Australia has lost to South Africa by 32 runs in their second ODI clash of the series, with the Aussie middle order collapsing.
Adam Zampa went for 0-77 from his 10 overs and Josh Hazlewood went at seven runs an over while claiming three wickets.
What's next?
Australia and South Africa will play the third ODI in the series at Potchefstroom on Wednesday night (AEST).
Australia's world champions have been found wanting again, falling well short in a chase for the second time in four days as South Africa prevailed by 32 runs in Johannesburg to seal the three-match ODI series triumph.
As a reconnaissance mission for their World Cup defence in southern Africa in a year's time, the loss overnight felt like another alarming capitulation after a fine start to their pursuit of a big Proteas total was wasted, just as on Thursday in the first-match collapse at Durban.
Chasing South Africa's formidable 9-365, which featured superb hundreds from captain Temba Bavuma and the ever-reliable David Miller, Australia's stand-in skipper Mitch Marsh and Travis Head, who had teed off with a brisk 90 together in Durban, this time clattered 130 off 17 overs at the Wanderers.
But the same old failings of cheap dismissals and inability to build partnerships came back to haunt the visitors, with not even a rousing late show of defiance from Xavier Bartlett, with a thumping 50 off 28 balls, able to get them to within a sniff of the target as they succumbed to 333 all out with one ball remaining.
After losing a second-straight match in which they had won the toss and sent the Proteas in, Australia, who again kept captain Pat Cummins on ice with the Test series around the corner, were left with further big concerns over their middle order stuttering in the face of quality spin.
"Really disappointing — we came here to ensure the series went to the last game but, fair play to South Africa, ultimately we've been outplayed again," Marsh said.
"In both games, the way we've set up the innings has been really good but we just haven't been able to execute in those middle phases.
"We've got to keep improving, we don't want to be whitewashed."
A third match will be played in Potchefstroom on Wednesday.
Cummins was unquestionably missed and a side injury that ensured Australia's outstanding quick Nathan Ellis could bowl only four overs meant their attack was always under pressure, even if Jack Edwards offered genuine all-round promise with his 5-67 and a solid knock of 25 in support of Bartlett.
Josh Hazlewood took three wickets while going at seven an over, but more alarming was Adam Zampa's continuing struggle, as he went for 0-77 off his 10 overs, in stark contrast to South Africa's excellent spin trio of Keshav Maharaj (2-54), Bjorn Fortuin (2-70) and Aiden Markram (1-55).
They helped put the brakes on Australia's chase after Marsh and Head had cracked 84 apiece, the captain's knock featuring five sixes and 10 fours off 53 balls and Head's start coming off 103 balls, with one six and 12 fours.
Apart from the openers, though, Australia was soon struggling, Cooper Connolly chipping one tamely off Lizaad Williams (3-54) to short midwicket to depart for 10 and wicketkeeper Alex Carey trapped lbw by Maharaj, who then did the same to dismiss Matt Renshaw for 32.
Cameron Green had a struggle, limping to 17 off 34 balls, before Bartlett showed him the way belatedly with his five mighty sixes, only for his innings, and Australia's last hope, to be ended by a cracking leg-before yorker from Williams.

The MTV VMAs are here with Taylor Swift making history and Madonna leading the nods: How to watch
The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards are here and Taylor Swift is set to make history

The 2026 MTV Video Music Awards are here and Swifties, it looks like the night is already yours.
Earlier this week it was announced that Taylor Swift will receive the inaugural Artist Director Honors, becoming the most awarded artist in VMA history.
Swift is currently tied with Beyoncé for the title of most-awarded musician in VMA history. They have 30 each. (Eminem is the male artist with the most VMAs with 15.) The new award, which according to the VMAs is meant to recognize artists “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling,” will bring her total to 31.
She will also debut the music video for her new song, “Patient Zero,” during the award show. Swift directed the visual, which stars Colin Farrell and Dakota Johnson.
“Patient Zero” is also her first single since marrying Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden in July.
Here's what else to know ahead of Sunday night's show.
How to watch the show
The two-hour MTV Video Music Awards show will broadcast live on CBS on Sunday, Sept. 27, at 7:30 p.m. Eastern and 4:30 p.m. Pacific, from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.
It is the first time since 2017 that the VMAs have picked a location that is not in New York or New Jersey.
The VMAs are also simulcast on MTV and be available to stream on Paramount+ in the U.S. It will become available to stream globally the next day on Paramount+ and MTV.
Snoop Dogg, a 13-time VMAs nominee and three-time winner, will host. Snoop made his debut on the VMAs stage in 1994. He closed the show in 1999 with Dr. Dre and Eminem and returned for a tribute to the Notorious B.I.G. and again for a performance with Eminem in 2022.
Who's nominated at the 2026 MTV VMAs
Madonna leads the 2026 MTV Video Music Award nominations. The pop superstar has been nominated in every decade of her musical career. She has 19 competitive MTV VMA wins and in 1986 became the first solo female artist to receive the Video Vanguard Award.
She is up for 11 awards at this year’s ceremony, including video, artist and song of the year, as well as best collaboration, dance, direction, art direction, cinematography, editing, choreography and visual effects.
Taylor Swift follows with the second-most nominations with nine. She is up for video and artist of the year as well as best pop, direction, art direction, cinematography, editing, choreography and visual effects.
Madonna and Swift are followed by Ariana Grande and Sabrina Carpenter with seven nods each to their names, as well as Bruno Mars, PinkPantheress and Zara Larsson with five. Blackpink’s LISA has four and Shakira, Tate McRae, GENER8ION and Yung Lean are tied for three.
Who’s performing at the 2026 MTV VMAs
Madonna will open the show. It will mark her first performance at the VMAs in 23 years.
Kacey Musgraves will pay homage to the late, great Dolly Parton. The country music icon, whose soaring vibrato vocals, poignant songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, died in Nashville of cancer in August. She was 80.
Raye, Sombr and Teddy Swims will pay tribute to George Michael, who died 10 years ago on Christmas Day. He was 53.
It's double duty for Raye, who also will perform solo.
Other performers include GENER8ION with Yung Lean, Shaboozey with Gunna, as well as Lisa and Sienna Spiro.
Who's presenting at the 2026 MTV VMAs
Alex Warren, Belmont Cameli, Charli xcx, Ciara Miller, David Corenswet, Ella Bright, Isabel May, Jeff Probst, Rachel Dratch, Teyana Taylor, Tyla and Troye Sivan will present.

Russia and Ukraine exchanged strikes overnight and on Sunday (September 27, 2026), killing at least six people in Ukraine and one in Russia, officials said, hours after Moscow rejected German calls to ease off its escalation toward NATO.
Russia's top diplomat on Saturday (September 26) brushed off what's believed to have been the first face-to-face meeting with his German counterpart since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The meeting was held during the UN General Assembly's annual gathering of world leaders, as an intensifying aerial war between Russia and Ukraine showed no sign of slowing.
Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport that Berlin blamed on the Kremlin.
With front-line positions largely unchanged since last year, Moscow has hammered its neighbor with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months. Meanwhile, Kyiv's long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses.
In Kyiv, a man was found dead after a Russian drone hit a non-residential building overnight, according to Ukraine's emergency service.
Later on Sunday (September 27), Russian drone strikes killed one person and wounded at least five on the outskirts of the capital, according to local administration head Tymur Tkachenko. In Kyiv itself, a drone hit a 9-story apartment block, wounding at least one woman, according to municipal authorities.
In Russian-occupied Ukraine, a strike by Kyiv's forces on Sunday (September 27) killed a civilian woman in Enerhodar, the town housing Europe's largest nuclear plant, according to its Kremlin-installed Mayor. Maxim Pukhov said the Ukrainian drones also wounded two others.
Russian forces also attacked Ukraine's southern Odesa region, which surrounds the country's main Black Sea port, multiple times overnight into Sunday (September 27), killing one person and wounding two, according to the head of the local military administration, Oleh Kiper.
On Sunday (September 27) afternoon, a woman and a 16-year-old girl were killed as Russian guided bombs struck the city of Sumy in northern Ukraine, regional administration head Oleh Hryhorov reported. He said five other people were wounded.
In Russia's Belgorod border region, a woman died in a hospital on Sunday (September 27) after being wounded in a Ukrainian strike, regional authorities said.
Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia struck twice at a data center in Kyiv on Sunday (September 27) morning, wounding two children and an adult. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces struck multiple data centres in Kyiv on Sunday (September 27) that it claimed were providing internet to Ukraine's armed forces.
Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly blamed each other for damaging power lines supplying Enerhodar's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, which Moscow captured early in the war. The plant is not in service, but needs power to keep cooling systems running and maintain safety.
Lavrov brushes off Germany meeting
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was dismissive after the meeting in New York, which was held at German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul's request. Lavrov said that Wadephul “simply reiterated his official position condemning Russia”.
“You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not,” he said.
Mr. Wadephul expressed openness to a better relationship but said it required a genuine willingness from Russia's leadership to end the war in Ukraine, according to a German delegation official.
An overwhelming majority of UN member nations have repeatedly condemned Moscow's invasion. The Kremlin describes the war as a “special military operation” intended to ensure Russia's security and the rights of Russian speakers.

The pros and cons of using a foldable phone
They're neat, but are they worth the price?
Apple, Google, Samsung — all the big-name manufacturers offer foldable phones, and consumers are growing more curious about them. While the category isn't huge, accounting for approximately 2 percent of the entire smartphone market, they are growing as shoppers decide the features they provide justify their significantly higher price.
But perhaps it is true to say that when you are spending a good slice of $2,000+ on a device, you want it to be able to deliver on the higher end of the features it promises. So, what are the pros and cons of using a foldable phone?
Foldable phones: The pros
To name a few, people like foldables for:
- Wow factor
- Display size
- Flexible use
- Multitasking and multi-app support
- Folding device caters to multiple needs
We'll start with the "Wow" factor. The physical transformation of the device when you fold it out, and the satisfying "snap" as you fold it back again, attract attention and provide unique physical feedback you don't get in standard smartphones. These devices are novel enough that 59 percent of smartphone owners are interested in the category, though cost and durability concerns remain.
With displays up to 8 inches, the category provides users with much larger displays in a product they can pocket. That's space for leaned-back experiences like browsing, streaming video or reading; it's also space for productive work, writing, editing and creative applications.
Manufacturers are optimizing the operating systems used by smartphones. That means better multitasking, multiple apps that open alongside each other, easy swiping through content between different apps and more. App developers are also improving their apps to make use of these unique folding platforms.
Because of how they are constructed, devices are flexible to use — use them folded like a phone, open them out to become a small tablet, half-fold them to deploy them as a mini-laptop or turn the device into a tripod-supported camera for video conferencing, selfies or photography. That flexibility means these phones can be used in ways others cannot.
Foldable phones: The cons
For all their versatility, there are several downsides to consider:
- Folding resilience
- Mechanical durability and dust/liquid resilience
- Display prone to scratches
- Camera quality
- Bulk and weight
- Apps may not yet be optimized
- Repair and replacement cost
Folding devices are tested for folding resilience — the number of folds they can support — but no current models last forever. Some older models display visible creases which look unpleasant and get in the way when using apps. The flexible plastic or ultra-thin glass displays used can be prone to scratches.
Those complex hinge mechanisms can become jammed by dust. Ingress Protection (IP) numbers help us evaluate the potential for this; the higher the first digit in an IP rating, the more resilient the device should be.
Earlier devices were relatively heavy and thick; some still balk at the weight. For example, the four most popular U.S. foldables weigh over 200g, partly due to the larger battery required for the displays. To make devices thinner, designers dispensed with bulky camera mechanisms, which means the cameras in most devices in the category are less advanced than those in high-end smartphones.
When it comes to app optimization, some apps still struggle to scale or transition smoothly between the outer and inner displays. Manufacturers and app developers are working to improve user experiences, but at this time, if you depend on any mission-critical apps, you should ask developers to confirm their support for foldables.
Finally, there's repair and replacement. With more moving parts, repair costs will be high. iFixit warns these devices are currently "not repairable." As the "Wow" factor nurtures a steady street trade in lost/stolen devices, making smartphone insurance essential.
Should you buy a folding smartphone?
Considering all the above, should you buy a folding device? It comes down to what you want from your phone. If you need a bigger display for reading, work or multitasking and don't mind paying a premium, the category has certainly become mature enough to be your daily driver. If you're rough on your devices, rely on apps that don't support folding screens, need better cameras or are price-conscious, a traditional smartphone remains your best bet until foldables close the gap.

Finding harmony with nature in the pearlescent waters of Oku-Matsushima’s oyster farms. Tucking into dishes made with unique alpine vegetables in the sacred hills of Dewa Sanzan. Forest bathing, imbibing in local sake and relaxing in wood-fired saunas nestled in Okutama’s lush mountains.
This is just a sampling of recent promotions for ecotourism destinations in Japan as destinations jostle to grab the attention of an annual influx of 40 million foreign visitors.
These destinations promise to immerse visitors in an “authentic” Japanese experience, all the while delivering sustainable experiences that minimize carbon emissions and environmental impacts.
But tourism is inherently a carbon-intensive activity. One U.S. dollar earned in tourism generates 1.02 kilograms of GHG emissions. Tourism’s footprint is four times higher than the service sector’s per-dollar emissions and 30% higher than the global economy’s average of $0.77 per kilogram of GHGs.
The story is no different in Japan.
In a 2020 paper that was released just as the tourism sector was beginning to shut down due to COVID-19, researchers with Tokyo City University estimated that Japan’s annual carbon emissions from the industry had reached 136 million tons per year. Meanwhile, Japan’s total emissions in 2019, the year before the study was released, totaled 1.1 billion, according to Our World in Data, highlighting the large carbon footprint of the sector.
Since Japan reopened its borders to tourists, the nation’s tourism boom has only accelerated.
Essentially, every year that brings more tourists accelerates greenhouse gas emissions and puts new strains on ecosystems, threatening to keep Japan off track from its 2050 goal of carbon neutrality.
To curtail emissions, a mix of government frameworks and entrepreneurial initiatives are underway, but with the current speed of tourism development, keeping up is proving to be a major challenge.
Emerging government frameworks
Temsegen Assefa, chief consultant at JTB Tourism Research & Consulting, says that Japan’s geography poses a particular challenge, given nearly all foreign tourists arrive by air.
“Because Japan is an island country, it relies heavily on aviation for inbound arrivals, and aviation is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize,” he tells The Japan Times.
Every nonstop roundtrip flight from London or Chicago to Tokyo adds over 3,000 kg of greenhouse gases to the atmosphere per passenger in economy class, equivalent to 40% of the annual energy-related emissions of an average American home, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
“Although the majority of arrivals do come from nearby Asian markets, arrivals from the U.S., Europe, and Australia are increasing, where the emissions per journey are considerably higher,” Assefa said.
Yusuke Kitamura, a researcher at Waseda University, calculates that over 50% of the emissions of Japan’s tourism industry come from transportation — and reducing those emissions presents a “significant challenge.”
Instead, Kitamura says local destinations should start where they can: on the ground. In 2020, Assefa and JTB Tourism Research & Consulting worked on a project in support of the Japan Tourism Agency to develop the Japan Sustainable Tourism Standard for Destinations, also known as JSTS-D. The standard provides local governments with a common framework for environmental protection and destination management, including cultural heritage preservation and benefits for local communities. It establishes benchmarks for emissions reductions, water use, pollution, resident attitudes, visitor volume management and more.
So far, dozens of approved destinations, ranging from ski towns such as Otaru and Niseko in Hokkaido, to Sumida Ward in Tokyo, to the entirety of Okinawa Prefecture, have signed on to the program. But using the guideline does not mean that the destination has achieved a particular level of environmental performance.
“Destinations need monitoring and implementation,” advises Assefa. He recommends that destinations also adopt the U.N. Tourism International Network of Sustainable Tourism Observatories (INSTO). The system involves quantitatively monitoring a huge number of indicators, from water energy and water consumption to economic impact.
Some destinations are going a step further.
Norikura Kogen, located in Nagano Prefecture’s Chubu Sangaku National Park, registered as the nation’s first “Zero Carbon Park” in 2021, for which stakeholders in hospitality, industry and local governments collectively agreed to advance zero carbon initiatives. “The community has decided to prioritize the environment, recognizing that it may come with some economic contraction,” says local guide and hotel operator Yuma Fujie. The area struggles with invasive species, rapidly expanding deer populations, and high emissions associated with the hospitality industry in a cold, snowy climate at 1,500 meters above sea level.
The Zero Carbon Park plan involves disseminating renewable energy from solar power and local biomass, reducing plastic use, and prioritizing the development of sustainable tourism. Fujie’s hot spring inn, Raicho, emphasizes long-term “workation” stays that minimize emissions by facilitating adventures on foot and bicycle, since Norikura Kogen restricts private vehicles. Fujie himself helped launch the Shinpi Trail, an 117-kilometer walking trail across the Japanese Alps from Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture to Takayama in Gifu Prefecture, in order to promote slower and more eco-conscious ways to experience the national park.
Up north, Hokkaido’s ultra-popular ski resort town Niseko is seeing international luxury hotels popping up at an unprecedented rate as wealthy foreign investors purchase local forestland to build winter chalets and private resorts. One measure in response is a new decarbonization subsidy for local businesses and residents. The subsidy is available for solar panels, energy storage batteries, energy-efficient air conditioning and water heating systems, and new houses that meet certain high standards of sustainability.
Atsuko Matsui, from Niseko’s environmental planning department, says that 42 subsidies worth a total of around ¥24 million have been awarded since 2024.
“While we haven’t experienced a significant environmental impact yet, there are growing local concerns about tourism development regarding energy consumption, waste generation and wastewater discharge,” Matsui says. “Niseko’s plan expects tourism operators to reinvest a portion of their earnings into environmental conservation activities.”
Finding a green niche
Amid the significant headwinds, there is some good news when it comes to tourism and sustainability: Operators in the carbon-intensive industry are starting to care.
“We’re seeing sustainable certificates not only on the rise in the luxury market, but also in mass market tourism,” Assefa says. “The hospitality sector is facing considerable international pressure to become more sustainable, and hotels in particular are seeking the marketing appeal of sustainability certifications.”
The number of Japanese hotels certified by Green Key, an international eco-certificate for the hospitality industry, has grown to 41 facilities as of this month compared with just seven in 2024. The local Japanese certifier Sakura Quality has now certified 247 facilities, nearly triple the 2024 figure.
One high-profile representative of that shift is Hoshino Resorts, with properties including Hoshinoya Karuizawa, Iriomote Hotel and Risonare Nasu all promoting sustainability and ecotourism.
Hoshinoya Karuizawa general manager Kazuya Shuto says that his resort, not unlike Fujie’s locally owned inn, emphasizes extended stays that promote low-emissions activities. This helps reduce emissions-heavy travel, while also increasing the hotel’s revenue per customer.
“We want guests to immerse themselves in one area and fully appreciate its unique charms, rather than hopping around multiple locations,” he says.
Hoshinoya Karuizawa produces the bulk of its energy on its own through hydropower and recycling heat from hot springs. The hotel first achieved a 100% recycling rate in 2011 and transports food waste directly to farms for composting. It is also built around ecotourism activities, specifically in the Karuizawa National Wild Bird Sanctuary Forest that surrounds the hotel: Hoshino’s affiliate NPO Picchio offers nature tours and conducts wildlife research and conservation activities in the forest.
Combining ecotourism and conservation may prove to be a strategic path forward for the industry. In the village of Onna in the center of Okinawa’s main island, local operators have started to offer coral reef restoration experiences, combining scuba diving with restoration work.
The volunteers help counter the decline of coral numbers in Okinawa, which is caused by wastewater and sediment pollution attributable to tourism and development, in addition to rising sea temperatures.
In spite of the rising availability of such experiences, tourism industry insiders say that the vast majority of visitors aren’t concerned about having particularly sustainable experiences.
“I can’t specifically remember any client, or even a potential client, asking after a low-environmental-impact tour,” says Noah Oskow at Unseen Japan, a Tokyo-based tour operator.
The company’s tours target visitors looking for cultural integration and experiences off the beaten path, but that hasn’t coincided with requests for sustainability.
“I think the image of Japan, real or not, is that it’s a fairly environmentally sound country, perhaps driven by how clean urban areas appear,” Oskow says.
Japan faces a difficult balancing act: while the government is seeking to disperse visitors from overcrowded urban areas into smaller towns and rural destinations, reaching these places often involves additional emissions in the form of flights or car journeys. Visitors may find sustainable ecotourism activities in remote areas of the country, but they’ll have to emit a lot of carbon to get there.
“There’s no one-size-fits-all solution,” says Assefa. “I personally believe destinations need to consistently monitor local tourism conditions and impacts.”
Once destinations can actually identify their challenges, finding solutions becomes far easier.
Gifu Prefecture established the first INSTO observatory in Japan in 2023, monitoring over 10,000 square kilometers and 1,000 accommodation facilities. The initial report identified private car transport as one of the largest energy management crises, as over 80% of tourists traveled in the prefecture via private car. With data procured through the U.N. initiative, the prefecture could swiftly designate electric vehicle proliferation as a key measure and created a goal to expand its EV charging network.
On the long road toward decarbonization, Kitamura believes that tourists have an important role to play.
“I hope that visitors will understand the challenges that Japan faces, but also raise their voices about areas where further action is needed,” he says. “That will enable tourists to enjoy their experiences while advancing sustainability for local businesses and residents.”
Kitamura notes that it’s also up to operators to create environments and systems within which tourists can help lessen their impact.
Essentially, what’s needed is a tourism environment where operators offer green choices, and tourists choose them. When both businesses and consumers consistently prompt one other to take small steps toward sustainability, Japan might finally see great, green progress.

Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
- Published
When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.
Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.
It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.
"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.
There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.
That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.
It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But it it something that match-going supporters actually want?
What the law says
Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.
It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.
The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.
Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.
The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.
It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.
However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.
It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.
The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.
The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.
The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.
Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".
The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".
It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".
Fans' views differ on drinking in stands
The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.
Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.
"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.
"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.
"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."
The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.
Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.
Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.
The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.
It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.
The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.
Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.
Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine".
"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.
"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.
"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."
For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.
Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".
"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.
"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.
"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."
Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".
"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."
But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.
What is it like in other sports and different countries?
Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.
Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.
The restrictions differ around Europe.
There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.
In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.
In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.
In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.

As Apple’s Tim Cook era draws to a close, we’re seeing more experimentation with the iPhone’s design than we’ve seen in a long time, but you wouldn’t know it from the iPhone 18 Pro. This absurdly fast, full-featured handset might be eclipsed by the hype around the iPhone Duo this year, but it’s still just as good as its immediate predecessor.
Of course, not too much has changed since the iPhone 17 Pro. There’s the new variable aperture and other camera controls for those who want to get granular with their mobile photography, a welcome addition given the iPhone’s reputation for inflexibly opinionated computational photography.
Beyond that, though, all the most important changes are under the hood: a new chip, better battery life, and much-improved thermals that both give the phone better sustained performance and make it cooler to the touch in many situations.
I think we’re seeing something of a transition for the “Pro” iPhones. They may still be the flagships in a sense, but Apple is at least for now saving its flashier design ideas for new products like last year’s iPhone Air or this year’s iPhone Duo.
The Pro phones aren’t the sexy, cool ones right now; they’re the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink, cover-for-every-kind-of-obsessive-user workhorses. I think that’s a great space for them to occupy, and this year’s iteration is no exception.
Design
The iPhone 18 Pro mostly looks and feels like last year’s flagship. It’s a function-over-form design (at least compared to something like the iPhone Air) with good materials.
I’m not normally one to care too much about color in these phones. For my personal phone, I’ve always just grabbed whatever was closest to black. (Apple says this year’s black is the blackest yet, of course.) But I have to admit the new burgundy color of my review unit is appealing, even though it’s quite the fingerprint magnet, in a long tradition for iPhones.
The main design difference this time around is a smaller Dynamic Island, that cut-out at the top of the screen that houses the front-facing camera and sensors. Apple has achieved this by moving the IR camera underneath the OLED panel, now in the top-left corner of the screen.
A new pixel arrangement allows infrared light to pass through in that spot, while the pixels in this region operate at twice the brightness to compensate for lower density, so there’s little visible effect on the image on the display. You can tell there’s something subtly going on in that corner if you know what to look for and look closely, but I don’t think most people will notice.
As I wrote when the Dynamic Island was first introduced, the way Apple combines the per-pixel brightness and absolute blacks of the OLED panel with creative software to turn what should be something of an albatross—a big, chunky hole in the screen—into an appealing feature by displaying live activities and other information around the sensors is one of the company’s more impressive design ideas in recent years. The execution is excellent and remains so.
Now, that hole is less big and chunky, making it sensible for Apple to now show up to three live activities at once in the region, not just one. The middle one has more information, while those on the left and right are basically dots with just enough to tell you something useful.

It’s also now possible to show more information on a second live activity when there are just two being displayed; I found this even more appealing than showing three live activities.
This isn’t enough of a reason to upgrade from an earlier Dynamic Island phone, of course, but it has made a good feature a little bit better.
Performance and thermals
Let’s talk specs, performance, and the main story with this phone—heat management. For most specs, this is last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. But the A20 Pro chip has some improvements that make this one of the more notable performance steps in a while.
A20 Pro
First up is the new A20 Pro chip. Apple has gone from a 3-nanometer process node in the A19 Pro to 2 nm here. It has a 6-core CPU with four efficiency cores and two performance cores—nothing new there. The GPU has seven cores, each with a Neural Accelerator that Apple says helps improve GPU-based AI workloads. (There’s hardware-accelerated ray-tracing support, too, though few games or apps utilize it.)
Also for local AI features (which are a big emphasis for this year’s iOS 27), there’s the dual 16-core Neural Engine.
Apple also says the A20 Pro has “the widest memory interface ever shipped in an iPhone” (naturally) with 50 percent more bandwidth. Based on what Apple has said so far about it, that seems to be mainly to improve AI performance. I’m speculating here, but given that Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features work fine on other recent iPhones, I imagine that’s a bit of padding to enable support for future AI features that won’t work on the 16 Pro or 17 Pro.
Unsurprisingly, and as the 3DMark benchmark chart below shows, that could make a big difference in graphics performance, too. It’s not like many people were complaining about the 17 Pro’s frame rates in Genshin Impact or Diablo Immortal, but hey, they definitely won’t be now.
Improved heat management
The chip has been re-architected in a couple of ways. New chip packaging promises improved heat management, thanks in part to a design that puts the system-on-a-chip next to the memory instead of stacked on top of it.
The most notable improvement is arguably a larger vapor chamber. Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro introduced the vapor chamber as an additional cooling measure, meant to help the phone sustain good performance for longer and distribute heat more sensibly. A copper material on the display plate helps keep the display cooler, too.
Apple promises up to 40 percent better sustained performance compared to last year’s Pro and up to 100 percent better than the iPhone 16 Pro before that. That’s neat, but sustained performance wasn’t a big problem for most users before. The main benefit is that the phone feels cooler and is less likely to overheat.
In my view, the better thermals are the most welcome addition to the iPhone 18 Pro. Many of us who have tried to use our phone as a GPS on the car dashboard on a hot summer day know the frustration of features shutting down when the phone goes into crisis heat-management mode. And even in normal use, like during online gaming or web browsing while streaming video, iPhones from a couple of years ago or earlier tended to get quite hot.
It’s been quite cool and overcast in Chicago this week—fall is here at last—so I haven’t been able to test the former of those extreme cases, but I’ve used the phone enough to be able to report that there is noticeable improvement in the more day-to-day scenarios. It still gets warm in some situations, like when I read the 3DMark benchmarks, but most of the time, it subjectively seems better than a couple of generations ago.
It’s normally hard to notice the absence of a problem, but my own iPhone 16 Pro has gotten hot frequently enough over the past couple of years that the contrast has been real and felt.
We’ll leave the camera specs to the cameras section of the review, but there are a couple of other spec changes worth noting.
A beefy battery (and other updates)
First off, there are further battery life improvements. Apple has long used offline video playback as one of its measures, and it says the iPhone 18 Pro can offer up to 36 hours of that on a single charge, compared to 33 for its predecessor. (It’s up to 45 for the 18 Pro Max and 39 for the 17 Pro Max.)
Subjectively, I’m impressed by the battery performance here. My personal daily driver is an iPhone 16 Pro Max, which is currently sitting at 86 percent maximum capacity per Apple’s battery health panel in the Settings app.
I have no complaints; I charge it for about an hour in the morning, then do whatever I want with it (other than maybe intensive 3D gaming) with the brightness cranked up until the next morning, when I charge again.
I noticed the iPhone 18 Pro showing higher percentages when I wake up in the morning than my 16 Pro Max with similar use, which is impressive for a smaller phone—even though my 160 Pro Max’s battery has aged a bit.
In terms of other additions, Apple has put its proprietary C2 cellular modem in the 18 Pro, which uses less energy than the Qualcomm modem in the 17 Pro, so that’s part of the battery life story here, too.
And if you’re inclined to charge wirelessly rather than with a USB-C cable, the iPhone 18 Pro has wireless charging at up to 25 W.
Cameras
If you’ve read my iPhone reviews before, you may recall I am not a photography geek. This is not the review to read if you want a deep dive on optics or how well this thing will work in a professional photo shoot scenario. (I’ll leave it to more skilled and knowledgeable people to assess the phone from that perspective, as there are already many such reviews out there.)
I’m a point-and-shooter. Thanks to both new hardware features and developments in computational photography, that’s actually where some of the more interesting and fastest-moving developments have been happening in the iPhone and its Android competitors over the past few years.
Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro is “pro” in the sense that it will be used by content creators and others who approach snapping photos or capturing videos far more seriously and creatively than I do. But really, it’s the phone that sometimes lets non-pros like me produce quasi-pro-looking images despite ourselves.
Take the new variable aperture feature, which got the most fanfare when this handset was announced. The ability to tweak this setting manually is a niche proposal, really; many people will rarely, if ever, touch it. That said, it adjusts automatically based on what’s in the scene by default, so in many cases, even folks like me will get slightly better photos.

There’s also Photographic Styles 3, the latest generation of Apple’s set of non-destructive presets for the general appearance and vibe of the photos you’re taking. Think Instagram filters, but less blunt-force. Previously, Photographic Styles were basically just color balance settings, but Photographic Styles 3 allows for texture tweaks, too.
This includes four texture options: film, glow, soft skin, and standard. These options—especially the film one—allow the iPhone’s built-in Camera app to compete with some third-party apps that tried to give photos warmer, more film-like looks. I won’t say it’s enough to make everyone drop those alternatives, but it’s good to have more options for those who are loyal to the main app.
Apart from these and a few other minor tweaks, it’s the same triple-48 MP rear camera system that we reviewed in last year’s iPhone 17 Pro, paired with the same front-facing 18 MP camera.
With the variable aperture and the other custom camera controls that are now accessible in the built-in Camera app (all the others are available on other recent iPhones), Apple has finally done plenty to address long-standing complaints that iPhone cameras were a little too opinionated for some users’ tastes.
Yes, these new features enable better point-and-shoot photos in some narrow situations, but user control seems to be the main pitch for the cameras this year.
For those who just want a good phone
This was Tim Cook’s last year as Apple’s CEO, and the iPhone 18 Pro is the quintessential iPhone of the Tim Cook era: practical, pricey, loaded with features to cover ever-more niche edge cases, and not especially bold in its design or ambitions—all to a high standard of quality.
This is the formula that has made it the world’s most popular flagship smartphone. There’s nothing wrong with that formula. Its recent predecessors were all great phones, and this one is, too.
But we all know the era of buying a new smartphone every year or two to enjoy amazing new features has passed. (Which is also great, by the way—for our pocketbooks, for the environment, for a whole bunch of reasons.) If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, there’s little reason to upgrade. Yes, we’re seeing some notable performance improvement year-over-year here, but I don’t think too many of us were complaining about the A17 Pro’s performance to begin with.
My personal daily driver is an iPhone 16 Pro, and I won’t be pulling the trigger this year, either. In fact, I think you’re still in great shape with your iPhone 15 Pro, if that’s what you have, provided your battery is still holding up.
Go further back than that, though, and all these little things start to accumulate into something enticing. That’s where we’re at, and that’s where we’ve been for a while now.
I wouldn’t go so far as to say the modern flagship smartphone is perfect in all respects; Apple and its competitors still find small ways to refine it and up the ante for specific types of users year after year, and I expect that to continue. And last year’s base iPhone 17 is still more than good enough for almost everybody.
But after almost two decades of competition and iteration, it’s at least directionally perfect. The basics are all here, and they don’t need to change. I wish the price hadn’t risen, but I suppose that’s the reality we live in right now.
If you want something new and flashy to impress your friends or to satisfy your brain with a novel experience, hold out for the iPhone Duo next month or venture into the slightly more energetic Android market. But if you just want a good phone that leverages all the latest technological progress without overdoing it for attention or progress’ sake, the iPhone Pro line is a good fit.
The good
Greatly improved thermal management has added up over two generations
Ditto for battery life
Very strong graphics and AI performance
New custom camera controls and photographic styles help you get (a little bit) out of the typical Apple processed look
The bad
Some might find it a little heavy
This isn’t really a bad thing, but there’s not much here to excite you or to inspire an upgrade if you already own a recent iPhone

Delhi woke up to a cloudy sky on Sunday, September 27, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) predicting thunderstorms and gusty winds for today. The weather agency has issued a ‘yellow alert’ for light rainfall. “Generally cloudy sky is expected to persist. One or two spells of very light to light rain at most places are expected,” an IMD official said, adding that thunderstorms, lightning and strong winds could accompany the rainfall. The city received 5mm of rain from 8.30 pm on Saturday to 8.30 am on Sunday. For the first time in the past seven years, Delhi has received rainfall so late in September. The minimum temperature settled below the season's average at 21 degrees Celsius on Sunday. The weather department has predicted a cloudy sky with the maximum temperature expected to touch 31 degrees Celsius. According to the IMD, temperatures throughout the upcoming week will stay mostly below average. While early winter typically begins in late October in Delhi, the below-average temperatures this week have brought a pleasant drop. Social media users, however, have already declared this dip in mercury as the start of winter. “Delhi weather suddenly feels like early winter. Feels like the season changed overnight,” a user said. “Kambal lene ki naubat aa gayi thi kal😭 (Had to use a blanket last night)” another added. A user said, “Hoping that this stays. Otherwise, Delhi winters are now only felt in oct. That's too late, October. So if it's happening, let's hope it stays.” “Just wake up feeling chills in the fan .. not winter feel but definitely cooler day compared to last year 🔥🙌” another user said. However, a netizen rightly pointed out that the cool weather is due to Cyclone Arnab. “Don't get dragged away with it.. it is the effect of Cyclone Arnab in the Bay of Bengal across the Indian coast of West Bengal. In a week, temperature will rise again till 36° and feels liks 41°” the netizen commented. “Last time bhi aesa hua tha, but sardi sirf 10-15 din ki he thi..😂😂😂” added another netizen. The air quality was recorded as 'satisfactory' at 9 am, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 54, according to the Sameer App. As winter approaches, air quality is expected to deteriorate. According to the CPCB, an AQI between zero and 50 is considered 'good', 51 to 100 'satisfactory', 101 to 200 'moderate', 201 to 300 'poor', 301 to 400 'very poor', and 401 to 500 'severe'. While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific.
On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador.
“The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added.
“They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities.
But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US.
US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny.
It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk.
Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”.
Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday.
Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase.
“Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations.
Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place.
Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces.
This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered.
Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday.
“Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine.
Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election.
So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.
Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region.
Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity.
During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”.
Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”.
Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country.
Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks.
In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations.
None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence.
“Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”.
Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed.
The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag.
Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment.
A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”.
Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian.
The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success.
“They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

17-year-old Nikita Kumari shines as India beat Iran to win kabaddi gold
Haryana’s 17-year-old Nikita Kumari made her senior India debut count, delivering a crucial performance as India defeated Iran to win women’s kabaddi gold.
At 17, Haryana’s Nikita Kumari made a memorable senior debut for India, delivering a crucial performance in the final as the women’s kabaddi team defeated Iran to win gold at the international tournament on Saturday.
For Nikita, who is among the youngest members of the Indian squad representing the country at the International level, Kabaddi was never just a sport she discovered later in life. It was part of her surroundings.
Nikita started playing Kabaddi at the age of eight. Her coach, Sunil Dabad, believes that her surroundings and early entry into the sports helped her build mental toughness that Nikita now displays on the international stage.
“In the villages of Haryana, most children grow up playing kabaddi. Nikita and her three younger sisters have all taken to the sport, and I have watched her journey closely from a young age. I always believed that Nikita had the talent and determination to one day make her country proud,” Dabad said.
Before earning her place in the senior Indian team, Nikita had already established herself at the junior level. She had represented India in youth competitions and also had the responsibility of captaining the Indian junior side.
“The transition, however, is never easy. But she is a confident player and mentally tough, which really helps in Kabaddi,” Nikita said.
When India found itself in a difficult situation against Iran, she was brought onto the mat at a crucial juncture. Rather than allowing the occasion or the pressure to dictate her game, the teenager responded with an attacking performance that gave India the impetus it needed.
“For a 17-year-old, it was a performance that went beyond her years. I can see people are praising her on social media. This is just the beginning,” Dabas added.
The significance of Nikita’s contribution becomes clearer when viewed in the context of the opponent. Coach Dabas told HT that Iran is among the strongest teams in Asian women’s Kabaddi and matches between the two sides can become intensely physical.
“When the match becomes tight, Iran starts playing a rough game. That is when mental toughness becomes very important,” she said.
Nikita had to deal with exactly that kind of pressure. “She continued playing despite suffering injury, showing the determination required to remain on the mat,” Dabas said.
Nikita’s mother, Vinod Kumari, said her daughter showed a natural inclination towards kabaddi from a young age. “She started training when she was in Class 3. She took to the sport naturally and gradually became more serious about it,” she said.
For Vinod, seeing her daughter represent India on the international stage is a moment of immense pride. “It feels wonderful when people come to us and talk about Nikita’s performance. She has not only made our family proud, but has brought pride to Haryana and the country as well by representing India on the global stage,” she told HT.
“I will always support my Gudiya (Nikita’s pet name). When she comes back, we are planning a grand welcome for her. It has not been easy for us. We are from a village, while she has to stay in Gurugram for her studies and training. She has worked very hard to reach this stage, and no matter how difficult it gets, I will always stand by her and support her dreams,” she said.
For now, the celebrations have begun at home, with the family distributing sweets among neighbours to mark Nikita’s achievement.
Her three younger sisters, who are also kabaddi players, look up to her as an inspiration, a reminder that a girl from a Haryana village, with determination and hard work, can dream of making it big in sport and representing the country on the world stage.

The zardozi embroidery on a Dior dress, the T-strap leather sandals at a Prada show, the mirror-work technique used on a Fendi bag – for decades, the skill of Indian artisans has been an invisible force behind some of the world’s most coveted fashion.
Now, that work is beginning to claim its own place in the spotlight, and the Mumbai-based textile and embroidery atelier Chanakya International is at the forefront.
Chanakya marked its 40th anniversary this month, celebrating with three exhibitions that trace its journey from an embroidery powerhouse to a present-day craft and cultural institution. The person steering it is 49-year-old Karishma Swali, whose father set up the group’s operations in the 1980s.
“What we have as a country is unique,” she tells me of India’s rich textile and craft heritage. “It’s unparalleled in many ways, and it’s the only place where we continue to practise it.” During the Renaissance, she says, France and Italy had established and varied traditions. “But what we have in India today is [what] other parts of the world have lost.”
Chanakya has a network of 1,400 artisans, and says that some are 13th-generation craftspeople, skilled in hundreds of embroidery traditions and supplying almost every luxury label you can imagine. Among the techniques they have revived is the Mughal-era silver filigree lace, or chaand jaal, reintroduced in a lighter form that has since become a regular feature in couture collections.
In 2023, Dior held a show at Mumbai’s Gateway of India, showcasing its partnership with Chanakya, in a high-profile acknowledgment of Indian craftsmanship. The runway saw sari-inspired skirts, vibrant madras-checks sets and Nehru-collar jackets.
These collaborations are supported by expert craft knowledge passed down and refined over generations, and they need institutional support to survive. The Kalhath Institute, a craft-preservation centre in Lucknow, runs residencies that pair artists from across the world with local artisans.
Kalhath’s co-founder Mohammed Amine Dadda tells me that Indian craftsmanship’s defining quality is “intelligence of the hand” – a sensitive, slow and cumulative process underpinned by patience and dexterity. “Without this technical mastery, and the considerable time required to create the most demanding pieces, haute couture and contemporary luxury simply could not bring their most ambitious creative visions to life.”
This mastery is not limited to textiles. When it comes to jewellery, global luxury brands have long sought Jaipur-based the Gem Palace, established in 1852 by the Kasliwal family, who still run it today. Samarth Kasliwal, 33, says part of the appeal lies in the visual language of Indian artistry itself. “There is something about Indian artistry that is inspired by nature,” he tells me, pointing to the recurring use of floral patterns and animals across Indian art and design. These motifs are universal, and travel across the lines of culture and language.
One recent collaboration Kasliwal is particularly proud of is a collection for Dior featuring green onyx and rock crystals, with engravings of birds, animals and flowers. The combination, he says, is reminiscent of traditional Indian jewellery, while drawing on techniques that remain central to the atelier’s work today.
With increased visibility, the question of credit and appropriation has become harder to ignore. Last week, a Ralph Lauren gown from the designer’s spring 2027 collection attracted criticism after many Indians pointed out that the embroidery the brand described as “embellishments” looked a lot like Indian zardozi, but without any accompanying credit. (Ralph Lauren did not respond to my request for comment.)
Then, Fendi came under fire when people noticed that a baguette bag from its autumn/winter collection featured mirrorwork often seen in Gujarati crafts. In April, Fendi credited Chanakya artisans in a social media video showcasing the same embroidery. But the product description on its site failed to mention any Indian inspiration, and its final label read “Made in Italy”.
After I asked Fendi about the discrepancy, the brand cited its “creative partnership” with Chanakya of more than three decades, saying it “remains committed to supporting and recognizing India’s rich craft heritage”. The website descriptor now reads: “Made in Italy and India with Chanakya”.
A recent Financial Times report noted that under EU rules, garments embroidered in India can still end up with a European label – so long as the final construction and finishing take place in Europe.
Last year, Prada was accused of appropriating Indian culture with Kolhapuri-inspired sandals, a controversy that showed us these debates around recognition can sometimes produce a more structural response. “We acknowledge the sandals … are inspired by traditional Indian handcrafted footwear, with a centuries-old heritage,” Lorenzo Bertelli, the corporate social responsibility chief at the Italian fashion house, had written in a letter to the Maharashtra chamber of commerce at the time.
Prada subsequently partnered with state-backed organisations in Maharashtra and Karnataka to produce a limited-edition collection, Made in India, and committed to a three-year training programme for artisans specialising in the craft.
Might these collaborations, controversies and corrections represent a shift in India’s place in the fashion industry? Anthropologist Phyllida Jay, author of Inspired by India: How India Transformed Global Design, appears to think so, placing the debate in a longer arc. “The stories of the ateliers producing highly skilled Indian craft in the elevated realm of European luxury and high fashion is part of a broader paradigm shift,” she writes, “where over 70 years after the end of colonial rule, India is being looked at in a different way on the world stage.” It is, in a way, a reversal, moving from a colonial history of extraction toward one in which Indians themselves get a voice in how their craft is represented.
Swali is ensuring this visibility also lives on through the Chanakya School of Craft, which she set up in 2016. Its 18-month programme provides free embroidery training and a travel honorarium to dozens of women, some of whom have gone on to work at the main atelier. Others have set up their own independent studios.
I had a chance to visit the space – inside a high-rise in Lower Parel, where those as young as 18 learn intricate needlework alongside grandmothers in their 60s. “Craft in India has never been institutionalised,” Swali says of the ethos behind the initiative. “It’s intergenerational,” she says, adding that women have often been excluded.
India’s culture of craft has always been precious. Growing up, I loved having the choice to affordably create any type of clothing. At one point, I had a small army of tailors, each with a different specialisation, whom I’d go to for different needs. I’d buy ajrakh and mashru silks from Dastkar or Nalli, and hand it to the right Masterji to stitch, embroider and tweak to my size. So, to me, Indian craftsmanship is not just a part of luxury, but a luxury itself.

HATHRAS: A retired Army man and his wife were found hacked to death with a sharp-edged weapon at their house near the Agra bypass in Hathras on Sunday, with police forming five teams to identify the killers and determine the motive behind the murders.
The victims were identified as Shamsuddin, 58, and his wife Saddo Begum, 55. Their bodies were found lying in a pool of blood at their house in the Sadabad Kotwali area.
According to police, the killings took place during the night. The bodies were discovered around 9.30am on Sunday after the house did not open and people raised an alarm, following which police were informed.
Superintendent of Police Chiranjeev Nath Sinha and Circle Officer Yogendra Krishna Narayan reached the spot along with police personnel and inspected the scene.
Forensic experts and a dog squad were also called in to assist with the investigation.
"Prima facie, it appears that they were killed with a sharp-edged weapon. Necessary legal action is being taken," the SP said.
He said the motive behind the killings was not immediately clear and five teams had been formed to identify the perpetrators and solve the case.
Shamsuddin had retired from the Army around 20 years ago. Police said he had two wives and used to stay with them alternately.
He had been staying with his first wife, Saddo Begum, at the house near the Agra bypass on Saturday night when the incident allegedly took place.

Earth's days are not exactly the same length. Scientists have been recording small variations in for decades. These changes are minuscule—sometimes just a few milliseconds—and mostly imperceptible, but scientists are keen to understand them as they point to a much more monumental change: Our planet’s rotation speed is shifting.
Scientists have already pinpointed a handful of compounding causes. Fluctuations in the atmosphere and oceans can slightly speed up or slow down the Earth’s rotation; major earthquakes can redistribute part of the planet’s mass; and by depositing enormous amounts of water into the oceans, melting continental ice is also a factor.
These influences account for some of the more sudden and recent changes, but on a several decades-long timescale, some of the variation appears to originate from a source much deeper within the Earth. Beneath our planet’s rocky mantle lies the outer core—a 1,400 mile thick layer of ultra-hot liquid metal that is in constant motion. As these flows change, they can slightly alter the speed at which the rest of the planet rotates.
However, how these forces are transmitted from one region to another has remained a mystery. Friction between the core and the mantle is too weak, so geologists have been searching for other mechanisms operating in the Earth’s interior.
In a new study published this week in Nature, researchers believe they have identified one of these hidden gears. They propose that the gravity of the inner core pushes rotation in one direction, while other interactions between the core and the mantle oppose it. The result of this competition, accumulated over decades, would be small accelerations and decelerations in the planet’s spin.
The idea is based on the fact that the inner core does not rotate at the same rate as the rest of the planet, causing it to become slightly misaligned with certain mass irregularities in the mantle. But the core “wants to be aligned,” Mathieu Dumberry, a geophysicist at the University of Alberta involved in the study, said in a press release. What this means is that gravity tries to pull the layers of the inner Earth back into their more harmonic position, which influences—albeit minutely—the rotation of the planet’s surface.
The authors reconstructed how this interaction influenced Earth’s spin between 1964 and 2019 using seismic estimates of the inner core’s rotation and models of liquid metal flows in the outer core. Their gravitational model closely reproduced both the timing and the magnitude of real gradual changes that had been observed over the decades.
Other yet-unknown factors are likely involved, but this proposal unravels a major component of our variable days. The model also didn’t account for all the forces competing involved, but it didn’t need to to produce a compelling result. Because it might be a tug-of-war, Dumberry said, but “gravity still wins.”
