IIT Madras, IIT Madras Research Park (IITMRP), and Unicorn India Ventures have announced the first close of their deeptech-focused IITM Unicorn Frontier Fund I at ₹450 Cr (about $46.9 Mn). The fund has already deployed nearly ₹55 Cr across four startups — Hathor, Quanastra, Triolt Energy, and Carbelim. Launched in February, the fund has a base corpus of ₹600 Cr and a ₹400 Cr greenshoe option, allowing it to raise up to ₹1,000 Cr (about $104.4 Mn). It is targeting a final close by December 2026. The fund’s backers include IIT Madras alumni and family offices, with institutional investors and banks expected to participate by the final close. Managed by Unicorn India Ventures, the fund aims to build a portfolio of 25 startups, with cheque sizes ranging from ₹15 Cr to ₹25 Cr. Most of its investments will target early-stage deeptech startups at technology readiness levels (TRLs) 3-4, covering proof-of-concept development and laboratory validation. Its six focus areas are defence tech, spacetech, semiconductors, manufacturing technology, robotics, and automation, AI infrastructure and GenAI, and healthtech. The fund, in a statement, said it would assess potential investments for their export opportunities, ability to replace imports, and contribution to domestic technological capabilities. IITM Unicorn Frontier Fund’s First Four Bets Among its initial investments, Chennai-based Hathor is developing semi-cryogenic and cryogenic rocket engines for small and medium satellite launch vehicles. Delhi-based Quanastra is building single-photon detection systems and quantum instrumentation for research and industrial applications. Triolt Energy develops lithium-ion battery cells for drones and fast-charging electric mobility applications, while Carbelim uses microalgae technology in carbon capture and air purification systems. Beyond investments from the fund, Unicorn India Ventures plans to mobilise additional capital through co-investments to support portfolio startups’ funding needs. Deeptech Investments Gather Pace The first close follows Unicorn India Ventures’ ₹1,200 Cr final close of its third fund in February, exceeding its ₹1,000 Cr target. The fund invests across areas including semiconductors, quantum sensing, defence tech, and spacetech. Other investors have also announced dedicated funds for these sectors. On September 18, Asiana Fund and Taiwan-based JC Capital launched a ₹1,000 Cr fund targeting advanced manufacturing and robotics, semiconductors and computing, materials and sustainability, and aerospace and defence. Meanwhile, IIT Madras Research Park has been a significant contributor to the country’s deeptech innovation space, having incubated over 480 deeptech startups, 190 of which are now commercially active. Of these, two startups have reached unicorn valuation — Ather Energy and Uniphore.

Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

Researchers have documented the first confirmed snakebite envenomation and subsequent human deaths in India caused by the venomous Caspian cobra (Naja oxiana), which have never previously been reported in the country, according to a case report published in Epidemiology International, a peer-reviewed journal.
The study titled ‘First Report of Deadly Bites by Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) From India’ by Bharti O.K., Menon J.C., Phull A., Joy S., Sharma V. and Malhotra A. details two fatalities and two survivals from bites by the species, also called the Central Asian cobra, in Himachal Pradesh’s Chamba’s Pir Panjal mountain range.
“Envenomation and subsequent deaths from the Caspian Cobra (Naja oxiana) have never previously been reported from India. While collecting data for the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) project on snakebites, we came across two deaths due to the bite of N. oxiana,” said Omesh Kumar Bharti of Himachal Pradesh’s Directorate of Health Services, who led the study.
“Deaths due to N. oxiana have never been previously reported from India. Naja oxiana is primarily found in Central Asia, with high human mortality resulting from envenoming. This species has been reported from Pakistan and Kashmir and was recorded in 2019 from Tissa block of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh. Naja oxiana has been shown to have rapidly expanded its range from Iran towards the northeast and it has been observed to be slowly expanding its range in Chamba towards lower elevations as reported by local rescuers,” noted the study.
The first death occurred in July 2020 in Ullansa village, when a 40-year-old man was bitten twice on the leg while spraying an apple orchard. He was taken to a nearby faith healer. However, his condition continued to worsen and on the third day after the bite, he was taken to the Civil Hospital Bharmour, where he was seen by the doctor and was found to lack a detectable pulse. A second victim, a 62-year-old man from Bhanjraru village, was bitten in July 2021 while walking to work and collapsed within half an hour. He died before reaching Civil Hospital Tissa; a post-mortem attributed the death to the venom’s neurotoxic effects, the study said.
Snakebite envenoming (SBE) remains a major cause of preventable mortality in rural India. The big four species, namely the spectacled cobra (Naja naja), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii), common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), are responsible for the majority of snakebite envenomation and deaths in the country. The commercially available anti-snake venom (ASV) correspondingly covers these species only, it said. The study also noted that the available anti-snake venom (ASV), designed to counter the ‘big four’ species responsible for most snakebite deaths nationally, does not effectively neutralise the venom components of N. oxiana.
The researchers said that there is a need to create greater community awareness about the danger of this species of snake in affected areas and educate them about ways to reduce the risk of being bitten.

The death by suicide of Sahil Wakode cannot be viewed in isolation, alumni of Indian Institute of Technology-Bombay (IITB) said on Sunday (September 27, 2026). The incident pointed to a deeper problem within the academic environment, they said. In a letter written to the Director of the institute, a group of alumni have also expressed concerns over the increasingly “militarised campus” during exams. Calling for immediate, comprehensive reforms, they sought a survey of the students’ mental health and a humane approach to deal with instances of misconduct.
In the three-page letter, the alumni expressed deep anguish about a series of deaths by suicide at the institute. The 10 demands put forth by the past students include a call for an immediate and impartial investigation into specific allegations of caste-based harassment and improved mental health support, including diverse counselling and mandatory faculty sensitisation.
“We sincerely hope that the institute will take concrete steps to ensure that the academic climate at IITB is egalitarian, humane and conducive to intellectual growth. This requires addressing the caste, class and gender-based inequalities, as well as other forms of exclusion, that are deeply embedded in our society and can manifest within academic institutions,” the letter, accessed by The Hindu, stated.
Wakode, 20, a second year B.Tech. student at IIT Bombay, allegedly died by suicide on September 18, 2026. His parents have alleged caste discrimination against him. An internal probe by the IIT, and a criminal probe by the Mumbai Crime Branch are underway.
“In the last one year alone, there have been four student suicides at IIT Bombay. In the last three years, two of the students who died—Sahil Wakode and Darshan Solanki—belonged to the Dalit community. The wider picture across the IITs is equally concerning,” the letter stated.

It cited media reports that alleged 45 suicides had been reported across 23 IITs over the past five years. There was a disproportionate representation of Schedule Castes (SC)/Scheduled Tribes (ST) students and female students among those who died by suicides in India’s premier institutes over the last few years, they said. “These figures point to a deeper problem: the compounding effects of performance pressure on students coupled with deep rooted caste/class/gender situations, and their alienation from a creative, inquisitive and, enjoyable academic life,” the former students said.
‘Militarised campus’
The alumni expressed strong reservations about a change in the academic culture of the institute in the last few years. “In recent times, the campus has increasingly resembled a militarised zone, with the deployment of police and other security forces during examinations. Students are being frisked by private security personnel before entering examination halls. This was not part of the academic culture during our time at IITB, and such measures fundamentally alter the character of an academic institution,” they said.
The alumni have demanded a comprehensive survey of students’ mental health, including an assessment of the impact of supervisors and teachers, ensuring this accounted for the gender, caste, religious, and linguistic diversity of the student community. They have also urged that the institute’s medical unit should be adequately staffed with diverse counsellors and therapists, including those from LGBTQ+ and SC/ST/OBC (Other Backward Classes) communities, to create safe spaces for marginalised students, and improve the quality of mental health support with empathy and dignity.
Faculty sensitisation
The letter called for compulsory and regular sensitisation programmes for faculty members on mental health issues, and the specific challenges faced by students from marginalised backgrounds. “This sensitisation must extend beyond mere discrimination prevention to actively cultivating an understanding and response to student needs,” the letter stated. An improvement in the current 1:18 teacher-student ratio has also been suggested.
The alumni demanded an impartial investigation into allegations of caste-based harassment faced by Wakode, and a fair inquiry into allegations against the concerned teacher. They welcomed the institute’s decision to suspend the Dean of Academic Affairs pending investigation. They also demanded complete institutional support for Wakode’s family through the investigation and legal proceedings, especially given the loss of their only son.
The letter has demanded that protesting students should not be criminalised. “We call upon the Institute to maintain a healthy academic environment during this difficult period. The IITB administration must listen to the genuine grievances of the protesting students and address their demands through a peaceful, transparent and democratic process, without the use of force or coercive measures,” the alumni said.
The said letter has been signed by 79 past students of IIT Bombay. It was sent to the Director by email on Sunday night. Despite repeated attempts, the institute’s Public Relations Officer did not provide a response to queries about the letter.
This article contains references to suicide and mental health issues. Those in distress may contact Sanjivini, Society for Mental Health suicide prevention helpline: 011-40769002.

US complete thrilling comeback to retain Presidents Cup
- Published
The United States completed a thrilling comeback on the final day to beat the Internationals and win an 11th successive Presidents Cup.
The hosts, containing eight of the world's 11 top-ranked players, trailed by three points going into Sunday and were looking to avoid just a second defeat since the biennial competition began 32 years ago.
They dominated the singles, winning nine of the 12 matches, to seal a 17-13 win at Medinah - the scene of Team Europe's famous Ryder Cup comeback win in 2012.
Jacob Bridgeman secured the decisive point by holing a four-foot par putt at the 18th to seal a one-up win over Australia's Min Woo Lee.
There were also wins for Cameron Young, Justin Thomas, Scottie Scheffler, Chris Gotterup, Collin Morikawa, Patrick Cantlay, Xander Schauffele and Jackson Koivun.
"I told the guys last night that funny stuff happens here. Medinah's got a history of funny things happening," said US captain Brandt Snedeker, who was a member of the team beaten by Europe in 2012.
"All these guys fought for each other, fought for this country, fought for this team."
International captain Geoff Ogilvy said: "The US team came out firing, we knew they would.
"It was on a knife edge all day. If some of those one downs we had out there had flipped to one up, the numbers looked really good and who knows what momentum that could give."
US President Donald Trump was in attendance in his role as honorary chairman, greeting the players and making a speech before the matches got under way.

With the changing weather brings many things: colder mornings; changing leaves; and, most important (particularly in this economy), a wave of sale events as the holiday season creeps around the corner.
There are plenty of early Prime Day deals already underway, but given that I’m WIRED’s resident vacuum tester, it’s no surprise vacuum sales caught my eye. Robot vacuums are tested near daily in my house with the help of my constantly sand-covered 4-year-old and litter-tracking cat, and I’ve changed the lives of multiple friends after persuading them to try a modern robot vacuum.
“Modern” is the key term here. If you’ve had the same cheap robot vacuum from years past that can’t map your home or connect to an app, you’re missing out on everything robot vacuums actually have to offer. Especially since most models can double as a mop and can detect where they should mop and where they should only vacuum. If you have yet to get a robot vacuum like this for your home, sales events like Prime Day (and pre-Prime Day!) are the perfect time to buy.
One of the best brands out there is Roborock, which has already put a few of its robot vacuums that we’ve tested and loved on sale. Here are the ones to snag.
Roborock’s On-Sale Robot Vacs
Roborock has finally started updating its more affordable Qrevo line this year after a period of inactivity, and the Qrevo 2 Pro is my favorite vacuum I’ve tested from the brand so far. Since it launched last month, this is the second time the 2 Pro has been on sale in the $500 range, though it was a little cheaper during Roborock’s anniversary earlier this month. Still, this is a good price for a powerful robot vacuum that packs 20,000 Pa of suction, easy app control, and an extendable mop arm that helps it get into tricky corners. Bill Gates joins call for AI safeguards, wants to discuss concerns with Trump
'No one thinks self-regulation is enough,' the Microsoft co-founder told NBC
AI requires safeguards that go beyond self-regulation, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said in an interview that aired on Sunday, calling for legislation to be passed in Congress.
"You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like," Gates said in a taped interview on NBC's Meet the Press program. "And that has to be a required thing."
A sudden groundswell has risen in favour of federal intervention after OpenAI said in July that an autonomous AI agent went rogue during a security test and hacked into another company, subverting human control. Gates joined that chorus, saying government must be involved.
"No one thinks self-regulation is enough," he said.
In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, OpenAI, Google's DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI have called for slowing the development of increasingly capable AI systems.
OpenAI said Friday it had paused training of its latest AI models, just hours after the company disclosed it was reviewing several incidents from the summer in which OpenAI agents searching U.S. federal government websites acted in unexpected ways beyond what was asked of them while gathering and distributing information.
Separately, AI evaluator Transluce said agents that appeared to come from OpenAI tried unsuccessfully to hack into a U.S. Department of Education website, a detail that OpenAI has not confirmed.
'It's not a hoax at all'
But U.S. President Donald Trump and other opponents of additional regulation for AI say new government restrictions would simply give China the upper hand in the AI revolution. Trump has publicly dismissed calls for new laws on AI as a "hoax."
Gates argued that safeguards would not dramatically hinder the industry, and that the risks of not implementing them are real.
"It's not a hoax at all," he told NBC.
Gates has said he wants to meet Trump to discuss AI.
"I hope that, given my life's work in the field, my saying how unique and different this is and how concerned I am will add to what he's hearing from other people," Gates said.
- OpenAI pauses training of latest models after AI agents probed U.S. government sites in unexpected ways
- AI's 'warning shot': Tech companies, experts raise fears of more rogue swarms after alarming Hugging Face hack
Axios reported that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei will have dinner on Sunday with Trump at the White House. Anthropic and the White House did not immediately return a request for comment on the Axios report.
Warnings about AI's risks are not new. But they took on added urgency this month after researchers in leading AI labs attached both a timeline and a probability to those concerns.
Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI could kill us all by the end of the decade, prompting U.S. lawmakers to call for new rules to govern the technology. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's alignment science lead, echoed Coxon's warning, saying there was a more than 10 per cent chance of such an event within the next decade.
Some policymakers have proposed mandating a "kill switch" that would allow federal authorities to halt AI models. Gates said that while he was not opposed to some sort of kill switch, it would not be enough if other safeguards were not also implemented.
The U.S. and China agreed to launch a dialogue on AI following President Xi Jinping's recent visit to Washington.

The M.S. Swaminathan Research Foundation (MSSRF) has inaugurated a water ATM at its heat stress study site in Perungudi, to improve access to drinking water. The 3,000-litre water ATM can dispense 20-litre cans at ₹5 each.
Mohan Kumar, director, Health Systems and Nutrition, MSSRF, said the initiative followed feedback from residents during field visits about the lack of access to drinking water.
The foundation is conducting a four-year longitudinal study across four sites in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka to assess the impact of heat on physical and mental health. Perungudi and Poompuhar in Mayiladuthurai are the two study sites in Tamil Nadu, while Sirwar in Raichur district, and Challakere in Chitradurga district are the sites in Karnataka.
“We wanted to make an immediate contribution to the community we are working with. Unlike water ATMs that dispense smaller quantities, this allows residents to collect 20 litres at a time at a minimal cost,” Dr. Kumar said. MSSRF plans to set up similar facilities at its other study sites.
MSSRF chairperson Soumya Swaminathan, who inaugurated the facility, said the foundation would assess its usefulness and explore other practical interventions based on the findings of the study.
The inauguration also featured an exhibition of photographs taken by local youngsters, as part of a photovoice study on heat and nutrition.
The broader heat study aims at assessing household and individual heat exposure, heat-related illnesses, coping mechanisms, mental health and well-being, and the preparedness of health systems to respond to heat-related situations. It will also examine the possibility of developing early warning systems at individual, sub-district, and district levels.
Speaking about the study, Dr. Swaminathan said the researchers were examining how changing weather patterns affect nutrition, heart rate, sleep, and overall well-being, particularly among vulnerable groups such as new-borns, older people, and those living with diabetes and hypertension.

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

“Avengers: Doomsday” co-director Anthony Russo has opened up about the pressure that comes with evolving the franchise’s iconic superhero characters, explaining that finding the balance between moving the story forward and honoring those already-beloved characters can be “very difficult.”
“It’s a very difficult part of the process because, I mean, we basically just have to use our own meters because we love the characters, we love the history, we love them in the same way that many fans do,” Russo said during a Q&A after a screening of “Avengers: Endgame Encore” (via GamesRadar+).
He continued: “But the one thing we always like to remind people of, you know, fandom does not speak with a single voice. There’s a wide variety of opinion in terms of who responds to which characters and which versions of which characters people respond to, it’s a very complex relationship that people have with the characters.”
Popular on Variety
Russo also said that he and his brother and co-director Joe have “a lot of respect for the storytelling journey that these characters have had up to this point.” “That’s part of their magic, a big part of their magic. But at the same time, we need to surprise ourselves in terms of who those characters are, where they can go, what they can do, what can happen, and in doing that, we hopefully surprise audiences as well.”
The director’s comments come nearly a year after an “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer spotlighted a much more serious Thor (Chris Hemsworth) than Marvel fans had seen in 2022’s “Thor: Love and Thunder.” The Taika Waititi-directed film performed well at the box office upon its release, but it divided fans who felt the character had become, in Hemsworth’s own words, “too silly.”
Russo also revealed that the film’s full cast has yet to be announced. “The cast is so large, and we’ve announced some of the cast, and we haven’t announced some of the cast,” said Russo. “I get confused myself over who we’ve announced and not announced, so I have to just slow down.” So far, the confirmed cast includes Hemsworth, Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans, Paul Rudd, Simu Liu, Tom Hiddleston and more.
“Avengers: Doomsday” will hit theaters on Dec. 18.

How to use Spotify's Running Mode on iOS and Android
Maximize your stride with the streaming service’s AI-powered feature.
Spotify launched its dedicated Fitness hub earlier this year, another move that shows how streaming service is looking to go beyond music and podcasts. Now, with the addition of Running Mode, it's more obvious than ever.
The new AI-powered feature is now available on both iOS and Android, exclusively for Premium subscribers in select markets, delivering a custom experience that tailors playlists to your fitness goals. Each Running Mode playlist is built around the music's BPM to align with the type of run you select.
Unlike Spotify Running, which was sunsetted in 2018, it doesn't play songs based on pace detection; now, it mainly lets you choose what to listen to. Instead of forcing you to skip tracks mid-workout or keep running back that same old playlist you've had for years, the new mode lets you dictate everything with added customization through the Prompted Playlist feature, structured intensity curves and voice guidance.
Whether you're lacing up for a low-key jog, a high-cadence speed workout or an interval run, setting up Running Mode on Spotify to find your ideal running soundtrack only takes a few quick steps.
How to activate Running Mode
Tap into Spotify on your iOS or Android device, then go to the Fitness hub, where you'll find Running Mode. There, you'll find a variety of genres and pre-structured workout types to choose from, including Intervals, Pyramids, Easy and Long, and Advanced.
Intervals will automatically swap between rapid stretches and breaks, using BPM as a designator to help you slow down and speed up as needed. Pyramid runs will start with a Warm Up period before leading into Build, Peak, Downshift and Cooldown sections with BPM tailored to each phase.
If you prefer a steady cadence, the Easy workout defaults to a manageable 135 BPM across a quick 20-minute run. On the other end, the Long and Advanced session pushes the tempo to 150 BPM over 45 minutes to keep your preferred rhythm locked in for the long haul. No matter which you choose, Spotify lets you adjust the length from 10 to 90 minutes.
For added personalization, the Beat Matching feature lets you set the pace. According to Spotify, most users prefer to stay around the standard 160 BPM mark, but many runners prefer to up the ante. If you want a rapid-fire tempo, you can dial it up to 170–180 BPM.
In case you don't want to fiddle with your phone before dashing out the door, Spotify accounts for that, too. Select one of the 20-minute sessions called 'Just Run,' so you can get a move on without having to scroll through the plethora of presets.
What can you listen to?
All four workout options are accompanied by genre-specific playlists. Whether you're feeling pop, hip-hop, EDM, country or rock, you can easily decide what songs serve as your workout's soundtrack. Each Running Mode playlist updates daily, but Spotify lets you save the ones you enjoy the most so you can revisit them for future runs.
For runners who want more control over what they're listening to, the "Prompted Playlist" feature is a game-changer, offering unique customization without too much effort. Tap "View prompt" and type in your request to DJ the session as you see fit; you can go broad with prompts like "high-energy songs that I haven't listened to since last year" or get specific with "hip-hop tracks from 2013 that make sense for a Sunday morning jog through the suburbs," and Spotify will add songs that fit the mood.
Tunes aside, if you need more of a push, you can also activate optional audio cues for mid-workout pep talks and motivational check-ins along the way, or simply mute them when your favorite songs are enough motivation.

Public health experts have called for tighter regulation of celebrity endorsements of harmful products following President Droupadi Murmu’s appeal to artistes to refrain from promoting substances detrimental to health, made against the backdrop of Maharashtra’s action over a Vimal Elaichi advertisement featuring Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.
The President, speaking at the 72nd National Film Awards in Gujarat on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), said popular artists, particularly those who influence children and young people, should promote disciplined lifestyles and refrain from endorsing substances harmful to health.
The remarks come as the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines whether the Vimal Elaichi campaign amounts to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala. The FDA has issued show-cause notices to the three actors, alleging that the advertisement creates an association with a pan-masala product whose manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale have been prohibited in Maharashtra.
The issue has also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court on September 14 declined to entertain a challenge to the FDA notices on territorial-jurisdiction grounds and directed the petitioner to approach the appropriate court in Maharashtra. The court did not adjudicate on whether the advertisements amounted to surrogate advertising.
Public health advocates have long raised concerns that celebrity endorsements can give socially acceptable imagery to products associated with tobacco, areca nut and other harmful substances, particularly among younger audiences. Cancer specialists have also warned about the health consequences associated with tobacco and areca-nut consumption.
Also read| Due diligence: On surrogate advertising
The Vimal campaign is not the first instance in which Bollywood celebrities have faced scrutiny over such endorsements. Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar have, at different times, been associated with advertisements for pan masala or related products. Kumar withdrew from a Vimal campaign in 2022 following criticism.
The renewed debate raises a broader public health question over whether regulations governing advertising are keeping pace with the influence of celebrity endorsements, particularly where advertisements for apparently permissible products may create associations with products that are restricted or harmful.
Speaking to The Hindu, Arun Gupta, convener of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi), said appeals to celebrities needed to be backed by a clear legal framework covering the endorsement and advertising of harmful products, including tobacco and ultra-processed foods.
“I wish appeals were taken seriously and work in India, especially when it comes to endorsement and advertising of harmful products which include ultra-processed food products and tobacco products,” he said.
Mr. Gupta said the government should act on the President’s appeal and enact a clearly worded law to prohibit the marketing of unhealthy products.
“This is the only way to curb the trend. Why I am saying this is because the current legal framework is more of self-regulation and is ineffective even though the government believes it to be working,” he said.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman — Oncology and executive director — Surgical Oncology and Robotic Surgery, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the President’s remarks highlighted the public-health consequences of celebrity endorsements of tobacco-linked products.
“As oncologists, we witness daily the catastrophic impact of pan masala, alcohol and tobacco addiction in our clinics. When high-profile icons lend their names to these brands, they inadvertently glamorise carcinogenic products for millions of impressionable youth,” he said.
Dr. Nayak said products such as silver-coated cardamom and flavoured mouth fresheners marketed under tobacco-associated brand names could function as surrogate advertisements.
“Using identical brand titles, logos and colour palettes — whether for pan masala or alcohol extensions —” creates a strong association with the primary brand, he said, calling for tighter regulation of such brand extensions.
Giving an insight into the scale of tobacco use in India, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found that 21.4% of Indians aged 15-49 used smokeless tobacco, with the prevalence higher among men (29.6%) than women (12.8%). The latest Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), conducted in 2016-17, estimated that 28.6% of Indians aged 15 years and above — nearly 267 million people — used tobacco. The survey also found that smokeless tobacco was the most prevalent form of tobacco use in the country.
A World Health Organisation study estimated the economic cost of diseases and premature deaths attributable to tobacco at ₹1.77 lakh crore in 2017-18, more than 1% of GDP, while treatment of tobacco-related diseases accounted for 5.3% of total health expenditure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has estimated that smokeless tobacco and areca-nut use caused more than 120,000 oral-cancer cases globally in 2022, with 88% occurring in South-Central Asia.

South Africa reels from spate of mass shootings that killed 38 people in a week
Johannesburg — A spate of mass shootings in three major South African cities killed nearly 40 people this week, with such incidents increasingly common in a country already known for its high crime rates.
On Saturday night, South African police said at least 10 people were killed at a shisanyama — a common kind of local restaurant selling barbecued meat — near Cape Town, while eleven others were injured.
The same night, near the commercial capital Johannesburg, 17 people were killed when a group of men with AK-47s burst into a township tavern where people were drinking.
The perpetrators "allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident," police said in a statement.
Police have not indicated a motive for either of the latest attacks.
Earlier in the week, another mass shooting occurred in the coastal city of Durban. Police said 11 people, including a pregnant woman, were killed on Tuesday by multiple gunmen in an attack on a house party.
A motive for that crime was also unclear, but several people at the house were known to authorities as part of investigations into criminal activity.
Illegal guns are common in South Africa, where mass shooting events are usually linked to gangs and organized crime, sometimes surrounding activities involving illegal gold miners known as "zama-zamas."
In June, in another mass shooting, 12 people were killed when gunmen stormed an informal settlement in Johannesburg, where people live in tin shacks without access to running water and electricity. That shooting was blamed on turf wars between zama-zamas.
At the scene, NPR saw pools of blood under a snooker table in a makeshift bar roped off with police tape and traumatized residents described their fear when they heard the gunshots.
"I hid under my bed," said Angela Mopayi, 54, at the time, "I couldn't breathe, I couldn't do anything, I thought I was dying."
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, averaging 60 a day. But even so, the number of mass shootings has become a national crisis.
President Cyril Ramaphosa has called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development," and deployed the army in some of the worst-affected areas.
President Trump has also been vocal about crime in South Africa since returning to office, but he has focused on the murders of white people on farms. While these do occur, official statistics show the vast majority of victims of crime are poor Black people.
And they are often also women. This month South Africans have been protesting amid a spate of brutal femicides in Johannesburg. On Saturday a tenth woman's body was discovered, despite police promises to crack down on gender-based violence.
South Africans head to the polls in November for local elections in which crime is expected to be a key issue.

Colombian police capture wife and daughter of Ecuadorian gang leader extradited to the United States
Colombian police say they have captured the wife and daughter of Jose Adolfo Macias Villamar, a notorious Ecuadorian gang leader
BOGOTA, Colombia -- BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Colombian police on Sunday said they captured the wife and daughter of a notorious Ecuadorian gang leader who was extradited to the U.S. last year on drug trafficking charges.
Police said the two women, who are wanted in Ecuador for money laundering, were arrested in Sabana de Torres, a small town in northeastern Colombia, in an operation backed by the FBI and Ecuadorian authorities.
“Colombia will not be a safe haven for the finances of transnational criminal groups,” Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a message posted on X on Sunday. “I will send these (women) with pleasure to my friend President Daniel Noboa, so that they face Ecuadorian justice.”
José Adolfo Macías Villamar, whose nickname is “Fito,” escaped from a prison in Guayaquil, Ecuador in January 2024. The gang leader’s prison break prompted Ecuador’s government to declare a state of emergency that was followed by deadly prison riots and chaos in the streets of Guayaquil, where gang members stormed a television station during a live broadcast.
Macías Villamar was recaptured last year and sent to the United States, where he has been charged with importing thousands of pounds of cocaine. His organization, Los Choneros, was designated as a terrorist group by the U.S. State Department last year.
Despite capturing powerful kingpins like Macías Villamar, and deploying the military to patrol some cities, Ecuador is struggling to contain drug violence.
The South American country’s homicide rate has quintupled since 2020, and last year Ecuador recorded its highest homicide rate in recent history — with 50 homicides per every 100,000 residents, according to the Interior Ministry.
Noboa’s response to drug trafficking outfits has come under criticism from human rights groups, as the military commits abuses that include the slayings of four children aged 11 to 15 in 2024. Despite these setbacks, Noboa was reelected to a four-year term last year by voters increasingly concerned with crime.

In a dramatic blend of cinema and diplomacy, the Iranian Embassy in Hyderabad has drawn a parallel between Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's defiant address at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) and the iconic battle scenes from the Telugu blockbuster Baahubali. The embassy shared a video featuring the film's protagonist taking on the enemy army, accompanied by a message asserting Iran's determination to stand firm against external pressure.
The video features scenes from Baahubali: The Beginning, in which Amarendra Baahubali, played by Prabhas, leads his forces against the Kalakeya army.
"Dr. Pezeshkian, President of Islamic Republic of Iran at UNGA: 'Will never bow our head or bend the knee' Like Baahubali standing against the Kalakeyas, we also shed our own blood in sacrifice for the homeland," the embassy wrote alongside the video.
The comparison draws on one of the film's most memorable sequences, in which Baahubali refuses to retreat despite facing a formidable enemy.
The post follows Pezeshkian's address at the 81st UNGA in New York on September 23, where he rejected the prospect of Iran surrendering to US pressure. Responding to US President Donald Trump's remarks a day earlier, Pezeshkian said that sanctions, pressure and threats would only strengthen the Iranian people's resolve. 
"We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he declared, while also expressing Iran's willingness to pursue dialogue and diplomacy without accepting coercion.
Pezeshkian's speech came amid escalating tensions between Iran and the United States.
He accused Washington and Israel of attacking Iranian territory and defended his country's military response, while maintaining that Tehran remained open to negotiations. He also criticised sanctions and raised concerns about civilian casualties and the conflict in West Asia. These remarks formed the backdrop to the embassy's subsequent social media post.

Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
- Published
You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.
You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.
Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."
Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.
FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.
The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?
The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.
Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.
"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.
Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.
Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.
Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".
"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."
What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.
Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.
Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.
"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."
He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.
The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.
The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.
Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".
"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.
For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.
What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

Andy Burnham brings good vibes to Labour’s annual conference but tough choices are coming
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been in office for two months, and his party seems content for now
LONDON -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been in the job for two months, and so far his party isn’t demanding his head. These days, that’s an accomplishment.
The governing Labour Party opens its annual conference beside the River Mersey in Liverpool on Sunday, with Burnham pledging to turn the page on a decade of economic and political turmoil that has made him the U.K.’s seventh prime minister since its 2016 vote to leave the European Union.
He says his message in a keynote speech on Tuesday will be: “It’s time for Britain to have hope again.”
“We’ve had a decade since Brexit and it’s been a decade of too much drift, too much division, and we need to draw a line on that,” Burnham said as he arrived in Liverpool on Saturday.
His message is aimed at both the British public and a center-left party that is hopeful but nervous — ready to embrace his promise of better times, but worried about economic damage rippling out from conflict in the Middle East.
University of Manchester political science professor Rob Ford said Burnham’s difficult task is to win over “a skeptical electorate" eager for change, "while at the same time doing that within the constraints of a very difficult economic and fiscal situation.”
In short: “How do you serve people a bowl of cold porridge and convince them it’s a pepperoni pizza?”
Britain’s main political parties all hold conferences in September and October, combinations of pep rally, social gathering and policy forum that set the political tone and agenda for the year ahead.
Last year’s Labour gathering was gloomy, as members despaired about Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s deep unpopularity, little more than a year after winning power in a landslide, and the seemingly unstoppable rise of the anti-immigration opposition party Reform UK.
Burnham, then the popular mayor of Greater Manchester, was followed around Liverpool by journalists as speculation grew that he would challenge Starmer.
Events came to a head months later when a panicky party forced Starmer’s resignation and his replacement by Burnham as party leader and prime minister in July.
Now, Labour is seeing a “Burnham bounce” driven by the new leader’s upbeat talk and modest moves to put money in voters’ pocketbooks by cutting tax on electricity bills and capping bus fares.
Meanwhile, Reform is facing parliamentary and police investigations over its finances – though it also recently received a whopping 72 million pounds ($95 million) from two cryptocurrency billionaires.
Burnham has already set out some priorities, including handing more power to local leaders in order to generate "good growth in every post code.” He says he’ll reform Britain’s privatized utilities, especially the expensive, leaky and polluting water network.
While the party is relatively united behind Burnham, he faces a divisive decision about whether to approve new oil drilling in the North Sea – opposed by environmentalists but backed by trade unions – and pushback over plans agreed under Starmer to make it harder for immigrants to settle permanently in Britain.
The next general election does not have to be called until 2029, but Labour’s revival has sparked talk of a snap election – something Burnham denies he’s considering.
“All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead,” Burnham told broadcaster ITV on Friday.
But no matter how upbeat Burnham is, economic pain is coming.
Burnham must explain to party members and voters how he will deal with economic turbulence from the on-off U.S.-Iran war, which has severely restricted the movement of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.
Treasury chief John Healey is set to deliver the Burnham government’s first budget on Oct. 28, with rising energy prices tightening a cost-of-living squeeze. Like other countries, Britain also needs to find money to increase defense spending to counter threats from Russia.
That means tax rises or spending cuts – or both – could be on the cards.
One thing that might bring an economic boost is to ease some of the trade barriers erected by Brexit. Burnham has pledged closer ties with the European Union, but it’s unclear how close.
Under Starmer, Labour was elected in 2024 on a promise not to seek to rejoin the bloc or enter its single market for goods, services and employment. Many Labour members would like to break that pledge, including former Prime Minister Tony Blair, who said last week that the U.K. and EU should start negotiations “where everything is on the table.”
Burnham has said that’s a discussion for another time. Meanwhile, progress toward closer ties has been slow.
An EU-U.K. reset summit initially penciled in for July has slipped to November at the earliest because the two sides are wrangling over the bloc’s “made in Europe” rules, which the U.K. says will hurt British producers.
Ford said that unlike Starmer, who quickly squandered the public’s goodwill, Burnham has held onto his reputation “as an optimist and an effective communicator.” But he said Burnham's “really stern test” is yet to come.
“The bills are still going to land on the doormat,” Ford said. “He’s going to have to be the prime minister who can sell the average voter on, ‘Yes, that is indeed a bowl of cold porridge in front of you, but it will get better.’”

Living on the coast of Maine has its advantages. Beaches and islands are close. "Not that close," my husband said when my daughter told us her high school English teacher had recommended her for a summer job. The opportunity was on a small island, a ferry ride away, and it would mean driving her into Portland from our house in the suburbs just outside, affecting our summer routine.
The ride is 30 minutes. With drop-off and pickup, that would take at least an hour. Traffic from local pedestrians and tourists is outrageous. Her new job would require a lot of effort from both of us, but it would also give her a chance to do something meaningful.
I thought she had a cooler first job than me
"She'd be working at a seafood place on an island off the coast of Maine," I said to my husband. "What a cool first job and amazing experience." I worked at a clothing store in the mall for my first job, where we had to upsell everything. If a person bought shorts, we pushed them to buy the matching shirt or headband. It was the 90s. Matching meant everything.
After my daughter interviewed with the manager, she got the job. Her text was enthusiastic and hopeful: "She offered me the job, and I really, really want to take it." Negotiations began later that evening. We went back and forth as she pleaded her case. I wondered aloud if I would make it through an entire summer driving in and out of one of the busiest sections of Southern Maine, but her excitement fed my own.
My husband was less than enthusiastic, but I understood that she needed this job. I also knew I needed to let her accept it, even if it meant hours of vacationers crossing in front of us at the crosswalk. Even if I had to shift my schedule and rethink my summer priorities. I wanted this experience for my daughter.
We bought a ferry pass and planned the drive into Portland. She agreed to pay for half of her monthly pass from her paycheck. She would also have to go in early since I was driving her, which wasn't ideal during the summer when I teach extended school year. The extra time spent on the island wouldn't be too painful since she could wait out the time until her shift at the beach. The job required compromise, but it would be worth it.
Her first job was on the island we visited when she was little
For her training shift, which started right after school ended, we went to the island together. When the kids were little, we used to visit as a family once a year. We'd walk around the whole island and have lunch at a local inn. It felt good to return after so many years, and to see her beginning her own experience there.
While she was training, I grabbed some lunch. Watching her work was amazing. She picked things up quickly and did her job accurately and efficiently. On the way home, we enjoyed the ferry ride. I left feeling sure this would be something she'd always remember. In the weeks since, she's been offered more hours and made some good friends.
It also gave me an excuse to take the family out to the island. I went with my two great-aunts to visit Kyle at work. We took her older sister, who is attending Arizona State. The youngest also came to our goodbye lunch. We rode out on the ferry and marveled at how beautiful my daughter's commute was. Tourists and locals crowded onto the ferry, taking pictures to remember the moment. It is one my daughter gets to enjoy all summer long.
It wasn't just a stunning morning and evening commute to work that made her job so cool, or the fun of introducing family to the island. The job also gave her her first work experience and her first paycheck. She managed to save up a good amount toward a car. It was great to watch her figure out what to keep in her checking account, what to spend each week, and what to save.
Seeing her make those choices showed me this job was teaching her more than how to earn a paycheck. She was learning about responsibility and gaining the confidence to make her own decisions. Her first cool job was also a chance for her to gain independence.
Next year, she hopes to return to her job on the island. While it will continue to require some effort from both of us, I know it will be worth it because this first job gave her more than experience. It gave her a first glimpse of adulthood — one of the many milestones that will help her through the arduous and uncertain journey ahead.

Nagoya – South Korea found its composure when it mattered most to win the women’s basketball gold at the Asian Games, surviving a huge scare to beat host Japan 75-70 in Saturday’s final.
The South Koreans took control of the game early and looked to be cruising towards their fourth Asian Games title and their first since 2014.
But Japan, backed by a noisy crowd at the 17,000-capacity Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, roared back to within two points late in the game until South Korea finally saw out the win.
Kang Lee-seul, who scored 21 points for South Korea including three crucial late free throws, said the pressure almost cost them the victory.
“I could feel our players’ minds were getting too busy, so I kept telling them to stay calm and to be a little more precise,” she said.
“I think I was constantly trying to encourage them and calm them down.”
The win came six days after South Korea beat Japan in the men’s final.
The South Koreans dominated in the first quarter, building a 15-3 lead to set the tone.
They looked comfortable until Japan finished the third quarter strongly and hit a three-pointer right at the buzzer.
Japan then closed the gap further in the fourth quarter, but South Korea held on to get the win over the line.
“We could actually have won by a much bigger margin but they caught up with us,” said Kang.
“Putting all of that aside, in the end we achieved this great result of winning the gold medal, so right now I’m extremely happy.”
Lee Hae-ran was South Korea’s top scorer with 24 points. Japan were led by Haru Owaki with 23 points.
Every player in South Korea’s squad also featured at the Women’s World Cup in Germany earlier this month, where it lost to the host in the first knockout round.
Japan was also eliminated at the same stage at the World Cup but it brought an entirely different squad to the Asian Games.
Japan was looking to win the Asian Games title for the first time since 1998.
Japan’s Miyu Okamoto said her team matched South Korea for skill at the start of the game but “we were overwhelmed by their spirit.”
“If we had a better start, I think we would have had a much better chance of winning,” she said.
China won the bronze medal, beating Taiwan 77-64.

'Gyanu must go,' says Dipke after ex-bureaucrat claims Gyanesh Kumar offered him BJP candidature
The CEC is at the heart of a controversy surrounding the commission after reports of alleged differences between the two election commissioners and Kumar.
Cockroach Janta Party leader Abhijeet Dipke on Saturday renewed his call for Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar's resignation after a former Kerala chief secretary alleged that Kumar had offered him BJP candidature in the general elections.
According to a report by Onmanorama, former Kerala chief secretary Jiji Thomson alleged that Kumar asked him if he was interested in contesting the 2019 Lok Sabha elections while travelling together on the same flight in 2016.
ALSO READ: EC says poll commissioners' letters to Cabinet Secretary not over policy matter, but 'related to...'
"We were together on a flight. He was waxing eloquent about Prime Minister Modi and openly asked me if I was interested in contesting as a BJP candidate from Pathanamthitta in the 2019 general elections. He was very persuasive; I declined it promptly," the report quoted him as saying. Jiji Thomson retired from the top post in 2016.
Deep Dive
Sharing the report on his Instagram handle, Dipke wrote, “Gyanu must go.” In a post on X, Dipke took a dig at Kumar saying, “Ye karwayenge free and fair elections. (He will ensure free and fair elections.)”
Citing the report, Congress MP Rahul Gandhi also launched an attack on Kumar and accused him of “match-fixing elections”. “First, Gyanesh Kumar - then a serving IAS officer - was used to recruit for the BJP. Then Modi and Shah made him the umpire and put him in charge of match-fixing India's elections,” he wrote on X.
CEC Kumar is at the heart of a huge controversy surrounding the Election Commission after an investigative report by The Indian Express alleged differences between the two election commissioners and Kumar.
The Election Commission on Saturday reasserted that key decisions, including the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls, were taken unanimously by the full commission.
The poll body has maintained that differing views and observations are a normal part of institutional deliberations and asserted that its orders have full legal sanction and follow statutory procedures.
Earlier on Friday, Dipke said CJP would launch a nationwide protest from Mumbai on October 2 and take it to cities across India if Kumar did not quit. The Dipke-led group has also warned of a nationwide agitation, including what it called 'Jantar Mantar 2.0'.
Launching its "Election Commission Thik Karo" campaign, the CJP said it would focus on the exclusion of more than 13 crore names from draft electoral rolls across 30 states and Union Territories during the ECI's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
CJP's call for protest was supported by Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray as he said, "If Gyanesh doesn't go, Mumbai will step out against Vote Chori from 2nd October, in huge numbers!"

Should you ditch your tablet for a foldable phone?
The new form factor offers convenience at a premium.
Book-style foldable phones feature enough screen real estate to rival compact tablets, and at this point, it's reasonable to wonder if the former should replace the latter. For instance, the latest iPad Mini features an 8.3-inch screen, only 0.3 inches larger than the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. At 7.6 inches, the iPhone Duo is slightly smaller, but the difference is minor. Most people aren't carrying a compact tablet around, but if an 8-inch device folds down to a typical smartphone size, that's different.
In fact, that convenience is the strongest argument in favor of replacing your tablet. You can use all of the features you normally use on a smartphone and unfold the screen when you prefer a tablet experience. A foldable also simplifies mobile data because most tablets need a second cell plan if you're moving around and need full access to its features. If you don't have a second plan, you may have to pay extra for a hotspot on your phone.
The foldable consolidates those uses into a single device and slides into your back pocket when you're done. It's not perfect, and it's not a universal replacement, but it's more than enough to replace a casual tablet, especially on the go.
Tablets still win for long sessions and serious work
It's a different story if your tablet is a major part of your daily work. A foldable is great for two, maybe three-app multitasking and portable entertainment, but it can't match the comfort and larger workspace a tablet typically brings to the table. This is especially true with tablets designed for video editing, graphic design or work that benefits from a larger canvas.
Granted, foldable phones can connect with most of the same peripherals a tablet can, which makes them fairly capable travel tools for basic work. But that's not the same as being a true workhorse. Using your phone as your full-time work machine puts a lot more strain on the battery, which is a huge compromise because it's also your main device for everyday use.
The price difference is also worth considering, because foldables aren't very budget friendly. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Galaxy Z Fold 8 start at premium prices, so combining your phone and tablet into one product can still cost more than purchasing separate devices, depending on what you need from each.
What are the disadvantages of a foldable phone?
Foldable phones still come with more compromises than either a standard smartphone or a dedicated tablet. The biggest reason is the hardware. Much has been said about hinges and folding displays, but ultimately, they just add complexity and cost, along with another element of wear and tear.
The design introduces a few trade-offs in day-to-day use. It offers more screen real estate, but that also means a bulkier, heavier device, with an inner display crease that's visible under certain lighting conditions. To be fair, foldable phones are becoming thinner and lighter, though they still have a way to go.
There are occasional software compromises as well. Android handles large screens and split-screen multitasking better than it used to, but occasionally an app uses the unfolded screen less than gracefully. Some apps simply stretch a vertical layout across a wider panel, and the result is... interesting.
Foldable phones are a premium convenience, but not quite full-blown replacements for every phone and tablet. They can absorb the job of a casual compact tablet, but there are a few compromises along the way. For those who aren't looking for any new compromises just yet and need a mobile workhorse, sticking with a dedicated tablet is still the best bet.
