My heart flutters every time I spot a unique vintage treasure in the tchotchke aisle at the thrift store. But then I realize it has a chip or a crack, so I decide to put it back. The object may have sentimental value, but it's not a match for my vintage shop, where I always try to feature high-quality items that have survived the test of time.
When my younger sister, Hillary, and I turned our love for vintage collecting into a small business nearly three years ago, we had no idea how hard it would be or how long it would take to sell a single vintage item.
Most people think it's as simple as plucking an item, taking a few photos, crafting a savvy title, and plopping it on a platform. But there's way more that goes into running our tiny online vintage shop.
We had to figure out the best places to source great items, how to navigate moody markets, how to do deep-dive historical research, how to clean and restore fragile pieces, how to set up systems, how to determine the value of our vintage objects, and, most importantly, how to learn to tell their stories.
We have to dig, sift, and sort
To source great items for the shop, Travel Far Now Vintage, my sister and I love a good thrift haul, estate sale dig, antique mall stroll, or flea market frenzy. But in the early days of selling vintage items, we started with the stuff in our own childhood home.
Our mother collected all kinds of objects, from porcelain flowers to royal portraits in filigree frames, and we didn't know quite what to do with them all when she died. We were excited to discover a vast online world of collectors seeking niche nostalgia.
As the shop grew, we widened and diversified our search. We learned that consistency is key. These days, we source items three to five times a week.
This work has led us into all kinds of scenarios: scaling mold-infested shelves, digging deep into dusty boxes, and sorting through basement barrels.
Sometimes we walk away with a bundle of goodies. Other days, we leave empty-handed. But we always shop with criteria for what we're looking for and how much we're willing to spend.
Pricing is a bit of a puzzle
We consider the item's quality, rarity, and what we paid for it. But it's more art than science.
Within an ecosystem of secondhand goods at increasingly competitive prices, we determine the price of an item based on the current market. We sometimes research the "sold rate" of similar items, but that's not always accurate as trends change.
I try to land on a price that accurately reflects the value of the item itself, as well as all the hidden labor that goes into presenting it. This includes digging in chaotic environments, restoring objects, researching their histories, telling their stories in listings, and promoting them on social media.
The price of an item also includes costs like gas, shipping, and packing supplies, as well as platform fees and ads.
This usually means there's a markup over the original price — sometimes more or less — depending on the object's rarity as a collector's item.
What are the ethics?
At a recent estate sale, I picked up a vintage paperback of Jack Kerouac's "The Dharma Bums," a mid-century classic popular among Beat Generation collectors. I bought it for a very reasonable price in great condition. The demand for a rare item like this allows for a higher markup, and I'm OK with that. It makes me happy to know this book will find its way into the hands of someone who will truly appreciate it.
Some people may consider this to be taking advantage of someone else's loss or lack of knowledge. When I buy or sell vintage items, I value integrity, fairness, and transparency on both sides. But this work is about finding gems in the junk, reviving objects that might otherwise be overlooked or tossed.
I store and care for these items and then connect them with people who value them. The markup reflects that work as much as it reflects the item's scarcity or market value.
It's impossible to sell vintage online without hearing complaints that Goodwill and other thrift stores are driving up vintage prices. But all the stuff people don't want anymore has to go somewhere — and that, too, comes at a cost.
Like any other business, charity shops, antique malls, and flea markets must calculate the costs of storing, cleaning, and selling these items.
My sister and I entered the vintage reselling world as grieving daughters and remain as enthusiastic storytellers — eager to connect people with vintage items that bring them joy. We factor in all the invisible work that goes into this business, but ultimately it's a labor of love.

No handshakes between Republic of Ireland and Israel
- Published
The Republic of Ireland and Israel players did not shake hands with each other before Sunday's controversial Uefa Nations League game in Hungary.
After walking on to the pitch at Nagyerdei Stadion, the Republic of Ireland squad stood for their national anthem and appeared to bow their heads before Israel's anthem.
Following the anthems, the two teams did not line up for the traditional handshakes.
There was also no exchange of pennants between Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel skipper Manor Solomon, who did not shake hands.
The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since February when the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.
The Republic of Ireland players have faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.
However, the players voted to fulfil the fixture during a lengthy meeting at the team's hotel in Debrecen on Saturday.
Later on Saturday, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu confirmed he had withdrawn from the squad, saying he felt it "would be wrong to participate" in Sunday's game and the return fixture in Serbia on 4 October.
The Irish players wore black armbands, which Football Association of Ireland chief executive David Courell said on Saturday was a gesture "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict".

Why Democratic Senate hopes are rising
With Republicans on the back foot, Democrats are eying an expanded Senate map.
We’re officially inside 40 days until the 2026 midterms — and Republicans are feeling the pressure.
Nearly every poll seems to bring more bad news for GOP candidates, even in what would normally be comfortably red seats. And one of the clearest signs of how the party is feeling is how they’re talking — or not talking — about President Donald Trump and his record.
As my colleague Andrew Prokop reported, some Republicans are slowly, tentatively starting to edge away from Trump and his least popular policies, including the Iran war and mass deportations.
In Florida, Rep. María Elvira Salazar — who won with more than 60 percent of the vote in 2024 — released an ad addressing Trump directly and criticizing his immigration enforcement efforts for having “gone too far.” Two Republican incumbents in Iowa, which has been hard-hit by soaring diesel prices, voted in favor of a resolution to end the Iran war.
Whether any of those gestures toward moderation will matter is another question, especially after almost a decade of unquestioning Republican fealty toward Trump. But they’re reflective of an environment that, even by usual midterm standards (when the president’s party almost always loses ground), is looking increasingly dire for the GOP.
The battle for the Senate
As things look worse for the GOP, Democrats are starting to eye an expanded Senate map and a very real chance of reclaiming the upper chamber, which once looked like an uphill battle.
Over the last two months, according to election forecasters like the Cook Political Report, more Senate races have slid into the tossup column or otherwise moved left.
Among them are the open Senate seats in Iowa and Texas — currently Republican-held — which Cook now considers tossups. Kansas, where incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is on the ballot, has shifted from likely to lean Republican. And even South Carolina has drifted out of the solid Republican column, though it’s still an extremely long shot for Democrats. (The New Hampshire Senate race, where Democrats are defending an open seat currently held by retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, has also shifted into the tossup column, from leaning Democratic.)
Texas, in particular, would be a prize for Democrats; polls have consistently shown Democratic state Rep. James Talarico leading against Republican Ken Paxton, Texas’s scandal-plagued attorney general who defeated incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn in a primary.
And Kansas has emerged as a surprise pickup possibility, with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, giving Marshall a tough race. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Marshall, a doctor, sued hundreds of patients for medical debts, sometimes resulting in their arrest; one of those patients has since appeared in a Hamilton campaign ad.

➨ We should be partying more. Vox’s Explain It to Me podcast talks with a party historian about our long — think medieval — history of having fun together, how it’s manifested over time, and why it’s so important societally and culturally, above and beyond purely being a good time.

Nationwide bank strike from tomorrow: Will online services still work? Which banks will be open? Key details
Branches of new generation private sector banks, including ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank and Axis Bank, will remain open during the three-day strike.
Banking services are expected to face disruptions for three days from Monday as bank unions begin a nationwide strike over their demand for a five-day working week and other pending issues.
The strike is likely to affect services such as cheque clearance, cash deposits and withdrawals, particularly at public sector banks, old generation private sector banks and regional rural banks. However, digital banking and other online services are expected to remain available, news agency PTI reported.
Branches of new generation private sector banks, including ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank and Axis Bank, will remain open during the three-day strike.
What services may be affected?
Customers using public sector banks and other institutions could face delays in branch-based banking services during the strike. Most public sector banks and other institutions have already issued advisories warning customers about possible inconvenience.
State Bank of India (SBI), in its advisory, said it would make every effort to provide essential banking services at branches and offices, but some services could be affected during the strike.
"Customers are therefore requested to complete their essential banking transactions well in advance of the proposed strike dates to avoid any inconvenience. Customers are also requested to make use of ATMs/ADWMs for their cash requirements and utilise YONO, Internet/Mobile Banking, UPI and other digital channels for their banking needs, wherever possible," it said.
Why are bank unions on strike?
The strike has been called by the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU), an umbrella body representing seven bank employees' and officers' unions. The unions are demanding a five-day working week along with several other pending issues.
The latest three-day strike comes after a one-day nationwide strike held on September 11. The UFBU has also threatened an indefinite strike from October 26, 2026 if its demands are not addressed.
The demand for a five-day banking week has remained unresolved for several years. Union leaders said the government did not give any commitment on the issue during recent conciliation meetings before the Chief Labour Commissioner.
"Agitation has been forced on the unions due to the actions of the government and management," said Rupam Roy, general secretary of the All India Bank Officers' Confederation (AIBOC).
What are the other demands?
Apart from a five-day working week, the unions are seeking changes to pension benefits, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to shift to the Old Pension Scheme (OPS).
"A five-day working week is already followed by central and state government offices, the RBI, LIC, GIC, NABARD and several other institutions. The stock market, money market and foreign exchange market also function on a five-day basis," said L Chandrasekhar, general secretary of the National Confederation of Bank Employees (NCBE).
What has the finance ministry said?
The finance ministry earlier this week urged bank employees not to go on strike and asked them to resolve their remaining demands through dialogue.
"Given that most concerns of the unions have been substantially addressed, that the remaining demand continues to be examined, and that the government continues to proactively introduce welfare measures for the banking workforce, bank employees are urged to refrain from resorting to strikes, work towards resolving issues through dialogue, and ensure that banking services remain uninterrupted," it said.
The ministry also said that one of the unions' key demands, withdrawal of the performance-linked incentive (PLI) scheme, was put in abeyance earlier this month following detailed discussions.
Despite the government resolving one of the two major demands raised by the union and continuing discussions, a one-day strike was held on September 11.

- Following Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 24, 2026, social media users shared a clip purportedly showing him saying "America deserved 9/11" as he shook his finger in the air.
- The clip was authentic, meaning it wasn't generated with artificial intelligence or digitally altered.
- A longer video of Netanyahu's speech, however, showed he was not expressing his personal belief but rather quoting the left-leaning influencer Hasan Piker. Piker truly made that statement during a live stream in 2019.
After Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 24, 2026, a rumor spread that during his speech, he said the U.S. deserved the 9/11 attacks.
Several users on X made the claim (archived), expressing disbelief using a supposed video clip of the speech of Netanyahu saying "America deserved 9/11" as he shook his finger in the air.
While the clip was authentic, meaning not generated with artificial intelligence or digitally altered, it omits critical context from Netanyahu's full remarks. He was not expressing his personal belief when he said those words. A longer video showed he was quoting Hasan Piker, a left-leaning influencer, who did say "America deserved 9/11" during a livestream in 2019. We've left this claim unrated to account for those nuances.
At the 27:10 mark in the video, Netanyahu addressed New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, saying Mamdani was antisemitic and he and Piker were friends. As he did so, he quoted Piker (emphasis ours):
So to all those that are spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: Shame on you. Shame on you for distorting the facts. Shame on you for inverting victim and aggressor. Shame on you for spitting in the face of truth.
Mr. Mamdani, since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York. They talk to me. They tell me, "This isn't the city we remember. It changed so quickly."
Now it's no wonder. You praise criminals convicted of supporting Hamas. You count as friends people like Hasan Piker, who said "America deserved 9/11. America deserved 9/11." Some friends you have.
You invite into your home a Palestinian journalist who filmed Hamas terrorists beating and torturing Israeli hostages, and later admitted that he refused to publish the videos in order to protect, you guessed it, the terrorists. Your wife liked a post praising the Oct. 7 massacre. She liked another post saying Tel Aviv shouldn't exist.
It is true that Piker said these words in August 2019 while live-streaming on Twitch:
"America deserved 9/11, dude," he said. "F*** it. I'm saying it."
For further reading, this is not the first time Snopes has investigated claims attributing this quote to someone other than Piker. In August 2026, we found U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat, hadn't expressed the belief that the U.S. deserved 9/11.

What does it take to make a morning cup of tea in Gaza?
For Alaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.
For 12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.
Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?
Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, when aid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.
Most of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.
There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.
There is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.
Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, deciding how many calories it will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.
Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans a plethora of ordinary objects from entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.
From the story of Rajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.
But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.
A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.
Still, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human. Prof Mahmoud Seydam wires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike. Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.

Mohamed Salah given six-month driving ban
- Published
Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding.
Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents.
The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge.
He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court.
A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce.
The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team.
Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history".
He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season.

How school districts are coping with diesel’s high cost thanks to Trump’s war: ‘We rob Peter to pay Paul, basically’
Diesel powers more than 87 percent of the buses that shuttle about 23.5 million students to school and school-related activities

The high cost of diesel fuel is blowing holes in school budgets across the country — forcing officials to scramble to keep their bright yellow buses on the road.
Diesel powers more than 87 percent of the buses that shuttle about 23.5 million students to school and school-related activities, according to the Engine Technology Forum, an industry group.
And with the national average price per gallon hovering near the record $6.53 reported Tuesday by AAA - an increase from the $3.74 a year ago in September - some administrators have consolidated routes, reducing daily trips and forcing kids to take longer rides on buses crammed with more passengers.
Prices have spiked after Donald Trump launched a war against Iran, choking off the world’s oil supply and causing both regular gasoline and diesel prices to soar.
“We rob Peter to pay Paul, basically,” Nick Klemisch, superintendent of the tiny Garrison Public Schools district in North Dakota, admitted. “We may have to not purchase a piece of equipment for the classroom.”
A survey of 188 school officials earlier this year found that 40 percent had adopted the strategy of consolidated routes, with 27 percent cracking down on idling and 20 percent cutting back on field trips to save on fuel.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for the price-tracking website GasBuddy, said Thursday on social media that the high cost of diesel “comes down to one thing: how hard it is right now to turn oil into diesel, and how many people around the world are fighting over getting it.”
In addition to Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz over President Donald Trump's war against the Islamic Republic, De Haan blamed diesel export bans by Russia and China, moves that Trump said Wednesday he was considering copying in a bid to bring down domestic prices before November's midterm elections.
Here's what The Independent found about how some school districts are tackling higher prices:
North Dakota
Klemisch oversees the district about 65 miles northwest of Bismarck and said he's budgeted about $100,000 for diesel this school year, up from about $80,000 in 2025-26, and $65,000 in 2024-2025.
Up to half of the district's 370 students get to and from school on the district's five bus routes — one of which stretches 42 miles each way — but they're already “bare bones” and can't be consolidated any further, he said.
With state law limiting school tax increases to 3 percent a year, the added cost of diesel “cuts into the general fund balance,” Klemisch said.
A shortage of bus drivers also regularly puts the superintendent behind the wheel, with Klemisch saying he's racked up 80 hours since classes resumed in late August.
“I'm usually the lone sub,” he said. “I drive activities. When you're in rural America, you get other activities as assigned.”
On Friday, Klemisch planned to take the football team to a game in Ray, North Dakota, a trip of about 130 miles.
The bus was scheduled to leave around 2:30 p.m., he said, adding, "Hopefully, I'll be home by midnight.
Wyoming
Carbon County School District No. 1's transportation director, Scott Hannum, said he expected diesel would cost about $4.50 a gallon when he prepared his budget for this school year.
But when he drove to work on Wednesday, he saw a pump price of $5.99.
“It's always a guess,” he said of the budgeting process.
Last year, the district's fleet of 32 buses logged about 470,000 miles ferrying about 750 students to and from its three schools in Rawlins, about 100 miles northwest of Laramie, and also taking kids on trips, Hannum said.
The district has already consolidated its routes, Hannum said, adding that he didn't foresee any more changes and that the only way to cut costs would be to "cut back activity trips."
“We travel hundreds of miles each way,” he said, noting that the football team recently played a game in Jackson, Wyoming.
“That's 285 miles away. Wyoming's a rural state. We drive 100 miles, easy, everywhere,” said Hannum, a former Rawlins city manager.
The district's business manager, Margaret Quintrall, said this year's school budget allocated $85,000 for diesel, with about one-quarter of that — $21,455 — already spent.
Both Hannum and Quintrall said Wyoming's method of funding education includes the full reimbursement of fuel costs. The state education budget has “sufficient funds to cover the higher diesel prices for the current school year,” said Trent Carroll, chief operations officer of the Wyoming Department of Education.
Nevada
The sprawling Clark County School District, headquartered in Las Vegas, ranks No. 1 in the nation based on the distance covered by its buses, which traveled a total of 31 million miles last year, according to statistics compiled by School Bus Fleet magazine.
During the 2025-2026 fiscal year, it spent $15.1 million on fuel to transport 120,000 students, up $2.4 million, or 19 percent, from 2024-2025, the district said in a prepared statement.
“Our current fiscal outlook projects this upward trend in expenditure volatility to persist through the better part of the 2026-2027 school year, equating to an additional $2.9 million in fuel-related expenses,” the statement said.
The district, which had an August enrollment of 270,975 students and 15,500 teachers, also said it was “working to absorb these costs through the Central Office budget,” without elaborating.
The projected higher fuel costs pale in comparison, however, to the anticipated loss of $100 million in state funding due to a higher-than-expected decline in enrollment of 10,400 students that the district announced earlier this month.
The district trimmed its budget by about $50 million in the spring, eliminating about 1,200 jobs, and it plans to slash another $51.6 million through cuts that will include an unspecified number of layoffs, according to a news release.
Florida
The mid-sized Bay District Schools in Panama City has more than 28,000 students, with about 8,000 riding buses that travel about 7,000 miles a day and more than a million miles a year, according to its 2026-2027 budget.
The fleet of 40 buses also carries kids on more than 1,000 field trips around the Florida Panhandle, the district's website says, and its spending plan includes $1.8 million for 10 new buses.
A spokesperson said in an email that officials initially earmarked $800,000 for diesel, the same amount as in 2025-2026.
That's since been increased by about $84,000 from other, unspecified sources to offset higher fuel prices, with no plans to alter any services at this time, the spokesperson said.

There are numerous reasons why you might want to record what’s happening on your phone. Maybe you’re having a problem with an app and you want to share what’s going wrong with a tech-savvy friend; or maybe you're the tech-savvy friend, and you want to show someone else how to fix a bug.
Perhaps you’re starting up a YouTube channel of smartphone tutorials. Or it could be that you want to capture evidence of a new high score in a mobile game—not just a screenshot of it, but the actual act of you achieving it.
For these reasons and more, screen recordings are useful, and they’re not difficult to capture no matter what the make and model of your handset. You’ll find instructions below for the two most well-known Android phone brands, and the iPhone.
Record Your Screen on a Google Pixel
If your phone of choice is the Google Pixel, unlock your handset then swipe down from the top of the screen with two fingers to bring up the full Quick Settings selection. You should see a widget for Screen recorder—if you can’t see it, try swiping left or right. If you still can’t see it, tap the pen icon (lower right) to add it to the Quick Settings menu.
Next you’ll see a panel of toggle switches: These options let you choose whether or not the screen touches are visible in the recording, and whether you want the selfie camera feed to be visible as an overlay (handy if you’re narrating or reacting to what’s on screen). You can also opt to include audio from your phone’s apps or from the microphone.
The drop-down menu at the top lets you decide between recording the entire screen or just a single app. When you’re happy, tap Start. You’ll see a short countdown, then the recording begins. To end the recording, tap the red recording timer in the status bar at the top, then Stop. The video will be saved to Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on a Samsung Galaxy
On Samsung Galaxy phones, the process is similar but not quite identical to screen recording on a Pixel. With your phone unlocked, swipe down from the top of the display, then swipe down again on the central pane (with icons for features including Wi-Fi and the flashlight) to reveal the Screen recorder icon.
This brings up a settings panel. You can choose between Full screen and Partial screen for your recording, and there are three options for audio: None, Media (whatever your phone is playing), and Media and mic (whatever your phone is playing plus the microphone input). There’s also a toggle switch for showing taps and touches on screen.
When you’re good to go, tap Start recording. You get a short countdown, and then the recording begins—up in the corner of the screen you’ll see a widget overlay for adding annotations or a selfie camera overlay, and for pausing or stopping the recording. When you tap the stop button, the video is saved in Samsung Gallery and (if you’ve got it installed) Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on an iPhone
For iOS, the screen recorder is launched by swiping down from the top right corner of the display, then tapping the screen recorder button (it’s a circle with another circle outside it). If the icon has been removed from the Control Center somehow, tap the + (plus) button in the top left corner to add it back.
You can either tap the record button once to start the countdown and launch the recording, or press and hold the record button to choose a different app for the recording besides the default Photos option—so you can use this to broadcast your recording to Facebook or WhatsApp for example.
Pressing and holding on the record button also lets you choose whether or not to include the iPhone mic audio. (The iPhone’s native output audio is always included.) To stop the recording, tap the recording indicator at the top of the screen, then the red stop button. You’ll find your saved video stored in the Photos app.
Third-Party Screen Recording Apps
It’s worth noting that iOS restricts what third-party apps can do in terms of screen recordings, for security and privacy reasons. Most apps in this category in the Apple App Store simply tap into the iPhone’s own recording capabilities, though Record It! is worth a look if you want to add commentaries and selfie cam reactions—you just need to add these after the main recording. Clips over three minutes require the $6 Pro purchase.
On Android, there are fewer limits on what apps can do. AZ Recorder has been a popular choice for years, giving you one-tap recording options, a choice of video quality settings, and some basic editing options included as well. To remove the ads in the app and the watermarks on your exported videos, you can pay $4.49 a month for the Pro version.
Mobizen Screen Recorder is another of the leading screen recorders on Android, and comes with a similar set of features as AZ Recorder: A widget overlay for instantly starting recordings, editing tools, and a few options for video quality (both resolution and refresh rate). Again, payment is required to remove the ads and watermarks—that will set you back $3.35 a month.

Shooting leaves 4 dead in Caribbean nation known for luxury tourism, police say
A manhunt is underway in St. Vincent and the Grenadines after a shooting left four people dead
PORT-OF-SPAIN, Trinidad -- A manhunt was underway Saturday after a shooting that left four people dead in the small Caribbean island nation of St. Vincent and the Grenadines, where authorities have struggled to contain gang violence.
The Royal St. Vincent and the Grenadines Police Force said late Friday that officers responded to reports of gunfire in Green Hill, a district located just outside of the capital city of Kingstown.
“Two bodies were met lying on the public road, the body of a female was discovered in a vehicle that was parked on the public road, and on an adjacent piece of land another body was discovered,” acting Police Commissioner Trevor Bailey said at a news conference Saturday.
Bailey said the corpses had what appeared to be gunshot wounds.
Four people were also injured in the shooting, with two of them still hospitalized.
There were no immediate arrests and police said they were still trying to determine the motive for the crime. Police said they registered another killing on Saturday, and were investigating whether it is linked to Friday night’s shooting.
St. Clair Leacock, the minister of national security, condemned the “unfortunate” and “unnecessary” shootings, while speaking on NBC Radio, a local news outlet Saturday. He said that while St. Vincent and the Grenadines remains a peaceful country, gang violence has plagued many communities.
According to police, 37 murders have been recorded this year in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, a country with a population of 110,000. The former British colony is made up of 32 islands and cays in the eastern Caribbean and has long relied on tourism as its main source of income.
The small archipelago is known for its volcanic landscapes, untouched coral reefs and white sand beaches that have made it a popular yachting destination. It is also home to several private islands that cater to the rich and famous.
“These homicides create a serious nightmare for us,” Leacock said.

UP mandates use-by-date on loose sweets and bans hazardous coolants in milk
Uttar Pradesh has ordered all sweets sold in the state to carry a use by date from October 15. The move, along with a glycol ban in milk units, aims to improve transparency and reduce health risks.
The Uttar Pradesh Food Safety and Drug Administration Department has ordered that all sweets stored and displayed for sale across the state must carry a "Use by Date" from October 15, officials said on Sunday. The move is especially significant for loose sweets, for which there was earlier no mandatory requirement to display an expiry date or "Use by Date".
In a separate step, the department has also banned the use of ethylene glycol and diethylene glycol in milk and milk product processing units in the state. Officials said the measures are aimed at giving consumers clearer information about the food they buy and reducing health risks.
According to the department, inspections at sweet manufacturing and retail outlets found that in many cases consumers were not being given clear information about the date of manufacture and the expiry date of sweets. As a result, consumers were unable to make informed decisions about the freshness and shelf life of the products they were purchasing.
An order issued by Food Safety and Drug Administration Commissioner Dr Roshan Jacob said the shelf life of sweets varies according to their nature and type. Different sweets can have a shelf life ranging from one day to 30 days, and their quality, taste and freshness are affected over time. The department said displaying the "Use by Date" would help consumers know the appropriate period for consuming the product and make better-informed choices about freshness and quality.
Under the existing system, packaged sweets are already required to carry an expiry date or "Use by Date". However, there was no clear mandatory provision for displaying such information on loose sweets. Officials said the initiative is meant to improve transparency in the sweets trade while ensuring that consumers receive essential information about the food products they buy.
The department also said enforcement and inspection activities had found that some milk processing establishments were using ethylene glycol or diethylene glycol as coolants during processes such as pasteurisation and refrigeration. It said these chemicals pose serious health risks if they contaminate food products, and the ban was imposed because of the possibility of the substances mixing with milk in the event of a leak in processing equipment. The department added that propylene glycol can be used as an alternative and is already being used by many milk processing units.
With the new rules, the department has sought to ensure that sweets sold in Uttar Pradesh carry a clear "Use by Date" and that milk processing units avoid chemicals that could contaminate food products.

Helicopter crash near Canadian city of Montreal leaves 4 dead, police say
Police say a helicopter has crashed southeast of the Canadian city of Montreal, killing all four people on board
MONTREAL, Quebec -- A helicopter crashed Saturday southeast of the Canadian city of Montreal, killing all four people on board, police said.
Audrey-Anne Bilodeau, a spokesperson for Sûreté du Québec provincial police, said the helicopter reportedly experienced difficulties before crashing around 2:30 p.m. in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, which is roughly 50 kilometers (31 miles) southeast of Montreal.
Firefighters managed to extinguish the blaze within an hour of the crash, but the four occupants were pronounced dead at the scene, Bilodeau said.
The provincial police have not yet identified the victims or the cause of the crash.
The spokesperson said the helicopter seems to have been a private aircraft.
The Transportation Safety Board of Canada has sent investigators to the crash site.

A twenty-two-year-old sociology student from Guwahati University was found dead after being discovered unconscious at a homestay in Guwahati. Her boyfriend claimed she died by suicide by hanging herself from a ceiling fan, but police state his version is still being verified. Her father has alleged that she was sexually assaulted and that she had informed her mother about the assault before her death, while the boyfriend's parents have countered these claims. Family and friends staged a protest demanding justice and seeking the intervention of the Assam Chief Minister, while the Vishva Hindu Parishad has alleged murder.
Protests over an alleged rape claim at Lovely Professional University in Phagwara escalated into violence on the second day, with students blocking the Phagwara-Jalandhar stretch of National Highway 44. Demonstrators pelted stones and vandalised vehicles, setting a Punjab police vehicle on fire and leaving several personnel injured. Police registered an FIR and formed a special investigation team to examine CCTV footage, forensic evidence, and phone records, stating that no corroborating evidence has been found so far. The university administration denied the incident occurred, while authorities called in additional forces to assess and control the situation.
A massive rescue operation is underway in Faridabad after a three-year-old girl fell into an eighty-foot open borewell. The child fell inside while playing around 5:30 p.m. Relief, rescue, and police teams arrived at the site to take charge of the operation. Emergency responders are excavating the ground adjacent to the borewell to reach the trapped child. Fire brigade units alongside an advanced life support ambulance remain stationed at the location to assist. The victim's father stated that the borewell was left uncovered and demanded that authorities ensure the safe return of his daughter.
In an interview with India Today, former Chinar Corps Commander Lieutenant General Satish Dua detailed the operational planning, strategic doctrine, and tactical execution of the 2016 cross-LoC surgical strikes following the Uri terror attack. Recalling the loss of 18 soldiers at Uri, Dua revealed that then Defence Minister Manohar Parrikar authorized the retaliatory mission during operational briefings in Srinagar. Indian Army Special Forces crossed the Line of Control to strike multiple terrorist launch pads simultaneously north and south of the Pir Panjal range at depths of four to five kilometers from stand-off positions. Intelligence assessments indicated between 40 and 60 terrorists were neutralized, while Indian forces suffered zero casualties. Dua emphasized that the operation combined tactical military action with diplomatic maneuvering at the United Nations General Assembly, establishing a precedent of proactive deterrence below the nuclear threshold that shaped subsequent responses, including the Balakot airstrikes.
A special broadcast of Pollution Ka Solution examines the escalating air pollution crisis across major urban centres, focusing on Delhi NCR and Mumbai, where hazardous Air Quality Index levels and winter toxic smog are creating an influx of pollution refugees. Residents and professionals, including Bharat Singh Kanwal, former advocate Prashant Kalra, and fashion designer Anuradha Prasad Dhawan, detail abandoning their careers and homes to relocate to destinations like Bengaluru and Goa after severe pediatric respiratory emergencies, persistent asthma, and health complications forced their departure. The discussion highlights broader urban systemic issues such as deficient waste management, unchecked deforestation, and rising cancer and respiratory burdens among children and senior citizens, with lifestyle expert Luke Coutinho noting that dietary adjustments cannot reverse cellular lung damage caused by toxic exposure. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd for alleged non-compliance with food safety norms in three infant nutrition products.
According to FSSAI, it examined NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, Lactogen Pro 1, and a follow-up formula along with their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.
In NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to "5HMOs" and "Whey Protein," while in Lactogen Pro 1, it observed a claim describing "Whey Protein" as easy to digest, the regulator said in a social media post.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India on these claims.
Both the products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, which restrict promotional claims or material aimed at increasing the saleability of infant foods, as well as Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which bars the advertisement or promotion of such products.
Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found sub-standard for Biotin content during laboratory analysis. The sample was sent for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the Biotin requirement prescribed under the 2020 regulations.
In light of these findings, FSSAI has filed three separate adjudication cases against Nestle India in respect of the three products, it added.
At 1.10 p.m., shares of Nestle India were down nearly 2% at ₹1,345.45 on the BSE.

Contract manufacturing company Aequs’ board has approved a fund raise of up to ₹650 Cr via a preferential issue of warrants to the promoter group, Mellwood Trustee Services Pvt Ltd. In a filing with the exchanges yesterday (September 25), the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.8 Cr warrants at an issue price of ₹231.55 per warrant. Of the total issue size, ₹325 Cr will be payable upfront upon allotment of the warrants, representing 50% of the issue size, and twice the regulatory minimum. The balance will be payable upon exercise of the warrants. The promoter issued an investment commitment letter dated September 25, 2026 to the company, confirming its intention to subscribe to the warrants for cash consideration. On full conversion of the warrants, the aggregate holding of the promoter and promoter group will increase to 60.73% from 59.09%. The issue is subject to the shareholders and regulatory approval. The company will seek shareholder approval via an EGM on October 22 (Thursday). The company plans to use the fresh capital to expand capacity across its aerospace and consumer businesses, including the development of its Hosur facility, investments in subsidiaries and joint ventures, and other general corporate purposes. "The equity will also provide the base against which the Company raises its term borrowings for the expansion. The board has assessed the Company’s current equity requirement through FY28 and has decided to meet it through this issue. A broader capital raise will be considered as and when required by the company’s growth plans," the company said. Founded in 2006 by Aravind Melligeri, Aequs provides manufacturing services to enterprises. It initially started with catering to the aerospace industry and later diversified its offerings to other sectors such as toys and consumer durable goods and products. It counts the likes of Airbus, Boeing and Collins Aerospace among its clients. Aequs is investing in building an aerospace engine component ecosystem in India. Its Hosur facility is expected to be operational next year, with shipments likely to begin by 2028. Brokerage Nuvama Institutional Equities initiated coverage on the aerospace contract manufacturer with a ‘Buy’ rating and a 12-month target price of ₹444, implying an upside of over 90% from July 6 closing price. The brokerage said Aequs’ $889 Mn order book provides strong revenue visibility, and projected a 42% revenue CAGR and an 84% EBITDA CAGR between FY26 and FY29. On the financial front, Aequs reported a net loss of ₹53.2 Cr in Q1 FY27, against a net profit of ₹3.6 Cr in the last year quarter. Operating revenue for the June quarter jumped 55% YoY to ₹395.6 Cr. The fresh fundraise comes almost a year after Aequs raised fresh capital via its initial public offering (IPO) in December 2025. The company's public offering comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹670 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.03 Cr shares. Amicus Capital, the Dempo family trusts, and individual shareholders Ravindra Mariwala and Raman Subramanian, alongside promoter entities Aequs Manufacturing Investments and Melligeri Private Family Foundation, offloaded shares via the OFS. Since listing, the company’s shares have more than doubled from the IPO price of ₹124. Shares of Aequs ended Friday’s trading session 1.38% higher at ₹246.20.

India stands at a critical demographic crossroads. With one of the world’s largest youth populations, the country possesses an immense economic advantage. Yet, a youthful population becomes a genuine demographic dividend only when young citizens are educated, skilled, gainfully employed and provided with meaningful opportunities. Otherwise, that demographic promise risks turning into social disillusionment.
China, despite its comparable population, is moving in the opposite demographic direction. Decades of low fertility have accelerated the ageing of its population. India, by contrast, possesses an extraordinary reservoir of young people entering the workforce. The central question is whether the country can create the economic opportunities and infrastructure needed to harness this potential.
The aspiration-reality gap
The smartphone revolution has intensified this challenge. A young person in a town or remote village can now see within seconds how the rest of the world lives, studies, works and travels. Global possibilities are visible on high-definition screens, even as tangible opportunities remain painfully out of reach.
This has created a widening divide between aspiration and reality. The horizons of young Indians have expanded far faster than the institutions and economies around them. Access to higher education has widened, yet meaningful employment opportunities have not kept pace. A college degree is no longer a guarantee of a job, leaving many without financial security or the dignity that comes with economic independence. When heightened aspirations collide with limited opportunities, frustration inevitably follows, often finding expression in protests over recruitment, examination irregularities, examination and test paper leaks, unemployment and systemic failures.
Kashmiri youth share these aspirations but carry a compounding historical burden. Decades of conflict, political uncertainty and economic isolation have deepened their sense of insecurity and constrained their opportunities. Too often, young Kashmiris have been viewed through a narrow security lens, as potential liabilities rather than national assets.
Yet, Jammu and Kashmir, like the rest of India, has a large young population with its own aspirations. Its youth seek the same basic things as young people elsewhere: economic independence, dignity, opportunity and a future in which they are not permanently viewed with suspicion.
Jammu and Kashmir possesses an exceptional combination of natural wealth and geographic significance. Its rivers offer substantial hydroelectric potential, its mountains contain valuable mineral resources, and its landscapes sustain a major tourism economy. Yet, its most underutilised strategic asset may be its location.
Also read | The importance of reform in higher education in India
Focus on Kashmir’s historic crossroads
For centuries, Kashmir was never a cul-de-sac. It was a thriving crossroads. Historic caravan routes linked Kashmir and Ladakh with Central Asia, Tibet and the broader Indian subcontinent. These routes carried far more than merchandise. They connected people, ideas, philosophies, literature, cultures and skills. The arrival of Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, revered as Shah-i-Hamadan, is deeply embedded in Kashmiri history and is traditionally associated with the arrival of Persian and Central Asian craftsmen who enriched Kashmir’s celebrated handicraft traditions. The historical lesson is clear: connectivity creates economic ecosystems.
Today, Indian strategic thinking needs to look beyond the immediate constraints posed by the Line of Control with Pakistan and the Line of Actual Control with China. Where political and security conditions permit, India needs a pragmatic framework to gradually restore Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh to the role they historically occupied: that of a bridge connecting South Asia with Central Asia and the wider Eurasian landmass.
For this, India needs a diplomatic road map alongside its infrastructure road map. Reopening traditional routes towards Pakistan or Central Asia cannot happen without sustained engagement with neighbouring countries. With Pakistan, the objective should be to explore confidence-building measures and trade connectivity wherever feasible. With China, India should pursue practical dialogue on trans-Himalayan connectivity wherever economic interests and security concerns can be reconciled.
This transition could begin with a phased connectivity strategy. India should identify historically important trade corridors that could eventually be revived as modern economic corridors, beginning with those where security and diplomatic conditions are most conducive. This does not mean opening every route at once. Pilot corridors could be developed and expanded progressively on the basis of experience.
Security cannot be ignored in any such endeavour. But security and connectivity need not automatically be treated as opposing objectives. Properly regulated connectivity can create greater economic interdependence and potentially provide stronger incentives for stability.
The same principle should guide India’s approach to Central Asia. Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh could become India’s northern economic gateway, giving Indian businesses greater access to Central Asian markets while bringing investment, tourism and commerce to the region. The benefits would extend far beyond Kashmir.
A road to opportunity
A functioning land corridor creates opportunities at every stage, from construction, transport and warehousing to hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, finance, technology and services. Unlike air connectivity, whose economic benefits are concentrated around a limited number of nodes, a trade corridor can generate economic activity across a wider geography through which it passes.
Most importantly, it could give the young people of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh something far more valuable than another promise. It could give them wings to fly towards new horizons.
India’s demographic advantage is a window of opportunity, not a permanent condition. We cannot afford to allow a generation to grow up watching possibilities on smartphones while encountering closed doors in the real world.
For Jammu and Kashmir, the answer may lie partly in reopening doors that history once kept open. The Silk Road was never only about silk. It was about the movement of goods, people, ideas and possibilities.
It is time to view Kashmir not merely through the prism of conflict, but through the lens of enterprise, connectivity and integration. Former Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee spoke of abandoning beaten paths and searching for new ways to address difficult issues. The ancient roads across the Himalayas do not belong merely in history books. Reimagined as modern economic arteries, they could become pathways to opportunity, giving the next generation not another reason to wait, but a road towards a better future.
Mehbooba Mufti is President, Jammu and Kashmir Peoples Democratic Party (PDP)

India vs West Indies: Virat Kohli joins Sachin Tendulkar in passing 15,000 ODI runs as his 55th ton fires India to victory
Virat Kohli smashed an unbeaten 139 off 88 balls, including 10 fours and nine sixes, as India successfully chased down 296 in just 41.4 overs to beat West Indies by eight wickets in first ODI; the 37-year-old now only plays ODI cricket internationally after retiring from Tests and T20Is
Sunday 27 September 2026 19:58, UK
Virat Kohli celebrated his return to the international arena by hitting his 55th ODI hundred as India beat West Indies by eight wickets in the series opener on Sunday.
India's star batter - who now only plays this format in international cricket - smashed an unbeaten 139 off 88 balls, including 10 fours and nine sixes, as India successfully chased down 296 in just 41.4 overs.
In doing so, the 37-year-old also became only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar (18,426) to pass 15,000 runs in ODIs.

"My focus has never been on milestones. Just looking back at the start of my journey, it makes me feel very grateful," Kohli said. "I enjoy each and every minute that I am out there playing for India, and I am able to do the job for my team. As a cricketer, this is all I could dream of."
Skipper Shubman Gill also notched a century, scoring 110 off 108 deliveries as India registered an easy win - clinched with a Kohli six - to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.
Earlier, West Indies had posted 295-7 from their 50 overs after being put into bat. Opener Justin Greaves (101 off 108) scored his maiden ODI ton, sharing in an impressive 135-run opening partnership with John Campbell (62 off 60) inside the first 20 overs.
Wrist spinner Kuldeep Yadav (4-40) ultimately accounted for both as he wreaked havoc in the middle overs to see West Indies reduced to 198-5 by the 36th.
Amir Jangoo's unbeaten 58 off 43 balls helped revive the innings, but their target of 296 ultimately proved an under-par one on a batter-friendly pitch.
It was a quick-fire chase for India as openers Gill and Rohit Sharma added 74 off 72 balls, Sharma scoring 32 off 35 before he fell to Alzarri Joseph (1-81) in the 12th over.
Kohli came to the crease and promptly eased his way to fifty in only 40 balls, hitting the 15,000-milestone on the way - the fastest to do it at 303 innings, compared to Tendulkar's 377.
He and Gill put on 151 off 132 balls for the second wicket before the captain departed against the run of play to Roston Chase (1-64) in the 34th over.
But Kohli cruised to a 74-ball hundred, before finishing the game in style with 8.2 overs to spare. Kohli's nine sixes were his most in an ODI innings.
Guwahati and Chandigarh will host the second and third ODIs on Wednesday and Saturday, followed by a five-match T20 series starting on October 6.

Getting my Canadian permanent residency should have felt like a win. But I've lost a lot along the way
Many of my friends who also applied for PR have left
This First Person is the experience of Areena Shrestha, who lives in Vancouver. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
I was 18 when I moved to Canada as a Nepalese international student, carrying two suitcases and a simple dream: to study, build a career and eventually call this country home. However, I didn't fully understand when I first arrived how uncertain and emotionally exhausting the journey to permanent residency could be.
While I studied psychology and international relations at the University of British Columbia, I interned at the Canadian Cancer Society and worked as a research assistant in a lab. I said yes to opportunities, built connections and slowly started to feel like I belonged here.
By the time I graduated four years later, my path felt clear. I wanted to work in the non-profit sector and give back to the same kind of communities that had supported me. So I began building a career in social services, supporting vulnerable communities as a program assistant, crisis responder and youth worker.
Today, I work as a case manager at a rent bank, helping people facing housing insecurity access financial support to avoid eviction. My job focuses on helping others find stability during times of a crisis.
Yet while I help others find stability, my own future in Canada has often felt uncertain.
For years, my future in Canada depended on my immigration status and the ticking clock of my work permit. I applied for permanent residency in December 2023. I would check my application status late at night, calculate points for Canada's comprehensive ranking system, and refresh the draw page for permanent residents over and over again. I thought about moving to a rural area just to increase points, hoping something would change.
As time passed, that uncertainty started to take a toll, especially six months before my permit was due to expire.
My closest friends — the same people I had grown up with and went to UBC with — began to leave. One by one, they packed up their lives and returned to countries they hadn't planned on going back to. They told me it wasn't worth sacrificing their mental health for a system that felt so unpredictable. Before one can even apply for permanent residency, you have to get an invitation to apply (ITA).
One of my friends even received an ITA for permanent residency — something we had all been working toward. But their application was rejected over a small mistake: uploading the wrong document.
Just like that, years of building a life here came to an end as they had to leave Canada within a 60-day period. Watching that happen made everything feel even more sad.
As my own work permit expiration date got closer, the anxiety became harder to ignore. I would wake up in the middle of the night with panic attacks, overwhelmed by the thought of losing everything I had built. Every phone call with my parents ended in tears — not just from stress, but from a growing sense of hopelessness.
I felt I had done everything "right." I had paid international tuition fees, built a career in the non-profit sector and was contributing to my community. And still, it felt like it might not be enough. I was not enough for Canada.
Going back to Nepal didn't feel like an option. My dad's job took him to work in many different countries which meant my parents no longer lived in Nepal. I realized how disconnected I had become since I grew up speaking Nepali, but couldn't read or write it.
Canada was the only place that felt like home. Yet I wasn't sure if I would be allowed to stay.
Out of desperation, I started relearning French — not out of passion, but because it felt like one of the only ways to increase my chances of getting an ITA.
Then everything changed.
After two years and eight months, I received my permanent residency approval through the health-care and social services occupations draw, which is a specific, express entry draw for individuals who are currently working in those fields. On March 22, 2026, my PR card finally arrived.
I expected to feel overwhelming joy. Instead, what I first felt was something quieter: Relief.
Relief that I could finally breathe without checking immigration updates. Relief that my life here was no longer temporary.
But the feeling is complicated.
Because while I stayed, many of the people who were part of my journey did not.
The friends who once made Canada feel like home are now scattered across different countries. The support system I built over the years is no longer here in the same way. And now I find myself starting over again, like when I was 18 and new to Canada: building new friendships, considering moving to a new city, trying to reshape what "home" looks like.
When I think back to the 18-year-old version of me who had just arrived in Canada, I realize she believed that if she worked hard enough, everything would fall into place.
In many ways, it did.
But what I didn't expect was how much waiting, uncertainty and quiet fear would come with it. I am grateful to be here. But I also carry the weight of everything it took to stay. And sometimes, that feeling doesn't disappear overnight.
When I voiced my concerns on TikTok, my videos went viral with more than 900,000 views. I realized that my story is not unique. Across Canada, immigrants like myself are navigating the same uncertainty while continuing to contribute to the country's workforce and communities.

Dating startup Rivet has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100.6 Cr) in seed funding from Peak XV Partners, Shine Capital, and Blume Ventures to build and scale its community-driven matchmaking platform. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to develop its product, expand distribution, and scale across the US. It announced its nationwide US launch yesterday. Besides US, Rivet has an office in Delhi NCR, with its engineering and machine learning teams largely based in India. Founded in 2025 by former Tinder and Match Group executive Taru Kapoor and Rajat Sahni, who previously served as CEO of CarDekho’s used-car business, Rivet offers a dating platform built around community recommendations. The startup calls its model “social matching”. Users can join as “matchers” to assess potential pairs and recommend introductions they think would work. These recommendations contribute to a social matching score for each potential pair. Pairs with high scores are introduced to each other, after which both individuals independently decide whether to connect and begin a conversation. People who are not looking to date can also join solely as matchers. The startup describes its model as a “give-to-get” approach, allowing users to help others find connections while receiving recommendations for themselves. The startup also counts former Tinder and OkCupid CEO Elie Seidman among its early investors. Seidman advised and mentored Kapoor during Rivet’s development. The startup competes with dating and matchmaking platforms such as Tinder, Hinge, Bumble, The League, and Wingman. Its community-driven approach makes participation by people willing to recommend matches an important part of its expansion, alongside attracting singles seeking connections. Rivet’s pitch centres on addressing the frustration of browsing profiles without finding a connection. Kapoor argued that while dating apps expanded the pool of potential partners, they also made the experience feel transactional and isolating. The startup is betting that recommendations from other people can help surface potential matches that users might otherwise dismiss on swipe-based apps.

William Lawrence is a Democrat running to represent Michigan’s Lansing-area Seventh Congressional District with a campaign that largely focuses on data centers and affordability. It’s not an unusual story in 2026 — but not long ago, Lawrence was cutting his teeth in progressive politics as a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, primarily focused on organizing around the climate crisis.
Why Democrats stopped talking about climate
A Sunrise Movement co-founder is running for Congress. He’s talking more about data centers than climate.
His arc, from progressive activist to politician, is emblematic of a bigger trend, as a wave of millennial progressives in midterm races across the country try to lean into issues that have broader, more immediate appeal with voters.
But that arc also raises big questions about the left’s changing priorities. In a recent interview for Vox’s podcast and video series America, Actually, host Astead Herndon spoke with Lawrence about his past activism and how he has pivoted. “It can sometimes feel like…folks hop from issue to issue, whether it’s climate, even anti-AI right now, without those things being solved,” Herndon told Lawrence.
According to Lawrence, “that’s the reality of the time. It seems like everything is unraveling, and it is because the whole social, economic, political compact is being renegotiated, not just in this country, but on a global stage.” Still, Lawrence said, that earlier organizing shapes how he sees different challenges today.
The two also discussed whether opposition to data centers and AI has wide, regular-voter appeal in places like Michigan and how Lawrence went from hopeless and disengaged to regaining a sense of agency through organizing.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
You started in Sunrise and were at the forefront of a young progressive movement that was aligned at that time — in 2018, 2019, and I think still — with progressive members of Congress like Rashida Tlaib or Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
I remember reporting about Sunrise at the time. The goal was to elect a Bernie Sanders, but the other goal was to have the party largely embrace things like a Green New Deal. How would you grade the efforts of the climate movement of that time, looking back?
I think we did some things very well.
We put climate jobs and justice at the top of the agenda for the incoming Biden administration. I think the Bernie-Biden task force is an often overlooked but very important chapter of that whole story, where Bernie and Biden both understood they had to bring their people to the table.
And that’s how Build Back Better got negotiated. We fought hard for Build Back Better, and ultimately came up two votes shy in the United States Senate.
Do you see that as a success or a failure of the climate movement?
I think Build Back Better was a success in coming to the table and negotiating, from the Green New Deal to Build Back Better, and then what we ended up with was the Inflation Reduction Act after it passed the final filter, which was Sen. Joe Manchin and Sen. Kyrsten Sinema. At the time, now, how I felt about it was, this is historic. This is the largest investment in green jobs and infrastructure in United States history. I know how hard it was to get here. I’m tremendously proud of the work that I did and so many others did.
Just in my district alone, we’ve delivered $26 billion in investment for manufacturing and sustainability because of the Inflation Reduction Act. But at the time, we knew that this is maybe 5 percent or 10 percent of what we need in scope. And now we’re experiencing the consequences of that.
Obviously, we still have a very volatile economy. We still lack energy security because we now have closed the Strait of Hormuz. We’re still too dependent on a global oil market, and we could use many more investments in solar and other kinds of renewable energy than we have now.
And ultimately, it wasn’t enough for the Biden-Harris administration to be able to win reelection, because people didn’t feel it enough in their pocketbooks.
Why do you think Democrats are talking less about climate?
I think it’s the intensity of the crises that we face. It feels like we’re falling through midair, after the end of all of the constitutional protections, the rule of law, and the economic security that people had previously enjoyed.
There are a lot of very acute and urgent crises, and I think that that has bumped climate, which is a super massive but also somewhat slow-moving crisis, a little bit lower on the priority list just in terms of what comes up for people on the Hill.
You went back to Michigan to focus on housing and advocacy. Did that make you think a little differently about the national work you were doing?
I think it’s fair to say that when I was younger, I got very focused on this climate issue, and I was very focused on it because it is this existential crisis we all face.
But it was after the pandemic that I wanted to bring my work closer to home. I wanted to do the work of putting down roots in the place that had raised me and make my life there. And in seeking to organize there, it was clear that we needed an in to organize that was more immediate.
“I believe in the agency of regular people taking charge of our own lives and working together to build a better future.”
More immediate than the Green New Deal.
Than the Green New Deal or than the looming climate crisis. People know that that’s an issue, but they’re like, “I’ve gotta pay rent at the end of the month.” And as an organizer, I believe that you have to listen to people, you have to hear what’s going on for them, and then work on issues that have the potential to bring people together.
Housing is one of those issues. Whether you’re in the city of Lansing, whether you’re in small towns, urban, rural, suburban, young or old, everybody can agree that the rent is too damn high and it’s too hard to buy a home anymore.
Were you surprised Trump won the state in 2024?
No.
Why not?
Because I saw it all unfold. We hoped to deliver more through the Biden-Harris administration than we ultimately did through Build Back Better. We didn’t deliver as much to relieve the economic anxiety that people were feeling. And then I do believe that the war and the genocide in Gaza and our blank check to allow that to happen with our money and our tax dollars destroyed the Democratic coalition that had been assembled from 2017 through 2020 for the purpose of beating Trump.
I just saw that unfolding over the course of the whole year, just like a slow-motion train wreck.
I want to ask locally, what do you think is most important in this race: housing, data centers, or pushing back against Donald Trump?
If I had to choose, I’d say data centers because that’s where people in the district are finding some common ground across the spectrum — in fighting back against the concentrated power in Silicon Valley, which has been fully enabled by [incumbent Rep.] Tom Barrett and Donald Trump.
So you’re saying that’s the issue that allows you to create cross-ideological coalitions?
Yeah.
Our last question is, just thinking through the scope of your career and the kind of progressive work: It can sometimes feel like folks hop from issue to issue, whether it’s climate, even anti-AI right now, without those things being solved, right?
Like, we still have a climate crisis. The rent is still too high. All of these things are still happening. How am I to trust that AI is the crisis of our time when I’ve heard so many crises of our time?
Some have called it a polycrisis — overlapping crises.
That’s the reality of the time. It seems like everything is unraveling, and it is because the whole social, economic, political compact is being renegotiated, not just in this country, but on a global stage. I don’t think it serves us to lie about that. I mean, here’s the reality, folks.
Everything is up in the air. Does it feel like you’re falling through midair? It’s because we are. All the old protections, all the old agreements have been chopped up. So we have got to come together. This is what I believe in more than anything, if there is a through line…I believe in the agency of regular people taking charge of our own lives and working together to build a better future.
That’s what I learned as an organizer, and that’s what gave me hope actually, at a time when I was doomer-ing in my younger years. And I told you, I wanted to just drop out of society and all that. It was seeing that regular people have come together before, and they’ve won a better future for their kids and grandkids, that gave me a path to follow in.
It does feel like a powerless time, I have to tell you. And a lot of this AI revolution, to your point about control or about agency. We’ve talked to so many people who just think that these things are happening to them, rather than feeling that they are participating in the changes afoot.
But you’re telling a kinda hopeful story.
I’m a hopeful guy. I was angry too, even when I got into this race. I was angry especially about the wars. But then in campaigning, I’ve met so many people across the district, old friends, new friends, and they give me a lot of hope because you just see the way that people are already performing miracles on a daily basis.

In an effort to extend social support and care to persons with mental illness, Chennai-based NGO The Banyan, Aaladamara Foundation, and the Banyan Academy of Leadership in Mental Health (BALM) inaugurated the Centre for Mental Health, Social Care, and Livelihoods, and the Last Mile Mental Health and Social Care Praxis Lab on Sunday.
Speaking at the event, former Chief Secretary of Keralam S.M. Vijayanand said, “Village panchayats are the natural frontline of any service delivery. When the whole government disappears, the panchayats and SHGs (self-help groups) work together in most parts of India.”
He further said they were repositories of social capital, and that SHGs and panchayats also help raise awareness of mental health in the community.
The centre brings clinical, social, and economic responses together as one integrated approach across five domains: income and social protection, livelihoods, relational stability, support for vulnerable caregivers, and access to basic healthcare.
A press release said the lab will study how social determinants and structural violence, including poverty and homelessness, are significant metrics in mental health care practice.
Director of The Hindu Group N. Ram said information asymmetry could weaken the administration and effectiveness of social care formulations for severe mental illness.
“The problem is particularly prominent in India because information is distributed through structures already marked by inequalities of class, caste, education, and gender. It is important to remember that power determines which information counts,” he said.
Deanna Jejeebhoy, the centre patron and sister of Ratan Tata, and Mr. Ram unveiled the centre and the lab respectively.
Co-CEO of BALM Preetha Krishnadas said, “Our health is shaped by the conditions in which we live, work and age, yet care systems stabilise symptoms and send people back to the very conditions that caused them distress. When they return, we call it relapse and locate the failure in the person rather than in the structure.”
Advocate Gitanjali Diwakar said that while the courts in India are burdened, the role of legal aid goes beyond providing case expertise and strategy to making time for people and communicating with empathy and sensitivity.
Actor Revathi, Commissioner of Central Taxes S. Nagarajan, Co-CEO of The Banyan Archana Padmakar, former Advocate General of Tamil Nadu P.S. Raman, and CEO of Aaladamara Foundation Mrinalini Ravi participated.
