Rishikesh rafting halted indefinitely as Ganga water level rises: Officials
Rafting resumed in the Ganga on September 23 following the annual monsoonal break that began on July 1
River rafting operations in the Ganga River in Rishikesh have been halted indefinitely following continuous rainfall over the past two days. Authorities decided to resume activities only after the weather improves and the river recedes to a safer level.
According to tourism officials, rafting and related adventure activities in the Ganga at Muni-ki-Reti have been prohibited until further orders. The water level was recorded at 339.50 metres on Sunday. Meanwhile, State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and Jal Police personnel made announcements at Ganga ghats and riverbed areas, cautioning people against going near the river.
“As it is currently raining across the Garhwal division and in view of Meteorological department advisories, river rafting has been halted with immediate effect until further directives are issued. Rafting will resume only after an assessment of weather conditions, the monsoonal forecast, the Ganga’s water level and the weather forecast for next week. All river rafting operators, the rafting association and stakeholders have been directed to strictly adhere to the order,” said Tehri Garhwal district tourism and adventure officer Sobat Singh Rana.
Police officers in the Lakshman Jhula, Muni-ki-Reti and Tapovan areas have also appealed to residents, pilgrims and tourists to exercise caution and avoid going near Ganga ghats, riverbeds and picnic spots, citing the high water level and increased risk of slips and falls.
“All rafting operators are complying with the administration’s directive prohibiting rafting and related adventure activities. Safety of all stakeholders is the prime concern,” said rafting association president Dharmendra Negi.
Rafting resumed in the Ganga on September 23 following the annual monsoonal break that began on July 1. The fresh suspension, within days of the resumption, has disappointed rafting operators.
“After a two-month monsoonal break, rafting resumed with religious rituals and prayers to Ganga. The buzz had returned to Muni-ki-Reti and Rishikesh, but the sudden rainy spell has led to the cancellation of dozens of bookings. Many people have left their resorts and hotels as the weather forecast for the next two days also predicts rain and cloudy conditions,” said Sohan Singh Negi, a lodge operator in Tapovan, about 10 km from Rishikesh.
Rafting operates at various points along the Ganga, including Kaudiyala, Marine Drive, Shivpuri, Brahmapuri and Clubhouse track towards Lakshman Jhula, across Tehri Garhwal, Pauri Garhwal and Dehradun districts. The rafting stretches range from five kilometers (km) to 30km.

Bihar is reportedly seeking to rebuild its mineral economy after decades of being left with little of the mineral wealth that remained with Jharkhand following the states’ bifurcation in 2000. Geological investigations conducted between 2021 and 2024 have identified mineral resources estimated at more than ₹21,000 crore across Rohtas, Jamui, Gaya and Jehanabad, reported The Indian Express. The discoveries could potentially generate more than ₹5,000 crore in annual mining revenue once the identified resources are converted into operational mines, according to state officials. That would be significantly higher than Bihar’s current record mining collection of ₹3,592 crore, which comes predominantly from minor minerals such as sand and stone. However, the transition from geological discoveries to commercial production remains a major challenge. The state is targeting mineral extraction across different projects between 2026 and 2031, with exploration, auctions, clearances and mining leases still to be completed. Rohtas accounts for a major share of the identified resources. Geological surveys have found around 130.11 million tonnes of glauconite across the Pipradih-Bhurwa and Chutia-Nauhatta blocks, with an estimated value of ₹14,048 crore. Glauconite can serve as a source of potassium for fertilisers, a potentially significant resource for India given its dependence on imports for potash fertilisers. The Bhora-Kathra block in Rohtas has also been identified with 33-39.68 million tonnes of high-grade limestone, valued at about ₹1,761.42 crore. The mineral is widely used in cement manufacturing and for producing quicklime. Rohtas is also home to the Amjhor pyrite deposits, which account for nearly 95% of India's known pyrite resources. Pyrites are used in sulfuric acid production and other industrial chemical processes. Jamui has emerged as another important mineral zone, particularly for magnetite and gold. The Majos block contains an estimated 48.40 million tonnes of magnetite, with an assessed value ranging from ₹3,817.60 crore to ₹6,000 crore. The Bhanta block has another 6.49 million tonnes, valued at around ₹511.91 crore. Magnetite is primarily used as iron ore in steelmaking and other metallurgical applications. The Sono area has also attracted attention for its gold-bearing resources. Exploration has identified 222.88 million tonnes of ore containing an estimated 37.6 tonnes of gold metal. The Sono resource is classified as a remaining resource rather than a reserve. Preliminary exploration has been carried out, with trial production targeted for 2027-28. Exploration in Gaya and Jehanabad has identified vanadium-bearing magnetite, ilmenite, rare earth elements and lithium-bearing pegmatites. These minerals have applications across strategic industries. Vanadium is used in high-strength steel and energy-storage technologies, while ilmenite is a source of titanium dioxide. Lithium and rare earth elements are important for technologies including electric-vehicle batteries, wind turbines and defence equipment. The discoveries could therefore expand Bihar’s mineral ambitions beyond traditional mining and into minerals considered strategically important for emerging industries. The ₹21,000 crore estimate is based on geological assessments that consider factors such as extraction, beneficiation and logistics. The Geological Survey of India generally progresses exploration through four stages — G4 reconnaissance, G3 preliminary exploration, G2 general exploration and G1 detailed exploration. Bihar has been aligning its legal and administrative framework with mineral-rich states such as Odisha and Jharkhand to move identified blocks towards commercial extraction under the amended Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act. The Ministry of Mines has also introduced reimbursable private-agency models through the National Mineral Exploration Trust to reduce investment risks during the early exploration phase. Under the proposed administrative roadmap, mining plans are expected to be submitted within six months, environmental clearances targeted within 18 months and lease execution completed within 12 months. The state's timeline includes advanced G2 and G1 drilling under composite licences during 2026-27, trial production from the Sono gold resource in 2027-28 and broader commercial mineral extraction between 2026 and 2031. The eighth tranche of critical mineral auctions was also launched in Patna in August 2026, adding another step towards bringing Bihar’s newly identified mineral resources into the commercial mining pipeline. The scale of the discoveries does not automatically translate into state revenue. Early auction rounds for some glauconite and nickel blocks had to be cancelled because of limited participation, with prospective miners hesitant to make large bids based on preliminary exploration data, the report noted. Technology and investment are additional hurdles. Extracting agricultural-grade potash from hard-rock glauconite and recovering vanadium from magnetite require capital-intensive processing technologies, some of which are still developing domestically. Land acquisition could pose another challenge. Although several mineral blocks are located outside forest areas, land ownership in agricultural regions is often fragmented among numerous private owners. Securing surface rights could therefore add to project timelines, alongside mandatory environmental approvals and Pollution Control Board clearances. Illegal mining is another concern as the state moves towards commercialisation. Bihar has announced plans for a specialised 1,000-member Mines Police Force to strengthen enforcement and protect mineral-bearing areas. Garvit Bhirani is a journalist based in Gurugram. I don’t think I’m going to hurt anyone’s feelings by pointing out that Decap doesn’t have the name recognition of Kendrick Lamar, Olivia Rodrigo, or Charli XCX. But his fingerprints are all over tracks from them, as well as many other artists, including Freddie Gibbs, Bad Bunny, Mac Miller, BTS, and even Ludwig Göransson’s score for Oppenheimer.
Decap is the man behind the drums behind your favorite song

Decap is the man behind the drums behind your favorite song
Producer and sound designer Decap’s ‘Drums That Knock’ are all over some of the biggest hits of the last 10 years.
Nicholas Piantedosi, better known as Decap, is a record producer, but perhaps more importantly, he’s the man behind Drums That Knock, a series of sample packs that have found their way onto countless records across genres. The line is so successful that, after debuting in 2016, it’s now on its 11th installment. Kenneth Blume, formerly known as Kenny Beats, the producer behind hits from Denzel Curry, Vince Staples, Rico Nasty, Idles, and FKA Twigs, said that Decap “changed a million lives with a single snare.”
Unsurprisingly for a man so obsessed with low-end, he’s got a real beef to pick with phone speakers. And even with all the modern tools at his disposal in his digital audio workstation of choice, Ableton Live, he still can’t give up his trusty Boss SP-202 Dr. Sample from 1998.
What is your most indispensable tool?
Ableton Live. It’s how I get my ideas out.
Which is the most underappreciated?
The clipper. A soft clipper can give your drums that warm analog sound, or it can make them hit super hard. It’s the tool that changed my music.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
The speaker. I wish I could hear a fat 808 on my phone. A raw 808 with no processing is basically inaudible on a phone speaker. So many people listen to music all day on their phone without ever truly feeling the low end. If I can make my drums knock on a phone anyway, I’m doing something right.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
My Boss SP-202 sampler. It’s the first sampler I ever had, back in junior high when I first started making beats. I chopped my first samples on it, and it was the start of everything I’m doing now.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
Gatekeeping over gear. This idea that you’re not a real producer unless you use hardware, or unless you use this DAW or that one. It’s not true. If you’ve got a computer, you already have everything you need. The dopest producer might be a kid in North Africa with Skullcandy headphones. The only thing I care about is if you’re dope or not.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
My honest answer is nothing. I’m happy making the music I make, because it’s meaningful to me and it’s my expression. I don’t need to make anyone else’s.
What creation are you most proud of?
Creating a hard-hitting sound that I love and watching it make its way across genres.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
From my dad. No matter what, make a decision and put a stake in the ground. But remember what a stake is. You can always pull it up and move it.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I meditate. It aligns my mind and my body, and when those two are lined up I can focus way more clearly. If the mind isn’t right, everything will always be a little off.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
The 3M technique: make it, mix it down, move on. It doesn’t have to be perfect. It’s about staying in the action of creation, because that’s where the magic happens.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Really good food. Living in Los Angeles, there’s no shortage of incredible restaurants, and I love going out for a nice dinner.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
“This all started with not wanting a real job”

On July 15, Raj Rani, 52, an ASHA worker in Yamunagar, Haryana had just completed her tasks for the day when she felt a throbbing pain in her left arm and in the middle of her chin. Since this pain had persisted for a few days, she went to the Community Health Centre (CHC) in Vyaspur to get an electrocardiogram (ECG) done.
The Additional Senior Medical Officer at the centre, Gunjeet Singh, saw the results of the ECG, gave her a dose of drugs including blood thinners and clotbusters, called a ‘loading dose’, and asked her to rush to the district hospital at Ambala Cantonment, two hours away, for further treatment.
Raj Rani had single-vessel disease, with a major coronary artery blocked. “At the district hospital, they scheduled my angioplasty the next day and I got one stent in my heart,” said Raj Rani. “I told my doctors to give me good treatment so I could resume my work as an ASHA. They reassured me that I would be able to do my duties, because I was lucky: I came in time,” she said.
Had this happened even two months ago, Raj Rani would not have received the diagnosis that would have led to quick treatment. Even though the Vyaspur CHC had an ECG machine, there was no technician to conduct it and while the medical officers could interpret the results, they were not very confident.
What changed
On May 29 this year, the Haryana government tied up with Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech startup, as part of Public-Private Partnership (PPP), to set up a tele-ECG network called Spandan One. Each medical centre in Haryana received a tele-ECG device that connects to smartphone and tablets, can be operated by frontline workers and gives a clinician-reviewed result in less than three minutes.
To date, nearly 600 government health facilities including primary health centres (PHCs), CHCs, sub-divisional hospitals and district hospitals have been equipped by a tele-ECG device along with training in using it. As of September 17, 33,854 ECG tests were conducted; 9,287 ECGs were abnormal and 1,342 critical cases were detected according to the Spandan dashboard.
In the remote Ranjitpur PHC in Yamunagar district, there is a steady increase in the footfall of patients due to the tele-ECG service available. “This is a new building we started using just six months ago; there is no fixed nurse or staff or even furniture,” said Varun Singh, medical officer who has been running the centre with staff on deputation and through borrowed furniture from other centres. “Ever since we got the tele-ECG, people have been coming to the centre asking for it,” he said.
One recent morning, Ram Saran, 75, come to the PHC with his son Mangaram to get his reports examined by Dr. Singh. Mr. Saran had been experiencing a feeling of his heart racing and breathlessness for many months. He had gotten an ECG and blood tests for ₹1200 at a private hospital at Vyaspur but wanted confirmation from the government doctor. The nursing officer at the PHC put the electrodes on Mr. Saran and an ECG graph formed in the tablet in her hands, with a message that the report was being analysed. Two and half minutes later, the report was ready to be downloaded. Mr. Saran had an ‘abnormal ECG’ and he was asked to consult a cardiologist and a copy of the report was sent to his mobile phone.
Dr. Singh then consulted with Mr. Saran and his son and told them to visit the hospital at Ambala Cant. at the earliest. “Before this initiative, I would not be able to interpret ECGs with this level of sophistication. The patient would need to visit a cardiologist available two hours away and wait a long time in the OPD for the diagnosis,” said Dr. Singh. For patients who are diagnosed with critical ECGs, an alarm goes off in the tablet to draw the attention of the healthcare worker and a prescription is generated so that patients receive life-saving medicines while the referral to a higher centre is being made.
“We never thought that we would get results within a few minutes of doing the ECG. This tele-ECG service is available in all centres in Yamunagar and is available in even other remote locations in the districts. This is a very welcome step,” said Shama Parveen, senior medical officer, Yamunagar CHC.
Primary care matters
Even though PHCs are the first point of contact of medical care for rural patients, they often do not have the necessary equipment or manpower to diagnose and treat heart ailments. A 2024 pre-print that assessed the availability of cardiac care in Vadodara district in Gujarat found only 44.11% of the surveyed PHCs had functional ECGs and employed them where indicated. In most cases patients were simply referred to higher centres for treatment. The time lost due to travel between centres can prove to be fatal for patients.
The impact of Haryana’s initiative has been incredible, said Kuldeep Singh, former Director General, Health Services (DGHS), Haryana who spearheaded the partnership. ECGs and early treatment for heart attacks is now available in rural centres that had earlier not registered a single heart attack due to lack of diagnosis. “We are already witnessing a 20% reduction in deaths in the emergency departments of district hospitals because patients are being stabilised before rushing here,” he said, adding that these are early assessments and more data is still being collected.
After primary care
Once the patient is stabilised with a loading dose, they are sent to higher centres such as district hospitals with Catherisation Labs where angiographies and angioplasties are performed. “Given the geography of Haryana, most patients reach the higher centre within one hour of the diagnosis, saving lives and heart muscles,” said Dr. Singh.
The Haryana government is also in a PPP with private providers to equip and run cath labs in four locations in the State–Panchkula, Gurugram, Faridabad and Ambala Cant. and is planning to soon expand to more locations.
As part of the agreement with the Haryana government, Sunfox Technologies provides equipment, training and on-going support for its tele-ECG system apart from maintaining a live dashboard monitoring cases. “Through the dashboard, we have real-time patient information which has given us rich insights–for example we now know that patients between 30-49 years have a higher incidence of cardiac issues than those over 50 years,” said Rajat Jain, CEO of the startup. Data has also shown that the incidence of critical ECGs among women in the age group of 30-49 is as much as men and greater than men in the age group of 70+, dispelling the belief that men have a greater risk for heart disease than women. “These kinds of insights are very important for policymakers but were never accessible before,” he said.
Challenges in the process
While the project is picking up steam in Haryana, there are some teething issues – many of the centres have to conduct repeat ECGs to get accurate ECG readings if they were not conducted properly the first time. A bump in the road was that the State’s nursing union had issued a diktat stating that nurses should not be conducting the ECGs as the post of ECG technicians has remained vacant in most health centres. The DGHS, however, later issued a letter stating that healthcare workers cannot deny conducting life-saving diagnosis and would face disciplinary action if they failed to do so. There is also the question of what happens when the partnership between the government and Sunfox Technologies ends: would the pathway to diagnosis and treatment change or would it have improved by then?
Looking ahead
Making ECGs available at PHCs is a great start but we need to do much more to improve the public health system as a whole to respond well to non-communicable diseases and their complications, said Chetanya Malik, a doctor who practices in Surguja, a remote district in Chattisgarh for the non-profit Sangwari. In Chhattisgarh, an ECG facility is only available at the district hospital, revealing the vastness of the need and the unevenness of primary care provided within the country. Dr. Malik also noted the need for patients to be given support in finding transport and for referrals to higher centres to be seamless to help solve the problem of cardiac emergencies.
India’s public health systems have, for decades now, remained focused on infectious diseases and maternal and child health — both still important, but the time has come to also realign the systems to care for non-communicable diseases. Heart disease alone is estimated to account for nearly 27% of all deaths in India. The need is enormous, and the technology is available. It is time all States implement such programmes, pointed out Dr. Kuldeep Singh.

Bengaluru man kills wife, dumps body in vacant plot; civic workers find it days later
A senior police officer said inquiries at the mall helped investigators establish woman's identity and trace her address.
A 32-year-old man from Odisha allegedly kept his wife’s body inside their Bengaluru home for three days after killing her during an argument over finances, before wrapping it in a bedsheet and dumping it at a vacant plot, police said on Saturday.
The accused, Sagar Chandra Rawat, was arrested more than three weeks after the highly decomposed body of his wife, Anusuya, was found at a vacant plot in MS Nagar near Sampigehalli, police said, according to news agency PTI.
According to police, Sagar and Anusuya had an argument over finances on August 11. Sagar allegedly assaulted and strangled his wife during the argument, resulting in her death due to suffocation.
He allegedly left her body inside their house for about three days. He then wrapped it in a bedsheet, tied it with a rope and carried it out of the house around midnight, police said.
Fearing that he would be caught, Sagar allegedly dumped the body at the vacant site before returning home.
He then collected his belongings, locked the house and began staying on the premises of the small hotel in Yelahanka where the couple worked, police said.

How was the body found?
The body was discovered on September 2 by workers cleaning the vacant plot following the Greater Bengaluru Authority's (GBA) directive to property owners to maintain their premises. The workers alerted the authorities, police said.
As the body was highly decomposed, police and local residents performed the last rites soon after the post-mortem.
With the body beyond recognition, establishing the woman's identity proved difficult. Police, however, found a mall tag on her clothing that led them to the billing details for the garment. A Ganesha pendant and technical analysis subsequently helped corroborate her identity as Anusuya, police said.
A senior police officer said inquiries at the mall helped investigators establish Anusuya's identity and trace her address.

When police reached her house in MS Nagar, they found it locked. Local inquiries revealed that Anusuya and Sagar worked at a small hotel in Yelahanka and had been living there, police said.
Police said Sagar had come to Bengaluru about five years ago and married Anusuya around two years ago.
He was subsequently taken into custody and, during interrogation, allegedly confessed to the killing after investigators confronted him with discrepancies in his statement.

Plans for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua’s long-awaited heavyweight clash were in doubt on Saturday after promoter Dana White said he was unsure whether the fight would go ahead.
Fury and Joshua were announced on Thursday as opponents for a December 11 showdown at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium, a contest billed as one of the biggest fights in British boxing history.
However, Fury said in a video posted on social media late on Friday that the fight was in jeopardy because Joshua and his promoter, Eddie Hearn, were trying to withdraw from the all-British heavyweight showdown between the former world champions.
Hearn’s promotional company, Matchroom Boxing, did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent on Saturday.
White, the UFC president and head of Zuffa Boxing, told reporters in London on Saturday that he did not know whether the bout would proceed as planned.
Asked about a scheduled press conference in the coming days, White said he was also uncertain whether it would take place.
Hearn has said he and Joshua had insisted on the bout being staged in Britain, while the promoters had proposed holding it in New York’s Madison Square Garden.
The dispute over promotional rights has also sparked claims of contractual breaches and talk of replacement opponents.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

Fishermen of Pulicat –from Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh– have urged the respective State governments to mark the respective fishing grounds using global positioning systems (GPS) as soon as possible.
In a joint meeting held in Tiruvallur district on Saturday, where fishermen, MLAs and officials from Sulurpetta in Andhra Pradesh and Tiruvallur took part, the fishermen representing 25 fishing hamlets that depend on the brackish-water lake that sprawls across the two States, said that they could no longer depend on the palmyrah tree trunks that were placed as demarcations. The tree trunks rot as they stand in the salt water, and when new trunks are placed, disputes could arise.
Sources said after the violent incidents of April 2014, when houses, boats, nets and engines of Chinna Mangodu village in Pulicat were set afire by fishermen from Andhra Pradesh in retaliation following a fishing border dispute, men from Tamil Nadu have refrained from fishing in waters under the control of Andhra Pradesh.
“We had imposed strict control, and someone would only very rarely fish in those areas. A total of 199 police cases are still pending against men from fishing hamlets in Tamil Nadu. We want the dispute to be settled once and for all. Fishermen from both the States have been staging protests and submitting petitions to the respective district administrations,” said a source in the know.
After hearing both sides, the Tiruvallur District Collector S. Kavitha and Tirupathi Additional Collector R. Govinda Rao decided that the present system of fishing would continue until the respective governments took a call.
Fishing community leader Durai Mahendran said the GPS marking should be done as soon as possible. “Fishermen are suffering due to this. Clear marking of fishing grounds would bring peace to the villages. The cases on the men too should be dropped,” he added.

Wish you looked at your phone less? Then you’ve probably heard of Brick, a $59 device that claims to help you block distractions. You tap your phone against the Brick when you want to avoid distractions—the bundled software stops you from opening whichever apps you’ve decided you need to stop doomscrolling.
The idea is to add a physical barrier between you and apps like Instagram—if you want to scroll, you need to physically get up, find the Brick, and tap it. It’s a good idea, and implemented in a way that makes it easy to get started. But what if you don’t want to buy a chunk of plastic?
Good news: the Brick is basically just an NFC chip, not that different from the one in your credit card or passport. You can buy a blank NFC chip for a dollar. Even better, free applications can use these chips to block distractions, exactly like the Brick. Or, if you prefer, these apps also support QR codes, meaning all you need is a printer. Here are two free distraction-blocking apps—complete with physical barriers—for iPhone or Android.
Best for iPhones: Foqos
The oddly named Foqos is a free, open source app for iOS by Canadian developer Ali Waseem. Many open source apps lack polish, but not this one—it’s easy to configure the necessary permissions, set up a profile, and start blocking distractions.
While creating a new profile, you first choose which physical object you want to use to start and stop your blocking sessions. The two most popular options are NFC tags (there’s a handy link to buy some in the app) or a QR code. But you can also block using a daily schedule, if you prefer, or by scanning any barcode. The barcode option is nice because you don’t need to buy or print anything—scan the code on your favorite book, beverage, or anything else you keep around the house.
Foqos can block you from managing apps while a profile is running. This means you can’t just delete Foqos to get around a block you set up, which is exactly what someone fighting against their own urges needs. You can allow a limited number of breaks, if you want.
I’ve been using this to break my Reddit habit and can report that it works. I keep a printed QR code inside a cabinet, far from the couch where I tend to scroll. It creates just enough friction that I can finish reading a book instead. The application has an excellent privacy policy—no data leaves your device.
Best for Android: Switchly
Foqos is sadly iOS-exclusive, and I couldn’t find an Android equivalent that’s quite as polished. But Switchly, by Vienna-based developer Saltyy, stands out as one of the more feature-complete apps I tested. You will need to spend some time fiddling to get it set up, granted, but once you do, you’ll find it every bit as flexible as Foqos.
To get started, open the app, which you can install from Google Play. A wizard will guide you through the relevant permissions, then talk you through setting up your first profile. You will need to read everything carefully, because it’s a little bit tough to navigate the first time. You can block apps and URLs. You can use an NFC chip or a QR code to trigger locking and unlocking. You can also block based on a schedule; Premium users can trigger when connected to a particular Wi-Fi network, or when a certain Bluetooth device is nearby.
If you’d rather not block Instagram entirely, but never want to see a Reel again, good news: there’s support for blocking particular features inside certain apps. The feature is labeled as experimental, but worked well in my testing.
There’s a lot of flexibility, but Android’s open nature means how well it works depends in part on your phone model. The developer acknowledges this. Also, you don’t need the Premium version—the free tier offers plenty of features for most people.
Another application Android users should check out is Lock. This app is more polished than Switchly, but only supports NFC chips. Give it a try if Switchly doesn’t quite work the way you like.
Distractions don’t just live on your phone. We’ve written about how to block websites on your computer, with multiple free options. But let’s face it: the phone is the ultimate distraction machine. Learn to control your impulses there.

Former Disney exec Kevin Mayer, who oversaw his former employer’s 2019 acquisition of 20th Century Fox, has shared his thoughts on the Paramount-Warner Bros merger.
The pragmatic exec, who has been co-CEO of Blackstone-backed media company Candle Media since 2021, told a panel at the Zurich Summit this weekend that consolidation in the media and entertainment sector was inevitable in a period of declining revenues.
“If we’re going to be intellectually honest about answering this question, you have to also ask yourself, what would happen if the merger didn’t happen,” he said in a response to a question on the merger.
Mayer said the film industry was in a phase of decline with “fewer and fewer” great financial outcomes, and that the status quo of a number of independent studios working with declining revenues no longer made financial sense.
Watch on Deadline
“Their ability to finance, to distribute and to market product is going to start to deteriorate very substantially. It already has, frankly. If we keep the standalone, the status quo, you’re going to have a larger number of very weak companies unable to do much in the future. That’s the future you’ve got to measure this consolidation against, in my opinion, not against some fanciful future where everything is as good as it was five, 10 years ago”.
Mayer said he expected Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison to keep his promises around producing 30 movies a year for at least five years after sealing of the deal.
“I did this once. I negotiated Disney’s purchase of 21st Century Fox, and I was responsible for integrating those two companies,” he said.
“David Ellison made some promises. I expect he’ll keep them. We have public promises that are that explicit… are very hard to reverse yourselves. I think for a period of time… for five years, he’ll do what he says. He’ll make the movies and he’ll release them theatrically, he’ll do it all.”
Mayer said he felt it was likely that Warner Bros. would continue to operate as a separate entity, based on his own experiences at Disney.
The biggest rub in the deal, he suggested, would be job losses in the industry, even if believed consolidation has “necessary”.
“When you hear these promises of $6 billion in synergies, that’s a euphemism for a lot of layoffs… That’s an extremely difficult thing, obviously, and that’s what I think this merger portends.”

Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
- Published
"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."
The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.
Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.
It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.
Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.
We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.
Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting.
It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire.
"Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.
He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals.
"I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."
He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.
At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach.
"We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.
Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.
The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.
Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.
Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.
We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.
About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.
As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.
We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.
Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.
Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.
There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line.
"It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.
The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.
Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.
In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.
Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.
She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.
A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.
About 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.
We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.
Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day.
"We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.
Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain.
"We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.
Fatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."
Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.
She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said.
"I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."
A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.
On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.
It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.

Four people died while more than ten were injured when a three-storeyed building under construction collapsed at Dhulkot village near Ambala City on Sunday (September 27, 2026), officials said.
The incident unfolded in the late afternoon when the concrete slab (lintel) for the roof was being cast on the first floor, prompting locals to initiate rescue efforts before informing the police and emergency services.
One of the injured workers claimed that some labourers were working on the ground floor, while others were engaged in the casting work above.
Ambala Civil Surgeon Renu Beri told reporters that 12 injured labourers were brought to the hospital, of whom five are still admitted, two were discharged on request, while the others were discharged after first aid was applied.
"Four were brought dead to the civil hospital in the evening. Their bodies have been shifted to the mortuary," she further said.
Talking to reporters in the evening, Ambala's Superintendent of Police, Ajit Singh Shekhawat, confirmed that four people had died in the incident.
NDRF, State Disaster Response Force, police and civil administration teams were engaged in the rescue operations after the incident, he said.
When asked if more people were trapped under the debris, the SP said, "Two to three people have been located, and efforts are on to rescue them.”
Police and senior administrative officials immediately arrived at the site with rescue equipment and engaged in removing debris.
An official said that heavy earth-moving machines and other machinery were pressed into service. When asked if the building belonged to a realtor, police said an investigation into the cause of the accident, the owner’s identity, and all other matters is underway.
"Our immediate priority is the rescue operation at the site. Details regarding the building owner and other relevant details will also be shared later,” Mr. Shekhawat said. “Whether it is unauthorised construction or if any negligence was involved, all this will be investigated,” he added.
When asked whether the three-storey building had necessary permission from the authorities concerned, the police officer said, "We will ask for records from the Ambala Municipal Corporation, whether it had permissions, whether it was legal. But all of it will be done once the rescue operation is over."

సౌదీ అరేబియా రాజధాని రియాద్లోని విమానాశ్రయంపై వైమానిక దాడి జరగడంతో భారీగా మంటలు, దట్టమైన నల్లటి పొగ వ్యాపించాయంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సౌదీ అరేబియాలోని రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై జరిగిన వైమానిక దాడికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో రియాద్కు చెందినది కాదు. ఇది రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జూన్ 2026లో డ్రోన్ దాడి వల్ల జరిగిన అగ్నిప్రమాదానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై హౌతీలు దాడి చేసినట్లు వార్తలు వస్తున్నప్పటికీ, వైరల్ వీడియో దానికి సంబంధించినది కాదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 జూన్ 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోకు చెందినది. మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్పై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడి కారణంగా వ్యాపించిన మంటలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతోంది.
వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 18 జూన్ 2026న మాస్కోపై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడిలో సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో మంటలు, పొగ వ్యాపించాయి. వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న ప్రదేశాన్ని గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, అది మాస్కోలో ఉన్నట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
అయితే, 19 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న రియాద్లోని కింగ్ ఖలీద్ అంతర్జాతీయ విమానాశ్రయంలోని ఇంధన డిపోపై తాము దాడి చేసినట్లు హౌతీలు పేర్కొన్నారంటూ పలు అంతర్జాతీయ వార్తా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) వెల్లడించాయి.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జరిగిన ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.

Beyond pay, work-life balance, and scheduling, there are other basic challenges affecting the US submarine workforce, including how workers get to the job, a Navy official overseeing workforce concerns shared.
The Navy's Submarine Industrial Base Program Office says it, along with its federal and state partners, has observed success in addressing region-specific problems, like transportation, that can be make-or-break for attracting new workers. Regional teams have been critical in examining the particular workforce needs around submarine construction and repair yards.
Erica Logan, the office's director of workforce, told Business Insider earlier this year that her team looks at local factors, including education, demographics, unemployment, and cost of living. Transportation is also part of the assessment.
"What does the transportation system look like? Is it a very rural area where there may not be transportation?" Logan said. "How would we get folks there? What could we do to help a supplier that lives in an area like that?"
The office, she said, has supported several transportation pilots with bus systems to make it easier for submarine workers to get to and from work. These programs have prompted further questions about free bus passes and van pools.
"I think we've done a lot in that area using this regional approach to really just get a good understanding of what that region has," Logan said.
The Navy's Submarine Industrial Base Program Office is working on rebuilding the network of suppliers, builders, and manufacturers that construct Navy submarines. As part of the broader efforts to fix decades-old shipbuilding problems in the US, the office has focused on attracting and retaining workers, as well as addressing everything from pay and work-life balance to problems unique to individual communities.
In one example provided by the office, General Dynamics Electric Boat partnered with the Rhode Island Public Transit Authority to provide direct service to the Quonset Point shipyard. Ridership has more than doubled year over year, the office said, and it came at no cost to the Navy.
In another, the Hampton Roads Workforce Council provides workers with gas cards and bus passes to help them get to work. Since September 2023, the Hampton Roads Maritime Training System program within the council has provided nearly $200,000 in transportation assistance, funded through grants, donations, and the Virginia state government.
Housing is also a challenge. The office hasn't funded permanent housing or related subsidies for shipyard or supplier workers. Instead, its efforts involve state and local engagement to expand affordable housing, as well as partnerships with specific yards or vendors.
Some initiatives specifically support trainees. For instance, the Accelerated Training in Defense Manufacturing program in Danville, Virginia, offers students housing during their 16-week training. The program quickly trains candidates in manufacturing skills and trades to create a sustained flow of workers for jobs in naval shipbuilding and the submarine industrial base.
Addressing these issues, along with competitive pay and benefits, is key to recruiting and retaining the workers that the Navy needs to meet its shipbuilding goals. Over the next 10 years, the service estimates it'll need to hire 250,000 skilled workers to account for the expected attrition and retirement in the workforce.

Jammu and Kashmir Bank is set to issue a recruitment notification for assistant and officer-level positions within the next few days, Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking during the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting (AGM) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC) here, Chatterjee said the bank had finalised negotiations with the agency that would conduct the recruitment examinations for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
“After 2021, the bank is going for recruitment of both assistants as well as officers. The agreement for conducting the examinations for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh is being finalised, and the bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” Chatterjee said.
He said the recruitment would be carried out in accordance with the bank’s operational requirements and would also take into account the need for employees with proficiency in local languages.
“As far as the bank is concerned, we will do what we have done in the past. There is a requirement for people with local language proficiency, though the numbers will be limited,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s presence across 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir had created a requirement for personnel familiar with local languages.
“The bank is present in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir, and we need people with local language proficiency to serve customers there. So, the bank may decide in future to hire a few employees to support our existing staff strength,” he said.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, which was chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.
The AGM was held under the theme “Trust, Tradition and Transformation”. Addressing shareholders, Krishnan said the bank’s future growth would have to be aligned with its wider economic and social contribution to the region.
“Our past gives us identity. Our present gives us strength. Our future gives us responsibility. Trust is our inheritance. Tradition is our anchor. Transformation is our obligation,” he said.
He also highlighted the bank’s role in supporting entrepreneurship and said its participation in Mission YUVA was significant in creating economic opportunities for a new generation of entrepreneurs.
On digital transformation, Krishnan said technology should ultimately serve the objective of improving customer experience and making banking “simpler, safer and more accessible”.
Chatterjee, meanwhile, said the bank had maintained its growth trajectory despite challenging circumstances and had recorded its fourth consecutive year of record profitability.
“Notwithstanding the challenging circumstances, your Bank maintained its growth trajectory and delivered a fourth consecutive year of record profitability. Net profit reached an all-time high of Rs 2,363 crore, registering year-on-year growth of 13.5%. The growth momentum has continued into the current financial year. By June 2026, the Bank crossed the historic milestone of Rs 3 trillion in total business,” he said.

“These outcomes demonstrate that our progress is broad-based, with profitability, asset quality, efficiency and capital strength advancing together. For our investors, this represents a resilient and increasingly diversified franchise, supported by strong fundamentals and a clear strategy for long-term value creation. On digital banking, he said investments in digital platforms, data analytics, cybersecurity and process automation were improving customer experience and operational efficiency.
“The rapid growth of up to 94% in digital transactions during FY 2025-26 demonstrates the increasing trust customers place in our digital ecosystem,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank would continue to invest in its workforce and technology while strengthening cybersecurity and customer experience.
“As we reflect with pride on a legacy spanning nearly nine decades, we remain conscious of the responsibility that accompanies it. Our aspiration is clear: to become the ‘Bank of Choice’. Towards this goal, we will continue to invest in our people and technology, reinforce cybersecurity, improve customer experience and institutionalise a culture of innovation and excellence,” he said.
During the question-and-answer session, shareholders raised queries on various aspects of the bank’s operations, including recruitment. Chatterjee responded to the questions.
DGM and Company Secretary Mohammad Shafi Mir also read out the Auditor’s Report, comments of the Comptroller and Auditor General and the Secretarial Audit Report. He informed shareholders that the e-voting results and Scrutinizer’s Report would be made available on the websites of the bank, its registrar and transfer agent, and the stock exchanges within two working days of the conclusion of the AGM.
The AGM concluded with shareholders appreciating the bank’s performance during the financial year 2025-26.

A delegation of the Kashmir Traders and Manufacturers Federation (KTMF), led by its president Mohammad Yaseen Khan, on Tuesday called on newly appointed Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone, Sujit Kumar Singh and discussed issues concerning the trade community across the Valley.
The delegation congratulated Singh on assuming charge as IGP Kashmir and expressed hope that his experience and leadership would further strengthen police-public coordination.
The meeting focused on traffic management, parking, policing, movement of commercial vehicles and timely resolution of traders’ grievances at the district level.
Representatives of various district trade bodies apprised the IGP of local issues affecting traders and business establishments and stressed the need for regular coordination between the police and the trading community.

KTMF senior member Javaid Ahmad Zargar, representing the Jamia Masjid and Downtown Srinagar area, raised the long-pending demand for a fire station near Jamia Masjid, citing the congestion in the area and the need for an effective emergency response mechanism.
Zargar also highlighted the shortage of adequate parking facilities in Downtown Srinagar, saying traffic and parking difficulties continue to affect traders, residents and visitors.
KTMF president Mohammad Yaseen Khan described the interaction as constructive and appreciated the IGP’s prompt response to the issues raised by the delegation.
He said traders were important stakeholders in maintaining a peaceful and orderly commercial environment and stressed that regular interaction between police and trade bodies could help resolve genuine issues before they escalate.

KTMF assured the police administration of continued cooperation in matters concerning public safety, traffic management, peace and a conducive environment for trade and commerce.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, police have said.
The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, south-west of Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.
In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as a shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.
The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.
No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.
South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.
Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.
“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a spokesperson, Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.
“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”
Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama joint at around 1.46am on Saturday night and starting shooting at customers.
“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained ... A court in Shopian on Tuesday sentenced a man to life imprisonment for the murder of a person in 2019, observing that the case did not fall within the “rarest of rare” category warranting the death penalty.
Principal Sessions Judge Shopian Mehmood Ahmed Chowdhary awarded life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh to Bilal Ahmad Seh, who was convicted under Section 302 of the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC).
The court said the convict had been in custody since his arrest on April 21, 2019, and had spent nearly seven years in custody during the trial.
The case, registered as FIR No. 19/2019 at Police Station Zainapora, initially involved charges under Sections 302, 307, 147, 148, 506, 109, 341 and 34 of the RPC.
While deciding the quantum of sentence, the court considered the mitigating and aggravating circumstances and referred to the Supreme Court’s guidelines on awarding the death penalty.
The court noted that the case was based on four eyewitnesses as well as circumstantial evidence. It also took into account that the convict was a first-time offender, was a farmer by profession and had been supporting his family.
The court observed that there were no aggravating circumstances of such an exceptional nature as to warrant capital punishment.
“Life imprisonment is the appropriate punishment to be awarded to the convict for commission of murder of the deceased,” the court said.
The court also noted that other accused named in the case, including the convict’s brother and two sisters, had been acquitted, while proceedings against another accused had abated following his death. A juvenile accused in the case is facing separate proceedings before the Juvenile Justice Board, according to the case record.
Since the sentence is one of life imprisonment, the court directed that the case file and judgment be submitted to the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh for confirmation of the sentence as required under law.
The convict was directed to be sent to Special Jail Pulwama to undergo the sentence. The court also informed him of his right to appeal against the judgment and sentence before the High Court within 15 days.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

Haptics tech company Taction sued Apple in 2021, alleging it infringed two of its patents. Now a federal jury in San Diego has awarded Taction over $5.7 billion in damages. According to CNBC, “The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input.”
Apple hit with $5.7 billion in damages over haptic patents
Apple’s Taptic Engine was found to infringe on two of Taction’s patents.
Taction argued that Apple’s Taptic Engine in its Apple Watches and iPhones used technology that it had developed without a proper license, and the jury agreed. It found that Apple had infringed on two claims in one patent and one in the other. However, the jury did not find that Apple willfully infringed. Taction had accused Apple of reverse-engineering the tech from two Kannon gaming headsets.
Apple has said that it intends to appeal the decision. We’ve reached out for additional comment and will update the story if and when we hear back.

CPI(M) and Congress condemned the alleged attack on the convoy of former Chief Minister Manik Sarkar at Bamutia assembly constituency in west Tripura on Sunday (September 27, 2026). Bricks and eggs were thrown at the vehicle of Mr. Sarkar and security escorts.
Both the opposition parties described the incident as a “fallout of the BJP’s frustration” as the saffron party is fast losing its support base in the State. They also linked the incident with recent controversies concerning the Election Commission of India.
