Luxury watch warranties are getting longer – but do buyers really benefit?
From Rolex and Omega’s five-year coverage to Hublot’s potential 10-year warranty, watch brands are promising more protection than ever. Here’s what that actually means for owners.
Luxury watch brands are locked in a perpetual arms race to win over enthusiasts and collectors. In this game of one-upmanship, ultra-thin movements, longer power reserves, better water resistance and hardier or more exotic case materials have all been pitched for battle.
But over the past decade, a new metric has entered the conversation: longer warranty periods.
Not too long ago, a two-year manufacturer’s warranty was standard. Now, brands such as Rolex, Omega and Tudor offer five years of international coverage, while Cartier and Jaeger-LeCoultre allow owners to extend theirs to as much as eight years through dedicated programmes.
In 2026, Hublot went further with a “5+5” model – eligible watches receive a five-year warranty, which owners can extend to 10 years by registering with the Hublotista programme.
“I’ve seen brands place massive importance on extended warranties recently, but it is largely a corporate arms race to attract clients, beat out competitors and lock in consumer loyalty,” observed Ken Liew, managing director of Watch Estate, a secondary-market dealer specialising in investment-grade timepieces.
That brands are now offering multi-year warranties should come as no surprise. After all, if watches are being marketed as heirlooms or purchases meant to last for generations, shouldn’t manufacturers be prepared to stand behind them for more than 24 months?
The timing isn’t entirely opportunistic, however. According to Singapore Watch Club founder Tom Chng, today’s watchmakers are better equipped than ever to make such promises.
“Production capabilities have advanced tremendously over the past two decades with the widespread adoption of CAD, CNC machining and increasingly sophisticated quality control processes,” he said.
“Components are manufactured to tighter tolerances than ever before, while durability and reliability testing have become far more rigorous and data-driven. Simply put, modern mechanical watches are generally more consistent than they have ever been,” Chng added.
Liew agreed. “Modern manufacturing, materials and quality control have made today’s watches genuinely more reliable. These defects happen less frequently, allowing brands to boldly project immense confidence in their craftsmanship while knowing the extended coverage actually costs them little to maintain.”
At the same time, some of the industry’s biggest players have raised consumer expectations. When Rolex introduced its five-year international warranty in 2015, competitors found it increasingly difficult to justify offering only two years of coverage, Liew pointed out.
“Extending the warranty is an easy way for brands to signal confidence in their products while remaining competitive in the eyes of consumers,” he explained.
For consumers spending five or six figures on a timepiece, an extended warranty offers peace of mind – the assurance that if something goes wrong because of a manufacturing defect, they will not be faced with a hefty repair bill.
Yet despite the industry’s increasingly generous warranties, collectors themselves remain pragmatic.
“When I buy a luxury watch, I already take it for granted that it comes with some form of warranty,” said watch collector George Tan. “The length of that warranty isn’t a dealbreaker for me. My main priority is always whether I love the watch and really want to buy it.”
Liew agreed. “For actual seasoned collectors, these long warranties aren’t a major deciding factor. A fine mechanical watch can always be fixed, with or without a warranty paper.”
But as longer warranties become increasingly common, are they actually delivering more value to buyers?
WHAT LONGER WARRANTIES SAY ABOUT LUXURY TIMEPIECES
Longer warranties are, in part, a public declaration of confidence. Standing behind a watch for five, eight or 10 years suggests that manufacturers are increasingly comfortable backing the reliability of their movements, materials and production standards.
“A manufacturer’s warranty is primarily about reassurance rather than necessity,” Liew maintained. “Mechanical watches are highly resilient – they aren’t like modern cars that constantly suffer from electronic or mechanical glitches, so actual factory failures are uncommon.”
The practical benefit, he added, is that owners can turn to an authorised dealer or service centre if a covered problem arises.
Chng has experienced this first-hand. “Longer warranties genuinely do make a difference,” he said. “I’ve personally benefited from an eight-year warranty, and there is real peace of mind in being able to wear a watch regularly without worrying about unexpected repair costs. It also softens the financial impact if the watch requires attention around its first recommended service interval.”
If owners are looking to sell their watches on the secondary market, does a longer warranty make any difference to desirability or resale value?
Liew said it would not. “In the high-end secondary market, a broken or unserviced movement can always be mechanically repaired back to perfect working order. But you can never ‘factory undo’ a gouged bezel, soft rounded lugs from over-polishing, or a damaged case.”
Warranties generally cover manufacturing defects rather than damage caused by wear, accidents or misuse. For experienced buyers, Liew argued, the remaining warranty period is therefore not necessarily the deciding factor.
“The metal holds the value, not the paper,” Liew said. “True collectors will gladly choose a watch out of warranty that is in pristine, unpolished, original condition over a heavily scuffed, poorly handled watch that happens to have four years of factory warranty left.”
EXTENDED WARRANTIES: WHAT BUYERS ARE ACTUALLY GETTING FROM LUXURY WATCH BRANDS
Beyond giving buyers peace of mind, do longer warranties translate into more comprehensive coverage?
Simply put, not necessarily.
A comparison of the six brands examined here – Cartier, Hublot, Jaeger-LeCoultre, Omega, Rolex and Tudor – found that despite differences in duration, their warranties are more alike than different.
All six warranties centre on the same core issue – manufacturing defects in materials or workmanship. They also broadly exclude normal wear and tear, accidental damage, misuse and unauthorised repairs.
That makes the quality of a brand’s after-sales support another important consideration at the point of purchase.
As Chng pointed out, warranty duration is only one consideration. “Equally important are the ease of making a claim, the quality and speed of service, and whether repairs are handled locally or must be sent overseas.”
Chng believes that a shorter warranty paired with strong after-sales support can provide a better ownership experience than a longer warranty accompanied by cumbersome service procedures.
HOW LUXURY WATCH BRANDS’ WARRANTY PROGRAMMES DIFFER
Rolex, Omega and Tudor have relatively straightforward warranty structures. Their five-year international warranties begin from the date of purchase, with no separate online registration or membership programme required.
For buyers, the process is straightforward: Purchase the watch from an authorised retailer and the warranty begins from the date of purchase.
Rolex and Tudor warranties are attached to eligible watches rather than explicitly restricted to the original buyer, provided the relevant guarantee conditions are met. That can be useful for buyers considering relatively new pre-owned watches.
Cartier and Jaeger-LeCoultre take a different approach, linking their warranty extensions to owner programmes.
Rather than granting their longest warranties automatically, both brands require eligible owners to register while the original manufacturer’s warranty is still active. Approved extensions can bring the total warranty period to as much as eight years.
Jaeger-LeCoultre’s Care Programme also includes services beyond the warranty extension, such as personalised information, maintenance-related services and functional checks.
Similarly, Cartier Care allows owners to apply for the extension as long as the watch is still covered by its initial two-year international warranty.
Then there is Hublot, which raised the stakes in 2026 with its “5+5” warranty programme.
Its five-year international warranty brings eligible watches in line with the five-year coverage offered by several major competitors. Owners who register an eligible watch through Hublotista during the initial warranty period can receive another five years of coverage – bringing the total to 10 years.
The full 10 years is not automatic. Connected watches and Hublot Certified Pre-Owned models, for example, continue to carry a two-year standard warranty under the current terms.
Omega differs in another respect. Its warranty terms provide for replacement with an identical or similar watch if repairs cannot restore normal use.
ULTIMATELY, DO EXTENDED WARRANTIES OFFER BETTER VALUE TO CONSUMERS?
Not necessarily. Longer warranties offer reassurance against covered defects, but routine servicing generally remains an out-of-pocket expense. Accidental damage is also typically excluded, while no warranty can prevent the dings, nicks and scratches that come with regular wear.
For Liew, an extended warranty barely factors into the purchasing decision. “No one buys a five- or six-figure luxury watch because of the warranty,” he said. “They buy it because of the raw emotional draw of the brand heritage, the design aesthetics and the price. A warranty is an afterthought – a minor checkbox item.”
Tan shared a similar view. “Most, if not all, collectors I know care way more about heritage, design and resale value,” he said. “The warranty doesn’t influence them all that much. People choose a watch based on how it looks and how much they want to wear it before they look at anything else.”
There is, however, one circumstance in which it might matter.
“If I love both watches equally and am genuinely stuck between them, a better warranty might break the tie,” said Tan. “Even then, the warranty would be the very last factor I look at.”
A longer warranty is unlikely to persuade someone to buy a watch they do not already love. But it may provide extra reassurance when choosing between two equally compelling options – or simply make ownership a little less daunting.
For brands, that reassurance can still matter. “When clients are spending six figures on complex, heavy pieces like tourbillons or perpetual calendars, they naturally demand a high level of reassurance because potential repair costs can be astronomical,” said Liew.
“Extending the warranty gives the client absolute peace of mind and acts as a smooth sales tactic, allowing brands to move these high-ticket pieces with confidence.”
Consumer expectations have evolved alongside the warranties themselves. According to Chng: “Buyers spending five or six figures on a watch increasingly expect ownership to mirror the broader luxury experience: Exceptional product quality supported by excellent after-sales service. A long warranty has therefore become as much a statement of confidence as it is a practical benefit.”
Looking ahead, Chng expects longer warranties to become more common.
“I wouldn’t be surprised to see 10-year warranties become increasingly common,” he said. “Eight years already puts the industry within touching distance of what feels like a psychologically satisfying milestone.
“More importantly, it reflects how confident manufacturers have become in their production methods and product reliability. Beyond a decade, however, I suspect the practical benefits diminish.”

The ministry of road transport and highways (MoRTH) has introduced a new Model Concession Agreement (MCA) on 18 September for highway projects awarded under the Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM), replacing the framework used for earlier projects.
The new MCA covers the entire project cycle, from conditions precedent and right-of-way to construction payments, operation and maintenance, termination and dispute resolution. It also introduces more granular milestones and monitoring mechanisms.
Mint explains what has changed, and what does it mean for developers, lenders and the government.
Why a new HAM agreement?
Under the HAM model, the concessionaire finances and builds the road and is subsequently paid through a combination of construction-stage payments and annuities. The new MCA explicitly covers design, financing, construction, operation and maintenance obligations.
The new agreement introduces more granular milestones and monitoring mechanisms. Most importantly, payments are now explicitly linked to independently certified physical progress.
For developers, this means a clearer framework for converting construction work into receivables, while the government gets a more direct mechanism to link payments to work completed on the ground.
How will developers get paid?
The most consequential change is the payment mechanism.
The new MCA provides for 40% of the bid project cost to be paid by government agencies during construction in 10 instalments of 4% each, against physical-progress milestones ranging from 5% to 90%.
The independent engineer has to certify achievement of each milestone, after which the authority is required to make the payment within 15 days.
The remaining project cost is to be paid through 30 biannual instalments beginning 180 days after the commercial operation date.
The agreement also provides for inflation adjustment through a 70:30 WPI-CPI formula, allowing the bid project cost to be adjusted for changes in the price index between bidding and invoicing.
For developers, this provides greater visibility on when construction expenditure can be converted into receivables. It also means, however, that payment is more directly dependent on measurable and certifiable physical progress.
Does it make construction financing easier?
The new MCA includes a significant liquidity-support mechanism. The authority can provide a mobilization advance of up to 10% of the total project cost, in two instalments, against a bank guarantee.
The MCA also introduces an incentive linked to newer construction technology. If a concessionaire purchases and registers qualifying alternative-fuel construction equipment—electric, hydrogen or biofuel machinery—or specified automated intelligent construction machinery within the prescribed period, the interest rate on the corresponding portion of the advance is reduced by 50%.
At the same time, developers bidding more than 10% below the estimated bid project cost will have to provide additional performance security equivalent to 10% of the difference.
Who bears the risk when projects are delayed?
The new agreement creates clearer consequences for both sides.
The authority must provide key conditions precedent, including right of way, relevant environmental permissions, forest and wildlife clearances and appointment of the independent engineer.
If the authority delays these conditions, it has to pay damages at 0.1% of the performance security for each day of delay, subject to the prescribed ceiling. Conversely, the concessionaire faces damages of 0.2% of performance security a day for delays attributable to it.
The MCA also provides a structured termination-payment mechanism. In the event of concessionaire default, the payment increases with the physical-progress milestone achieved, rather than being treated as a simple recovery of expenditure.
For example, termination after the 20% milestone provides for 50% of debt due or 3% of bid project cost, whichever is lower. The corresponding percentages rise progressively at later milestones.
This makes the point at which a project fails particularly important for lenders and developers, since the termination payment is linked to the project's physical progress.
What changes in construction monitoring and road safety?
The new MCA places greater emphasis on continuous verification rather than monitoring only at the end of construction.
Physical progress is to be measured using predefined weightages for individual construction activities. The agreement also requires monthly progress reporting, inspections, testing, video recording and technical audits.
Road safety receives a separate layer of oversight. The authority is required to appoint a safety consultant, including for a safety audit of completed construction works before COD.
The independent engineer is also to be changed every three years, potentially reducing the risk of one monitoring agency remaining associated with a project throughout its life.
What does this mean for highway construction?
The immediate effect is likely to be a more milestone-driven HAM construction regime.
Developers get a clearer payment calendar, inflation protection and access to mobilization funding. At the same time, the government gets stronger safeguards against low-ball bidding, delays and poor-quality construction.
The new MCA also extends the contract beyond simply building the road. Its maintenance framework requires creation of an asset-management system covering an inventory of road assets, their condition, maintenance needs, costs and a real-time database.
That could gradually shift HAM projects towards a more data-driven lifecycle approach, with the quality of the road during its operating period becoming as important as its construction.

For decades, Richland Parish remained a small farming community nestled in Louisiana's northeast corner.
Residents living in the parish — a spattering of rural towns and unincorporated communities — had come to know their home for its slower pace of life. Much of the area is filled with winding back roads, sprawling farmland, and a skyline free of towering skyscrapers. The closest major regional city is Monroe, about 30 minutes west, with a population more than twice that of Richland Parish.
It's the kind of place where everybody claims to know everybody, or at very least, has heard of them. 
Now Meta has arrived, and things are changing.
In December 2024, the company announced plans to build its largest data center to date in Richland Parish, specifically near the unincorporated community of Holly Ridge, which local outlets report has fewer than 2,000 residents. Meta said the $50 billion, multi-year project would support around 7,500 jobs at the peak of construction and around 1,000 operational jobs, eclipsing the local community by thousands.
Angel Crawford of Delhi, a town about 10 minutes west of Holly Ridge, first noticed a surge in construction and operational workers arriving in her community last year.
Around that time, she and her husband, Bryan, opened a mobile home park to help address the housing gap.
Angel and Bryan Crawford founded Antley Pines.
Bryan and Angel Crawford initially worked in the nursing industry, but pivoted careers in 2024 after becoming empty nesters.
"We started with real estate and rentals because they are very much needed in this area," Angel told Business Insider. "It's very rural here, so when there are fluctuating prices in the market, it doesn't really hit us because there are never enough houses for sale or rent."
They began buying older homes and fixer-uppers that year.
"We had a vision to create a mobile home park, and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center. That's what pushed us to keep going forward, " Angel said. "We understood there wasn't enough housing for residents, and our dream of building more multifamily houses was right in line to do that."
In 2024, the couple founded Parish Line Properties, which operates 18 homes in the area, including a mobile home park called Antley Pines. Of the 18 homes, 14 are considered workforce housing.
Many residents in the park are contractors working for Meta.
In many ways, Richland Parish is a microcosm of the debate about data centers across the US. Some Americans are optimistic about data centers, citing new jobs, revitalized economies, and the securing of the country's lead over China in AI development. Others are more critical, expressing concerns about the environment, the strain on utility grids, and how the acceleration of AI could impact the job market.
"Around here, people feel one way or the other about the data center. Either people are excited about the opportunities, or they hate them. There's no in between," Angel said. "I see it as an opportunity for us to have more experiences in our area and jobs for our children, so they can stay here instead of moving away."
The Crawfords opened Antley Pines in December 2025. Despite some locals' mixed feelings about the data center, the demand for housing is undeniable.
"All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said.
She said many of her tenants are subcontractors, like electricians, working with Meta.
The mobile home park is 15 minutes from Meta's construction site.
Although Antley Pines isn't directly in Holly Ridge, the mobile park is still reaping the economic benefits.
"Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," Angel said.
That kind of routine can take a toll on workers, many of whom are not from the area.
"One of the big things my tenants tell me is that if they live in Dallas and it's 30 miles to work, it takes about 30 minutes. Well, in rural areas, 30 miles could take 60 minutes because of all the back roads and little towns you have to go through," she said. "The closer they can get to the job site, the better."
The influx of workers has boosted market prices.
Antley Pines offers fully furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom homes, which Angel said gives workers the option of staying with family or rooming with colleagues. She said the homes, which come with amenities, cost an average of $3,000 a month with utilities.
"I don't have any problem with getting tenants in those homes at that price point," Angel said. "Before Meta arrived, an unfurnished house without utilities in the same area would probably go for around $1,200 to $1,500 a month."
In Richland Parish, the median household income was around $53,000 in 2024.
"We've assured our local long-term tenants that we won't increase their rent. That's not what we're about. We're not going to put local tenants in a bind. We're going to find different and new properties to help with workforce housing," she said.
Amenities like WiFi are in high demand.
Angel said there are a few common requests among the construction and operational workers under Meta.
"As soon as they get into their rentals, 'What's the WiFi password?' is their first question," Angel said. "Some don't have their family here, so they want to do FaceTime."
The tenants also value an escape from the bustling construction site.
"They're with a lot of people all day long. They don't want to come home to a lot of noise," Angel said. "All of them say they love the peace and quiet."
Workforce housing is more popular than ever.
The demand for lodging in the area has continued to grow, Angel said.
"I get phone calls or text messages almost daily. Most of them are from my current tenants who have met someone who's looking for somewhere to stay," she said. "If you go on any of the websites, like Realtor.com, not all local rental properties are listed on there."
That's what led her to create StayNELA, a third-party website connecting tenants with property owners in 2025.
"I did a lot of research for several months by driving around the area and looking at all the different signs in people's yards or at four-way stops that you couldn't read properly. I kept a log, took pictures, and kept them in a folder on my phone. If anything was on Facebook about a rental, I saved it."
Some locals are also working on the data center.
While some construction workers traveled to work on Meta's data center, others were locals leveraging the opportunity that arrived in their backyard, Angel said.
"A lot of young men in this area work offshore at oil rigs, so it's a lot of time spent away from home," she said. "We know a lot of young people who are working at the construction site right now who would usually be off working away from home."
She added, "Hopefully, it'll bring more jobs to the area for our kids and grandkids."
There's uncertainty around how long construction workers will remain in Richland Parish.
Construction on Meta's data center is expected to continue for several years, but there's uncertainty among workers about how long they'll be in Richland Parish.
"Most of them don't know how long they're going to be here. They hope they're going to be here long-term, but in construction, they don't get told until it's done," Angel said.
Month-to-month leasing is among the top requests from tenants.
A future without Meta.
Although Meta's presence in Richland Parish has become the new normal, it won't last forever.
The data center will eventually become operational, meaning construction will wane, and workers will leave. The Crawfords have thought about a future without Meta, and they're not worried.
"Each home in our mobile park is on one-fourth of an acre. After Meta's gone, we can sell them individually or rent them out," Angel said.
For now, though, they're focused on the economic benefits that have come to Richland Parish from the data center project.
"We've seen a lot of laundromats, RV parks, and mobile home parks come to the area," Angel said. "It's great for the economy in our area because people who we've worked with who install electrical systems, septic systems, plumbing, gravel, and all those things are busy because Meta's here."

New Delhi, Sep 23: The Congress on Wednesday alleged that for the Modi government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform but an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, as well as a tool for stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation.
The opposition party's assertion comes after former Bombay High Court judge Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra government's panel to prepare a draft for implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), citing serious reservations over its decision to restrict public feedback on crucial social issues to a "Yes/No" format.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said the resignation of a former high court judge from the Maharashtra government's committee to draft a UCC for the state raises larger questions, apart from his several concerns on the functioning of this committee.
Posting his statement on X, Ramesh said, "A retired High Court judge has shown courage to resign from a committee set up by the Maharashtra government to prepare a uniform civil code for the state. Here is our statement on the non-uniform 'Uniform' Civil Codes (UCC) the HM is trying to bulldoze through in every state."
"Did the Constituent Assembly ever imagine a situation in which every state would enact its own separate version of a UCC? The answer is a resounding no," Ramesh said.
Did the architects of our Constitution led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar ever conceive states competing with one another to have different UCCs according to the political machinations and calculations of one political party, he asked.
"Again, the answer is a resounding no," Ramesh added.
He pointed out that on June 17, 2016, the Modi government referred the question of the UCC to the 21st Law Commission of India for detailed examination.
"After extensive research, the Commission published its Consultation Paper on Reform of Family Law on August 31, 2018. Its conclusion appearing in paragraph 1.15 on page 7 of the Consultation Paper was clear: 'The formulation of a Uniform Civil Code is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage'. Instead it recommended addressing nor discrimination within individual family laws while preserving India's legal and cultural diversity," Ramesh said.
The Modi government has chosen to disregard the findings of the very Commission it tasked with examining the issue because the facts, as usual, did not align with its political agenda, the Congress leader said.
Over the last three years, one BJP-ruled State after another bulldozed through its own version of a UCC, Ramesh said.
The UCC came into effect in Uttarakhand from January 27, 2025. Subsequently the Gujarat Assembly passed the UCC Bill on March 24, 2026, the Assam Assembly on May 27, 2026 and the Madhya Pradesh Assembly on July 21, 2026," he pointed out.
Ramesh said these State-level UCCs, never envisaged in the Constitution, are not uniform.
"They contain different provisions, different penalties, different procedures and significant exemptions. Contrary to claims, the Uttarakhand UCC, the only one in force, continues with a number of patriarchal traditions and is creating many problems for perfectly law-abiding residents of the state," Ramesh argued.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah has made a typically bombastic announcement that a UCC will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before the 2029 Lok Sabha election, he said.
Evidently other NDA parties have lost their voices and are being silenced by the BJP, the Congress general secretary said.
"For the Modi Government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform to be implemented after the widest possible consultations and public debate and with the broadest possible consensus. It is, in reality, an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, a tool for harassment and intimidation, stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation," Ramesh said.
Later, asked about the statement, he said, "The UCC bulldozer is to permanently polarise society."
In a letter to the panel chairperson Justice Ranjana Desai (retd), former Bombay High Court judge Chavan criticised the committee's approach, stating that reducing complex societal questions, such as delayed marriages, perversions, infertility, and rising matrimonial disputes, to binary options undermined the primary purpose of consensus-building.
The former judge said he had misunderstood that the committee aimed to gather views of the people of Maharashtra and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, infertility, unstable marriages, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism and so on.
"Now that the misunderstanding is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses, in a 'yes or no' format to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy," the letter said.
In July, the state government set up a seven-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai to draft a framework for implementing the UCC, which seeks to establish equal laws across religions on issues about marriage, divorce, and property.
Justice Chavan, a former high court judge, resigned from the panel on September 19.
The Congress' statement also comes days after Shah said the BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce UCC before 2029. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.

Last year, Maddie Kowalski was a regular sophomore attending the University of Florida. Then a series of burner accounts on X started proliferating explicit, nonconsensual videos of her. This week, Zoë Schiffer sits down with WIRED’s senior writer Ej Dickson to discuss the burnerverse, a sprawling, loosely organized network of anonymous accounts that have turned the sexual humiliation of young women into an online participatory sport.
You can follow Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer and Ej Dickson on Bluesky at @ejdickson. Write to us at [email protected].

Maddie Kowalski: When I heard that someone had sent a nude photograph of me to his friends at FSU, and in this picture I was heavily intoxicated.
Zoë Schiffer: This is Maddie Kowalski.
Maddie Kowalski: So right after this, I started getting flooded with messages that I was being talked about all over my school's Yik Yak.
Zoë Schiffer: Yik Yak is a platform popular among college students where you can post anonymously if you're within a specific geographic radius.
Maddie Kowalski: Everything was just happening really fast, and I couldn't comprehend any of it.
Zoë Schiffer: What Maddie had heard about was a single photo, but there were a series of videos in which she was visibly out of it, naked, and performing sexual acts. Maddie remembers, well, she was really drunk that night.
Maddie Kowalski: I felt really detached from the girl in the videos because I had so little memory of the events.
Zoë Schiffer: Obviously, she hadn't consented to any of this, not to being filmed, and certainly not to those films being posted online. But now, it was all over X.
Maddie Kowalski: And at this moment, I just felt my whole world collapse. Everything was being shared and reposted so fast, and I couldn't do anything to stop it.
Zoë Schiffer: The videos had officially gone viral. #MaddieKowalski was trending on X nationwide, and it was viewed more than 8.5 million times. For the next 24 hours, Maddie sat paralyzed on her couch while anonymous internet people harassed her. They posted old photos from before the night the videos were taken. They called and texted her parents all throughout the night. One anonymous man told her father that he'd had sex with her and had since tested positive for HIV. People on X were placing bets on whether by the end of the week she would either start an OnlyFans or kill herself. Here's the thing. The people behind this weren't strangers in some far-off corner of the internet. In many cases, they were her literal classmates hiding behind anonymous burner accounts, mostly used to celebrate college sports. From WIRED's Uncanny Valley, I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor. WIRED senior writer Ej Dickson spent months following Maddie's story and what's become known as the burnerverse, a sprawling, loosely organized network of anonymous accounts that has turned the sexual humiliation of young women into a kind of participatory sport. Ej, thank you so much for coming on.
Ej Dickson: Thank you for having me.
Zoë Schiffer: Can you talk us through what exactly is the burnerverse? How is it organized? Who exactly is part of it?
Ej Dickson: So, the burnerverse is a very loosely organized network. It's unfair to even say network because it's just kind of an amorphous community of college sports fan burner accounts. So, they're all anonymous or mostly anonymous accounts. And I think it's important to note that a lot of them are pretty innocuous, but there is a segment of this community that has emerged that is pretty violently racist and misogynistic and antisemitic. And this is the corner of the subculture that has sort of made a sport out of systemically doxing women. So, I initially found out about the burnerverse in February 2025, a few months, about nine months, before Maddie went viral. And I found out about it because I saw this young woman's name trending on X, and her name was Mary Kate Cornett. And I was really curious. I was like, who is this person? And it turned out to be an Ole Miss college student who there was a campus rumor, a salacious, defamatory rumor, about her sex life that had gone viral on campus that had been elevated to the mainstream and was going viral on X nationally because a bunch of prominent people had picked it up. Barstool Sports personalities, Pat McAfee, talked about it on his podcast. So, I was like, how does this happen? How does a girl's name trend nationally based on a completely unverifiable rumor? This is a private citizen. There's no real news interest here. How does this happen? And that's how I started digging into the burnerverse and how burner accounts made her name go viral.
Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, she gets alerted to the fact that these images and videos are going viral on campus. What was her immediate response? What avenues were available to her, I guess, in terms of reporting or getting the content taken down?
Ej Dickson: So, she had the presence of mind to go to the police department in Gainesville, where she went to school, fairly early. And she was receiving harassing phone calls basically every second of the day at that point from these burner accounts, calling her slut, calling her parents, telling that she had AIDS, that she was a crack whore. Just the most horrible things you can possibly imagine. She couldn't even turn off her phone, she told me, because her phone was ringing so much. She couldn't even press the button to turn it off. And so, she went to the Gainesville Police Department to complain about this, and they basically just told her, "Change your phone number." And she was like, "Oh, OK. Well, that's not really going to do anything." Also, the university contacted her because the university found out about the images going viral before she did, even. That's how massively widespread they were. And they opened up a Title IX investigation, but it was closed after about a month because she says the university told her that there was no evidence that the videos had been filmed on campus, so it was not within their jurisdiction. So, her initial options for recourse were pretty limited, at least at first.
Zoë Schiffer: I'm curious, can you talk through her sorority's response? Were they helpful?
Ej Dickson: I think she considered that one of the biggest betrayals is how her sorority sisters responded to all of this. Her sorority basically disavowed her immediately. They allegedly held meetings discussing how this incident would reflect on them. Many of her sorority sisters blocked her, unfollowed her. Again, I mean, this was a girl who was struggling. She was in her second year of college, 19 years old, drinking heavily, needed support, and your sorority sisters are supposed to stick with you through thick and thin. I mean, you're supposed to be bonded for life. And basically the second that this happens, they completely abandoned her is the way she tells it.
Zoë Schiffer: And eventually, she and her family try and find a lawyer, and you write in the story that it was difficult for them to find someone who could understand the scope of the problem. I believe the line in the story is like, "This wasn't a typical revenge porn case. This was much bigger than that."

If this had been a simple case of a spurned ex-boyfriend posting a nude or a pornographic video nonconsensually, that would've been much easier to prosecute. That's something that law enforcement has seen before, but this wasn't that. This was a network of total strangers posting the nonconsensual intimate images of a girl they didn't even know, for no apparent reason. And there were so many obstacles in the way. They didn't know who was behind these accounts. They didn't know why they were posting them. They didn't know how they had obtained these videos. To this day, Maddie is not sure how her video was leaked. And I also think it really speaks to the real chasm between the speed with which the viral news cycle evolves and the speed with which our legislation evolves. It simply can't keep up.
Zoë Schiffer: So, there's a moment where I believe it's when she's starting to consult with lawyers. What does she ultimately decide?
Ej Dickson: She ultimately decides to go after the burner accounts, the anonymous men who shared her nonconsensual videos. My understanding is that it took a couple of months for the Gainesville Police Department to subpoena X for these guys' records. Two freshmen boys in a fraternity, Theta Chi, who she did not know. And a third man was also charged, who I believe was a former UF student who had transferred at that point.
Zoë Schiffer: You also write that people don't have a lot of recourse in terms of getting X to take immediate action. This is happening years after Elon Musk has purchased the platform formerly known as Twitter. He famously got rid of much of the trust and safety team. The content policies have been relaxed from what they used to be. And so, how responsive was the platform in getting the content to go away?
Ej Dickson: Well, I mean, the platform didn't respond to me when I asked for comment, and I had a lot of questions for them. I mean, I don't think that this would've happened were it not for Elon Musk acquiring X and dismantling the regulations because X's algorithm amplifies divisive or inflammatory content in such a way that it doesn't really matter what's trending. It's just going to be broadcast nationwide. And it's like a game of whack-a-mole. You can file a take-down request, and apparently the Kowalskis said that X was pretty responsive in terms of actually getting the videos down individually once they filed the request because they're legally required to do that because of the Take It Down Act. But, if you remove one, 10 more pop up in their stead. That's just the way the internet works.
Zoë Schiffer: As things stand now, has anyone specifically been held accountable for what happened to Maddie?
Ej Dickson: So, the men are being charged with sexual cyberharassment which is a misdemeanor that is punishable by up to one year in prison and an $1,000 fine. I believe one of them is ... The police department is alleging that he'd financially profited off of her humiliation. When I reached out to Theta Chi, their fraternity, they said that they were on interim suspension and completely disavowed their activities and said, "This is not what Theta Chi is about." I don't know if that was prompted by my reaching out or if that had already been underway prior. I don't want to speculate, but I had said that she will see them posting from parties and stuff.
Zoë Schiffer: And where does this leave Maddie?
Ej Dickson: She's traumatized. I mean, can you imagine the worst moment of your life goes viral when you're 19 years old, and you don't even remember it? She doesn't think she'll be able to date and find love. She thinks this is going to follow her wherever she goes for the rest of her life. And the first time I met her, she wasn't even particularly emotional about it. It was just fact for her. And I was just sitting there. I'm a parent. It broke my heart. And that's the thing that really haunted me after reporting this and what really stuck with me when I spoke to her best friend who's quoted in the article. They stole her youth. They stole her girlhood. They stole her optimism and her sense of hope and belief that she could do something great with her life. Because that's what college is all about, right? You're kind of on the precipice of all of that. And that just seems like the most egregious theft of all.
Zoë Schiffer: Her experience also isn't an isolated incident, right? How far-reaching is this? How many people has this happened to?
Ej Dickson: So, there are degrees of it. All told, I was able to identify about a little less than a dozen women across the country who had been doxed in this fashion and on this scale. They were all young women in their late teens, early 20s, college students or recently graduated from college, conventionally attractive, and they had all been subject to some sort of salacious rumor or had nonconsensual videos or images of them circulating and were perceived to have transgressed the boundaries of sexual norms, I guess, in some way was kind of the unifying criteria. But, the burner accounts were also doing this on a much smaller scale to teenage girls whose photos were posted on college's incoming students' Instagram pages. They were taking their photos and posting them and making fun of their bodies and the way they looked and posting their full names. Girls who weren't even in college yet, incoming freshmen, they were doxing on a much smaller scale. And they do that pretty regularly. Or, they'll take photos of somebody's dating profile, some girl's dating profile or a message, and they'll post it, and they'll release her name and make fun of her. So, it happens all the time. I think that it's really the scale that differs, but the exposure aspect of it happens all the time.
Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, I'm curious how she felt. Like you said, you talked to her after the article came out. Obviously, it's this decision that I think a lot of sources face where it's like, do you not speak out and hope that the story kind of goes away? Or, do you take the chance and try and take back a little of the narrative?
Ej Dickson: That was really difficult. That was something I was really concerned about because I thought that there was a possibility that it could renew the harassment against her. And we had a number of conversations about that. And I think she understood and understands the impact that her story has and that she has an opportunity to speak for other women who have been through this and to sort of ensure that shame switches sides, that she doesn't need to be ashamed of what happened to her. I think she was a little overwhelmed, but she's a very strong person.
Maddie Kowalski: I'd like to end this with something really important. Although I don't have control over what happened to me, I can control what I do moving forward, and I want to move forward with healing.
Zoë Schiffer: Here's Maddie again. We thought she should close out the story in her own words.
Maddie Kowalski: These last few weeks have been the darkest and hardest moments of my life, but I'm still here, and that's something that I'm really learning to be proud of. I'm taking steps to rebuild myself, to feel safe again, and to understand that what happened to me doesn't define me. And I know that this is a long path. I've unfortunately also realized that there are so many women and girls as well as men who go through things like this in silence, feeling alone or ashamed or afraid to speak. And if sharing my story can help even one person feel seen or teach one person why consent and decency matter, then it's worth it.

Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered
- Published
It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules.
Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024.
BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on all almost of the charges.
We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it.
But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end?
What are the 115 charges?
In February 2023, City were charged and referred to an independent commission over alleged breaches that were said to have taken place between 2009 and 2018.
The charges - relating to Premier League financial rules - are:
- 54 x failure to provide accurate financial information from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
- 14 x failure to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
- 5 x failure to comply with Uefa's rules including financial fair play (FFP) 2013-14 to 2017-18.
- 7 x breaching Premier League profit and sustainability (PSR) rules from 2015-16 to 2017-18.
- 35 x failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations from December 2018 to Feb 2023.
City have always denied wrongdoing and BBC Sport has been told they would appeal were they found guilty.
But what does that actually mean?
German newspaper Der Spiegel published leaked documents, including emails purportedly sent between top City executives (some of whom remain at the City Football Group), across several seasons following the club's Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.
It alleged these showed the club had inflated sponsorship revenue from state-owned airline Etihad and state-controlled telecoms firm Etisalat by disguising direct investment from their holding company (Sheik Mansour's Abu Dhabi United Group, or ADUG) as sponsorship income by channelling the funds through the companies' accounts.
This, it was alleged, was a means of meeting FFP rules introduced by Uefa in 2011 - and PSR brought in by the Premier League in 2012 - limiting clubs' permitted losses.
There then followed further allegations of misreporting financial information centred on documents that claimed to show secret 'off-the-books' payments to then manager Roberto Mancini via consultancy fees from a club in Abu Dhabi.
It is also alleged the club gave players more money than was officially going through the accounts so recorded spending was less than it actually was.
City, who have always maintained ADUG is a private fund rather than an arm of the state, refused to comment on any of Der Spiegel's revelations, saying the leaked emails were obtained illegally, and they were an "attempt to damage the club's reputation".
City - along with the companies involved - strongly denied breaking any financial rules. But that did not stop both Uefa and the Premier League launching investigations as a result.
What has been the timeline of the case?
November 2018: Football Leaks allegations emerge with Der Spiegel publishing claims Manchester City breached financial fair play rules.
March 2019: Uefa launches a formal investigation off the back of Der Spiegel's findings.
May 2019: City criticise the investigation and launch an appeal process.
November 2019: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) deems City's appeal inadmissible.
February 2020: Uefa announces a two-year ban for City from European competitions and a €30m fine.
July 2020: City's European ban is overturned after an appeal to Cas.
July 2021: City lose a jurisdiction ruling that allows the media to report the Premier League is continuing to investigate the champions for alleged financial breaches.
April 2022: Der Spiegel publishes a fresh report claiming the Premier League has been investigating the club for three years, providing detailed claims.
February 2023: The Premier League charges City with 115 financial breaches.
September 2024: The start of a 10-week hearing between the Premier League and City on the 115 charges.
February 2025: City manager Pep Guardiola says the club expect to learn the verdict "within one month". Guardiola left the Etihad at the end of last season.
September 2026: Reports emerge that a verdict has been reached, with sources telling the BBC that City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges.
What punishment could Man City face?
It was never expected the verdict would come complete with the sanctions.
We now face a waiting game for even that verdict to officially be made public by the independent panel.
We don't know who was on the panel that heard and ruled on the case, and that will only come once a written judgment is released.
All options are open to the disciplinary commission:
- Points deduction (immediate or suspended).
- Financial penalties (immediate or suspended).
- Removal from the Premier League.
Being removed from the Premier League would mean City lose their membership and are demoted to a lower division from the end of the season.
That could also happen through a points penalty so severe they would effectively be relegated.
What has been said?
The Premier League declined to comment on the case when approached on Friday.
City issued a statement that showed frustration news of the verdict had leaked.
It read: "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.
"As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."
Will there be an appeal? How long would one take?
An appeal from City is expected to be a formality.
City's legal team is being led by Lord Pannick KC, who is reported to charge £5,000 an hour for his services. He helped City overturn their two-year European ban in 2020.
However, considering we are already eight years into this process - and two years beyond the start of the hearing itself - it is impossible to speculate when this could come to an end.
Until now, the case has been watertight, with no media leaks from any of the parties involved.
This is just the latest chapter.
However, while the commission's judgement can be directly appealed against, it is not possible for City to take it to Cas.
What titles did City win and who was affected?
City won the Premier League three times during the period in question.
That includes their first in the Premier League era in 2011-12, plus 2013-14 and 2017-18.
They won the FA Cup in 2011, and the EFL Cup three times - 2013-14, 2015-16 and 2017-18.
Since their 2008 takeover by ADUG, City have won eight league titles, and multiple cups including the Champions League as part of a Treble in 2023.
If the commission choses to hand City's titles to other clubs, this is who could benefit:
Premier League
2011-12: Manchester United
2013-14: Liverpool
2017-18: Manchester United
FA Cup
2010-11: Stoke City
EFL Cup
2013-14: Sunderland
2015-16: Liverpool
2017-18: Arsenal
Could affected clubs claim compensation from City?
Earlier this year, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35m over the impact of a breach of the Premier League's financial rules.
The case - heard by a Premier League commission - relates to the 2021-22 season, when Everton were found to have broken PSR regulations over a three-year period.
Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
The Clarets were awarded £26m in damages and a further £9m in interest.
Clubs who had their league positions impacted by City's offences could potentially claim a loss of chance to win potential honours.
These would need to be individually heard by an independent commission.
How much has the case cost?
This specific case was six years in the making, so legal fees on both sides were estimated at tens of millions of pounds before the hearing even started.
Whichever side 'wins' can be expected to make a claim for costs.
For context, the Premier League wanted Everton to pay the full £4.9m legal costs of their first PSR six-point deduction case.
However, an appeal board ruled Everton should pay £1.7m and the Premier League cover the remaining £3.2m legal fees.
Any costs being paid by the Premier League at the end of the City case would have to be spread across the 20 clubs which make up the league.
Have there been other cases involving Premier League teams?
Comparisons have been drawn to the cases brought by the Premier League against Nottingham Forest and Everton respectively over breaches of PSR.
During the 2023-24 season, both clubs were docked points for making more losses than they were permitted to for the three-year period from the 2020-21 to 2022-23 seasons.
Those cases were of a single charge, were easier to decipher and involved significantly less evidence.
Everton were twice deducted points. For the first charge, they were docked six points - reduced from 10 points on appeal. The second offence led to them being handed a two-point penalty.
Forest, meanwhile, lost four points.
However, these relate purely to PSR.
Why are the Man City and Chelsea cases different?
Chelsea have faced 74 charges of rule breaches, but these were quite different and primarily focused on transfers that happened between the 2010-11 and 2015-16 seasons, including deals for Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o and Willian.
The Premier League fined Chelsea £10m and handed out a suspended transfer ban after admitting making £47m in secret payments.
Importantly, Chelsea reached a settlement with the Premier League in relation to historical regulatory matters that were self-reported.
This has not been the case with City, who have always denied wrongdoing.
The Blues were also fined by Uefa and the Football Association.

Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides.
The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city.
Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives".

In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties.
In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight.
"People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed."
Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians".
Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military".
Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan".
The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following an attack on a mosque at a police compound in north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP.
A group linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack.
Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem.
Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants.
Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed.
Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day.
Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026.
The worst single incident occurred in March, when more than 269 people were killed, external in a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure".
The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism".

Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
- Published
Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality.
More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed.
The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment.
Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties.
Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia.
"People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said.
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility".
While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference".
He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace".
Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe.
This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv.
Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees.
Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s.
Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe said on Sunday, September 27, 2026, days after the revelation that a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked the country's health-system database.

Beibhinn Parsons became Ireland women's all-time record try scorer as they held off a late comeback from Japan to register a 31-24 win in the WXV Global Series at Dexcom Stadium.

Ireland take control in Galway

Hogan once again showed her threat and extended Scott Bemand's side's lead when she finished a nice move from Aoibheann Reilly after the half-hour mark.
A mistake in the Ireland defence then gifted Japan a great opportunity to register their first try before Anna McGann rushed back to stop Nami Asari's run.

After turbulent summer, England head into winter schedule
LONDON, Sept 27 : England’s emphatic win over Sri Lanka in the last clash of their three-match One Day International series on Sunday brought down the curtain on a tumultuous home summer but there will be hardly any rest as the team head out on the road.
The sudden and shock retirement of captain Ben Stokes, the sacking of Brendon McCullum as test coach and more off-field incidents punctuated recent months as England played Test series against New Zealand and Pakistan and beat both India and Sri Lanka in ODI and Twenty20 contests.
They suffered a 2-1 Test series defeat to New Zealand, with Stokes quitting and McCullum being sacked, although he kept his role as coach of the ODI and T20 teams.
Stokes had been left out for the second test against New Zealand in June after breaking a team curfew and then announced his retirement from international cricket during the third test, which they went on to lose by 160 runs, citing exhaustion.
With Joe Root returning as captain, England were back on track with a one-sided 3-0 Test series win over Pakistan, who were hampered by their own problems and proved disjointed opponents.
But even then the build-up to the second Test was overshadowed by an incident involving bowler Brydon Carse outside a nightclub in Derby, where he was handcuffed by police and then dropped from the England squad.
Root described himself as "hacked off" by the growing list of alcohol-related incidents involving England players after the controversy of last winter’s tours, including Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($41,000) following an altercation in Wellington as well as reports of drinking during a mid-Ashes series trip to Noosa.
Now they go off again for winter action, with a tri-series next month in Pakistan that also includes Sri Lanka, then three ODIs and five T20s in Australia followed by a three-Test series in South Africa with former New Zealand captain Stephen Fleming as the new Test coach.
Fleming has promised a more measured approach to the Test side after Stokes and McCullum introduced a brand of cricket quickly nicknamed "Bazball".
England also have three ODIs in South Africa, who co-host the 2027 Cricket World Cup next October, and the one-off, pink ball, day-night 150th anniversary of Test cricket clash against Australia in Melbourne in March.
"I would love to be in charge of the number one Test team in the world. That would be my aspiration," Fleming said last week.

NEW DELHI: Festive shopping for a new fridge or air-conditioner is set to cost more, with consumer durable makers raising prices as higher component and freight costs, compounded by shipping delays, squeeze margins.
Blue Star has raised air-conditioner prices by 8%, managing director B Thiagarajan said. Thomson India plans to raise prices by 10% across categories after Oct, while Intex Technologies is holding off on a broad increase to support festive sales. Haier and Daikin have also raised prices or are preparing to announce increases.
"Commodity prices have been going up because of war and that has been a big factor," Thiagarajan said. Demand for copper from electric vehicles and data centres was also contributing to pressure, he added.
The latest revisions follow increases ahead of summer. Blue Star had raised prices by 8-10% in mid-Feb, while Daikin announced increases of up to 12% from April, depending on the model. Higher input costs, currency movements and revised energy-efficiency norms were among the reasons cited. For TV and appliance manufacturers, the pressure extends beyond metals.
"The consumer durables industry is facing pressure from both sides - sharply higher input costs and significant supply-chain disruptions," said Thomson India CEO Avneet Singh Marwah.
Memory, plastics, metals and open-cell panels have become substantially costlier, alongside freight, he said. Shipments are facing port delays of at least 20-30 days, disrupting inventory planning and production schedules. Manufacturers have absorbed much of the burden so far, but that is becoming difficult to sustain, Marwah said. "As a result, price corrections across categories such as televisions and appliances are becoming inevitable."
However, companies are weighing the need to protect margins against the risk of discouraging buyers during the festive season.
"We are not looking at a broad-based price increase at this stage," said Keshav Bansal, director, Intex Technologies.
Bansal said memory-chip costs were weighing on televisions, while commodities, energy, petrochemicals and currency movements were affecting air conditioners and other appliances.
"Rather than passing this on to consumers, we're absorbing a significant part of these pressures," he said. Intex is using Smart TV bundles, extended panel warranties on select large-screen models, retailer schemes and financing options to encourage upgrades. "Consumers today are willing to spend but are looking more closely at the value they receive," Bansal said.

Westmead Hospital has the longest emergency wait times in Western Sydney
At work one afternoon in late August, a sudden wave of pain hit Adnaan with such force he could barely stand.
The pain in his abdomen and shortness of breath was so intense he left work early, hoping bed rest might ease it.
By 5pm, it had worsened and he made the call to go to Westmead Hospital's emergency department.
"My dad came rushing upstairs and he saw that I was drenched in sweat," he recalled.
But when he arrived, he was confronted with what he can only describe as a "scary" scene.
"It just felt like a zombie apocalypse,"
"It was pretty much full, all the seats were taken, people were on the floor, some people were standing."
Adnaan, who wants to be identified only by his first name, spent the next 23 hours waiting on a hard chair.
By the next afternoon, with admission still hours away and no bed in sight, he decided to leave against medical advice, despite being told his kidney was slightly ruptured.
He said staff told him there were only three doctors on for 144 patients.
"They said to me very clearly that we do not have anything available right now … we've got no beds,"
Westmead worst performing in Western Sydney
Health figures released this month show Westmead, one of Sydney's largest hospitals, has the longest ED wait times of any hospital in its own district.
Just 49.1 per cent of patients start treatment on time, the lowest rate in Western Sydney, below Auburn, Mount Druitt and Blacktown.
The average wait is six hours 30 minutes, compared to a state average of three hours 49 minutes.
The median time for patients admitted or transferred was 16 hours 35 minutes, up 81 minutes on last year, the steepest deterioration of any measure at the hospital.
The Australian Medical Association's NSW president Fred Betros said the data showed EDs were under unprecedented pressure, with a record 395,000 ambulance responses statewide last quarter and a sharp rise in the sickest patients.
"They bypass the front door, they go straight into places like our resuscitation bays," Dr Betros said.
"The people out front with less urgent but still serious conditions … just wait longer."
He said such experiences like Adnaan's were common.
"I'm a general surgeon so I do a moderate amount of on call … I spend a significant amount of my time every on-call shift bringing patients out from the front of the emergency department, apologising to them that we don't have a bed for them," he said.
Health district apologises, points to rising demand
Western Sydney Local Health District, which runs Westmead, said the hospital was the district's major tertiary and quaternary referral centre and one of the busiest in the state.
It said Westmead saw a higher volume of complex, critically unwell patients than other hospitals in the district, including major trauma cases and patients needing advanced diagnostics.
A district spokesperson said it understood long waits could be distressing for patients and their families and apologised to those who waited longer than expected for care.
The district confirmed it had also reached out to apologise directly to Adnaan for the distress he experienced during his stay.
Minister points to bed block
NSW Health Minister Ryan Park acknowledged the wait times were "not good enough", and pointed to bed block, where aged care and NDIS patients are stuck in hospital awaiting package placements, as a key driver.
Minister Park also personally called Adnaan to apologise for his experience.
"This is not a buck passing exercise, it's just the reality of an acute hospital,"
NSW Health said one in eight ED-accessible beds statewide could not be used because patients were stuck waiting on aged care or NDIS placements, up from about one in 10 in 2025.
The government said it had committed $35.7 million to an Aged Care Response Package, and $38 million specifically to Westmead for more beds, staff and services, though Westmead missed out on a separate $130.7 million short stay unit expansion at six other hospitals.
NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said the government was not delivering.
"They keep talking about additional beds but they haven't delivered any of them," she said.
Federal government pushes back
A spokesperson for the federal Department of Health said a January funding deal delivered an extra $25 billion in hospital funding nationally, including $6.5 billion to NSW over five years.
The spokesperson said the Commonwealth also offered states a ring fenced $2 billion specifically for aged care, which the states rejected, choosing to direct the funding into hospital systems instead.
"We worked with the states and territories in good faith, and it is now time for them to deliver on their promises," the spokesperson said.
The department pointed to a $3.7 billion aged care investment in this year's budget and about 5,000 additional aged care beds being built nationally each year.
Shaping up as a key voting issue
With Western Sydney one of the fastest growing regions in the country, Dr Betros said capacity in the region's hospitals had not kept pace.
"We're already at that stage where we can't absorb any more demand," he said.
"Goodwill's only going to go so far."
With the NSW election due in March 2027, Dr Betros said hospital wait times would shape up as a key election issue.
"The people of Western Sydney … actually deserve better health care," he said.
Adnaan's pain has since eased with medication, but he still does not have a diagnosis and is waiting to see a specialist.
"I feel like if we can't even fix something as simple as the hospital system, then a lot of people will lose their lives," he said.
"It's made me rethink … who I do vote for."

Unlike most conglomerate-owned media companies, National Geographic is still pouring money into documentaries. Their latest docuseries “Africa Earth’s Wild Home” is a seven-parter that took four years to make and employed over 50 people. It’s the first series in a multi-year franchise that will document the planet, one continent at a time.
Nat Geo partnered with National Geographic Society’s global community of Explorers and scientists and Rolex’s Perpetual Planet Initiative to make the seven-series franchise.
Nat Geo president Courteney Monroe says that the partnership demonstrates a “shared commitment to protecting our natural world.”
“It’s proof of what’s possible when storytelling, science and a shared sense of purpose come together,” says Monroe. “Through this collaboration, we are expanding what natural history storytelling can reveal, whose voices it can elevate and how deeply it can connect audiences to the wonders of our planet.”
“Africa Earth’s Wild Home” is narrated and executive produced by Academy Award nominee Wunmi Mosaku. It was filmed in nearly 30 African countries and used new technology and cutting-edge CGI to reveal the continent’s history and the forces that shaped its natural environments. To capture how Africa’s varied ecosystems shape the animals that live within them, film crews were sent to deserts, forests, jungles, mountains and islands.
Showrunner and series editor Gavin Boyland says Africa became the first continent in the multi-year franchise because people often associate wildlife with Africa.
“Africa got the best wildlife,” says Boyland. “It’s got the most spectacle. It’s got the charismatic animals. So, what we wanted to do from the outset is show people a different side of Africa. So, while we absolutely filmed lions and elephants and all the kind of familiar wildlife, but we also wanted to show different environments, different landscapes and different species that live in those landscapes as well.”
Instead of reaching out to typical Western researchers and scientists, Boyland and his team went to Africa and approached wildlife guides, drivers, photographers, and locals who saw wildlife daily.
“Those people were able to point us towards new behaviors,” says Boyland.
“Africa Earth’s Wild Home” features sequences that have never been filmed before, including the smallest crocodile hunting bats in pitch-black caves, a grumpy black rain frog, a flying saucer beetle that digs trenches to harvest water from coastal fog, giant “vegetarian” land tortoises hunting birds, golden wolves hunting pelicans three times their size and a male fossa fighting to gain access to a female’s mating tree.
“The series inspires us to look closer, learn more and care more deeply,” says Jill Tiefenthaler, CEO of National Geographic Society. “That’s the same passion that drives our National Geographic Explorers, who are working every day to understand and protect the natural world. With partners like Rolex and Disney, we magnify the impact of their work, inspiring millions to care about our planet and its future.”
The final episode in “Africa Earth’s Wild Home” focuses on conservationists, photographers and scientists whose work safeguarding the continent underpins the series. Both the episode and the series build on a 70-year partnership between National Geographic and Rolex.
“Across seven episodes, the extraordinary filmmaking reveals that protecting Africa’s wild heart starts with understanding its fragile ecosystems,” says Rolex exec Arnaud Boetsch. “By shining a spotlight on the Explorers and scientists working on the frontlines of conservation, the series promises to spark not just wonder but hope for the future.”
“Africa Earth’s Wild Home” premieres Oct. 2 on National Geographic and streams on Disney+ and Hulu on Oct. 3. The series was produced by BBC Studios Natural History Unit for National Geographic.

Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
- Published
Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray after fighting broke out this week between regional forces and the national army.
Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the much smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray.
"Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme.
The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment.
Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody".
Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services.
Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting heightened tension and reports of panic buying.
During the two-year civil which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world.
Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions.
