New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.
Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.
Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland and Sweden were two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.
Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.
The two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”
A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.
“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”
The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”
What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”
Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”
It’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.
What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.
“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”
PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”
Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.
In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary, Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short, White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he made Evelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”
When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”

Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have required Switzerland to curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia.
All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP).
Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amid increasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia.
Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’s decision to mirror EU sanctions against Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the UN.
The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2m francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign.
Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party.
The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy”, leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate with Nato.
Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years.
Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve, leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation.
She also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests.
Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality.
The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.

Tax implications deterring homeowners from letting empty rooms as affordable rentals
In short:
Census data shows there could be up to 13 million spare bedrooms across the country.
Homesharing advocates say clearer rules could encourage owners to rent them out.
But owners say they're wary about complicated taxes, even though there are exemptions.
Homeowner Ali Bradley considers herself one of the lucky ones and would like to pay it forward by renting out some of her spare rooms at an affordable rate.
But the tax implications have so far dissuaded the Brisbane mum, who is now entering the empty nester stage, from doing so.
"Cost and complexity, capital gains tax implications, income tax and also the complexity of regulations," she said.
"From my point of view, we're in a housing crisis. We need a wider range of solutions and we don't need deterrents."
Ms Bradley said the goal would not be to make money, but to provide housing, and in return, she could continue to afford the hefty maintenance bill for her older home.
Boarding was once more common
Property economist Lyndall Bryant has been researching what she characterises as boarding arrangements for several years.
She said these had once much more common, with many younger people who moved to larger cities as students or apprentices renting a room in a larger house.
"That really sparked my interest into, why don't we do that anymore," the lecturer at Queensland University of Technology said.
"Why is it not normal for people to take in boarders, take in lodgers, and provide an affordable housing option for people who need it?"
Dr Bryant said her research had shown there were a few barriers, and chief among them was the fear of taking in a renter or boarder meaning a person was liable to pay both income tax and capital gains tax, as well as the impact it could have on a pension.
People were also concerned about safety and security if they took a stranger into their home, she said.
Dr Bryant said there were overseas examples, including in Ireland, of schemes which incentivised boarders. For example, the government could set a threshold for affordable rent for a room at which a person wasn't taxed.
"Countries are realising that new housing supply is a long way off and we do have a rental crisis and we need to be providing more affordable housing options to people," she said.
"This is also a cost-of-living crisis, so homeowners are trying to make ends meet."
In most cases, board arrangements mean the person is sharing the cost of the house including utilities, internet, power and insurance, rather than paying a certain amount in rent.
There are some exemptions set out by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) where these kinds of arrangements don't attract tax.
A spokesperson for the ATO said this included where children or close family members "boarded".
"These … are usually different from circumstances where a stranger is offered a tenancy at the property, or what is more commonly referred to as 'rent' which tend to lack the element of being a private or domestic transaction and are more commonly conducted at arm's length," they said.
Census data suggests there could be as many as 13 million spare bedrooms across the country.
Federal Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke reignited discussion about these rooms earlier this month in a speech about migration where he remarked on living styles having changed across the years to mean fewer people per household.
He said everyone had the right to choose how they lived.
Some data, including a 2019 survey of older Australians conducted by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute showed only small numbers of people wanted to rent out a room in their home.
Advocates agree renting spare rooms isn't for everyone but say those who want to do so should have clear guidelines.
Calls for clearer rules about boarding
The Homeshare Australia and New Zealand Alliance (HANZA) has long been calling for clearer rules and defined protections for boarders and homeowners.
In Queensland, where Ms Bradley lives, boarders and lodgers are not covered by standard residential tenancy laws in most cases where the owner lives at the premises and rents out three or fewer rooms.
A spokesperson for Queensland's Department of Housing and Public Works said the government was committed to ensuring everyone had access to safe, secure and affordable housing.
No changes to rental laws as they relate to boarding arrangements are currently being considered, they said.
HANZA chairperson Rosie Lawn wanted to see greater action by state governments in the space, saying home share arrangements were one strategy that could help with the country's housing crisis.
Ms Lawn said it wasn't just about renting, but about creating a relationship between the two people, like arrangements about chores or other household tasks.
"I think the government being able to provide clear information to them about how they're protected, that would really help more people step into home sharing," Ms Lawn explained.
The federal treasurer was contacted for further comment on clarifying tax settings for people renting out spare rooms but did not respond to specific questions.

As drones completely reshape how armored vehicles are used on the battlefield in Ukraine, the developers behind the British Army's next-generation tank are taking these lessons into account.
Britain's Challenger 3 main battle tank is intended as a major upgrade over its predecessor, which is in service with both the British Army and the Ukrainian military. The new tank will feature a digital overhaul and new weaponry that make it more compatible with other NATO forces.
"We're taking a load of data from Ukraine" and feeding it into the Challenger 3 development, a UK defense ministry spokesperson told Business Insider at an exhibition near London last week.
The tank has a smart targeting system built primarily for combating enemy armor, but it can be adapted to detect hostile drones, a major threat on the modern battlefield. For protection, the tank is equipped with explosive reactive armor.
New features for the Challenger 3 are modular, meaning they can be swapped in and out, the spokesperson said, adding that Britain has options for drone-related equipment that can be installed as needed.
British Army officers told Business Insider at the UK defense industry exhibition that the UK is learning lessons from Ukraine, not only for the development of the Challenger 3, but for armored vehicles in general, like how they can remain survivable on a modern battlefield.
The officers emphasized that the version of the new Challenger 3 tank that exists today is not a finished product; the core platform will continue to be improved to keep pace with changes in modern warfare.
In 2021, the UK defense ministry awarded Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land a $1 billion contract to upgrade roughly 150 Challenger 2 tanks, which entered service with the British Army nearly three decades ago and have seen combat in the Middle East and Ukraine.
The new upgraded tanks, designated as Challenger 3s, were designed as digital fighting vehicles with state-of-the-art targeting, fire-control, surveillance, and survivability systems. One of the biggest changes is the addition of a 120mm L55A1 smoothbore main gun that fires NATO-standard ammunition, replacing the Challenger 2's rifled gun that used ammunition unique to Britain.
Other improvements include a redesigned turret, better thermal imaging, enhanced armor, and upgrades to the tank's engine, suspension, and other key systems.
There are seven Challenger 3 prototypes, and an eighth is in production. The tanks have already completed their first crewed live-firing trials and are undergoing additional testing before expected delivery next year, which was pushed back from 2025.
The Challenger 3 is at the center of what British Army officers and officials describe as the new "20-40-40" model, a layered approach to armor operations designed to protect high-value assets such as tanks and helicopters by relying more on cheaper drones and robots.
The defense ministry spokesperson said this approach was taken directly from Ukraine, where cheap drones worth hundreds of dollars have been able to destroy armored vehicles that cost millions.
The 20-40-40 model underscores that while the war in Ukraine has raised questions about the utility of tanks and other armored vehicles on modern battlefields, British military leaders still see them as a core part of their strategy.

Soon after the news of Hindutva fanatic Swatantra Bhardwaj getting interim bail for three weeks went out, a 1.16-minute video of him got viral, in which he is with another person who boasts about Bhardwaj’s release and compares him with a lion on the hunt. Bhardwaj then threatens those who had attacked his supporters while he was in detention. He says (in Hindi), “You are like insects.. why did you target my brothers? if they wanted they could have beaten you up.. but for some reason, they followed the law… I will not do anything to you.. tell your father Chandrashekhar Azad (Bhim Army chief whom Bhardwaj compares to Ravana), that this Brahmin lion (referring to himself) will avenge the attack. It is an open challenge…”
Bhardwaj faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and an attempt-to-murder charge for an alleged assault on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Azaad. Pope Leo calls assisted dying ‘false compassion’ during visit to shrine known for miraculous cures
Leo had urged his home state to strike down a law allowing assisted dying before it took effect

Pope Leo XIV condemned the legalization of medically assisted death Sunday as immoral “false compassion,” reaffirming Catholic teaching on the sanctity of life during a visit to Lourdes, the French shrine associated with miraculous healings.
On the third day of his visit to France, Leo again waded into the end-of-life debate unfolding in his native U.S. and countries around the world. The issue roiled French politics for years before lawmakers recently approved legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication.
Leo also met on Sunday with seven survivors of clergy sexual abuse, in what has now become a regular appointment for popes on foreign visits. The aim is to atone for the Catholic Church’s failure to protect its youngest and most vulnerable members from predator priests.
“It was extraordinary,” said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos, who joined four others at a press conference afterward to praise Leo for the encounter, saying he listened and was informed of their cases. “I never thought I would have a pope before me.”
A message about end-of-life care
Leo’s visit to the once staunchly Catholic and officially secular France has been marked by huge crowds — 800,000 at Leo’s Mass on Paris’ iconic Place de la Concorde — and his messaging against abortion and assisted dying.
France’s National Assembly in 2024 enshrined abortion as a constitutional right and recently gave final approval to its end-of-life bill.
On Sunday, the American pope celebrated Mass before some 150,000 people — many in wheelchairs — on the prairie next to Lourdes’ main basilica. He then visited a care center for sick people on the sanctuary’s grounds. He sought to encourage especially those who live in “terrible pain” that they have inherent dignity that no law or algorithm can “eliminate.”
“On the contrary, it is precisely in the name of this inalienable dignity of the human person that we must reject the temptation to cause death under the guise of false compassion,” he said. "What is legal is not necessarily moral,” Leo said to applause from the crowd.
Catholic teaching holds that all human life must be protected and defended from conception until natural death, leading to its firm opposition to abortion, euthanasia and medically assisted dying.
Leo had specifically criticized a medical-aid-in-dying law that took effect on Sept. 12 in his home state of Illinois — the 13th U.S. state with such a law.
Lourdes became a major pilgrimage destination after the Catholic Church officially recognized visions of the Virgin Mary reported here by a young girl in 1858. The site near the Spanish border draws millions of pilgrims each year, especially sick and disabled believers hoping for a cure from the famed spring water in the Lourdes grotto where the visions purportedly occurred.
As a result in Lourdes, where the church has recognized 72 “miraculous” cures as authentic, the question of respecting even the most frail, sick and vulnerable is particularly acute.
Survivors visit Lourdes as part of their healing process
More recently, Lourdes has also become a place of healing for survivors of clergy sexual abuse, and it was chosen as the site for Leo's encounter with victims. Leo met with them in a group and one-on-one in an encounter that lasted nearly two hours, the Vatican said.
The pope "listened to their stories, the pain and suffering they had endured — sometimes, unfortunately, with the complicity or silence of those who could have helped them — and their suggestions for ensuring that this does not happen again,” the Vatican said in a statement.
Olivier Mardi, co-founder of Voix Libérées de Touraine, a survivor group, said he perceived that Leo was a decisive “man of engagement” who had done his homework going into the meeting. He said Leo knew Mardi's case and asked him precise questions.
“He's not fooled; he knows that these incidents will continue and that we must remain vigilant,” he said. “There was an emotional side to it, and at the same time, something very powerful when he spoke.”
The French church has faced a brutal reckoning with its legacy of abuse. An independent report in 2021 estimated 330,000 children had been abused over 70 years by some 3,000 priests and church workers.
Despite criticism of the report’s methodology and conclusions, French bishops put in place an independent system of compensation for victims that to date has recommended the church pay out more than 20 million euros ($22.7 million).
During a meeting with French bishops on Sunday morning, Leo praised their response to victims and urged them to continue. But he also acknowledged that the cratering in priestly vocations in the French church is related to the scandal, given the priesthood is now sometimes viewed with suspicion.
“For priestly vocations to flourish, the priest must be welcomed, accepted, and loved,” Leo said.
Monsignor Pierre-Antoine Bozo, spokesperson for the bishops’ conference, said Leo intentionally wanted to keep the encounter with victims small to facilitate an intimate encounter.
“When it comes to listening to them, you can’t have 50 people in front of you,” he said. “So I think that’s really what the pope chose: to listen so that we can act and respond more effectively.”
Mosaics are a painful reminder of alleged abuse
In Lourdes, Leo was also reminded of a prickly abuse case inherited from Pope Francis.
The façade of one of the Lourdes basilicas was designed by the Rev. Marko Rupnik, a religious mosaic artist.
Rupnik is currently on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them starting in the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks.
His case was covered up for three decades by his Jesuit superiors, and even Francis was suspected of having protected his fellow Jesuit. In response to a media outcry, Francis ordered a canonical trial in 2024, which is ongoing.
The Rupnik case posed the question of what to do with his mosaics, which adorn basilicas around the world.
Lourdes Bishop Jean-Marc Micas in 2025 decided to cover the façade of the Notre Dame du Rosaire Basilica, reasoning that abuse victims who come to Lourdes for healing shouldn’t be forced to see the mosaics.
On Sunday, Leo looped in front of the basilica in his popemobile, passing by the mosaic panels now covered by mustard-colored curtains affixed with plastic ties.

Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
- Published
A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after 48 hours of heavy rain left roads in the Thai capital submerged.
People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.
Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested.
The rain is expected to continue into Sunday, raising fears that more canals could burst their banks.
Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now.
"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now."
She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding.
Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding.
The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand.
All 50 of Bangkok's districts have been declared emergency zones.
Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported.
He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled."

Every year, my husband's family gathers on the Sunshine Coast of British Columbia, Canada, for a long weekend family reunion.
They fish, swim, hike, roast marshmallows around the campfire, and catch up on the back deck. The weekend culminates in the annual horseshoe tournament, where the winners add their names to the trophy and we all celebrate with a potluck roast dinner.
My husband, Colin, has been going up to the Sunshine Coast every year since he was a baby. There's a tree on the property that he planted in elementary school that now stands over 40 feet tall.
I started attending with him in 2015, first as his girlfriend and then in 2022, as his wife. And now we get to share this annual family tradition with our daughter.
Last year, our daughter joined the family trip for the first time
In 2025, we got to bring our daughter up to the Sunshine Coast for the first time. Not only was it her first time joining the family trip, but at 5 months old, it was her first trip ever.
It was so fun to bring our daughter along and to introduce her to my husband's extended family. We spent most of our trip out on the back deck, where our daughter lay on a blanket, entertaining her relatives. The fresh air even helped her sleep through the night!
In between naps and nursing, we squeezed in a family hike and a quick swim. But overall, it was a very laid-back vacation with our baby.
This year, with a toddler, it was a completely different trip
When we headed back up to the Sunshine Coast in July 2026, we knew it was going to be a totally different trip than the year before. This time, we had an 18-month-old toddler who was on the move, eating full meals, and only napping once per day.
It was a lot more work to keep up with our daughter this year. Colin and I were constantly checking that someone was with her and taking inventory of everything she might need (toys, snacks, a life jacket, a water bottle, etc.).
But it was also a lot of fun. Last year, she wasn't crawling or walking. But this year, she was running across grass fields, sitting in her own child-size camping chair, and helping herself to snacks from the kitchen.
My favorite part of this year's trip was seeing our daughter bond with her cousins. She was enamored by the big kids, and they totally took her under their wing. I loved watching her play piano with them and hold hands as they walked down trails together.
We can't wait to continue this family tradition with the next generation
When I first joined my husband's annual family trip in 2015, I knew I was so lucky to have this beautiful place to visit every year in the company of the nicest people. The Sunshine Coast became one of my favorite places in the world.
And now the trip is that much more meaningful because we get to share it with our daughter. I love that we're passing on this family tradition to the next generation and that we'll be able to mark the years of her life in annual trips to the Sunshine Coast.
This year, she was thrilled to meet the goats who live next door, go out on the boat to check crab traps, and blow bubbles with her cousins. I can't wait to see what she experiences on our trip next year!

The Opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Janata Dal (Secular) (JD(S)) have refused to be part of the proposed all-party delegation planned by the Karnataka government to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi to seek Central assistance for drought relief.
On Sunday, Union Minister and JD(S) leader H.D. Kumaraswamy and Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Assembly R. Ashok said that they would not be part of the proposed delegation.
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar is leaving for Delhi on Monday to take part in the Congress Working Committee meeting scheduled for Tuesday. The Chief Minister had earlier indicated that the government is seeking a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and an all-party delegation from Karnataka.
Mr. Kumaraswamy said that the State representatives could go on their own, and that there was no need for an all-party delegation. The Chief Minister, at the end of the four-day special session convened to discuss the drought, farm distress, and the Kasturangan Committee report, announced that an all-party delegation would be taken to the Prime Minister to seek Central assistance in drought mitigation efforts.
“What will you do by taking an all-party delegation to the Centre? It will add to the expenditure of the exchequer. Spending on flights and stay in star-category hotels is an unnecessary expenditure. Could someone not go and speak to the Centre?” the Union Minister told presspersons here on Sunday. Stating that he would not say that the State has gone bankrupt, he said: “It is you who has been sitting on an empty treasury.”
Meanwhile, Mr. Ashok said that they would not go to the Centre to seek funds for drought relief. “We are ready to meet the Union Minister with respect to the Kasturirangan report. We will not be part of the drought delegation,” he said. He accused the Congress government of lacking commitment to help the drought-hit farmers in Karnataka.
Central team to arrive for drought assessment
After Karnataka’s first memorandum to the Centre regarding the drought situation, estimating a loss of around ₹18,000 crores and seeking about ₹3,800 crores as assistance from the Centre, a team from the Union government will arrive in Karnataka for a drought assessment on October 3.
The team will be visiting the drought-affected areas for three days from October 4 and will be holding discussions with Chief Secretary Shalini Rajneesh on October 7.
Three Inter-Ministerial Central Teams will assess crop damage and geographic conditions. While one team will assess Tumakuru, Chitradurga, Davangere and Vijayanagara districts, the second team will visit Hassan, Mysuru and Chamarajanagar (it may include Mandya). The third team will visit Yadgir, Bagalkote, Raichur and Koppal districts.
While 177 taluks out of 240 taluks in the State have been declared drought-affected, ground-truthing exercises are being undertaken in another 50 taluks. Deputy Chief Minister and Revenue Minister G. Parameshwara has said that over 200 taluks could eventually be declared drought-affected, with an estimated loss of about ₹40,000 crores.

Srinagar, Sep 22: The ongoing Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly session has come under criticism from All Party Sikh Coordination Committee Chairman and senior political leader Jagmohan Singh Raina, who alleged that the House is spending more time on political confrontations and Jammu-versus-Kashmir rhetoric than on issues directly affecting the public.
The Assembly witnessed uproar over the cancellation of the December 5 holiday commemorating the birth anniversary of Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah, founder and leader of the National Conference. He questioned why legislators were engaging in political confrontation instead of using the Assembly to bring resolutions on issues affecting ordinary citizens.
Raina also expressed concern over what he described as increasing Jammu-versus-Kashmir rhetoric inside the House. He said issues surrounding Article 370 and Article 35A should not overshadow the pressing concerns for which people expect their elected representatives to work.
According to Raina, the Assembly should give greater attention to unemployment, vacant posts in the health sector, shortage of doctors and paramedical staff, and vacancies in educational institutions.
He alleged that thousands of posts remain vacant across different departments and questioned whether the government has a clear long-term strategy to address unemployment and staffing shortages, particularly in healthcare and education.
Raina said every MLA should use the Assembly platform to highlight problems faced by people in their respective constituencies and seek practical solutions.
He also referred to earlier Assemblies, saying that, in his view, legislators had maintained greater decorum and devoted more attention to government programmes, policies and public welfare.

Avalanche sweeps Nepal mountain, killing 2 and leaving 12 missing
An avalanche has swept a mountain peak in Nepal during bad weather, killing at least two people and leaving 12 others missing
KATHMANDU, Nepal -- An avalanche swept a mountain peak in Nepal during bad weather Sunday, killing at least two people and leaving 12 others missing, officials said.
The avalanche hit Mount Himlung, a 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) peak in north central Nepal, said Mukti Prasad Khanal, the chief government administrator of Manang District where the mountain is located.
All those killed or missing were Nepali nationals.
Rescuers brought two bodies and 10 survivors down from the mountain by helicopter to a nearby town, Khanal said.
The search was expected to resume at first light Monday, he said.
Authorities had warned of severe weather across the Himalayan nation over the weekend. It has rained across Nepal since Thursday, with snowfall in the northern mountain regions.
Nepal is recovering from devastating flooding in August that swept several villages, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and nearly 6,000 others missing.

The US and China agreed to set up a channel for handling artificial intelligence (AI)-related incidents, according to an announcement at the end of their three-day summit, even though president Donald Trump has claimed the technology doesn’t need any new guardrails.
Xi Jinping's first visit to the White House produced no major breakthroughs, but experts say it provided them an opportunity to nurture cooperation and set up working groups that could prevent problems from escalating.
The White House on Saturday said both sides would set up a communication mechanism for AI-related incidents, to discuss related risks and benefits, with further AI-specific talks scheduled for November.
During their summit, Mr Xi reportedly told Mr Trump that both nations can and must develop and manage AI “for good”, in contrast to the American president’s stance that safety fears over the technology are “a hoax”.
Mr Xi told Mr Trump: “Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. [We must] ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people.”
AI bosses in recent weeks have sounded alarm over the potential of the technology to threaten the future of the human race. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI maker ChatGPT, said the world was right to be afraid of AI, and the warnings have led to new calls for regulation of the technology.
Two researchers from Anthropic, the company behind the advanced AI assistant Claude, also warned this month that the rapidly progressing technology could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.
It prompted the UN human rights chief to ask AI companies to rein in development of the technology, cautioning that the world was “on the cusp of irreversible change" that could affect generations of humanity.
But at the UN General Assembly last Tuesday, Mr Trump dismissed calls for stricter controls, branding the warnings “a hoax”.
“During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and 'super-intelligence’,” Mr Trump said ahead of Mr Xi's arrival in Washington.
Analysts have cautioned that the two countries’ intense competition in the AI field is likely to reduce either side’s willingness to limit the technology beyond symbolic agreements.
Mr Trump claims Mr Xi had agreed with his push to rebrand AI as “super intelligence". He has instructed government departments to use the term in posts and documents.
The US president has also rebuffed calls for Congress to place new regulations on AI, saying: “The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades.”
Several executives from AI and technology companies attended the Trump-Xi state dinner on Thursday evening, including Mr Altman, Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, Tesla boss Elon Musk and Amazon chief Jeff Bezos.

Child predators are arguably the most reviled demographic in society.
So when someone like Chris Hansen, the former NBC Dateline journalist and host of the To Catch a Predator series, decides to take up the mantle of exposing them to the public, he is naturally praised as a hero.
But, as is revealed in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime—a dramatized snapshot of Hansen’s life at the show’s peak—it’s not as simple as that. Exposing allegedly bad people for public entertainment brings up a lot of ethical concerns and unintended consequences. And while many of the vigilantes carrying out these sting operations claim they are doing a public service, their motivations become a lot more suspect when fame and money are involved.
To Catch a Predator launched in 2004. In the show, Hansen’s team would pair up with civilian watchdog group Perverted Justice, using adult “decoys” to pose as minors online and exchange messages with men in chatrooms and private DMs. After the conversations became sexual, the crew would set up a sting, inviting these men to a home to meet the decoy, only to have Hansen confront them, uttering his catchphrase, “Have a seat.” The men were technically free to leave instead of sitting for an on-camera interview, but often police were waiting outside to arrest them.
The show developed an intense fandom that remains active to this day in subreddits like r/tcap, which has 52,000 weekly visitors, despite the fact that NBC stopped airing the original series in 2007.
In A24's Primetime, a darkly told character study in theaters September 25, Hansen (Robert Pattinson) clearly enjoys the praise and seems desperate for more accolades. He brags to his two young sons that he’s about to be on prime-time television, despite them not understanding the importance of that, and complains that the show has “never won an Emmy or any of the significance it deserves.” When a fan recognizes Hansen on a flight and becomes bloodthirsty, asking the TV host if he ever wants to “bleed” the predators he’s outing, Hansen smiles and admits that what he does by disgracing them on national television is “a little worse.”
In real life, Hansen cofounded the streaming service Trublu in November 2022, where he continues his investigations into alleged child predators. But these days, he’s far from alone. His work has inspired copycats, who thrive on social media and streaming platforms like YouTube, Kick, and Facebook. These groups and individuals are largely disorganized, and as such, hard to track, but a 2022 Washington Post investigation identified at least 160 in the US. Arguably, the people running these operations are more reckless, in part because they’re driven by virality.
One of them, who goes by Skeet Hansen, was featured in the 2025 MTV documentary Predators, about the Dateline show. In the film, directed by David Osit, Skeet Hansen responds to the criticism of the movement by saying, “There’s never been a detective that solved a murder that didn't get paid for it. So why shouldn't I be able to monetize off of catching these guys like the original show and making this content for people’s entertainment?”
One of many issues with that argument is that these hunters aren’t professional investigators—and sometimes they get things wrong.
In April, YouTuber and Kick streamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy apologized after publicly—and wrongly— accosting a man of Indian descent. He accused the man of wanting to “rape a 16-year-old” in a mock Indian accent and called him “Mr. Mumbai.” In March 2025, The New York Times reported that Zdorovetskiy’s tactics for ambushing suspected creeps included beating some of them up, dressing like the Joker; the Times piece found that there have been more than 170 violent vigilante attacks by predator-hunting groups since 2023.
I spent over a year investigating similar groups in Canada for Vice, starting in 2015, and found that some of the people being targeted in stings had severe intellectual and physical disabilities.
Law enforcement groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly denounced vigilantes, noting that their evidence often can’t be used within the criminal justice system and that confronting alleged pedophiles can allow the targeted person to escape before police can step in. In some cases, the so-called predator hunters have ended up being charged with child-porn offenses themselves.
Warning: The following contains spoilers for Primetime.
In Primetime, the catastrophic consequences of these rogue busts culminate in a sting taking down Louis William “Bill” Conradt Jr., a chief felony assistant district attorney in Rockwall County, Texas. Conradt doesn’t agree to come to a decoy house, so both the TV crew and police show up at his home, where he shoots and kills himself. (The real-life Hansen told the Hollywood Reporter he doesn’t regret the November 2006 sting. Neither he nor NBC responded to a request for comment for this story.)
There are no heroes in Primetime, and the movie doesn’t wrap up any of these threads neatly.
At the end, struggling actor “Decoy Dan,” played excellently by Skyler Gisondo, finally gets career validation when his appearances on the show earn him a SAG-AFTRA card, but it’s clear from his expression that he’s not comfortable with what he had to do to get it.
Meanwhile, Hansen’s character, who repeats the phrase “What would have happened if I wasn’t here?” to suspected predators throughout the film, leaves the audience to grapple with that question. The answers are far from black-and-white.

Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti over the last ten days.

- Fortnite pro Swizzy becomes the first player to win back-to-back FNCS Globals in 2025 and 2026.
- He shared his FNCS 2026 Globals win with HavoK pro Pixie and his FNCS 2025 win with Merstach and Queasy.
- Swizzy took home $400,000 along with the FNCS trophy and Axe of Champions with his latest win.
Fortnite Global Championship 2026 (also known as FNCS Globals) has now concluded, and the duo team of Swizzy and Pixie has been crowned FNCS Champions. The European duo, who are part of the esports org named HavoK, came from behind 5th place to climb the leaderboard in their final match.
But what makes this more thrilling for the duo is that this is Swizzy’s 2nd back-to-back FNCS Globals win as champion (2025 and 2026). In the previous FNCS 2025 Globals season, Swizzy shared the trophy with his trio Merstach and Queasy when he grabbed his first Fortnite LAN Championship. Now just a year later, after teaming up with Pixie for the duos format in the 2026 season, he became the first Fortnite player to have consecutive wins at the Fortnite Global Championship.
While most of the FNCS Globals 2026 scoreboard was dominated by vic0 and Malibuca for the most part, there was a high chance for Shxrk and t3eny to take home the trophy with their dominating performance. However, in the final game, after the leaders vic0 and Malibuca got eliminated early, Swizzy and Pixie marched on and continued racking up elims.
Furthermore, their Game 10 Victory Royale also helped put a dub on the scoreboard next to their name, which became a major factor in their win at Fortnite Global Championship 2026. When presenters asked Swizzy about becoming the first-ever Fortnite player to win a Global Championship back-to-back, Swizzy replied, “Bro, this feels amazing. I mean- back-to-back. We are here, and it’s ours!”
When it comes to the prize money, Swizzy and Pixie took home a huge chunk worth $400,000 out of the $2 million prize pool, which was split between the 50 duos. The champs also took with them an in-game Axe of Champions pickaxe, which is the rarest cosmetic item in Fortnite. Furthermore, if you don’t know already, the next Fortnite competitive season, FNCS 2027 will bring back Trios mode.

Spotlight on new coaches as road to Afcon 2027 begins
- Published
Just eight months on from the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) - and with the world still waiting to find out the ultimate destination of the title - the road to the 2027 tournament begins in earnest.
The 48 sides still in contention will play two rounds of qualifying in this extended international window, which gets under way on Thursday.
Two more matches follow in November, with the groups reaching their denouement with the final two fixtures in March.
The top two in nine of the 12 groups will progress to the 24-team finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Preparations for the tournament in East Africa may be lagging behind but, with the three hosts all guaranteed qualification, there is only one spot on offer in their respective groups. That means a second-placed finish may potentially not be enough.
Several managerial changes have occurred since the last Afcon in Morocco and this year's Fifa World Cup, while several star players have hung up their boots. Here's what to keep an eye on in the first two rounds of action.
- Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned 
  - Published24 July
Big names in the dugout
Among several coaching changes, two in particular have caught the eye.
Herve Renard, the only man to win Afcon with two different nations, has returned to the Ivory Coast job some 11 years after leading the West Africans to the title.
The 57-year-old Frenchman starts his second stint with the Elephants at home against Ghana on Thursday in what is the standout match in the first round of fixtures.
In the opposing dugout, the experienced Carlos Queiroz is back at the helm after leading the Black Stars to the last 32 at the World Cup. However, Tottenham's Mohammed Kudus is among a number of players to withdraw from his squad.
Patrick Vieira is another high-profile arrival, as the 1998 World Cup champion with France takes charge of Senegal, the country of his birth.
The former Arsenal midfielder, 50, describes the role as "an absolute dream" yet he will begin with two away games against Mozambique and Ethiopia because Dakar is getting ready to host the 2026 Youth Olympics.
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
Other new arrivals
Cape Verde were one of the great stories of the 2026 World Cup, pushing Argentina all the way in the last 32 before the debutants lost 3-2 after extra time.
Long-serving coach Bubista has since resigned from the Blue Sharks hotseat, with his former assistant Humberto Bettencourt stepping up.
He will begin his reign in Mali on Friday before hosting Rwanda on Tuesday.
Algeria, Tunisia and South Africa have also changed coaches since the World Cup.
The Tunisians have turned to former Esperance and Renaissance Berkane boss Moin Chaaban as they aim to move on from their disastrous World Cup campaign which saw Sabri Lamouchi dismissed after one game and Renard fail to orchestrate a revival.
Pitso Mosimane has been reappointed by South Africa some 14 years on from his last spell in charge - which saw Bafana Bafana miss out on the 2012 Afcon - and Brahim Hemdani has taken over Algeria after Vladmir Petkovic's departure.
Meanwhile, Afcon legend Claude Le Roy has returned at the age of 78 after signing on for a second stint with Congo-Brazzaville.
The Red Devils have not appeared at the finals since 2015, while Frenchman Le Roy is aiming to coach at a record-extending 10th edition of the finals.
Burkina Faso have turned to ex-Comoros boss Amir Abdou and, after a stint with Libya, 2021 Afcon-winning coach Aliou Cisse has his first competitive matches in charge of Angola.
The former Senegal boss starts with a tough away assignment in Egypt.
An era ends
Some big-name players have called time on their international careers since the World Cup, with several of them former Afcon winners.
Senegal are looking for a new number one after Edouard Mendy hung up his goalkeeping gloves.
The 34-year-old helped the Teranga Lions become champions at the 2021 and 2025 tournaments - even if the latter title is still disputed at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
Wing wizard Riyad Mahrez, who captained Algeria to the trophy in 2019, has quit international duty while Ivory Coast will have to cope without midfielders Seko Fofana and Jean-Michael Seri.
Ellyes Skhiri has also called time on his international career and will not be involved as Tunisia aim to reach a record-extending 18th consecutive Afcon.
Meanwhile, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has stepped back from Gabon duty, saying he felt "humiliated" by his treatment after their exit at the previous tournament.
The 37-year-old was excluded from the national team set-up after their group-stage exit. That sanction was later lifted, but Aubameyang ruled himself out of Sebastien Migne's Panthers squad despite his fine start to the season with Deportivo La Coruna.
Return of the Red Sea Camels
Elsewhere, Eritrea are back in the group stage of Afcon qualifiers - for the first time since the build-up to the 2008 edition - after seeing off Eswatini 4-1 on aggregate in the preliminary round in March.
Chad, Djibouti, Mauritius, Sao Tome and Principe and Seychelles are the other five nations already eliminated.
However, seven Ertirea players absconded after the away leg of their tie which was held in South Africa.
Occurrences of Eritrean sportsmen and women failing to return home to what is a one-party state and a highly militarised society has long been an issue, and was part of the reason for the East Africans withdrawing from qualifying for both the 2023 Afcon and 2026 World Cup.
Yet the Red Sea Camels, who have been drawn alongside Kenya, South Africa and Guinea in Group D, are now largely relying on talent drawn from the diaspora.
Just three home-based players have been named in the squad for their opening two fixtures, which see them take on the tournament co-hosts in Nairobi on Saturday before a 'home' game against Bafana Bafana in Cairo on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Somalia have reached the group stage of qualifying for the first ever time but face a very tricky draw alongside Ivory Coast, Ghana and The Gambia.
The Ocean Stars are ranked 53rd on the continent but, like Eritrea, can at least dream of reaching Afcon as the tournament returns to East Africa for the first time since 1976.

FilmNation Entertainment Founder and CEO Glen Basner will receive the Game Changer Award this evening at the Zurich Summit, the annual industry event aimed at fostering transatlantic connections taking place within the Zurich Film Festival.
As part of the honor, Basner participated in an onstage conversation on Saturday moderated by German Oscar-winning director Edward Berger.
Over the course of an hour, the pair dug into Basner’s trajectory from sales rep at his father’s garment business, to heading up one of the world’s top international indie sales, financing and production companies.
Basner and Berger go back a long way, having first met at the beginning of their film careers in the early 1990s at famed New York production company Good Machine.
Watch on Deadline
Basner arrived there from a five-year stint selling ladies knitted sweaters. He had been bitten by the movie bug while helping childhood friend Edward Burns in his spare time on his first film The Brothers McMullen. Burns then invited Basner onto his second feature She’s The One, which was produced by Good Machine. The rest is history.
Berger spent a year and a half at the company from 1994, where his paths crossed with Basner. They have stayed connected ever since, with the pair joining forces professionally again on Berger’s 2024 $100M global box office and streaming hit Conclave.
“32 years later, it’s such a full circle moment,” said Berger as they kicked off the conversation.
Looking back at his time working with Ted Hope, James Schamus and David Linde at Good Machine, Basner said the lessons he learned there had carried him through his career.
“I was taught that you could sell movies around the world and not lie to people… that you can value and appreciate the relationships that you develop around the world and treat people not just as if you’re selling them a product, but that you are really delivering them a work of art, and that you’re there to help support them as they go and release the films country by country,” he said.
Berger suggested working there had also taught them resilience, recalling how just prior to their arrival, the company had nearly gone bankrupt after it wrapped Ang Lee’s romantic comedy The Wedding Banquet.
“It taught us to go through hard times and get stronger… around the time of The Wedding Banquet, the company was basically bankrupt… they decided let’s cancel the photocopier and scrape every last bit together and go to Berlin,” said the director.
The film went on to win the Berlinale’s Golden Bear and then took off at the box office to gross some $23M, against the $1M budget, making it the most profitable U.S. film of 1993.
After subsequent stints heading up sales at Focus and then The Weinstein Company, Basner created FilmNation in 2008, initially uniquely as a sales company.
He said creating his own company had been a natural move for him given his family background.
“My father had his own business, and I wanted to be like my father, so I always had this entrepreneurial bug that I wanted to go out and sort of really test my mettle by being on my own and developing something and seeing if it could succeed,” he said. “So that was something I thought about since the first day that I started working in film.”
Eighteen years later, the company has expanded organically into finance, production and TV, with bases in New York and L.A., and string of award-winning features in its filmography including The Big Sick, Promising Young Woman, Anora, Conclave, Maria and upcoming pictures Bunker, Talent for Murder and I Play Rocky to name but a few.
“The opportunity was clear in 2008. In those days, there were only two strong and dominant, excellent American international sales companies that were unaffiliated with U.S. distribution,” said Basner.
“Pretty much at the same time, they both became U.S. distributors. Summit, which was run by Patrick Wachberger, became a U.S. distributor, and Mandate, Joe Drake’s company, was bought by Lionsgate… so there was this big hole for an American, unaffiliated-with-distribution sales company.”
Sales craft
Talking about FilmNation’s recent slate, Basner said he had wooed Florian Zeller ahead of getting involved in Bunker.
“I told him to his face he was my filmmaker crush of the moment,” he joked.
“You said that to me too,” replied Berger in mock disbelief.
“I know. It was a different moment,” fired back Basner jovially.
He recalled how Zeller had been on the cusp of approaching Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz as FilmNation quietly putting out international sales feelers.
“He had said, ‘If they say yes, we’ll move forward. If they don’t do the movie, I don’t think I’m going to do the movie.’ Fortunately, they said yes, and then we just really started the work,” said Basner.
The film took a traditional pre-sales route thanks to Zeller’s track-record with Oscar-winner The Father, followed by The Son, it’s A-list cast and a “exquisite” script, with the bulk of the international sales tied up at Cannes in 2025. The U.S. deal to Sony Pictures Classics was sealed in collaboration with CAA Media Finance later on, on the basis of the completed film.
“There were distributors that were willing to take the risk. It’s not the easiest thing to say: ‘Here’s the script, here’s the director, here are the actors, and here’s your price’. They don’t really get to sit and have hour-long conversations with the filmmaker to fully understand the movie,” said Basner .
“They have to trust us to be able to articulate exactly what the movie is and what the intention is of that filmmaker, so that they can then decide to take the significant risk on a movie like this of pre-buying the film.”
Talking about their collaboration on Vatican-set thriller Conclave, revolving around the secretive Vatican process of electing a new Pope, Basner said part of the challenge had been conveying Berger’s vision for the film to buyers.
He suggested that on the basis of the screenplay alone – it felt like a story about “a bunch of old men talking in rooms” with a potential $12M to $15M price tag.
“But that really wasn’t the movie that you were looking to make… You talked about The Parallax View being a point of reference for you,” said Basner, referring to Alan J. Pakula’s 1974 political thriller.
“You talked not just about the architecture of the locations, but the architecture of how you wanted the camera to move and the film to feel… all of a sudden this became a political thriller,” continued Basner.
The sales veteran said estimating a value of a film, country by country, came down to a mixture of experience and expertise.
“You’re responsible to hit these estimates. And human nature takes over, and sometimes you can get a little bit conservative to make sure that you deliver,’ he said.
“What we’ve learned over the years is to trust the business acumen and the marketplace experience that we have, and not be too conservative, but actually just deliver the valuation that we think, and be prepared to stand by it in a real way because it’s our money that we’re investing.”
“Part of that is, instead of talking all the time about what the market says and what the market will bear, it’s really about just sitting and listening to the filmmaking team so that you really understand, not what I, Glen Basner, thinks the movie is going to be or should be, but the movie that the filmmaker wants to make.”
Basner revealed he was wary of going down the packaging route of attaching known talent when helping get big projects of the ground, suggesting attempts to mitigate risks on films, whether via the cast or other factors, can sometimes lead to less exciting films.
“Sometimes we have to take more risk on an unknown actor because they are the best person for that role to make the best version of the movie, and we have to trust that filmmaker to deliver on that, not in a naive way, in a thoughtful way, but really trust that that’s really what’s going to drive the value for that movie,” said Basner.
“I really am encouraging everybody to look around, look at what’s working in the marketplace. There are a lot of films that, on paper, did not make sense. The history of our company is predominantly on films that did not make sense to the marketplace at the beginning.”
Conclave clash
Berger revealed they had not always seen eye-to-eye in the final stages of bringing Conclave to fruition.
“After quite a long edit… I was basically done with the film. I’d run out of ideas… I really wanted to go to Venice or at least show them the movie and see if they’d show it,” recalled Berger.
“This was in in May. Glenn got on the phone and made me furious. I hated him. He just kind of said, ‘I’m not sure the movie’s ready, don’t rush it…Venice is going to be expensive, and we don’t have American distribution in place’,” he recalled.
Lead producer Tessa Ross also felt the movie was “missing something” and after test screenings with friends and family sparked an “ok” response, Berger went back to the edit suite and even reshot one or two scenes.
Berger credited Berger and Ross for pushing the extra mile on the film, while his energy levels were low after an arduous months-long edit process.
“This is going back to Good Machine, and what I took from Good Machine… which was you can always do better… whether its budget, contract or the cut of the movie,” said Berger.
“We just edited and edited and edited and made the music again and revised it, and finally something cracked… little things, just shifted and gave us the confidence that the movie was ready. But it was really half a year later.”
Organic expansion
Taking stock of FilmNation’s trajectory since 2008, Basner said the expansion into production and TV had been organic.
“We never really anticipated becoming the company that we have over time, but things changed. One, as we continued to do our jobs and have success, we gained confidence through experience, and we were ready to do things like fund our own films,” he said.
A second development was the convergence of film and TV and other entertainment formats, which has seen the company also embrace TV, podcasts and theater, while retaining its original mission of being a place that enables filmmakers to not just make their film, but to make the very best iteration of their film.
“When we’re at our best, that’s exactly what we’re doing. It’s no more complicated than that. And when we are doing it, nothing feels more rewarding than doing that job well,” he said.
Looking to near-term goals, Basner said the company was ramping up its productions in the arrival of former 20th Century Fox, DreamWorks and Universal Pictures exec Stacey Snider in the new role of Chief Creative Officer in January.
“We are being more ambitious by investing more and making more films. This year we will make four films and a television series, and next year we already have four films in pre-production and hope to make another three,” said Basner.
“The arrival of Snider as the Chief Creative Officer was an articulation of our desire to take more risk and to be more productive,” he continued.
“Working with her these last nine months, you see this incredible creative talent, you see a skill set and a maturity that we don’t have ourselves, or that I don’t have myself, and it is definitely building confidence to invest further. But it’s really also, as she would say, it’s about making it better. The conversation that you had before: let’s take another look at this. Let’s do it a little bit better. That’s something she reminds me pretty much every day.”

Why Premier League faces uncertainty and chaos after Man City ruling
- Published
If you were getting the impression that the saga over Manchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again.
Two years and 10 days since the hearing began, and 1,329 days after City were charged, we now know a verdict has been reached, with the club guilty of the majority of financial rule breaches.
That is not because the Premier League or Manchester City have told us - it is thanks to the Athletic finding out and breaking the story., external
BBC Sport was later told the verdict was sent during the week to club executives, who had to sign a non-disclosure agreement to open the file.
A process can appear to be completely watertight, as this one certainly had been, but when the circle of trust is expanded, the chance of information getting out increases.
Despite this, public silence from the Premier League continues.
City did not address whether they had been found guilty in a statement making it clear - with an appeal expected - that the "process remains ongoing" from their point of view.
It all points to the suggestion that the long-awaited decision of the independent panel was not a case of this process nearing an end, but perhaps instead reaching the end of the beginning.
It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now.
City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion.
The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who have always insisted they have done nothing wrong.
When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole.
And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation.
Enzo Maresca's side go to Liverpool on 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless?
Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing.
Scenario one: Nothing is announced this season on punishments
Deciding the punishment should be quicker than ascertaining guilt, but nothing is certain in this case.
As the charges have been denied, it will have to go to a sanction hearing convened by the independent panel.
BBC Sport has been told this hearing could still be months away, and the result may not be published until the appeal is completed.
At the hearing, everything will be on the table. Fines, points deductions and even demotion.
This differs from Chelsea's case earlier this year, as the Stamford Bridge club self-reported and admitted guilt. That allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League and reach a sanctioning agreement.
It is possible that City could decide to hold their hands up and try to agree a deal - which would be better for the league - though that seems unlikely given the club's consistently strong denials over many years.
The panel will have to comb through the hundreds of pages of evidence and determine the punishment.
Remember, Everton were docked six points, reduced from 10 on appeal, and then two points in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR). Nottingham Forest were deducted four points.
These were considered to be minor breaches, while City faced seven separate charges on PSR breaches in the Premier League alone, as well as a further five related to Uefa competitions.
This aspect alone suggests a large points penalty.
That is before you get into the inflated sponsorship revenue allegedly channelled through the companies' accounts as a means of meeting financial fair play rules, payments to players and managers, and a failure to comply with investigations.
Take all this into account, and it places an asterisk against the Premier League between 2009 and 2018.
Chelsea and Manchester City, two of the competition's most successful clubs, have been part of that. While Chelsea admitted effectively cheating, City have been found guilty. They got around the financial rules to put them in a position to be able to sign more expensive players than their finances should have permitted.
And if this season passes with no decision on the sanction while it is known City were guilty of the majority of counts, what does that mean for the integrity of the competition?
Could a penalty be backdated to this season when finally awarded? Unlikely.
So what if Manchester City win the league?
Coventry are third from bottom right now. What if they finish in that position, are relegated, but would have stayed up had City's punishment come this season?
This inertia is terrible news for the Premier League as a competition.
There's a strong argument that a sanctioning agreement is the cleanest way out of this.
But that may not be palatable to the league as they would have to negotiate with City, who would presumably want a lesser punishment.
- Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation 
  - Published1 day ago
- Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict 
  - Published1 day ago
- Man City legal fight could spiral out of control - Purslow 
  - Published23 hours ago
Scenario two: Man City punishment is levied this season but they appeal
The usual process when any points penalty is handed down is that it is applied immediately, subject to appeal.
It could be a points deduction so large that it is effectively a relegation.
Alternatively, if City's membership of the Premier League was revoked, it is unclear how that might be applied mid-season.
It could also be that the punishment is a huge fine, although that would seem unlikely given points deductions to other clubs.
The question would be how soon we hear, and how long after the appeal is heard.
Usually, the league asks for an expedited process from the independent arbitration company which handles disciplinary cases.
But, as ever in this case, the complexities indicate this is not straightforward.
There is the chance, though slim, that the punishment is only applied to the league table after the appeal.
That would surely lead to protests from impacted teams this season, who will demand it should, as usual, come into effect immediately.
Scenario three: Appeal is heard quickly and full decision announced
For the integrity of the Premier League, so all clubs know what they are playing for, this would need to happen sooner rather than later.
Last season, a points deduction for West Bromwich Albion related to breaches of profit and sustainability regulations was not announced until 24 April.
While ultimately they stayed in the Championship, it plunged them back into a relegation fight when they thought they were safe. It also gave some hope to the teams in the relegation zone.
The Premier League does not want this to drag on until the penultimate month of the season, but nothing is guaranteed in this story.
In this scenario, let's not forget City could also win their appeal, like they did over Uefa's punishment back in July 2020.
While this would be celebrated at Etihad Stadium it would likely not be the end of the acrimony over the case.
Scenario four: Even after the case is closed, this is not over
Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation from Manchester City over the case.
One source, who held a senior executive position at two Premier League sides, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims against Manchester City.
Another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could even be centralised by the league.
Premier League rules allow clubs to seek legal action against each other for compensation.
In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35m after they broke PSR over a three-year period.
Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.
Everton are appealing, with sources previously saying they would "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to the Manchester City case.
There is uncertainty over a statute of limitations, which would set a cut-off point for claims.
Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham Hotspur reportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation two years ago.
This is not just about Manchester United (twice) and Liverpool, who finished as runners-up to City in their title-winning seasons.
It is about those clubs who just missed out on the Champions League, or failed to make Europe, or even those who were relegated.
And it could even result in claims over the prize money for each Premier League place, or the potential commercial earnings lost by rival clubs.
Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport it would be considered a "denial of an opportunity" by complainants.
Maguire explained that the "statute of limitations is not referenced" in the Premier League's traditional handbook, though that could be subject to a legal challenge from City.
But what of the compensation? Just looking at Champions League qualifying could bring huge financial claims.
"The Champions League in those days was worth a minimum of £30m," Maguire said. "I think by the time we got to 2018, it was probably worth £60m or £70m, and that's in prize money.
"On top of that, you could claim for loss of gate receipts, loss of sponsor bonuses. This is highly unlikely, but it's certainly being discussed.
"Players get bonuses for qualifying for the Champions League. Those bonuses, if you talk to people connected to the elite clubs, are normally in the region of 25%.
"An average salary in those days would probably, if you go back to 2012, be in the region of £80,000 or £90,000 a week. Twenty-five percent of that is four or five million pounds a year. That's how the issues stack up."
Points deductions, fines, and compensation claims.
This is an extremely messy situation for the Premier League, and it does not look like being resolved anytime soon.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Expansive red flags raised by two Election Commissioners within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision of voters list triggered a massive political storm on Wednesday, with the Opposition accusing CEC Gyanesh Kumar of indulging in "one-man autocracy" and demanding his removal.
Officials said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voters' list.
The reactions poured in after a report in The Indian Express revealed that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared the screenshot of the media report on X.

Sea level rise is reshaping a beloved California beach town and threatening a busy rail line
After years of erosion, California is bracing for flooding and landslides ahead of this year’s expected super El Niño
