Opponents of Anthropic's Dario Amodei are circulating a highly negative brief about him to the White House ahead of an important dinner with President Trump, per an Axios review of the document.
Why it matters: No company wants to be on Trump's bad side — and a Sunday night dinner between the president and Amodei could be what thaws relations after a year of tension.
Behind the scenes: The brief, which is not an internal White House document, casts Amodei as having "a long record of attacking Trump" and having "deep Democratic ties."
It notes the company's falling out earlier this year with the Pentagon as a "clear example of Dario showing he doesn't trust President Trump."
The brief is intended for Trump's eyes and is likely to get in front of him, according to a source familiar with the internal workings of the White House. Its origin is unclear.
It even reads in "Trump Talk," a name the president gives to his style of posting: "Dario claimed that AI would eliminate half of all entry-level white collar jobs as soon as this year. WRONG!"
Between the lines: The brief's creators are appealing to a president who prizes loyalty and puts a premium on praise.
Amodei's failure to communicate properly with the Trump administration has previously cost the company.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Yes, but: Trump has also been laser-focused on winning the AI race and Anthropic is one of the few companies on the frontier of the technology.
Anthropic is also valued at hundreds of billions of dollars and has plans to go public soon, making it even harder for the White House to ignore.
"The WH is trying to get everyone seated at the table," one source told Axios.
The bottom line: Anthropic and the White House both have something to gain from Sunday night's dinner, so long as Amodei's critics don't get there first.

NATO militaries need to learn how to disperse weapons production, as Ukraine does, before entering a war to preserve their ability to keep producing while under attack, a senior defense official advised.
Raivis Melnis, the defense minister of Latvia, an alliance and EU member state bordering Russia, told Business Insider that industry in the West might not be ready to operate as it would need to in wartime.
Ukrainian arms makers split up manufacturing across multiple sites, operate underground, and even move around to prevent a single successful Russian strike from having a huge impact on their operations. But in Europe, many companies run projects from larger factories, which could become a single point of failure.
"Our industry is a peacetime establishment" that has been built under conditions where "there is no threat," Melnis said.
NATO companies work in a far more concentrated way, he said, and "the question is whether we are ready to produce the systems in different locations, dispersed, and how we organize that."
He said this is why he encourages partnerships between Latvian and Ukrainian defense companies, so they can learn from how the Ukrainian companies operate, including how their systems are "built for war purposes."
Ukraine has also demonstrated how a country "can provide that reassurance if, for instance, an industry site is destroyed." Kyiv offers compensation for some business properties damaged or destroyed in Russian attacks and is planning additional support.
Ukrainian officials and company leaders have been pushing for Western companies to adopt a more disaggregated approach to prepare for the possibility of a wider conflict.
Davyd Aloian, the deputy secretary of Ukraine's National Security and Defense Council, told Business Insider that the Russian threat to Europe is so substantial that companies across NATO should "definitely" start breaking up their production more.
Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian arms maker Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that some alliance defense firms have sought Frontline's advice on dispersing manufacturing operations. The company, he said, has adapted to "endure the loss of any site." Any loss is still "painful," but the company survives. Operations are designed so it's "as easy as possible to move," he added.
Oleg, a company executive at Ukrainian drone maker TechEx, told Business Insider that "every day we are facing another level of threat from Russia trying to hit the factories."
The company, he said, has to find "creative ways to switch the locations every couple of months to raise the level of security for our people, because, of course, you want to take care of the people and keep them safe." He said the company warns its international partners that their conventions are "slightly outdated." He requested that only his first name be used for security purposes.
The CEO of Ukrainian-Estonian defense tech company Ark Robotics told Business Insider that his company makes different components at different sites, something he said is "necessary" even if it's not ideal. A single site is "the best way to do it," but, he explained, the company has to be "smart about it and not create a big enough target for it to attract too much attention or to disclose where our operations are happening."
He said this should be the "default for defense-based manufacturing going forward," even outside Ukraine.
Some companies are already taking heed. Estonian company Krattworks, which makes drones used by Ukraine, agreed with these assessments. Karmo Saar, the company's head of sales, told Business Insider that for Ukrainian companies, it "would be a lot more economical, cheaper, and better to run this operation in one big facility, but they cannot do that."
"In Europe, we do that," Saar said. "And when the war strikes, I think we're going to be punished."
Srđan Kovačević, the CEO of Croatian drone technology company ORQA, which has signed up to begin working in Ukraine, told Business Insider that it is "our deep philosophy that distribution is more resilient" in Ukraine.
"Distributed systems are much more resilient to any disruption than concentrated systems, centralized systems," he said, noting that the thinking appears to be shifting across Europe. "This distributed nature actually reinforces resilience, even though there are economic downsides to it," he added.
Latvia is one of the NATO countries most worried about a Russian attack or invasion and has been a vocal supporter of increased defense spending within the alliance, helping to arm Ukraine, and taking lessons from Ukraine's fight. These lessons are being fed into a new automated anti-drone defense wall and the acquisition of Ukraine-tested gear.
Melnis wants Latvian firms to learn directly from Ukraine's battlefield experience and has announced a series of deals to deepen cooperation between the two countries' defense industries.
He told Business Insider that he wants Latvia's companies to learn from Ukraine's "proven, combat-tested" systems and combine that with Latvia's "peacetime establishment, where our scientist engineers can work and can develop and bring those two together."
Ukraine's wartime experience and understanding, he said, is something for which "you can't just sit in a normal office and build and simulate and create."
Ukrainian companies, he said, work much more closely with front-line units than Western firms do. Ukraine's "military industry has established really close cooperation with the armed forces," he said. "We don't have such experience."
"This is something I want to bring as well, that experience in," Melnis said, saying he wants to "take those best practices."
Deterring Russia, he said, requires strong capabilities and also continued support for Ukraine. Russia wants "to destroy that support for Ukraine," he said. "Therefore, it is important for us to support, and we will be supporting Ukraine to build the victory."

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Bagsewania police on Sunday booked another suspect in the case involving alleged fake IAS officer Tripti Singh, who is accused of cheating people on the promise of arranging government jobs and official work.

The latest US-Canada trade tensions are hitting an unlikely corner of the food market: whey protein. Whey, a by-product of cheese-making, is a key ingredient in protein powders, shakes, snacks, and increasingly popular high-protein foods. Now, manufacturers on both sides of the border are scrambling to deal with tariffs and restrictions that could make the ingredient more expensive and harder to source. The US is set to prohibit imports of several Canadian dairy products, including certain whey products, from 29 September. The move follows Washington's decision to impose additional duties on Canadian dairy products, while Canada has responded with its own tariffs on US goods. The Canadian government has listed whey protein concentrate and several forms of powdered whey among products facing a 50% counter-tariff on US imports. For businesses that rely heavily on the ingredient, the disruption is already being felt. Jim McMahon, chief executive of British Columbia-based Fit Foods LP, told CNN that his company depends on US suppliers because the highly processed whey it uses has limited availability in Canada. “If there’s no tariff relief, it’s devastating for consumers, retailers and us,” McMahon said, according to CNN. The problem is not simply a matter of finding another source of protein. Canadian farmers produce whey, but the country has significantly less cheese production than the US and fewer facilities capable of processing whey into the concentrated forms required by protein manufacturers. That makes switching suppliers difficult. Companies could theoretically turn to alternatives such as pea protein, which is not subject to the same tariffs. But changing an established product is far more complicated than swapping one ingredient for another. Manufacturers may have to reformulate recipes, adjust production processes and rebuild parts of their supply chains. Aaron Skelton, president of the Canadian Health Food Association, told CNN that businesses were already struggling to identify alternatives. “Economic tools can be turned on and off fairly quickly. Supply chains can’t,” he said. The pressure is also reaching the wholesale market. According to USDA data cited by CNN, US whey protein concentrate prices reached a record $13 per pound in June, about 250% higher than a year earlier. Prices later eased to around $10-$11 per pound, but manufacturers have warned that consumers have not yet absorbed the full effect of those increases. That could mean higher prices for protein powders and ready-to-eat products containing whey in the months ahead. The impact will not necessarily be identical across the two countries. Canadian manufacturers face particularly acute supply concerns because of their reliance on US whey, while American consumers could see higher prices as the broader disruption works its way through the market. The latest measures are part of a much wider deterioration in trade between the two neighbours. The US announced a ban on selected Canadian dairy products, alcohol and motorcycles from 29 September, while Canada introduced retaliatory tariffs on roughly $20 billion of US goods earlier this month. For the fitness industry, however, the trade dispute has brought a surprisingly simple concern into focus: keeping protein on the shelves without making it significantly more expensive. You never need a cup of coffee tomorrow. You need it now. An empty bag signals panic, tragedy, and a trip to the store in your pajamas. The WIRED guide to the best coffee subscriptions is designed, in part, to make sure this moment never happens.
The promise of the internet is that you can access the best coffee delivery services in the country, and therefore the best coffee, from anywhere you live. The WIRED Reviews team has been testing and recommending monthly coffee subscriptions since 2018, when online coffee ordering became the norm. I've been writing about coffee on both coasts for more than 15 years, and it's not unheard of for me to go through four bags a week while testing coffee machines.
Featured Products

My top coffee subscription for most people, Atlas Coffee Club, brings in flavors from all over the world in a round-robin. Trade Coffee appeals to the widest variety of palates for cold brew, espresso, or drip. Podium Coffee Club offers wild surprises for true aficionados, among prize-winning coffee.
This list represents the best and most interesting coffee bean subscriptions of 2026. Updated September 2026: I’ve newly tested and added Beanz coffee subscription as a top pick, streamlined WIRED's selections, updated prices and descriptions, rearranged and retested some subscriptions, and updated tariff information.
Best Coffee Subscription Overall: Atlas Coffee Roasters
Atlas Coffee Club offers a true world tour of coffee: high-quality, single-origin beans from a different far-flung part of the world each month. This includes lesser-known coffee-producing regions such as Thailand or Yunnan, China, or a truly rare, chocolaty-nutty bag from Uganda.
Each month, the Austin, Texas-based roaster offers beans from a different region—whether an Indian variety that tastes gently of marzipan, or one from Peru that brims with toffee. Those countries and farms keep changing, as Atlas forms new relationships with growers all over the world. I find the monthly switch to be an excellent rhythm for espresso in particular, since I'm dialing in a new bean for a new flavor each month.
Atlas’ roasts are excellent, the bags look pretty, and the service is outstanding. Because Atlas is the sole importer and roaster of each bean variety, you skip the middleman and save money. Each bag arrives at your doorstep at a price competitive with the premium (but far less fresh!) beans at your local supermarket. Bags are a full 12 ounces—not the diet bags that have become popular among many subscriptions and roasters.
Choose between light-to-medium or medium-to-dark roasts, remaining mostly in the fat part of the bell curve where aromas are most pronounced and easy to extract. Whatever the region or roast, I've also found that Atlas' roasting profile tends to lead to a smooth character that's common among Atlas’ beans. Roaster. Delivery: Every two or four weeks, anywhere from a half-bag to four bags per shipment. Coffee changes each month. Priced $15–$20 per 12-ounce bag, depending on order size. $6 shipping.

After testing multiple months' worth of beans, I can say each coffee from Podium has been interesting, special, or downright unique in some way—especially a bag of beauteously floral and pine-forward beans from Colombia growing legend Elkin Guzman, roasted by Podium cofounder Sam LaRobardiere's excellent coffee brand Theory Coffee.
Expect light-roast beans, best for lovers of drip, pour-over, and Aeropress. (Light-roast espresso lovers will also find a home here.) The Gold subscription is generally excellent, balanced, and aromatic. The Platinum tends to be adventurous, surprising, or maybe just rare: It's coffee that tastes like other coffee doesn't.
So far, I've had no misses. Consider Podium a source of discovery, and an indulgent gift to yourself (or someone you like) each month, to supplement your more usual coffee habit. It does cost what an indulgence costs, however.
Multi-roaster. Delivery: Monthly. $25 (Gold) or $20 (Platinum) per 10.5-ounce bag. Also available in 3-pound or 5-pound bags.
Best Coffee for Espresso Lovers: Bean Box
Seattle-based Bean Box was a pioneer among multi-roaster coffee subscriptions, and it still has one of the largest selections of roasters to choose from if you pick out your own bags. In particular, while a lot of the newest, trendiest coffee subscriptions lean funky and fruity and light, I've found that the curation for Bean Box leans toward depth, balance, and rich chocolate or toffee notes.
Bean Box's full-flavored, rich coffee selections are perfect for lovers of the brown-sugar and coffee notes often favored by lovers of cold brew and traditional espresso. Indeed, Bean Box's espresso-specific subscription is quite the best coffee subscription for espresso lovers that I've yet found. Every two to six weeks, you'll receive a new and expertly curated bag of beans that's good for rich, syrupy shots and full-flavored lattes.
Bean Box's prices are often low for retail craft coffee of this caliber, the bags are big (or at least they're the full 12 ounces), and prices can often beat direct-ordering from the roaster if you subscribe. But take note that for most options, you'll be adding $6 to $8 for shipping on each delivery.
Bean Box isn't just for espresso, however. Drip or pour-over lovers who favor balance and chocolatey notes over funk and fruit may find a home here. Even many of the light roasts meant for pour-over often favor balance and roundness, like a truly excellent single-origin Ethiopia by Seattle's Middle Fork Roasters.
Retailer. Delivery: Once every two to six weeks. Priced per 12-ounce bag.
An Excellent Coffee Subscription From Breville: Beanz
Beanz is a coffee subscription service I had not encountered until quite recently, and it's been a wonderful discovery. This is a smaller coffee subscription, but it's also one of the best-selected subscriptions I've encountered if you're looking for roasters on the forefront of both sourcing and interesting flavors.
If there's a super-special coffee roaster that java insiders like to whisper to me about, it's often available on Beanz. Recent drops included funky blends from Australia's adventurous Proud Mary, a beautifully balanced light roast from Pennsylvania Amish country's cult-popular Passenger Coffee, and a wildly distinctive blend from hipster-beloved YES PLZ out of Los Angeles.
The other surprise is that Beanz is owned by Breville, and by extension Baratza coffee grinders. This means new owners of Breville or Baratza machines get 25 percent off on coffee, with up to hundreds of dollars in savings over the course of a subscription. This is the sort of discount that inspires true loyalty: It means better prices than if I'd ordered directly from the roasters, on some of the best and most exciting coffee in America. Hot dang.
If you don't have Breville or Baratza, prices are still quite good, and the coffee is still delicious. But take note that there's a two-bag minimum on subscriptions—which is less flexible than most roasters if you're a solo coffee drinker.
Retailer. Delivery: Once every two to eight weeks. $20 per 12-ounce bag.
Best Adventurous Single-Roaster Subscription: Equator Coffee
One of my favorite bags of light-roast coffee I tried last year came from Equator Coffee. It was funky, cool, weird, and roasted feather-light, a single-origin bag from Mae Chedi in Thailand with tasting notes of raspberries and aged rum. But then one of my favorite decaf bags came from Equator, too: a lovely single-origin Ethiopian that was gently reminiscent of a chocolate blueberry muffin.
This 30-year-old Bay Area pioneer, once a maverick best known for roasting the French Laundry's house blend from its founding partners' Marin County garage, is now a powerhouse. Equator offers wonderfully diverse tastes, sourced from farms in 50 countries—one of few single-roaster subscriptions to rival any multi-roaster in breadth, depth, and the capacity for surprise.
Equator's coffee bean subscriptions include wild single-origin coffees, espresso-friendly roasts, fair trade and organic beans, and balanced blends. A rotating supply of interesting decaf is also available as a subscription. These days, Equator is maybe the oldest craft roaster to still consistently taste so fresh. Just pick your style and let the coffee come.
Roaster. Delivery: One through eight weeks. Priced per bag, generally $19 to $22 for 12 ounces.
Best Decaf Subscription: Swiss Water
Decaf has come a long way, with a few new-school, more natural decaf makers that have emerged as the jitter-free darlings of the premium coffee world. Perhaps the most famous is British Columbia's Swiss Water, the company behind the Swiss Water decaffeination process, which provides decaf to some of the best premium roasters across the United States. But Swiss Water also offers its own subscription service to bring you some of the very best decaf roasts—genuine heavy hitters that remain full-flavored, robust, and delicate without keeping you up at night.
Retailer. Delivery: Weekly, biweekly, monthly, or bimonthly. Priced per bag.
Best Fresh, Seasonal Coffee: Origin Roasted
No matter where the beans come from, nearly all coffee sold in the United States is roasted in the US, often after sitting in a warehouse for weeks or months. But Origin Roasted is truly globetrotting and truly seasonal. Each month they send a 10-ounce bag of specialty beans that are roasted, packed, and then shipped directly from the same part of the world where the coffee was harvested.
Shipping straight from the source within one to three days of roasting means the beans are not merely fresh, but roasted in season. It also means the beans will be a cosmopolitan affair, roasted according to the tastes of exotic locales. A side benefit is that more of the proceeds from sales go directly to the growers and roasters in their home countries.
WIRED reviewer Michael Calore has been drinking Origin Roasted coffee since the service launched five years ago—and anecdotally, fresh bags roasted when the fruit's still fresh … taste fresh. They also retain floral and fruity notes you can't find in supermarket bags. But Origin's beans are also pretty special, and hard to find. Calore's favorite bags (Jalapa Producers from Guatemala, Azahar from Risaralda, Colombia) are actually cheaper through the Origin subscription than if you tried to find them individually.
Roaster. Delivery: Ships on the last Friday of every month. $25 per 10-ounce bag.
Best Instant Coffee Subscription: Cometeer
Cometeer is unlike any other coffee subscription I have tried. It arrives frozen, as a little pod that you can thaw out with hot water. I was, of course, skeptical. But I couldn't believe how aromatic and straight-up distinctive each roast was, despite being flash-frozen.
In part, that's a function of the coffee itself. Cometeer pods contain brew from some of the finest specialty roasters in the world—Black & White, Onyx, Proud Mary, you name it—that's been brewed and condensed with the power of science, then flash-frozen and vacuum-packed to maintain freshness. All you've gotta do is drop them into a cup, then thaw them with 5 ounces of boiling or near-boiling water. And then, blammo—an oddly terrific cup of coffee, miles above powdered instant or pods. It's not quite the same as a fresh cup: The mouthfeel is different. The flavors are rounder, smushier, and less crisp. But on light roasts especially, the aromatics are big, bold, and wild. I truly enjoy it.
They don't come cheap if you order a single box at a time, but subscription prices are reasonable—about $2 a capsule for very fancy beans. They'll keep in the freezer for months, but you'll need to drink them soon if you thaw them: They keep full flavor for one day at room temp or three days in a cooler or hotel fridge. The introductory box these days is a wild and woolly world tour of coffee beans with 32 capsules from 16 coffee-producing countries.
Retailer. Delivery: Variety packs or single-varietal packs arrive once every four weeks.
Best Coffee Subscription for Rare Beans: Bean & Bean
Bean & Bean sources some of the rarest and most precious coffee beans on the planet, and roasts them to delicate fruition. There are only about 400 certified Q Graders in the United States—basically, the master sommeliers of coffee. Two of them are the mother-daughter team of Rachel and Jiyoon Han at New York's Bean & Bean. Together, they roast some of the world's most exquisite beans, like Geshas from Taiwan and honey-milled Cup of Excellence winners from El Salvador.
You can shop these bags individually. But the more fun option is to let the Hans surprise you with their favorite ridiculously rare light roast of the moment. It's a more expensive subscription than some, and bag size may vary depending on the expense of each rare bean. But you have probably never tried coffee like the bag that will arrive at your stoop.
Roaster. Delivery: Depending on subscription type, anywhere from weekly to monthly. Priced per bag or selection.
Frequently Asked Questions
What Kinds of Coffee Subscriptions Are There?
There are two main kinds of coffee subscription providers: roasters and retailers. Both roasters and multi-roaster retailers sell great coffee. This guide includes both.
Roasters are cafés and small-batch producers who buy raw beans from farmers all over the world and roast them to perfection. By buying from a roaster, you're directly supporting the people who make your favorite coffees. The downside is you usually won't have as broad a selection. Roasters usually sell only their own coffee, but that often means special blends and single origins are available from a roaster that you can't get from a retailer. Your local roaster down the street may also have subscription offers, giving you the chance to buy local without leaving your house—and often catch a discount.
Retailers or multi-roaster subscriptions are coffee subscription providers who buy their beans from many different roasters, then ship bags of coffee to you. A multi-roaster retailer will often have a much broader selection of high-quality coffee available (from multiple brands) to ship to your doorstep—often selected and curated carefully by coffee experts. The downside of some subscriptions is that you're not buying directly from a roaster, which means the coffee may not be as fresh. (That's where this guide comes in. We can tell you how fresh they are because we always test each one and note the roast dates on each coffee bag.)
Subscription Beans vs. Locally Roasted Beans
Look: If you live in a big city with great coffee, the best way to try fresh roasts and new beans, and learn about them, is to go to your local roaster. Nearly every midsize city in the United States has at least a couple of excellent purveyors. Look up your local coffee roasters or visit your favorite coffee shop and ask where they get their beans. Buy the beans. Talk to people. It's fun, if you like talking to people.
Heck, this is also true when you're traveling. The best coffee you can find is often the cup you drink when you're on the road, in a new place, tasting something new. Even if you don't live on the road, it's fun to explore different shops when you do travel.
But the wonder of the internet is that you're not limited to only the best of what's local. Subscriptions allow you to take the temperature of the most interesting roasters from all over the country and world, without going anywhere in particular. Heard about that one roaster in Delaware or North Carolina making crazy coffee with co-ferments and natural fermentation? A roaster in Guatemala highlighting beans from their neighbors? Are you new to the world of premium coffee, and you'd like some help from the curators at Trade Coffee or Podium Coffee Club to learn what you like? Let them inform and surprise you.
This is why you might take a subscription. The world is at your door—even the world you've never even visited. I'm also lazy enough to order subscriptions from roasters a 15-minute drive away, but this is between you and your local ecologist.
But also, sometimes it's homesickness for what used to be local. For me, one of the best in this country is a tiny spot in South Jersey called Royal Mile. They used to be my favorite local coffee shop when I lived in Philly and would drive to Jersey to get the coffee. Now they aren't local at all, because I moved. But through the magic of the internet and the US Postal Service, I can still get their truly wild, surprising, mad-scientist single-origin bags anytime I want. What a privilege.
How We Test Coffee Subscriptions
To test these subscriptions, we try a variety of beans from each service, both our own picks and any curated options. We brewed each bag in different ways to see which beans were best suited to which brewing method. Over the subscriptions he tested, Scott Gilbertson covered the spectrum of grinds with espresso, moka pot, French press, pour-over, and Turkish or cowboy coffee. Matthew Korfhage wanders through espresso, AeroPress, drip, cold brew, pour-over, and a wealth of somewhat unclassifiable devices.
It's worth doing the same if you have access to different brewing methods, especially if you opt for a subscription that offers a lot of variety. A roast that makes a great shot of espresso does not necessarily make the best pour-over coffee, and vice versa. Some roasters, like the excellent Equator Coffee, offer one subscription specifically for espresso, one for decaf, and another for light single-origin roasts that lend themselves to drip and pour-over. It can also be rewarding to take notes on your favorites. Some of these services offer a way to do this on the site, which is handy, though a paper notebook works well enough. If you'd like some more pointers on brewing, be sure to read our guide to brewing better coffee at home.
Are Coffee Subscriptions Worth It?
A coffee subscription service often offers discounts on shipping or the base cost of each bag, compared to buying single bags for delivery. But usually, subscriptions will be premium beans, so it won't be as cheap as the less-fresh, often pre-ground coffee from your grocery store.
But if you're the sort who likes to try the best freshly roasted single-origin Ethiopian or Guatemalan beans from roasters all over the country? This is where coffee subscriptions shine. You're also often getting the best specialty bags a roaster has to offer, or a curated selection from a certified Q Grader—meaning you're a lot more likely to find new roasts and origins you wouldn't have come across on your own.
I have no dearth of local roasters that I love to support. Portland, Oregon, where I live, is perhaps the densest home to craft coffee in the country: Heart, Coava, Stumptown, Roseline, Sterling; multiple national coffee publications; and a craft coffee festival. I've been writing about coffee in Portland and elsewhere for more than a decade.
But a coffee subscription gives me access to beans from all over the country and world. It's a mix of ease and adventure, and a chance to be a barista at my own home multi-roaster café. I enjoy that I can get fresh-roasted beans from a coffee farm in Guatemala that roasts their own impossibly fresh beans onsite, alongside world-famous beans from other farmers right down the road—or taking a world tour each month with beans from my favorite globe-hopping roaster, Atlas Coffee Club.
But for others, a coffee subscription is just a way to get a steady drip of their favorite bag from their favorite roaster, guaranteed to arrive every week or every two weeks. Simple convenience is its own form of worth it.
How Does WIRED Select Coffee Subscriptions to Be Reviewed?
There's a lot of good coffee out there, and I am always trying something new—drip, espresso, cold brew. I've been writing about coffee for 15 years on both coasts, and I'm always on the lookout for new and exciting growers, roasters, and beans. I keep abreast of coffee industry publications like Sprudge, haunt subreddits, consult friends and industry contacts, and take tips.
Coffee can be subjective, of course, and everyone has their preferences. I include my personal favorite roasters among this list, rotate in discoveries I think readers might be interested in, and also solicit favorites from other WIRED (and very wired) reviewers with different palates. But when deciding what subscriptions to include in our curated list, I look into what it offers that others don't. I'm often looking for ones that best serve particular types of drinkers—a new service, a new delivery method, a clever way to cater to what you (whoever you may be) really want at your doorstep each week.
Often, a unique or uniquely useful or just kinda cool subscription model or roaster will be the first I'm in line to test. Other times, I get sent a sample bag of beans, and it sends me over the moon. Always feel free to send a note in the comments about a particularly terrific roaster or subscription.
How Have Tariffs Affected Coffee Prices?
Tariffs matter. So do fuel prices. Pretty much all coffee roasted and sold in the United States is imported. If it costs more to bring into the US, it will eventually cost more to buy.
This is one of many factors that affected coffee prices throughout last year, including extreme weather in Brazil and Vietnam, increasing demand, and relatively flat supply. All of these factors, including tariffs, have contributed to coffee prices rising dramatically in 2025. While coffee prices have dipped a bit this fall after coffee mostly escaped renewed tariff this summer, but prices are still higher than they were two years ago, and coffee roasters are still reeling from the wild spikes of 2025 and early 2026.
Subscriptions can absorb temporary high coffee commodity prices in part by selecting which beans get sent. In many cases, subscriptions are able to charge less than the individual bags you see at the supermarket because of guaranteed sales (the same way subscribing to a magazine costs less than buying at the newsstand).
But coffee subscriptions aren't immune to price hikes, even if they're better suited to weathering the vicissitudes of chance and the market. One service decreased the size of its bags from 12 ounces to 10 ounces last year, while others raised prices only on select bags. One way or another, I tend to see price increases on at least one or two coffee subscriptions every time I check. The volatility of US trade relationships is a key factor.
More Coffee Subscriptions WIRED Recommends
There are so many coffee subscriptions out there, and honestly, a lot of them offer very good coffee—some are even amazing. This list would need to be at least three times as long to capture every one of them. I have way more subscriptions I've loved than I have space to talk about them, so here I've gathered some past picks that we here at WIRED like. Have a favorite we haven't tried? Drop a recommendation in the comments.
Angels’ Cup: Angels’ Cup is more like a distance-learning coffee school than a box subscription service, and the Black Box subscription is like a blind coffee tasting from afar. You will learn what you actually like and dislike about coffee, along with some education through the app, roaster's notes, and notes from fellow tasters.
Mistobox: With more than 500 different coffees from 60-plus roasters, Mistobox makes a good gift subscription, especially if you don't know what kind of coffee to get someone. Somewhere in those 500 choices, your coffee fanatic should find something that will make them happy. One of the most compelling and surprising offerings: Misto lets you choose the most you're willing to pay per shipment, and your offerings will change accordingly. Delivery frequency can also be customized down to the day. We're due for a re-test after Mistobox retooled its website.
Sightglass Coffee: San Francisco's Sightglass Coffee is headquartered right in the middle of the city's South of Market neighborhood, which is SF's tech hub (and also home to WIRED). Just think of all the Github commits, UX prototypes, and vibe coding chatbot prompts that have been fueled by this roaster's beans. The subscription service is flexible, so you can pick to have the same bag sent every time, or you can have them curate the selection so you get something different. My personal recommendation is the single-origin Seasonal Variety Subscription. You'll get a bag of beans from different producers every month. The sourcing is all over the map: Colombia, Ethiopia, Guatemala, Kenya, Mexico. I tried one 12-ounce bag per week for two months, and everything was just outstanding, with unique and distinct flavors from each of the producers. —Michael Calore
Partners Coffee: Partners Coffee is a Brooklyn-based small-batch roaster that offers subscriptions by blend as well as a single-origin option that swaps out every two weeks. Partners roasts and ships all orders within two days, so it arrives at your door as fresh as possible. The whole bean Manhattan roast and Ghost Town decaf are great for those who like light to medium roasts. Even better, you can manage your subscription via text message.
Gento Coffee: Gento is part of a new and welcome trend: growers who roast their own coffee and ship directly from the source. In Guatemala, Gento takes this a step further, roasting beans from other local growers that rank among the most esteemed bean farms in the world. But in this case, the beans might only travel down the road to be roasted. The single-origin subscription is really the play here. Alongside roasts from Gento's own beans from the Prentice family farm, you might find roasts from highly regarded Guatemalan growers like Genaro Juárez and Petrona Perez. If those names don't mean anything to you yet, they will after you try them.
Camber Coffee: Bellingham, Washington, roaster Camber Coffee slipped under the radar for me for maybe too long, but amid its 10-year anniversary celebrations, I finally remedied this. Camber makes distinguished, aromatic, balanced single-origin coffees and a truly chocolaty espresso blend called Big Joy that lives up to its name: it's like a fudge brownie in espresso form. Subscriptions net you 10 percent off list price on each bag.
Sweet Bloom Coffee: Colorado's Sweet Bloom Coffee, unlike most roasters in America, pays attention to the growing season for each region and brings in beans when they're at their best “seasonal sweet spot,” to use Sweet Bloom’s terminology. Sweet Bloom's single-bag Roaster's Choice subscription ships single-origin coffees from small producers around the world, many of which Gear team director Michael Calore had never encountered until the beans arrived, and some from coffee-growing regions that he had to bust out the map to locate. The flavors are easier to put a finger on: Sweet Bloom tends to favor fruity and floral coffees, and presents them in lighter roasts that let all those provocative flavor notes express themselves at full volume. If you prefer bright, slightly acidic, and very fragrant coffees, this is a roaster for you.
Sunday Coffee Project: Portland's Sunday Coffee Project produces some of the most distinctive, funky, fruity, and interesting coffee I know in this country. This could be a yeast-fermented Thai light roast that tastes a whole lot like Sangria, or an Ethiopian so floral you'll swear you got invited to a spring wedding. Plus, the coffee comes in a little art box, designed to look like a coffee-themed children's cereal complete with games on the back and a little cartoon character on the front: maybe a sheep lifting weights or a snake playing tennis. It's a small roaster, and they've dialed back their offerings from weekly new roasts to monthly. But if you like light and adventurous coffee, a box from Sunday Coffee Project may be your favorite thing you get in the mail that month.
Trücup: Are you sensitive to the acids in coffee, but you love coffee? Trücup makes unique, low-acid coffee through what it calls a natural steam process, which makes it a great option for caffeine lovers with sensitive stomachs or those who suffer from gastroesophageal reflux disease or heartburn. (Disclaimer: If you've been diagnosed with GERD, talk to your physician before you try any coffee.) Either way, even those with well-fortified stomachs may want to take note. WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson loves this coffee for a more mellow cup in the afternoon or evening.
Wonderstate Coffee: Wisconsin's Wonderstate, previously named Kickapoo, is quite possibly the nation's first fully solar-powered roaster. Besides being an excellent roaster, it has a long and vocal commitment to paying farmers higher wages. The most recent batch of single origins I tried had a tendency toward light, subtle, mild-mannered, and lightly tannic brews—a cosmopolitan palate that's also Midwestern-polite.
French Truck Coffee: French Truck Coffee got its start in New Orleans and now has a dozen of its signature yellow storefronts scattered around town. Gilbertson is a fan of the Big River blend, which has a deep, rich, and very robust flavor profile that's especially well-suited to pour-over brewing. In fact, French Truck has some of the most detailed brewing instructions around.
Stone Creek Coffee: Milwaukee-based Stone Creek Coffee delivers its fresh, flavorful coffee in big 1-pound bags, with a variety of blends and single-origin options available. The Cream City blend in particular is a delightful medium roast with warmer flavor notes like chocolate and brown sugar, rounded out by fruity flavors—giving the coffee an almost cacao-nib flavor. Add a little milk, and it's almost like drinking hot cocoa. A monthly subscription delivers two bags per shipment.
Fire Dept. Coffee: Fire Department Coffee was created to support injured firefighters and underfunded fire departments all over the country. The coffee is mostly medium and dark—less trendy than a classic, chocolaty profile, especially in the blends. The basic coffee club subscription is best for those who love espresso, or a strong and roasty French press or moka pot. The premium coffee-of-the-month selections veer more medium and are more suitable for those who make drip coffee or pour-over. And what's best, each bag supports a fire department, in what's been among the worst years for wildfires in recent memory.
Grounds and Hounds: We've recommended this as a top pick in the past, for its mix of feel-good donations to animal shelters and excellent roasts. Grounds and Hounds offers small-batch roasted blends and single-origin beans, with 20 percent of its profits going to benefit animal shelters. The brand has some of Gilbertson's personal favorite coffees, especially the dark roasts. (Try the Snow Day Winter Roast when it's available.) Subscriptions are mostly recurring, individual-bag subscriptions.
Birds & Beans Coffee: Like birds? Clear-cut coffee farms can be hard on them. But Birds & Beans is a coffee roaster devoted to making sure its coffee is grown in Smithsonian-certified, bird-friendly farms with tree cover that helps birds thrive. The dark roasts in particular are delicious and genuinely dark: Scarlet Tanager is a favorite of Gilbertson's.

Spacetech startup GalaxEye has secured ₹63.84 Cr in financial support under the Centre’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund to develop its next-generation multisensor satellite technology. The Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), has signed an agreement with the Bengaluru-based startup to provide the support through optionally convertible debentures. The project has a total approved cost of ₹247.69 Cr, the Centre said in a statement. It aims to develop an indigenous satellite capable of OptoSAR imaging at a resolution finer than 0.5 metres. The project will take the technology from Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 to TRL 9, progressing from a demonstrated prototype towards a system proven in operation. GalaxEye's technology combines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and electro-optical (EO) imaging. While optical imaging can be affected by cloud cover and lighting conditions, SAR can capture images through clouds and without daylight. By combining the two, the startup aims to provide high-resolution Earth observation across different weather and lighting conditions. The proposed satellite’s applications include wide-area and long-range surveillance, detection of people and vehicles, and target classification, the government said. “The agreement with GalaxEye reflects TDB’s focus on enabling indigenous capabilities in emerging space technologies and supporting their journey towards commercialisation,” TDB secretary Rajesh Kumar Pathak said. GalaxEye Builds Its Satellite Capabilities Founded in 2021 by Suyash Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, Pranit Mehta, and Rakshit Bhatt, GalaxEye builds multi-sensor earth observation satellites designed to provide high-resolution imaging and geospatial intelligence catering to sectors such as defence, agriculture, infrastructure and disaster management. The startup raised ₹44.2 Cr as part of an ongoing Series A round earlier this year, with investors including Speciale Invest, Rainmatter, MV Core and Mounttech Growth Fund. The IIT Madras-incubated startup has raised nearly $27 Mn in funding to date from investors like Speciale Invest, Mela Ventures, and Anicut Capital. The startup claims to be building the world’s first multi-sensor earth observation satellite and aims to deploy a constellation of indigenous micro-satellites with data fusion capabilities. Earlier this month, GalaxEye received a US patent for satellite imaging technology, the first of its kind for an Indian spacetech startup. The patent covers the core architecture behind the startup’s proprietary OptoSAR technology. This came after the startup launched its maiden OptoSAR satellite under ‘Mission Drishti’ in May, which was touted as India’s largest privately built earth observation satellite and the world’s first imaging satellite using OptoSAR. However, it lost communication with the satellite in July due to an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. The startup is now targeting the launch of two new OptoSAR satellites in the next two years while expanding its in-house capabilities to further strengthen quality, reliability, and execution. Spacetech Funding Enters New Phase The agreement adds to support for spacetech startups under the Centre’s ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund, approved in July 2025 to increase private-sector participation in research, development, and innovation. The fund is designed to finance technology development and commercialisation through long-term capital. It operates through a two-tier structure, with the Anusandhan National Research Foundation acting as the first-level custodian and institutions such as TDB and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council serving as second-level fund managers. According to the government statement, TDB has approved 22 projects with a combined project cost of ₹4,744 Cr, involving ₹2,192 Cr in RDI support. GalaxEye joins other spacetech startups backed under the programme. In May, Dhruva Space secured ₹105 Cr for Project Garud, which aims to develop a standardised satellite platform for large-scale deployments across telecom, earth observation, and national security applications. The public funding comes alongside larger private investments in the sector. Indian spacetech startups have raised nearly $250 Mn in 2026 so far. These include Skyroot Aerospace’s $60 Mn round, which made it India’s first spacetech unicorn, and Pixxel’s $100 Mn Series C to expand satellite manufacturing and imaging capabilities.

As Trump brushes off the need for additional guardrails around artificial intelligence, Bill Gates is sounding the alarm.
In a recent interview, the Microsoft co-founder urged the U.S. government to implement regulations around the development of AI, following a meeting with CEOs of several of biggest AI companies, who agreed it’s necessary to slow down the pace of the growing tech.
“No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said on NBC News’ Meet the Press. “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like. And that has to be a required thing. And it will be a little bit of overhead for the industry, but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”
Watch on Deadline
Gates added, “AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths. You know, so even though it’s pretty hard to get to 100%, there’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools.”
Following recent warnings from those working in AI, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order this month to fast-track stringent oversight and control of AI. Convening “a group of world-leading experts” within the next 60 days, the order lays out a discussion of “safety plans” and “an emergency shutoff, or ‘kill switch,’ for frontier models.”
On a federal level, Trump has brushed off concerns about AI as “a hoax,” insisting the U.S. government “already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies.

JOHANNESBURG – South African police said 27 people were killed in two separate shootings within hours of each other, and they were hunting the perpetrators who attacked patrons at a tavern west of Johannesburg and then later at an entertainment venue east of Cape Town.
Gang violence and organized crime remain rife in South Africa, despite government efforts to curb one of the highest per capita murder rates in the world, including by deploying the army in some areas.
In Wedela township, about 80 km (50 miles) from Johannesburg, 17 people were killed and 15 injured at a tavern, the South African Police Service said in a statement posted on X.
“Suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols,” the statement said of the shooting, which occurred around 9:30 p.m. (1930 GMT) on Saturday.
The motive was unclear and no arrests had been made, the statement said.
In a separate attack in the township of Lwandle on the outskirts of Cape Town, gunmen opened fire in a venue selling grilled meat around 1:46 a.m. on Sunday, police said.
Five people died at the scene and another five died of injuries after being transported to medical facilities, while 11 others were receiving medical treatment, police said.
“Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident with no arrests effected yet,” the statement said.
Crime is expected to be a major issue for voters in municipal elections in November, when the African National Congress is facing further erosion of voter support.
A shooting at a house party near Durban last week killed 11 people, while a series of women’s bodies found near Johannesburg since July has renewed fear and anger over high rates of femicide.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

I’ll admit it: I’ve been a longtime Away apologist. Travel makes me anxious, and my coping mechanism is apparently color coordination. There’s something comforting about seeing my matching suitcases at baggage claim (after frantically tracking them through Find My).
So, I was skeptical when I swapped my beloved Away set for Quince’s Expandable Small Carry-On and Large Check-In Suitcase Set ($270). But my first thought when I opened the box was that Quince had made a compelling Away dupe. Side by side, they have the same shape, proportions, and minimalist look. And honestly, this tracks for Quince. The brand has a talent for producing relatively affordable versions of the things I love: Mongolian cashmere, wellness supplements, engagement rings … the list goes on.
I’ve tested Quince’s travel collection before and was impressed. Its All-Day Neoprene Duffle Bag ($102) and All-Day Neoprene Toiletry Bag ($35) survived a Canyon Ranch longevity retreat in Tucson with me, where I spent a week learning how to optimize every aspect of my existence. If that isn’t a stress test for travel gear, I don’t know what is.
If I were buying luggage for the first time in a long time or replacing an old set, I’d choose Quince. You’re getting polished, durable suitcases with reliable features, and without paying a premium for the brand name. At $270 for both an expandable carry-on and a large checked bag, it's an excellent value.
Away doesn’t offer a comparable bundle, but its Large Flex ($425) and Carry-On Flex ($325) are almost identical to Quince’s Expandable Large Check-In ($220) and Expandable Small Carry-On ($140). All four are polycarbonate hard-shell suitcases with similar exterior and interior dimensions, capacity, and weight, though Quince’s are both slightly lighter. They also have similar features: 360-degree spinner wheels, a Travel Sentry combination lock, a removable laundry bag, and, crucially, a lifetime warranty. After traveling with both, I found them to be equally sturdy. I was also able to pack the exact same clothes in both sets, and the Quince Large Check-In actually gave me more room once expanded.
Even the designs are quite similar. Take away Away’s emblem, and it would be tough to tell these suitcases apart. Quince’s branding is even more minimal; there are no flashy logos, which I aesthetically appreciate, but it does make the bags harder to spot on a baggage carousel. Both brands offer a solid range of colors, so that’s mostly a matter of taste. For me, the more important distinction is the price. Quince gives you essentially the same experience for less money, so why pay double for Away?
To further sweeten the deal, the bundle knocks another $90 off the combined price. And Quince’s value isn’t limited to its advantage over Away. It’s significantly less expensive than comparable luggage from popular brands like July, Monos, Travelpro, and Briggs & Riley. Quince also gives customers 365 days to return unused products, which is a much more generous window than competitors.
I’m sold on Quince’s luggage, and I’m already eyeing its Eco Compression Packing Cubes ($46) and Italian Leather Pouch Travel Set ($72) for my next trip. At this point, Quince has earned a suspicious amount of my trust.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed a draft amendment to the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011, to restrict the manufacture and sale of analogue products as “Paneer” and prevent consumers from being misled about the nature and composition of such products, noted a release issued by the Union Health Ministry on Thursday.
The proposed Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Amendment Regulations, 2026 seek to insert a new clause under Regulation 2.1.1 of the existing regulations, specifically covering “paneer made of constituents not derived from milk”.
Under the proposed amendment, products already licensed or registered under the ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category would be required to discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing.
The proposed amendment is aimed at ensuring that the nomenclature and presentation of food products accurately reflect their nature and composition, thereby enabling consumers to make informed choices.
As the notification is a draft regulation, FSSAI has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public. The draft regulations will be taken into consideration after the expiry of 60 days from the date on which copies of the Official Gazette containing the notification are made available to the public.

During the pandemic, we all heard some variation of “they died with Covid, not from it.”
The phrase is back, this time attached to measles. On Aug. 25, Pennsylvania reported two measles-associated deaths in Lancaster. That day, a county commissioner relayed the coroner’s office’s position that one person had died “WITH measles, but not FROM measles.” (The coroner has attributed that death, an infant’s, to a ruptured spleen; without the medical records or full autopsy, the public can only go on what the coroner has shared with reporters.)
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention then left both deaths out of its national measles update and put an asterisk in the deaths column. Pennsylvania has since reported two more, for a total of four. The CDC added one of these deaths to its data on Wednesday but still does not list the other three.
On Sept. 16, in her first interview as CDC head, Erica Schwartz was asked about the CDC’s decision to leave the Pennsylvania deaths out of its count. She pointed back to Covid, saying that when someone with COVID was hit by a bus, “often that was called a Covid-related death,” and that definitions matter.
Definitions do matter, and the question underneath the “with, not from” phrase is a fair one. A positive test and a death are two separate facts, and people want to know how one gets connected to the other.
That connection is documented on the death certificate, a form most of us will never fill out and may not understand without some background. One of our husbands is an emergency physician and has filled out many. He’s explained the process and has expressed frustration (and anger) over the distortion that’s playing out.
How the form works explains why a person who tests positive for Covid and is then hit by a bus isn’t a Covid death, and why a child who develops fatal pneumonia because of measles is a measles death.
Literally speaking, we all die of cardiac arrest
If we wanted to be literal about it, the cause of death for nearly everyone would be cardiac arrest, since in the end our hearts stop. We don’t record deaths that way because in almost every case something caused the heart to stop. The CDC’s handbook for physicians tells certifiers not to list cardiac or respiratory arrest as a cause of death for this reason. Pennsylvania’s death certificate manual says the same in capital letters: “DO NOT enter terminal events such as cardiac arrest” without showing what caused them.
Death is usually a cascade, and the certificate is designed to capture it. The first part of the U.S. standard death certificate lists the sequence in reverse order. The top line is the immediate cause, meaning the final disease, injury, or complication before death. Each line beneath it is the condition that led to the one above, and the last line is the underlying cause, the disease or injury that initiated the chain of events. The second part is for other significant conditions that contributed to the death without being part of that chain.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health’s training for certifiers uses this example. A patient dies of bleeding esophageal varices, which were due to portal hypertension, which was due to liver cirrhosis, which was due to hepatitis B. The top line of that certificate is the bleeding, and the underlying cause is hepatitis B because the virus started the sequence. Homicide law relies on similar reasoning when a gunshot victim dies of complications from the wound months later. We apply this logic to car crashes and gunshots all the time, and it applies to infections in the same way.
Where the bus story came from
The bus story has a traceable origin. Early in the pandemic, some federal and state officials said that anyone who died with Covid was being counted. Some early tallies came from case surveillance — the fast, preliminary reports that health departments send to the CDC when a person with a positive test dies. Death certificate data follows weeks later and becomes the basis for official mortality statistics. When a Washington, D.C., TV station went looking in late 2020 for crash victims counted as Covid deaths, it found a Florida motorcyclist who had been added to a county’s preliminary tally and was removed after the medical examiner reviewed the death. The CDC’s mortality statistics chief described that correction as the system working as designed.
On the certificate itself, the chain for a person who tests positive and is then hit by a bus starts with the injuries from the crash. If Covid neither caused that sequence nor contributed to the death, it doesn’t belong in part one or part two. The CDC’s certification guidance says Covid belongs on a certificate when it played a role in the death, and a CDC review of Covid mortality data adds that a contributing cause is one the certifier judged significant, not an incidental finding.
So, at least one trauma death did land in a preliminary tally at the height of pandemic chaos and was later corrected, and nothing in the reporting from that period supports the claim that such deaths were “often” counted in official mortality statistics.
Were Covid deaths overcounted?
To be fair, the “with Covid” concern had a real basis in hospitalization data. When hospitals were testing every admission during the Omicron wave, people admitted for something else could test positive and be included in Covid hospitalization counts, as physician Jake Scott described for CIDRAP. Death certificates show Covid’s role in deaths changing over the same period. Covid was the underlying cause on 88% of the certificates that mentioned it from 2020 through mid-2022, and that fell to 76% for 2022 as a whole as certifiers more often listed it as a contributing cause.
Excess mortality offers an independent check because it doesn’t depend on deciding what caused each individual death. It compares deaths from all causes with the number expected in a typical year. The CDC estimated about 299,000 excess deaths in the U.S. from late January through early October 2020, and about 198,000 of them were attributed to Covid. The rest likely reflect a mix of unrecognized Covid deaths and indirect effects of the pandemic.
Excess mortality can’t tell us whether every death was classified correctly. It does show that deaths rose by far more than the number attributed to Covid, so inflated certificates can’t account for the toll.
What this means for counting measles deaths
In the same interview, Schwartz described measles accurately, saying it can cause pneumonia and a fatal brain disease called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Those complications are how measles kills us, which means measles will rarely be on the top line of a certificate. If a child develops measles, then pneumonia, then respiratory failure, measles is the underlying cause because it started the chain. As the American Academy of Pediatrics explained, a child can die from complications of an infectious disease even if that disease isn’t the final condition listed.
Schwartz said the CDC is waiting for the National Center for Health Statistics to confirm measles as the underlying cause on the death certificates, and has asked the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists for a formal definition of a measles death. Underlying cause is the right standard for official mortality statistics, and a clearer surveillance definition would help. Final death certificate data can take months, though, and outbreak surveillance hasn’t traditionally waited for it. The CDC’s measles updates have relied on deaths reported by state health departments, and last year the agency counted a New Mexico death while that investigation was still open. During Covid, fast surveillance reports came first and certificates corrected them later. Holding measles deaths out of the national update until certificates are final reverses that order.
Every death has something that kicked off the cascade. Arguing over whether someone died “with” or “of” a disease gets us stuck on the last thing that happened, when the death certificate asks what happened first, whether that was a fall, a gunshot, Covid, or measles. Schwartz — who also emphasized that the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is safe and effective — has said her priority is rebuilding trust through accuracy and transparency. Showing the public which measles deaths states have reported, which are under review, and what standard is being applied would serve both.
Elana Pearl Ben-Joseph is a pediatrician and senior medical and scientific editor of Unbiased Science. Jess Steier is a public health scientist and founder of Unbiased Science.
