Law must not be weakened at any cost: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann on anti-sacrilege law
Bhagwant Mann met a government panel reviewing objections to Punjab's anti-sacrilege law alongside Akal Takht concerns. He said consultations may refine provisions, but life imprisonment and heavy fines for beadbi must stay.
Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann on Sunday said the Akal Takht is supreme for "all of us" and reiterated that his government will leave no stone unturned to protect the sanctity and dignity of the Guru Granth Sahib through the strongest possible legal framework against sacrilege.
At a meeting with a seven-member committee set up by the Punjab government to discuss amendments to an anti-sacrilege law passed in April, Mann said life imprisonment and heavy fines for those who commit 'beadbi' form the core of the law and cannot be diluted.
The meeting discussed the Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026, objections raised over some provisions, and the way forward through consultation and consensus, according to an official statement.
Mann asked the committee to hold detailed and regular meetings with the panel set up by the Akal Takht to review the proposed amendments, consider its suggestions and work towards a consensus, while ensuring that the law continues to provide the strongest possible protection to the sanctity of the Guru Granth Sahib and brings solace to the "deeply hurt sentiments of the Sikh Sangat".
"The spirit and core objective of the law must not be compromised while discussing its provisions with the panel constituted by the Akal Takht. The provisions prescribing life imprisonment and heavy fines for perpetrators of sacrilege constitute the core foundation of this law. Therefore, the law must not be weakened at any cost," Mann said.
He said the government's only objective is to ensure the strictest possible punishment for those guilty of sacrilege so that no person ever dares to commit such a grave offence.
Mann said certain concerns had been raised about some provisions of the Act and that the government had therefore formed a seven-member committee of eminent intellectuals and legal experts to examine them.
"The proposed amendments will be discussed comprehensively so that an amicable resolution is reached after taking into consideration all legal, constitutional and other relevant aspects," he said.
He added, "I have asked the committee members to hold meetings with the panel constituted by the Akal Takht Sahib so that, through mutual consultation and consensus, necessary amendments to the law can be initiated, if required. Our government will approach this entire process with utmost respect and sensitivity."
The chief minister said the state's objective was clear: the sanctity of the Guru Granth Sahib must remain fully protected and the law must effectively serve its purpose. He expressed hope that the committee's deliberations would lead to an outcome in line with the sentiments of the Sikh Panth and further strengthen the legal framework for protecting the sanctity of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Those present at the meeting included former Akal Takht jathedar Giani Raghbir Singh, Baba Sahib Singh representing Damdami Taksal, and Sant Baba Sewa Singh Rampur Khera.
The Punjab Assembly had unanimously passed the Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Bill, 2026, on April 13. It received the governor's assent on April 17 and was notified as an Act soon after. The Akal Takht later objected to several parts of the law, especially Sikh terminology, the use of the term "custodian" for the religious text, and the assigning of unique numbers to holy "Birs".
Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Kuldip Singh Gargajj on June 29 asked the state government to address these objections within a month. On July 30, Gargajj described the Punjab government's response as "unsatisfactory" and announced a five-member committee to engage with the AAP government on the issue.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

Pickford or Trafford? The battle to be England's number one is now on
- Published
You have to go back 10 years to find a major tournament where Jordan Pickford was not starting in goal for England.
The Everton goalkeeper has pretty much been England's number one since making his debut in 2017 - until now.
Saturday's 3-2 Nations League loss to Spain saw Leeds' James Trafford make his competitive debut for the Three Lions as manager Thomas Tuchel signalled the battle to be number one is on.
Pickford became England's highest appearance maker at World Cups, overtaking Peter Shilton when he started in England's 2026 quarter-final win over Norway.
During Gareth Southgate's tenure there was not a natural goalkeeper to rival Pickford, and that looked to continue under Tuchel as Pickford started all but one of England's World Cup qualifiers and then every game in the summer.
But it looks as though Pickford has finally got a rival in Trafford, with Tuchel saying that the pair get "two consecutive matches each" during this international break.
Trafford has impressed since making his move to Leeds for a deal worth up to £45m.
Against Spain, the 23-year-old showed his quality with the ball at his feet and made an impressive save to deny Ferran Torres in the first half.
But he was beaten three times as England lost their Nations League opener to the world champions.
"I think he deserved to get the two matches, that's why we gave him two matches," Tuchel said.
"He started the Premier League season well and gets minutes as number one at Leeds.
"Jordan [Pickford] did absolutely nothing wrong but we wanted to use this competition to see how far actually James is."
Trafford's journey to possible England number one
Trafford's form this season has helped Leeds to fifth in the Premier League table.
He has kept two clean sheets and now has his chance to stake his claim as England's future number one over two matches.
Trafford had only played 32 top-flight games before moving to Leeds following time at Burnley and Manchester City.
He came through City's academy and joined Burnley for an initial fee of £15m in the summer of 2023.
However, he conceded 67 goals in only 28 matches before losing his place towards the end of the 2023-24 season.
But after starring in Burnley's successful promotion in 2024-25 and the Clarets conceding just 16 goals, Trafford returned to City for £27m last summer with the hope of being Pep Guardiola's number one.
City brought in one of the best goalkeepers in the world in Gianluigi Donnarumma, just four weeks after Trafford's arrival and he became second choice.
Despite it being a frustrating campaign, Trafford did get vital experience and started both the FA Cup final and Carabao Cup final for City before his move to Leeds.
He has been part of England success too, winning the U21 European Championship in 2023 and saving a stoppage-time penalty as Lee Carsley's side beat Spain in the final.
Pickford has been England's reliable keeper
Pickford has kept 46 clean sheets in his 91 appearances for England and has been a huge part of the Three Lions' recent success at major tournaments.
"I think Jordan Pickford will be very disappointed," former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"Putting myself in that place, he will be questioning why he is not in that place. If he is number one, then why is he not playing against the world champions?
"You wonder whether this is the next generation coming through for Thomas Tuchel."
Pickford put in an excellent performance as England beat Mexico in the World Cup to progress to the quarter-finals, but it was not the goalkeeper's best tournament.
"Jordan Pickford has never let England down," Ian Dennis said.
"You have opposition against the Czech Republic and Croatia where you could give James Trafford an opportunity then. I do find the decision quite strange.
"Pickford against the world champions - you would back him to play in this game."
How do the two compare?
Pickford is in current possession of the number one shirt and played every minute of the World Cup until he was rested for England's third-place play-off win over France, with Dean Henderson starting.
The 32-year-old, who will be 34 at Euro 2028, has 91 England caps and has saved four of the 14 penalties he has faced in major tournament shootouts.
In the Premier League Pickford's overall numbers dwarf Trafford's. Since the start of the 2024-25 season no-one has prevented more expected goals than the Everton stopper.
But there is very little between the two this campaign with Pickford preventing more goals but Trafford having a higher save percentage and better passing accuracy.

Srinagar, Sept 23: PDP president Mehbooba Mufti on Wednesday warned that India could “resemble a banana republic” if electoral rolls continue to be altered according to the wishes of the ruling BJP, while praising two Election Commissioners for raising objections to decisions taken by the poll panel.
Speaking about reports that two Election Commissioners had raised objections on several occasions to decisions and positions taken by the Election Commission, Mufti said their dissent was important for the health of Indian democracy.
“Today they are trying to subvert the very fundamental of Indian democracy, which is the electoral process, by, you know, fudging the electoral rolls, which the two Election Commissioners have pointed out,” she said.
She said India and Pakistan, which she described as “sibling states”, appeared to be competing with each other in ways that harmed their own people and institutions.
“I feel that our both the sibling states, India and Pakistan, they are trying to undo each other, competing with each other — who can damage their people the most, who can damage their country the most,” Mufti said.
Referring to India’s description of itself as the world’s largest democracy, she said the country’s electoral process was central to that democratic identity.
“Our country India, which is seen as the largest democracy in the world and which our Prime Minister proudly talks about, ‘mother of democracy’, whenever he is abroad,” she said.
“But if it continues to be like this, you know, where electoral rolls — deletion and addition — happens at BJP’s will, then there are dangers that at some point of time our country, which is the largest democracy in the world, is going to resemble a banana republic.”
Mufti also contrasted the situation in India with developments in Pakistan, particularly the detention of the sisters of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan.
“At the same time, look at Pakistan, which goes around the world as a peacemaker, as mediator of peace, is crushing dissent within its country with an iron hand,” she said.
“Look at — I mean, detaining Imran Khan’s sisters, who are unarmed, who are protesting very peacefully, them detaining just because they are trying to stand up for their brother. What does it speak?”
She said the detention of women protesters was at odds with Pakistan’s international image.
“You are going around the world as a peacemaker and, in your home, inside your house, women who have no weapons in their hands, you are detaining them,” she said.
Mufti said the “only silver lining” she could see was that India still had officials willing to question those in power.
“The only silver lining I can see is that in India we still have people like the two Election Commissioners who have the courage and integrity to question the people in power,” she said.
She contrasted this with Pakistan, saying there were no comparable voices within the establishment willing to question what she described as the “arbitrary detention” of Imran Khan’s sisters.
“It’s a very, very sorry state of affairs,” she said.
Mufti also referred to the deletion of voters from draft electoral rolls, saying the scale of the changes made the independence of Election Commission officials particularly important.
“If we do not have people like the two Election Commissioners, I don’t want to take their name at this point of time. I don’t know what trouble they are going to go through,” she said.
“They will be ED raids now, Income Tax raids now. What will happen to them?”
She concluded by reiterating her warning about the consequences of continued changes to electoral rolls.
“But if we continue like this, I mean, there will be a time when we are going to resemble a banana republic. There will be no democracy,” Mufti said.

Another dedicated app that can help you understand what the doctor has written on your prescription is the Prescription Reader AI: Meds app, which is available on Android. This app is built by MS Productions and is arguably the most feature-packed app designed for this purpose. You open the app, point your camera at the prescription, the app takes a scan, and its smart medication recognition engine instantly detects the drug names and formatting. It converts your prescription into readable text, so that you can make informed decisions. Once the app detects a medicine, you don’t have to manually Google its uses, as the Prescription Reader AI app itself shows you the drug’s uses, precautions, and side effects.
Everything that you have searched for remains in your history, so that you can access it quickly. There is a pill reminder and alarm as well, so that you don’t miss your doses. Not only English; it supports multiple languages, supports light and dark modes, and you can also share or save the readable prescription in PDF format. The Prescription Reader AI: Meds app is available for free, but only available on Android.
Download: Android
Docus AI
While you can still apply some workarounds as mentioned above, to read prescriptions, lab reports are still the worst. A blood test report gives you a wall of numbers, acronyms, and reference ranges that are guaranteed to induce anxiety. Some numbers might look too high, while some may look too low, making a normal person confused. Docus AI helps to solve this specific problem. It is built for heavy-duty medical document analysis. You need to upload a PDF, screenshot, or photo of your lab test (blood, urine, swab, etc.). Using Docus AI’s “AI Doctor,” the app will then compare the specific numbers against standard medical guidelines to figure out exactly what is going on inside your body.
Docus AI breaks down hundreds of biomarkers like cholesterol, cortisol, or thyroid levels and lets you understand if the numbers are high or low. It goes a step further and also explains what these numbers actually mean for your health. This way, you can make necessary decisions in your lifestyle. Based on your results, this AI tool may suggest dietary changes, lifestyle adjustments, or prompt you to consult a human specialist immediately. The free version lets you access features like an AI doctor and lab test interpretation, but you can unlock full potential by paying a fee.
AI Prescription Reader
The name says it all. The AI Prescription Reader is a web tool that is good for those who don’t want an AI companion and don’t want to install an app. The AI Prescription Reader is for people who want a fast, free, no-nonsense tool that gets the job done in five seconds. The good thing about this tool is that, apart from being web-based, it is dead simple. All you need to do is upload a document, or you can take a picture with your camera and hit the Analyze button. The AI runs its OCR magic and gives you a clean, formatted text box with the detected medicine, strength, and frequency.
There is a built-in prescription dictionary as well that you can go through to understand the medical terms that doctors have mentioned in the note. You can also export the deciphered text into a PDF and send it to anyone who needs it. The best part about this tool is that it doesn’t ask you to sign up or sign in using any account. You can use it straight away by visiting its website.
Google Lens/Gemini
This list would be incomplete if we do not appreciate the powers Google Lens and now Gemini have brought to our phones. Google Lens wasn’t specifically built for medical prescriptions, but its world-class text recognition engine makes it one of the powerful tools out there. Recently, I also needed some help, and with the help of Google Lens, I was able to decipher what was written in the prescription, get it checked by the doctor, and it was 100% correct. Though this may not be the case with everyone. It is available for Android and iOS, and you probably already have the Google app on your phone.
It pulls out the medical details about the medicine it has detected and shares them with you, such as what the drug looks like, common uses, and side effects. If an elderly member of your household is using it, they can tap the Listen feature so Google Lens reads the prescription aloud.
Be cautious
Yes, AI is advanced, and things are going in the right direction, but it is to be taken with a quick dose of reality. AI is smart, but it is not 100% accurate. A smudge on the paper or rushed handwriting can still cause the AI to incorrectly determine the wrong medicine. It is easy to confuse 10mg with 70mg for two similarly named drugs. It is always important that you get it verified by experienced medical personnel or the doctor themselves and get the right medicine.

United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) has said they would go ahead with the three-day nationwide strike beginning September 28, as a conciliation meeting before the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner on Tuesday remained inconclusive.
The conciliation meeting was held a day after the Finance Ministry appealed to bank employees to refrain from resorting to strikes and resolve their remaining demands through dialogue.
UFBU, which claims to represent 90 per cent of the banking workforce, is primarily seeking 5-day banking among other demands.
The strike, if it materialises, may impact banking services for five days as the weekend before September 28 is a holiday. It would coincide with the half-yearly closing of the banking sector.
“Responding to the appeal made by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), Indian Banks’ Association (IBA), Bank managements to defer the strike, we informed them that if there is any concrete and positive development towards implementation of our demand for introduction of 5 days banking, UFBU will consider the same,” UFBU said in a statement after the meeting with the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner.
Otherwise, it said, UFBU will be constrained to go ahead with the proposed strike on September 28, 29 and 30.
Representatives of the DFS, Ministry of Finance, informed that the Government has been taking many initiatives for the welfare of the bank employees and the issue of 5-day Banking is also under consideration as they have to take into account the views of many other stakeholders before any decision is taken, it said.
Hence, it said, they requested the UFBU to defer the strike and continue the dialogue. Bank unions under UFBU had gone on nationwide strike on September 11 over their demand.
UFBU’s other demands include an update and improvement of pension, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to switch to the old pension scheme (OPS).
Many public sector banks have started issuing advisories to their customers to use digital channels such as Mobile Banking, ATM, Internet Banking, BC Point and UPI for banking needs if the strike materialises.
The proposed 3-day strike period also coincides with the half-yearly closing of banks on September 30, a date of particular significance for reconciliation, provisioning and treasury and market operations.
A disruption of this nature, combined with the preceding weekend, would result in an effective five-day closure of banking services at a particularly sensitive point in the financial calendar - causing considerable inconvenience to customers, businesses, Government transactions and international banking operations.
Strikes cause disruption in banking services that inconvenience the public, impact the business of the banks, and ultimately harm the interests of bank employees and there is no fruitful outcome that is achieved through strikes, the finance ministry had said on Monday.
The government assured that it remains committed to the welfare and well-being of bank employees and to addressing their genuine concerns through constructive engagement.

LPU suspends classes for 10 days amid campus unrest, midterms postponed
Lovely Professional University suspended classes and postponed exams after violent protests over an alleged rape on campus. Police have registered an FIR and formed an SIT as the university denies the allegation and asks students not to spread unverified claims.
Lovely Professional University (LPU) in Punjab's Phagwara has suspended regular classes for 10 days from Monday, September 28, following violent protests on campus over allegations that a female student was raped by an outsider.
The university has also postponed its mid-term examinations until further notice. A revised examination schedule will be communicated to students through the University Management System (UMS), LPU said in a statement.
The university advised students to remain calm and follow official instructions. Students have also been allowed to travel to their hometowns during the 10-day period in consultation with their parents or guardians.
Those who choose to remain on campus have been advised to stay inside their hostels or places of residence, avoid unnecessary movement and stay away from any unrest-related activities.
MID-TERM EXAMS POSTPONED
In its notice to students, LPU said the decision to suspend regular classes had been taken "to ensure the safety and well-being of all students".
The university said mid-term examinations would remain postponed until further notice. Students have been asked to stay connected through the UMS for further updates.
The decision came after a day of protests and clashes on the campus and a blockade of National Highway-44 by students.
STUDENTS CLASH WITH POLICE
The protests began near Girls' Hostel-3 around 1 am on Sunday after students alleged that a female student had been raped by a plumber three days earlier. The protesters also alleged that the hostel warden had been informed but no action was taken.
The allegations triggered a large protest, with students blocking NH-44 outside the university from around 8 am. Traffic was severely affected as the blockade continued through the day.
The situation escalated in the evening when police attempted to clear the road. Officials said protesters threw water bottles at police personnel, following which police resorted to a mild lathi charge.
The protesters then moved towards the campus and allegedly pelted stones at police vehicles. Two police vehicles were set on fire and four to five police vehicles were damaged, according to police. Several police personnel were also injured.
A heavy police contingent from Kapurthala, Jalandhar Rural and Hoshiarpur was deployed, with a team led by ADGP M F Farooqui later entering the campus.
Jalandhar Range DIG Naveen Singla said the situation had been brought under control and that traffic movement on NH-44 would be restored.
FIR REGISTERED, SIT FORMED
Police said an FIR had been registered against an unknown person based on the complaint related to the alleged rape. A special investigation team (SIT) has also been formed to investigate the allegations.
Singla said investigators would examine forensic evidence, CCTV footage and call records before reaching a conclusion.
The DIG said students had claimed that the alleged victim, who was staying in Hostel No. 3, had returned home after they believed no action had been taken.
Students also demanded that the hostel staff should comprise only women. Police said the university management would address the demand.
Singla also said a female student from Telangana studying at LPU had died by suicide around 15 days earlier. He said action would be taken if the students' allegations of foul play were established.
LPU DENIES RAPE ALLEGATION
LPU has denied that a rape took place on its campus, describing the allegations as rumours.
Registrar Monica Gulati said "false, baseless and fabricated" allegations were being circulated by anti-social elements to disturb the university's academic environment.
The university also released a video statement featuring three female students from Room No. 504 of the hostel. They said they had been staying there for around two months and claimed that no rape incident had taken place.
LPU said it would cooperate with the police investigation and urged students, parents and members of the public not to circulate unverified information.
The university alleged that some elements were making a "deliberate" and "concerted" attempt to damage its reputation.
VANDALISM AND HIGHWAY BLOCKADE
The protests also saw vandalism and damage to property on the university campus. Videos circulating on social media purportedly showed students damaging window panes and flower pots, while some objects were set on fire.
Other videos showed damaged vehicles, a vandalised ATM kiosk and alleged damage at shops in the university mall. Some protesters were also seen climbing onto a decommissioned MiG-23UM aircraft and a military tank installed on the campus.
The NH-44 blockade caused long traffic queues, with traffic diverted through the Phagwara-Jandiala road and other arterial routes.
Several rounds of talks between students and the university management failed to resolve the standoff. LPU Vice Chancellor Jaspal Singh Sandhu assured students that genuine grievances would be addressed.
The protesters, however, demanded that LPU Founder-Chancellor Ashok Mittal, who is also a BJP Rajya Sabha MP, meet them and give assurances on their demands. They also sought protection from action over their participation in the protest and demanded that access to the University Management System not be blocked.
POLITICAL REACTION
Punjab Congress chief Amrinder Singh Raja Warring criticised the AAP government over the law-and-order situation, saying students with concerns should receive transparent and time-bound answers.
He also criticised the prolonged blockade of NH-44 and questioned the absence of a representative of the state government at the protest site.
Meanwhile, the immediate focus, LPU said, is on maintaining student safety, with regular classes suspended for 10 days and mid-term examinations put on hold as the police investigation into the allegations continues.

The United States Food and Drug Administration has approved AbbVie's treatment for Parkinson's disease in adults, the health regulator's website showed on Friday, September 25, 2026.
The drug tavapadon, which AbbVie gained access to through its $8.7 billion acquisition of Cerevel Therapeutics in 2023, comes as a once-a-day pill.
It will be sold under the brand name Juvmo, according to the FDA's website.
Parkinson's is a long-term brain condition that gradually damages movement control, often causing tremors, stiffness and balance issues. More than 11 million people live with the disease worldwide, according to AbbVie.
Juvmo works by mimicking dopamine, a vital brain chemical that naturally decreases in people with Parkinson's.
The regulator's nod was based on data from AbbVie's late-stage trial program which showed the drug improved symptoms in patients with the disease. Common side effects reported in the trials included nausea, dizziness and headache.
AbbVie did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on the drug's launch and pricing.
Citi analysts had previously said the launch was expected in the third quarter of 2026, but that uptake was likely to be gradual as negotiations progressed on the drug's Medicare coverage.
AbbVie continued to target more than $5 billion in combined Parkinson's disease sales, Citi added.

The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.
Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.
Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.
As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.
“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.
“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.
After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.
“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.
Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

Kim Birrell claims her first WTA title but loses top spot in Australian women's tennis rankings
In short:
Australia's Kim Birrell won the first WTA title of her career after downing compatriot Maya Joint in the Korea Open WTA 250.
Birrell still lost her place as Australia's top-ranked women's player after Talia Gibson finished runner-up in the Singapore Open.
Alex de Minaur's Team World lost to Europe in the Laver Cup after a defeat in the doubles while playing with American Taylor Fritz.
Kim Birrell has been left reflecting on an emotional and thrilling breakthrough day for Australian women's tennis in south-east Asia as she scooped the first WTA title of her career, while also losing her national number one ranking.
Birrell rocketed into the world's top-50 for the first time with her long-awaited maiden triumph at the Korea Open WTA 250 event while admitting her landmark day wasn't easy as she had to get there by beating her Australian pal Maya Joint in the final.
While the popular 28-year-old Queenslander was celebrating her victory with sympathetic words for her young tearful compatriot, Talia Gibson was annexing her Australian number one ranking elsewhere on the Asian swing.
Gibson, another player enjoying a breakthrough 2026 campaign, had reached the Singapore Open final on the same day and even though she lost to Canadian Leylah Fernandez, missing out on her maiden title, her big points haul at the bigger WTA 500 event meant she will leapfrog Birrell in the rankings.
Birrell capped her breakthrough year, which had featured a sensational win over Jessica Pegula in the French Open, with a 6-4, 6-2 victory over Joint in the Seoul final.
It was the first all-Australian WTA championship match since Sam Stosur beat Daria Gavrilova at Strasbourg in 2017, with Queenslander Birrell ending up finally lifting a trophy after losing her two previous finals in Osaka in 2024 and Chennai last year.
"It was quite difficult for us today because we are very good friends," Birrell said before speaking directly to Joint.
"You've had a tough year, I know. I hope you know how proud I am of you and how amazing you are."
Joint has had an up-and-down year, with a back injury and a long losing sequence finally ended when she earned her triumph over the returning Serena Williams at Wimbledon that made worldwide headlines.
"It's tough against a friend and I'm really proud of you," Joint said, congratulating her compatriot.
Europe downs Team World at Laver Cup
A day after Alex de Minaur beat Alexander Zverev to keep Team World's hopes alive in the Laver Cup, a doubles loss featuring the Australian and American Taylor Fritz ended Andre Agassi's team's bid for victory.
Agassi had planned to lean on de Minaur again after the doubles to take on Carlos Alcaraz, but the loss to Italy's Flavio Cobolli and Czech Jakub Mensik meant Europe took an unassailable lead in the competition.
"We were very close," de Minaur said.
"Yesterday, we won two supers [10-point tiebreakers] and lost one with Taylor playing an epic match.
"We were up against it from the get-go; we were the underdogs and put in a hell of a fight. A couple points here and there could have changed the whole tie."

In a major push to make legal services more accessible, transparent and citizen-friendly, Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo today launched the ‘e-Nyaya Sarathi’ web portal and mobile application, providing citizens a unified digital gateway to legal information, judicial resources and government legal services.
The event was attended by senior officers including ACS PWD; Principal Secretary, Home; Principal Secretary, Culture Department; Registrar General, High Court of J&K and Ladakh; Sr. AAG Mohsin Qadri; Member Secretary, J&K State Legal Services Authority; Commissioner Secretary, H&UDD; Commissioner Secretary, Social Welfare; Commissioner Secretary, Science & Technology; Commissioner Secretary, Law; Secretary, RDD; Secretary, Legislative Assembly and other officers of the Department of Law, Justice & Parliamentary Affairs. Members of the technical development team also attended the launch event.
Developed by the Department of Law, Justice & Parliamentary Affairs, the platform brings multiple legal services under one roof, enabling citizens to access essential legal information and services anytime and from anywhere. The initiative seeks to simplify the public’s interaction with the legal system and replace conventional bureaucratic hurdles with a more transparent and digitally accessible service delivery mechanism.
Speaking at the launch, the Chief Secretary described the initiative as a significant step towards citizen-centric digital governance, emphasising that legal services should be accessible, reliable and easy to navigate. He said that e-Nyaya Sarathi would help bridge the gap between citizens and legal institutions by bringing critical legal resources directly to their fingertips.
Giving details about the platform, Commissioner Secretary, Law, Achal Sethi, revealed that the portal offers a range of services, including legal aid and pro-bono assistance, a central repository of Acts, Rules, Judgments and Government Notifications, in addition to facilities like ‘Search Your Case’ and ‘Find My Court’ and dedicated modules for Women & Child Development and Advocate Related Matters.
Adding a technology-driven dimension to the initiative, the platform also features an AI-powered chatbot to guide users through legal queries and assist them in navigating various services available on the portal. The integrated framework is aimed at making access to legal information simpler and more responsive, particularly for citizens seeking quick and reliable information.
Moreover, it was also apprised that the e-Nyaya Sarathi portal is now available at www.enyayasarathi.jk.gov.in, while its mobile application can be downloaded from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store.

Normally, we try to update you quarterly on what’s going on with the US electric grid since it provides a nice view of developing trends and smooths out some month-to-month randomness. Unfortunately, I was out of the office when last month’s data was released, so this will be a seven-month update on 2026 trends.
The top line item is that energy use is continuing to rise, albeit not as quickly as headlines about data centers might lead people to believe. Beyond data centers, there’s a growing electrification—things like EVs and heat pumps—that is shifting energy demands onto the grid. Despite all of this, electricity use has risen by only 2 percent compared to the same period last year. At this time the previous year, demand had risen by 3 percent compared to the year prior.
Some of this may be due to continued improvements in efficiency, which had largely kept electricity demand stable throughout the early 2000s. And some of it may be because more data centers are generating their own power so that demand doesn’t show up on the grid. So far, the growth in demand hasn’t reached apocalyptic levels.
Slowing solar
The other big story in recent years has been the explosive growth of solar power. The astonishing growth rates we’ve been seeing—over 30 percent year over year in many quarters—would inevitably come to an end as the ever-larger installed base would cause an identical increase to register as a smaller percentage change. But for the first seven months of 2026, there’s a smaller increase in generation.
Through September 2025, solar generated 48 terawatt-hours more than it had the year before. For the same period in 2026, that number was 39 TWh. That’s still good for a growth rate of 22 percent, but it’s a considerable drop-off at a time when demand is growing, and solar is the cheapest way to meet it. Obviously, the federal government is currently hostile to renewables and has removed incentives for their use, which may be slowing down solar’s previously astonishing expansion.
Coal is down and renewables are up, despite the Trump Administration trying to achieve the opposite result.

Coal is down and renewables are up, despite the Trump Administration trying to achieve the opposite result.

John Timmer
Small-scale solar, such as rooftop installations, has been growing at a slower rate, but still managed to increase by over 12 percent year over year. Combined with utility-scale generation, solar produced 72 percent as much electricity as coal over the first seven months of 2026, aided in part by coal declining by a bit over 10 percent from the same period the year before.
Beyond solar and coal, all the changes in major electricity sources were less than 10 percent year over year. Hydro is up by 9 percent, wind by 6 percent, and nuclear and natural gas both by less than 2 percent.
Overall, this leaves us with wind and solar now covering 21 percent of US electricity demand. Through the first seven months of 2026, the growth from these two sources alone was 55 Tw-hr, while demand on the grid rose by 51 TWh. In other words, their growth meant that increased use of electricity could be met entirely by renewable sources. (Again, excluding any on-site generation by data centers and the growth in small-scale solar, neither of which shows up on the grid.)

Adding in hydro means that renewables now cover 27 percent of demand. With nuclear, that adds up to the US covering 45 percent of its electricity use with non-carbon-emitting sources. For comparison, the EU generates about 30 percent of its electricity using wind and solar, and 65 percent is emissions-free. (That rises to 71 percent if you count bioenergy, which is largely carbon-neutral, but not emissions-free.)
What’s next?
The Energy Information Agency, which provides all the grid data, also keeps track of what they expect to be hooked up to the grid over the coming months, which provides some perspective on what we might expect to see over the next year. The latest version of this highlights a couple of trends and one almost-trend.
The almost comes in the form of two large offshore wind projects that will be completed off the East Coast, including a 2.6 GW monster off Virginia. The Trump administration has paid off developers to stop building anything similar, so these will likely be the last of their kind until the 2030s. Onshore wind development has continued throughout the Midwest and Plains regions.

Those areas, along with the South, are also seeing a lot of solar development. This includes some significant facilities in Michigan and Wisconsin, which were probably too far north for the economics to have worked out just a few years back. Another notable change is that battery installations are starting to spread beyond the hotbeds in California and Texas. Arizona and Colorado are seeing a number of grid battery installs; the new solar in Michigan will be paired with a few, and there’s a large one expected to come online in Georgia.
A smattering of new natural gas plants will be coming online, mostly throughout the Midwest and Texas. No new nuclear or coal plants will be completed; it has now been 13 years since the last new coal plant came online in the US, and none are currently being developed.

The Centre is considering an anchor investment of ₹15,000 Cr to ₹20,000 Cr in a proposed fund aimed at supporting frontier AI companies and expanding the country’s compute infrastructure. The proposed National Frontier AI & Compute Fund (NFAICF) could provide long-term risk capital to AI companies and finance GPU clusters, specialised data centres, and other infrastructure required to develop and deploy advanced AI models, ET reported, citing sources. The proposal is currently under consultation, and the fund’s final corpus, structure, governance framework, and the role of government capital are yet to be decided. It is also unclear whether the government would invest directly in companies and infrastructure projects or route the capital through an intermediary structure. The government is considering a model under which it and private investors would contribute capital in a 50:50 ratio, the report said. The proposed fund was discussed at a closed-door meeting on “Financing India’s Frontier AI & Compute Ecosystem” in Delhi yesterday. The meeting was attended by Sarvam cofounder Vivek Raghavan, Peak XV Partners MD Rajan Anandan, E2E Networks CEO Tarun Dua, MeitY secretary S Krishnan, and officials from the IndiaAI Mission. The government sought views from VC firms, infrastructure providers, and other stakeholders on its role in attracting private capital to the frontier AI ecosystem. The NFAICF could be structured as a SEBI-regulated Category I AIF, with investment decisions taken by a committee comprising experts from the technology, investment, infrastructure, and finance sectors. The fund could invest through venture and growth equity, convertible instruments, infrastructure equity, fund-of-funds commitments, and direct co-investments, depending on the requirements of a company or infrastructure project. Its proposed objectives include providing long-term capital to foundation-model builders, specialised AI systems and other strategically important AI technologies, while also financing GPU clusters, specialised data-centre capacity and other compute infrastructure. The government is also examining whether international institutions such as the International Finance Corporation could participate in the proposed fund. Centre Exploring Demand-Linked Compute Financing A key focus of the discussions yesterday was financing GPU infrastructure without creating excess or underutilised capacity. The government is considering linking compute investments to demand from AI companies and research institutions through capacity commitments, utilisation arrangements or pre-agreed commercial terms. The objective is to reduce the risk of stranded or underutilised infrastructure. It is additionally considering a follow-on and co-investment capability, allowing the proposed fund to participate in later funding rounds alongside private investors when strategically important companies require additional capital. The final design of the NFAICF will depend on stakeholder feedback and further assessment. This comes as the demand for advanced GPUs continues to outpace supply, with infrastructure providers facing longer delivery timelines and rising pressure to secure capacity. The capital required to build GPU infrastructure is also challenges for Indian cloud and neocloud providers, particularly as they look to expand their capacity for AI workloads. The NFAICF is being considered in addition to the existing ₹10,372 Cr IndiaAI Mission, which provides subsidised compute access and funding for indigenous foundation models. The government has also been expanding the country's AI compute capacity through the IndiaAI Mission. The Mission initially targeted access to more than 10,000 GPUs through a public-private partnership to make high-end computing resources available to Indian AI companies and researchers. The government has since onboarded more than 38,000 GPUs through empanelled cloud service providers and plans to expand the compute pool further. IndiaAI has also been supporting multiple companies and research teams to develop Indian foundation models across large multimodal models and smaller language models.

Australia fell to an ODI series defeat to South Africa with a game to spare as they were beaten by 32 runs in the second ODI match of three in Johannesburg on Sunday.

- Minecraft Dungeons 2 DLCs are officially planned by Mojang.

Minecraft Dungeons 2 has yet to be launched globally, but Mojang is already looking beyond launch. The developers have confirmed that Minecraft Dungeons 2 DLCs are planned, promising players a new destination and additional mobs in the ARPG sequel.
The confirmation for the new DLCs came alongside the details about the broader mechanics of Minecraft Dungeons 2, including the interconnected Overworld and mysterious Rifts. However, Mojang has not revealed the exact release dates, names, or prices of the expansions yet.

This story was originally published by High Country News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk Collaboration.
This weather threat costs us billions. And it’s about to get worse.
Scientists are chasing hail to understand what’s happening to these dangerous projectiles.
At a specialized cold lab in Boulder, Colorado, where indoor temperatures hover around minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 20 degrees Celsius), atmospheric researcher Anthony Bernal Ayala slices hailstones with a band saw, revealing layers of icy growth like the rings of a tree. These frozen rings — clear or cloudy, thick or thin — indicate the conditions in which the hail formed: A clear layer signals the water froze slowly, while a cloudy layer means it happened quickly, trapping air bubbles. Bernal Ayala then analyzes the crystalline structures, particles, and isotopes preserved in these layers.
“All that information can tell you a wonderful story of how the hailstone was growing, but nobody — not until now — was able to tap into that history,” said Bernal Ayala, who works for Atmospheric and Environmental Research, part of the JANUS Research Group.
Bernal Ayala’s research, conducted at the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR), is part of a historic effort to study one of the costliest weather hazards. Researchers hope their findings will help protect lives and property from the stones that careen to Earth, battering roofs, pummeling crops, and pockmarking cars.
From 2023 to 2025, annual severe thunderstorm losses exceeded $50 billion nationwide, according to the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety — more than double the losses seen just a decade earlier. Hail accounted for 60 percent to 80 percent of the damage.
In Colorado, one of the country’s most hail-prone states, hail — not wildfire — is the main factor driving up insurance premiums. And researchers expect larger, more damaging hailstones to become more common with climate change.
“It’s going to just keep getting costlier and costlier,” Bernal Ayala said.
Even basic questions about hail have been notoriously hard to study. But a long-awaited resurgence in research, including the first major US field campaign to study hail in more than 40 years, could help change that.
ICECHIP — the “In-situ Collaborative Experiment for the Collection of Hail In the Plains” — aims to improve forecasts, make warnings more precise and help communities better prepare. It received $11 million in funding from the National Science Foundation in 2024, just before deep cuts hit the foundation in 2025.
For six weeks in spring 2025, about 100 scientists and university students chased hailstorms across the Central Plains and Front Range, from the Canadian to the Mexican border, using radar trucks to track storms and drones to take aerial footage. Researchers photographed hail with high-speed cameras, measured its impact with a tool called a disdrometer, recorded hail’s distribution and size based on its imprints on foam pads, captured it in specialized funnels, and crushed it to test its strength.
Scientists from the Australian Bureau of Meteorology also used balloons to release golf ball-sized sensors into storms. Once aloft, each hail-like probe collected data on how fast it was traveling and whether ice was growing on it; a microphone even recorded water droplets and hailstones hitting it.
“This has really been the first time where we’ve been able to do a real comprehensive look at hail on the ground, hail aloft, the storm itself, the environment around the storm — just everything all at once,” said Becky Adams-Selin, ICECHIP’s lead investigator and a principal scientist at Atmospheric and Environmental Research, JANUS Research Group.
ICECHIP’s samples were packed into 26 cooler-sized boxes and brought to NCAR. This internationally renowned hub for weather and climate research has been used to study hail for decades. In one of its last major campaigns, in the 1970s, the US investigated Soviet claims that it could suppress hail.
Researchers say there’s no other US lab like it; the backup plan to store ICECHIP’s samples involved using a walk-in freezer from a fast-food restaurant.
Now NCAR’s own future is uncertain: In late 2025, the Trump administration said it would dissolve the center and transfer its work out of state. The University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), which manages NCAR, sued the administration in March, alleging that it’s targeting NCAR to punish Colorado for retaining its mail-in voting system and because Gov. Jared Polis initially refused to release former Mesa County clerk Tina Peters, a 2020 election denier imprisoned for breaching election security and undermining election integrity.
In June, a federal judge temporarily blocked the White House from dismantling NCAR. The government has until Sept. 30 to respond to the lawsuit.
“I can’t even quantify the impact that it would have to our community if we lost NCAR,” Victor Gensini, professor of meteorology at Northern Illinois University, told HCN. “They are the beating heart.”
Previous research has predicted climate change’s effects on hail, noting that warmer temperatures could melt smaller hailstones before they land but also fuel stronger updrafts, keeping hailstones airborne longer and allowing them to grow bigger, enabling the most damaging hail to become more common.
A record-setting stone recovered in Yuma County, Colorado, in 2023 measured more than 5 inches across. That year, the state logged 176 reports of hail 2 inches or greater, surpassing the previous record of 91 reports in 2018, according to the Colorado Climate Center.
Scientists say it’s difficult to know how much of the rise in damage is due to the increase in large hail versus the increased development in hail hotspots. The connection between a rapidly growing human footprint and higher insured losses has been dubbed the “expanding bull’s-eye effect.”
Gensini, a principal ICECHIP investigator, cites the development boom east of the Front Range, along Colorado’s Interstate 25 corridor, which has grown explosively in recent decades. The population of the Fort Collins metro area alone has doubled since 1990 to around 375,000 residents, according to the US Census Bureau.
This is happening across the Western US, as previously rural or open areas become densely populated, increasingly expensive targets for hail.
“Colorado is the poster child for what I expect the next 25 years to look like for hail,” Gensini said.
In 2019, Fort Collins became one of the first cities to adopt hail-specific roofing requirements for new builds and remodels. Marcus Coldiron, the city’s chief building official, said it was partly in response to all the shingles and roofing materials taken to the landfill after a catastrophic hailstorm in 2018.
It’s still unclear how well the requirements are working: Coldiron said fewer permits were being issued for roof replacements and fewer shingles were going to the dump. However, Fort Collins also hasn’t experienced a hailstorm as devastating as the one that hit in 2018.
A growing number of Front Range communities now require impact-resistant shingles in their building codes, and Colorado legislators recently passed a law offering grants to residents who install more resilient roofing.
ICECHIP’s researchers are also investigating how they can improve building materials as billion-dollar losses from single storms become more common.
“The dollars are simply piling up so fast,” said Ian Giammanco, a lead research meteorologist at the Insurance Institute for Business and Home Safety, one of ICECHIP’s key partners. “We’re still trying to understand how do we get the best materials onto roofs, onto people’s homes, onto businesses to actually start shaving off these losses.”

At least two dead after explosion destroys building close to Acropolis in Athens
- Published
At least two people have died and four more are missing after an explosion destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis, with local media reporting the building housed a holiday rental.
An American man and woman have died, with two more US tourists missing, AFP news agency reported citing local officials. A Greek national and UK national who lived in the building are also said to be missing.
Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with a Greek fire official later telling reporters the body of a man had also been found.
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
BBC News has contacted the UK Foreign Office.

TOI Correspondent from Washington:
 The United States and China may disagree about tariffs, technology, Taiwan and the future of the world order. But there is apparently one subject on which they can find common ground: everybody loves pandas.
Two giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, are arriving in Atlanta on Monday, just days after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington. Their arrival adds a furry footnote to a summit heavy on symbolism and somewhat lighter on earth-shaking breakthroughs. The pandas are headed for a 10-year stay at Zoo Atlanta under a conservation agreement.
They travelled in considerably greater comfort than most travelers. Handlers packed steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots for their 15-hour FedEx flight. Experienced American keepers accompanied them. The Atlanta zoo upgraded their quarters and arranged a steady supply of locally grown bamboo. A little more tantrum from Beijing and liveried waiters with silver platters could be standing by
China, of course, is the undisputed grandmaster of this branch of statecraft. In 1972, after Richard Nixon’s historic visit to Beijing, First Lady Pat Nixon is said to have mentioned her affection for pandas to Premier Zhou Enlai. Two months later, Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing arrived at Washington’s National Zoo. The Americans reciprocated with two musk oxen, Milton and Matilda, now long forgotten.
The panda relationship subsequently became more sophisticated – and more expensive. China stopped giving pandas away in the 1980s and shifted to long-term loans, generally for conservation and research, with cubs born abroad eventually returning to China.
Washington’s panda romance has therefore gone through several seasons: Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing; then Tian Tian and Mei Xiang; their famous cubs Tai Shan, Bao Bao and Bei Bei; the tearful departure of the family in 2023; and the arrival in 2024 of Bao Li and Qing Bao. The Smithsonian says the new agreement runs through 2034.
The spirit animating panda diplomacy is obvious. Pandas are cute, photogenic, rare and almost aggressively non-threatening. Put two world leaders beside a trade dispute, and everybody looks grim; put two pandas beside the same dispute and suddenly it's all cute and cuddly.
China is hardly alone in understanding the diplomatic value of charismatic fauna. India actually had elephant diplomacy before pandas became a diplomatic instrument. Veteran diplomats recall Jawaharlal Nehru sent a baby elephant named Indira to Tokyo in 1949 after receiving hundreds of letters from Japanese children asking for one. He subsequently sent elephants to Berlin and to many other countries including China, the Soviet Union, the United States, Turkey, Iran, Canada and the Netherlands. But India simply did not build a durable, institutionalised animal-diplomacy industry around them.
Perhaps that was partly wisdom. Unlike pandas, Indian elephants are social, intelligent, enormously demanding animals whose welfare becomes complicated once diplomacy ends and the photo opportunity is over. A 2024 examination of the practice, prompted by the plight of an elephant gifted to India by Zimbabwe, highlighted this problem precisely: diplomatic animals can be separated from herds, habitats and familiar environments for the convenience of human relations.
Besides, neither pandas and elephants -- nor koalas and platypuses from Australia, horses from Mongolia, and akita dogs from Japan, all of which were deployed in the case of diplomacy -- were consulted about their assignment. Humans have spent centuries deciding that critters make excellent ambassadors without ever bothering to ask the envoys.
Why? Because animals, unlike ambassadors, cannot resign their postings, request asylum or leak the contents of their diplomatic cables. And perhaps that is why they make such remarkably good diplomats. They never complain, never contradict the communique, never hold a press conference and -- most importantly -- never ask what happened to the promised breakthrough.

Mbappe, Vini and Konate obscure Real's Ceuta message
- Published
Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta.
Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.
Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city.
While most of the players wore the shirts fully, Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate had theirs rolled up to around chest height, obscuring some of the slogan.
Mbappe and Vinicius then removed their shirts before the pre-match handshake, while Konate kept his on for longer. Their team-mates and the Elche players continued to wear the shirts through the pre-match formalities.
This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. Before their Champions League meeting with Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabeu on 8 September, supporters in the south stand displayed cards featuring the coat of arms of the autonomous city, while the rest of the stadium joined the tribute with a round of applause.
The initiative was part of a wider show of support for Ceuta, following a major migration crisis in the Spanish territory after thousands of people entered from Morocco.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa.
Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
The representatives of the players have been asked for comment.
The episode came shortly before a dramatic night for Real Madrid, who recovered from surrendering a two-goal lead to beat Elche 3-2, with Carlos Espi scoring the winner in stoppage time.
Mbappe was among Madrid's scorers, while Vinicius started the game.
The pre-match gesture also highlighted the differing approaches among players and clubs to the Ceuta campaign.
Barcelona did not take part in the initiative, while players at other La Liga fixtures had worn the shirts as intended.

This past April, while attending his nephew’s bar mitzvah on Cape Cod, Eric Umansky woke up to an inbox full of emails from people from his past. They all wanted to know the same thing: Was he actually throwing a party Saturday night?
The New York–based journalist wasn’t sure what party they were referring to, or why random acquaintances he’d met in passing 15 years ago were emailing him. On deadline and already stressed about work, he checked his phone, where more messages inquired about a supposed Paperless Post invite he’d sent for a “Special Private Dinner Party” at 7 pm on May 2.
Except Umansky hadn't sent the invite, and he wasn’t planning to host a party anytime soon.
As it turned out, he was an early victim of an email scam that has since become more widespread. What Umansky didn’t expect was the positive effect it would have on his social life.
In May, after receiving increased reports, the Federal Trade Commission issued a consumer alert warning about scammers sending “unexpected messages that look like they’re from well-known invitation platforms like Evite or Paperless Post,” noting how some messages “make you enter your email username and password to see event details” while others “tell you to enter a phone number and share a special code to RSVP.”
Umansky wasn’t sure how it happened; he thought he'd taken the necessary precautions to safeguard his email, including using two-factor authentication. All he could think to do was post a message on Facebook, LinkedIn, and his other social networks to notify people that he was, in fact, not having a party and, more importantly, “don’t come to my house.”
Phishing scams, which have proliferated across the last two decades, remain one of the biggest security risks faced both by individuals and companies. Email scams, in particular, can now be highly sophisticated, incorporating social engineering techniques like creating urgency or fear in a target and even leveraging the personal relationships between two people to manipulate a victim, what’s known as “spear phishing.” AI has only made those deceptions harder to weed out.
But in some recent cases, like Umansky’s, the fake party invite is having an unintended outcome: It is encouraging people to check in to see whether the message was actually real and, in doing so, has reignited dormant relationships.
“It was so striking to me after it happened that I actually had a thought that I was like, ‘Oh, is this a net positive?’” says Umansky, who over the last several months has reconnected with a handful of old friends and colleagues over lunch and via text. He recently spent an hour on Zoom with a former coworker who now lives in Mexico City. They hadn’t talked to each other in over a decade. “I was like, Oh, you know, I actually want to catch up with you about something. There was an idea I wanted to bat around with him, which we talked about for maybe 10 minutes. The rest of the time we talked about our lives.”
According to a 2024 study published in the scientific journal Communications Psychology examining social withdrawal, which surveyed 2,400 adults in the US, UK, and Canada, people are sometimes unwilling to contact old friends because they believe the other person won’t want to hear from them or they fear the interaction will be awkward. The research noted that “high priority placed on work and productivity in North America has led people to cut back on social connections and social time to meet increasing demands at work,” in addition to other life transitions, such as parenthood or moving to a new city.
But a suspicious party invite is exactly the kind of low-stakes incentive that has made initiating contact easier because it represents the one thing we all crave: a sense of belonging.
According to Lara Aknin, a professor of psychology at Simon Fraser University whose research has explored the hesitancy around reconnecting with lapsed contacts, only 30 percent of people actually check in with an old friend “even when we make doing so as easy as possible by helping them identify a desirable, feasible, and low-risk contact.”
With email scams, “people are motivated and willing to reach out to an old friend because the scam provides a legitimate excuse or social cover to do so,” she says. “In fact, people may even be slightly grateful for the reconnection opportunity this context affords, even though they hope the scam is false.”
Most people will only have a small number of close relationships in their lifetime, and it is even fewer these days; nearly half of the population (44 percent) have five or fewer acquaintances. “In the course of [scammers] taking advantage of that real desire, they are actually helping fill it,” Umansky says.
He’s not the only one who has reignited old relationships after being targeted by a scam. “I heard from a friend of more than 30 years,” Larry Persily wrote in the Wrangell Sentinel, a local newspaper in Alaska, of the trend. One source confirms with WIRED that they are back in touch with an ex they haven’t spoken to in years after receiving a fake invite.
To be clear, the unintended consequence of scam attempts may be reconnecting with lost friends, but they’re not all Zoom reunions and brunch. The FBI estimates that scammers tricked Americans out of $21 billion in 2025 alone, with help from AI.
Some of us remain impervious to the lure of the phishing trap invite. In late August, I received an unexpected Paperless Post invite—“Raise a Glass! Dinner & Drinks” the subject line read—from an acquaintance I hadn’t spoken to since 2017, though I immediately deleted it because I could barely remember who he was or why we even exchanged emails. I probably should have reached out. Maybe we both would’ve enjoyed the catch-up.
