In Summary
- Google recently unveiled the first batch of Googlebooks, its new kind of notebook, with devices from Lenovo, Dell, Asus, Acer and HP.
- The first batch of Googlebooks comes packed with top-of-the-line hardware and premium design, and has premium prices beginning at USD 899.
- While we wait for them to hit the market (they go on sale on October 4 and 5), we take a look at eleven features of Google’s new notebook concept.
Is it a rejigged Chromebook? Or is it a new attempt by Google to get Android into the notebook space? Google took the wraps off its much-talked-about Googlebook notebook recently, with Googlebooks from five leading brands: HP, Asus. Acer, Lenovo and Dell. What exactly is so special about them, and should you be interested in one? Here are eleven things that we think you need to know about the new Googlebook that might help you make up your mind about them, even as the first batch of Googlebooks gets set to arrive in early October:
Table of Contents
Built on Android, designed to work in sync with your (Android) phone
“If you use an Android phone, your laptop shouldn’t treat it like a stranger,” says Google, so it is hardly surprising that one of the USPs of the Googlebook is the fact that it works seamlessly with your phone, provided it is an Android phone. Googlebooks are built on what Google calls a “share Android foundation,” so you can log in to them with your Android username and password, and access apps and files on your phone on the Googlebook, and do much more, effortlessly. We have no news on compatibility with iPhones at the time of writing.
Comes with a touchscreen
While touchscreens were broadly optional with Chromebooks, as of now, all Googlebooks come with a touchscreen display of up to 2.8K resolution. The touch interface is an integral part of the Googlebook experience. As of now, there is no talk of Googlebook tablets, but given the touch UI, we expect to see them at some stage.
Premium innards (Top-of-the-line chips, lots of RAM)
Unlike Android and ChromeOS, which were both optimized to run even on relatively modest specs, the Googlebook is clearly a high-end beast. All Googlebooks have to come with Intel Core Ultra Series 3 or Snapdragon X Elite with dedicated NPUs capable of over 45 TOPS. They also come with a minimum of 16 GB RAM. The Googlebook at this point seems clearly to be designed for high-end work.
…and outards too
It is not just their hardware; the Googlebook itself also has to be made of premium materials, such as carbon fiber, magnesium and aluminum. Trackpads also have to be made of glass, and the keyboards have to be backlit.
A bar that glows!
They might be sleekly designed and made of premium materials, but perhaps the most striking feature of the Googlebooks is the thin glowing bar on their lids. This Glow Bar lights up in different shades when one starts up the Googlebook, shows battery level, and also “supports other playful patterns” on different occasions, such as when one is using Gemini.
Keyboards that are slightly different
While the keyboards on Googlebooks are broadly similar to those seen on Windows notebooks, there are some subtle differences. Keyboards on the Googlebook come with two special keys – a special key labeled G to invoke Gemini. The capslock key on a Googlebook also acts as a Quick Insert key. Pressing it gives you access to a number of features such as clipboard history, instant translation, emojis, and local search tools. There is also a dedicated shortcut key for Rambler, Google’s voice dictation app that’s making waves these days. Don’t get fooled by those classic keys – there’s a lot under the surface of a Googlebook keyboard!
Runs on Googlebook OS
The operating system of the Googlebooks is – well – Googlebook OS. It is a blend of Android and ChromeOS, and was codenamed Aluminum. It is built on Android and has the same security architecture as ChromeOS. Yes, not many prizes for innovative nomenclature, but then this is the tech world which has operating systems called One and Nothing, so who are we to judge?
Gemini is literally a cursor wriggle away
Every Googlebook comes packed with AI and AI tools, and a super special way of summoning Gemini, Google’s AI assistant. You do not need to hit a button; just wriggle the cursor, and Gemini will pop up! Google calls it the Magic Pointer, and it certainly adds a new dimension to accessing AI on notebooks.
All of Android’s apps and a “desktop Chrome” experience
At the time of writing and based on what has been made public, the Googlebook’s main source of apps is the Google Play Store for Android. What’s more. Android apps and games run natively rather than in a special environment (as on Chromebooks), delivering smooth performance. You also get a proper “desktop” Chrome experience, so all extensions will work, and there is also support for Office 365. What’s more, Android apps and games on a connected Android phone will also work smoothly on a Googlebook. Many of the apps are optimized to run on the large screen and come with support for keyboard and mouse. We do not know if APK files can be installed or if apps can be “sideloaded” onto Googlebooks at this time, though.
PC games can be played…but on the cloud!
But what about PC games? After all, the Googlebooks do boast some seriously powerful hardware, including high-resolution displays, flagship chips, and stacks of RAM. Well, at the time of writing, PC games cannot be directly installed on the, but one can stream PC games via GeForce NOW. We hope that changes in the coming days, given Google’s specs and price tags.
10 years software support
Impressed by the seven years of software support on the Pixel phones? Well, the Googlebooks come with a massive ten years of software support. And given that the hardware inside is top-notch and the frame is made of premium materials, there is every chance that these notebooks will stand the test of time.
And one more thing: They are going to be premium devices as of now!
The current set of Googlebooks unveiled by Google starts at USD 899, with some even starting at prices in excess of USD 1000. Given the current hardware and material requirements laid down for them and the trend of rising component prices, it is likely that Googlebooks will remain premium devices for a while. Of course, we would love it if they became more affordable. Premium tech is wonderful, but affordable tech is love.

EC extends deadline for claims, objections to October 12 in Maharashtra amid SIR row
The move comes after reports of differences among the three-member Election Commission over decisions and directions regarding electoral roll revisions.
The deadline for filing claims and objections related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Maharashtra has been extended to October 12, while the deadline for their disposal has been moved to November 10, the Election Commission announced on Saturday.
The poll body has made similar changes in Delhi, extending the deadline for claims and objections to October 30 and the deadline for their disposal to November 30.
The move comes after reports of differences among the three-member Election Commission over decisions and directions concerning electoral-roll revisions, including the deletion and addition of names, changes to forms for new voters and access to voter data.
Key decisions announced by EC
At a meeting at Nirvachan Sadan attended by all three election commissioners, the Commission said voters who received notices during the SIR "for being unmapped and logical discrepancies" will no longer have to appear for a personal hearing before the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO).
Booth Level Officers (BLOs) will visit these voters at their homes to collect the required documents. These will then be uploaded to the ECINet portal "for decision by the ERO."
A hearing will be held "only in exceptional circumstances, as decided by the ERO," and will "preferably" take place online. The Commission said facilities for online hearings will also be strengthened.
District election officers have also been directed to "create adequate number of help desks/hold special camps" for people living in night shelters, as well as labourers, the poor and the homeless, "as per requirement."
The Commission said the declaration attached to Form 6 for the SIR "has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court," while outside the SIR period, forms "applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used."
CEC under fire over ‘dissent’ row
The decision comes after a report by The Indian Express, based on internal documents and interviews, said election commissioners SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had separately written to cabinet secretary TV Somanathan. They objected to changes in the allocation of work, saying they had removed a layer of oversight over the IT backbone of the electoral rolls.
The Commission reiterated that its SIR order of June 24, 2025 was issued "with the unanimous approval of the Commission," and had "been upheld by the Supreme Court of India," while the schedules for SIR were also issued with unanimous approval.
The Commission said SIR "has already been completed in 20 states/UTs including Bihar and West Bengal," and instructed chief electoral officers, district election officers and EROs to "immediately launch a special drive for enrolment" of voters left out of the rolls. This includes "young/first-time voters," under the process of continuous updation.

An ironic development emerging alongside the “Make America Healthy Again” movement is the portrayal of nicotine as a wellness and performance-enhancing product. Across social media, podcasts, natural medicine communities and tech startups, prominent wellness personalities and other influencers are portraying nicotine as a misunderstood compound whose potential benefits have been overshadowed by its negative association with cigarettes.
In these circles, nicotine is now being hailed as a natural product that can be used for everything from improving focus to protecting against cognitive decline. As a pulmonary physician-scientist who studies nicotine addiction and the health consequences of tobacco and nicotine products, I am concerned about these claims.
Some of this rebranding stems from the observation that nicotine is a naturally occurring plant compound found primarily in tobacco and in nightshade vegetables such as tomatoes, potatoes and eggplant in trace amounts. Proponents of nicotine use also draw on studies suggesting that nicotine can affect certain aspects of cognition and brain function. However, extending these findings to broad claims about productivity, brain health, longevity or wellness goes well beyond what has been shown in human studies.
The greatest health risks arise when tobacco is burned, which generates thousands of toxic substances, including carcinogens, carbon monoxide, and fine particulate matter. Repeated exposure to these combustion products can cause cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease, and numerous other smoking-related illnesses.
Nicotine’s comeback as a wellness product is more about non-smoking options, such as nicotine pouches, or some combine nicotine with other substances marketed as cognition enhancers, like caffeine and nootropics. While many smoking-related diseases result from the chemical products of combustion, nicotine itself has well-known negative effects on the brain and body.
Nicotine activates the sympathetic nervous system—the body’s “fight or flight” response—which increases heart rate and blood pressure and disrupts sleep. Repeatedly kick-starting this system can place additional strain on the heart. Exposure is also of particular concern during critical phases of development.
Not to mention the extremely well-known risk that nicotine is addictive. It activates reward pathways in the brain, acting on receptors for acetylcholine, a key neurotransmitter involved in attention, learning, and memory. Though it may temporarily increase alertness and attention, nicotine does not reproduce normal acetylcholine signaling. The effects last much longer and alter activity throughout the brain.
With repeated exposure, the brain adapts to nicotine’s presence. Receptors become less responsive, and so the brain compensates by increasing the number of nicotine receptors, contributing to dependence. Activation of these receptors also influences the release of other neurotransmitters, including dopamine, which plays an important role in reward and reinforcement.
A common claim within wellness communities is that nicotine is a cognitive enhancer that improves focus and productivity. While there are some studies indicating that nicotine may temporarily enhance attention, vigilance, reaction time, and some types of memory, the results are mixed.
If any benefit does exist, the research suggests that this may only be the case for people with mild cognitive impairment. For healthy individuals, it doesn’t appear to offer any boost and may even worsen cognitive operation among higher-performing people.
In addition, many of these studies include people already dependent on nicotine. When these regular users stop consuming nicotine, they’re likely to experience irritability, anxiety, restlessness, and impaired attention. Reintroducing nicotine often relieves these symptoms, making it difficult to determine whether any improvements reflect true cognitive enhancement or are simply the reversal of withdrawal symptoms.
Wellness influencers also promote nicotine as a tool for managing stress and improving mood. Nicotine does activate reward pathways in the brain, which can create a sense of pleasure and wellbeing—temporarily.
Long-term users of nicotine often find that the substance makes stress and anxiety harder to manage. Research consistently shows that people who quit smoking experience reductions in anxiety, depression, and stress, along with improvements in mood and overall quality of life over time. In fact, long-term discontinuation of nicotine use is associated with better mental health.
But the most ambitious claims emerging from the pro-nicotine wellness movement suggest that nicotine protects against Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s, and other forms age-related cognitive decline. Or further, that nicotine slows biological aging and promotes longevity.
There’s some kernels of research underneath these claims, such as laboratory studies showing that nicotine can affect cellular pathways related to oxidative stress and animal studies suggesting effects on inflammation and other mechanisms linked to aging and disease. However, such findings have not translated into anything that indicates nicotine promotes healthy aging, extends lifespan or prevents age-related disease in humans.

A special broadcast of Pollution Ka Solution examines the escalating air pollution crisis across major urban centres, focusing on Delhi NCR and Mumbai, where hazardous Air Quality Index levels and winter toxic smog are creating an influx of pollution refugees. Residents and professionals, including Bharat Singh Kanwal, former advocate Prashant Kalra, and fashion designer Anuradha Prasad Dhawan, detail abandoning their careers and homes to relocate to destinations like Bengaluru and Goa after severe pediatric respiratory emergencies, persistent asthma, and health complications forced their departure. The discussion highlights broader urban systemic issues such as deficient waste management, unchecked deforestation, and rising cancer and respiratory burdens among children and senior citizens, with lifestyle expert Luke Coutinho noting that dietary adjustments cannot reverse cellular lung damage caused by toxic exposure. Panellists address policy implementation challenges surrounding the National Clean Air Programme and Graded Response Action Plan, calling for year-round interstate governance, strict environmental compliance accountability, and civic participation to counter urban air quality deterioration.

Senior police officers on the ground confirmed efforts to stabilise the area and identify individuals involved in arson and vandalism.

The death of an Anna University student at Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday (September 18, 2026), due to scrub typhus, has once again brought this bacterial infection to the fore. University authorities have said they have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis
What is scrub typhus?
Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It is spread by the bite of infected larval mites or chiggers -- it is not a mosquito-borne disease.
Scrub typhus is a major public health burden in South and Southeast Asia. A 2021 systematic review noted that scrub typhus, a common acute febrile illness, is “a grossly under-recognised public health problem in India.” It stated that the proportion of scrub typhus among acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) studies was 25.3%, and community seroprevalence was 34.2%. The review also noted that the disease causes severe morbidity and accounts for a large number of deaths, with its bueden “underappreciated.”
A 2025 multi-centre study of 587 children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu revealed that scrub typhus is now the most common infectious cause of AES in southern India.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms usually begin within 10 days of infection. The United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists symptoms of scrub typhus as: fever and chills, headache, body aches and muscle pain, a dark, scab-like region at the site of the chigger bite (also known as eschar), mental changes ranging from confusion to coma, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash.
Timely treatment is critical. If left untreated, severe illness from scrub typhus infection can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), shock, meningitis and kidney failure, which can be fatal, notes a research paper, Incidence of Scrub Typhus in Rural South India published in The New England Journal of Medicine last year.
In India, there is a high mortality of scrub typhus, primarily due to late diagnosis and treatment.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
Since the symptoms of scrub typhus are common to those of several other diseases, diagnosis is often delayed. A blood test (IgM ELISA or PCR) can help confirm the diagnosis.
Scrub typhus should be treated with the antibiotics doxycycline or azithromycin. If the treatment is begun in time, it is effective. Results of a trial carried out in seven centres in India, published in 2023, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive a combination therapy of doxycycline and azithromycin, showed faster resolution of complications compared with two other arms where patients were given monotherapy with either doxycycline or azithromycin. The frequencies of respiratory, renal, hepatic, and central nervous system complications were lower in the combination-therapy group than in either of the monotherapy groups.
How can it be prevented?
There is no vaccine as yet for scrub typhus. The infection is not contagious.
Chiggers live in areas with lots of grass, thick vegetation, agricultural fields, plant litter and bare soil across rural areas of Asia, and usually feed on small mammals such as rats and shrews.
Keeping oneself safe from bites through protective clothing, covered footwear and the use of insect repellent may help. Ensuring surroundings are clean and well maintained can also go some way towards reducing mite habitats.
“Early diagnosis and prompt treatment can significantly reduce complications and mortality. Establishing good surveillance and instituting appropriate control measures are urgently needed,” the 2021 review notes.

In Egypt, leaving prison does not mean escaping the security state
From the very beginning of his detention, Abdelrahman ElGendy, who had just turned 17, was forced to reckon with the constant assault that is prison life in Egypt.
After being unlawfully detained in October 2013 for being close to a protest, and categorised as an alleged Muslim Brotherhood "terrorist" (read: protester), he found himself interned in Egypt's spiralling archipelago of political prisons, along with his father.
The assault that is prison life is not just in the physical act of detention, or the violence and torture enacted by captors; it is in every sound and movement made in the prison. Contrary to popular understanding, an assault in law is not an act of violence itself, but the apprehension that unlawful violence might take place - and nothing better describes life in Egypt's prisons than a constant assault.
On his first night, given no actual reason for his arrest other than the amorphous accusation of being Ikhwan (Muslim Brotherhood), ElGendy recalls in his memoir, Huna:
"Are they going to torture us?" I blurted. I could not look at Baba.

"Well, they haven't so far. So that's a good sign." Aboulfetouh shrugged. "Maybe they'll pass us tonight."
Ten minutes later, the locks clanked outside, and I stiffened. The guard pushed open the door and signaled to me and Baba to follow him.
They came for us.
The movement of the guards outside, the sound of the keys jangling in the door, the clank of a door being opened - these are part of the ongoing violence of the prison. They are constant, everyday, audible reminders that at any point it may well be your turn, and so the body turns hypervigilant, stiffening at the prospect that the violence you have been apprehending has finally come for you. Sometimes it does.
In a hyper-militarised state, there is no escaping the assault. One would imagine that for ElGendy, the relief of release after six years of hell inside numerous prisons would provide the necessary balm for his healing. But there is no escaping the constant assault while living under the false god of what the academic Walaa Quisay and I call the deified national security state.
Political barzakh
It is tragically fitting that ElGendy refers to the period immediately after his release as barzakh - in Islam, the space that exists between this life and the eternal afterlife, but a space confined inside a grave.
Release, while welcome, becomes a barzakh of sorts for ElGendy, because he is still in Egypt, where the self-proclaimed all-seeing eye of the state continues to operate with impunity, and because the continuous assault of the prison experience carries through into the sounds and sensations of everyday life:
In prison, I had hunted for silence, cutting out sound until I lost my ears. But this noise was different...
The noise fascinated me, like a collective, conspiratorial effort to drown out the void. To forget that we were all hurtling toward death.
The noise interrupted the void; prison noise had summoned it.
The notion that release from prison in Egypt is akin to freedom is a form of gaslighting. Release places the person in a political barzakh, where everyday activity becomes yet another reminder of how tenuous the state of release might be.
The notion that release from prison in Egypt is akin to freedom is a form of gaslighting
One morning, ElGendy notices a plain white van parked by his building. Hypervigilance, coupled with a dysregulated amygdala and hippocampus, results in a state of anxiety. For ElGendy, the state is back. "They've come for me," he gasps down the phone to his Baba. Yet it wasn't the state - those he calls "the Arms" throughout the book - it was simply a gardening company parked up.
The assault is continuous precisely because of the unknowability of how the Arms operate in everyday life - just as they would walk past the cell, and it was never known whose door the keys would jangle for, and whose name would be called for interrogation.
This experience of the barzakh is not limited to the national security gaze in Egypt. In so many ways, ElGendy's post-detention experience reminds me of The Suspect by Rizwaan Sabir, who recounts being interrogated as a terrorism suspect by UK police for seven days before his eventual release.
Sabir experienced extreme paranoia after his release because of the ubiquitous presence of the national security state in his life, including in the mental health services that were there ostensibly to help people like him. It is in this ubiquity that the apprehension of unlawful state violence festers - it is seemingly everywhere.
'Mind-forg'd manacles'
I lived in Egypt in the Hosni Mubarak era while studying Arabic in Nasr City, walking constantly under the shadow of the infamous Amn al-Dawla - the State Security headquarters. It was the period in which I was least political in my life, or at least since I became aware of injustice in the world.
I recall being told by veterans of Arabic language programmes: don't talk politics to your teachers, to taxi drivers, to random people in the street. Keep yourself to yourself and never speak about the regime, about Palestine or any other matter. Stick to football.
That was in 2009, and I realise now that this is precisely what the security state requires: our best apolitical versions of ourselves, a self-erasing scrutiny that eviscerates any vestige of critique of the violence we live under. It is what William Blake termed "the mind-forg'd manacles".
As social media travellers relate their scuba-diving holidays in Hurghada, or tulab al-ilm (students of knowledge) relate their stories of studying Shafi'i jurisprudence at the prestigious Al-Azhar University, it can be difficult to remember what Egypt actually is: a country ruled by a military for the purpose of maintaining the interests of others in the region. As ElGendy read in an inscription on one prison wall:
اكتب على حيط الزنزانة، حكم العسكر عار وخيانة
Write it on the cell walls: Military rule is shame and treachery
Under such rule, it can be difficult to remember how limited one's agency is. When ElGendy's Baba rebukes him for wanting to proclaim out loud, inside prison, the betrayal that is military rule, it is hard to remember that the fault lies with the security state, not with those desperate to shout it from every rooftop.
So we find there are layers to the barzakh as it operates in every place Egyptians find themselves.
Those who are out in the open-air prison cannot speak, because to do so will invoke the state's ire against them. Those who are detained cannot speak, because to do so will invoke the spectre of the Ikhwan against their name. Those who are imprisoned cannot speak, because to do so will only decrease their chances of a pardon or release.
And so all resort to ameliorating their conditions in whatever small way they can - except this is what existence looks like, not the freedom to live. As ElGendy's cellmate and friend Tooha noted one night:
"The constant push to improve prison life. We've accepted confinement as the norm, Gendy, and that's how they win."
Somewhere in the liminal space between I am imprisoned and I am a prisoner, we had stopped trying to climb the tree.
'Shame and treachery'
The tree cannot be climbed by negotiating a settlement with the security state, as the Muslim Brotherhood found out in its attempt at normalising the facade of democracy through elections. Nor can prison life be negotiated through nepotism, protecting one's own sanctified group at the expense of other siyasi (political prisoners) and gena'i (criminal prisoners), because the entire system oppresses them all.
To fight our way out of this barzakh is to admit that "military rule is shame and treachery", a lesson most profoundly learnt in the midst of the genocide of the Palestinian people, where ElGendy ends his stunning account.
Seeing Egyptian soldiers take bribes from Palestinians, as ElGendy recounts, and an Egyptian state-linked firm charge them thousands of dollars each to escape, seeing Egyptian authorities bar access to humanitarians seeking to enter Gaza, and witnessing the repression of pro-Palestine sentiment reminds us that Egypt's military shame is tied inextricably to its role as a garrison for western interests.
Until we acknowledge this khiyana (treachery) and treat Egypt as a hostile entity, we will continue to normalise Egypt's role in the structure of violence that maintains the status quo of genocide.
ElGendy's memoir, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, is the starting point for us to acknowledge the true face of Egypt, and the true face of the hostile entities that rule it. Through engaging with his profound reflections on his time in prison, we might better understand how we collectivise across our disparate groupings, and how we might eventually fight back.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

The world of Mirzapur has largely revolved around power struggles, violence and rivalries between its male characters. However, the franchise has also given its female characters some of its most layered storylines, with Beena Tripathi emerging as one of the most intriguing figures.
After Mirzapur – The Movie’s success, Rasika Dugal’s Beena Tripathi deserves her own spin-off, and the time is right!
Played by Rasika Dugal, Beena has undergone a significant transformation through the series. From navigating the dynamics within the Tripathi household to making difficult choices for her own survival, her journey has often unfolded alongside the larger battle for power in Mirzapur.
With the franchise now expanding beyond streaming, the possibility of exploring individual characters in greater depth could offer another way to build on its universe. Beena, in particular, has a backstory and set of relationships that could potentially lend themselves to a standalone story.
One of the more recent additions to her arc came through her relationship with Birju Lohar, played by Mohit Malik. The storyline offered viewers a glimpse into Beena's emotional past and provided more context for the woman she eventually became. It also introduced a comparatively softer dimension to a character whose journey has largely been shaped by survival, power and difficult choices.
The use of the classic song 'Saanson Ki Mala' during Beena's track further underlined the emotional conflict surrounding her character. The song played against a moment in which Beena was faced with a difficult decision, adding another layer to the sequence and highlighting the contrast between her emotions and instincts.
The track has also generated attention on social media, with the song finding traction through Reels and other user-generated content. This has added to the ongoing conversation around Beena and the different facets of her character.
A potential Beena Tripathi spin-off could explore parts of her life that the main Mirzapur storyline has only touched upon, including her past, relationships and evolution within the Tripathi family. While there is no official announcement of such a series at present, Beena's journey leaves enough unanswered questions for the character to potentially carry a story of her own.
For now, Rasika Dugal's Beena remains one of the franchise's most complex characters, with her story continuing to offer possibilities beyond the central power struggle that has defined Mirzapur.

In September 2026, some people on social media shared an image that appeared to show U.S. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump frowning as they stared into the camera lens.
For example, one X post (archived) said of the image, "For just a moment, the world saw their true nature. This is a real photo."
The same image was shared to Reddit (archived) and Threads (archived). Some social media users doubted the authenticity of the image.
The image is authentic, though cropped. The original photo, which includes Chinese President Xi Jinping and first lady Peng Liyuan during their state visit to the U.S., was taken on Sept. 24, 2026 by Getty photographer Chip Somodevilla. We were unable to find any verifiable information as to why the Trumps were frowning at that moment.
The caption of Somodevilla's photo reads:
A military aide, U.S. first lady Melania Trump, U.S. President Donald Trump, President of China Xi Jinping, and first lady of China Peng Liyuan depart a balcony after watching a Silent Drill Platoon Review at the White House on September 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. President Trump is hosting President Xi for a three-day state visit to Washington, DC where the leaders are expected to discuss trade practices, artificial intelligence and furthering 'strategic stability' between their countries.
An almost identical photo taken by Reuters photographer Evan Vucci is featured on Reuters Connect, Reuters' licensable photo repository. That caption is less specific than the Getty caption, instead reading, "President Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping after watching a military demonstration from a balcony of the White House in Washington, September 24."
Reuters Connect also offers two other, more zoomed-out versions of the same photo. These versions photo match Somodevilla's Getty photo by including Jinping's wife, Peng Liyuan, on the far right of the same balcony.
The four can be seen watching the referenced military demonstration in another Reuters photo.
The Associated Press' own photo repository has photos from just before and about the same time as the Getty and Reuters photos were taken. One shows Melania Trump still looking at Jinping, while the other has both Trumps looking just past the camera, similar to the Reuters photo.
Two other AP photos, one of Trump gesturing for Jinping to walk ahead of him and another of the pair walking side-by-side, suggests the four were heading inside the White House from the military demonstration with the two presidents walking ahead of the two first ladies.
Somodevilla apparently shot another photo a couple of seconds after his first one. In that photo, the Trumps' frowns are less pronounced than in the photo that spread on social media.

The Trump administration is seeking to join Elon Musk’s appeal against a €120 million EU fine of the billionaire’s social media platform X, the latest escalation in the transatlantic clash over Brussels’ efforts to rein in US tech companies.
The US Department of Justice on Thursday filed an application to intervene in a pair of cases brought by Musk and X seeking annulment of the penalty, which will be heard at the EU’s General Court in Luxembourg.
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,” assistant attorney general Brett Shumate said.
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” Shumate added.
The European Commission in December last year fined X €120 million for breaking the Digital Services Act, the first such penalty under the bloc’s online safety regime. It accused the platform of breaching its regulations for transparency, providing insufficient access to data and the deceptive design of its blue-tick system for verified accounts.
The DSA, a more aggressive set of rules to police online players, has become a flashpoint between Brussels and US tech companies. Donald Trump’s administration has supported claims by US companies that the EU is unfairly targeting American groups and infringing freedom of speech principles championed by the Maga movement.

Google has been trying to have its AI assistant make phone calls on your behalf for almost 10 years. Remember Duplex? It enabled the now-defunct Google Assistant to call restaurants and book tables. That service was shuttered a few years ago, but now comes round two, powered by modern large language models.
On Thursday, Google announced Call for Me, an experimental beta feature exclusive to its latest Pixel 11 smartphones in the US (and in English). Pixel 11 owners need a Gemini subscription and have to be enrolled in the Phone by Google app’s public beta. Google has instructions on how to participate here.
These calls are designed to reach businesses. Gemini can call your local hardware store to ask if they stock a specific tool, or chat with a barber to schedule a haircut. Just tell Gemini to make the call—it may ask you follow-up questions for more context—and the chatbot will introduce itself and can have a back-and-forth conversation to ensure your request is handled. If it runs into an automated phone menu, it can navigate it and even wait on hold. On your end, you can view a live transcript on the Pixel and take over at any point.
Google says it works best with businesses, but there are some establishments Gemini won't call, like emergency services. That said, you can ask Gemini to call specific numbers. For example, if your tattoo artist doesn't have much of a web presence, “Gemini will try to search for a phone number, but you may provide one as well,” a Google spokesperson tells WIRED. During these calls, the assistant's voice will be the same one used in Gemini Live interactions, even if your preferred Gemini voice has an accent.
Call for Me expands on Google’s suite of smart calling features on Pixels and Android. The Phone app can already screen incoming calls and block robocalls and telemarketers. Hold for Me lets the assistant listen for when the hold music ends and a live person is on the other end; it alerts you to pick up the phone when it’s finally your cue. Direct My Call can display the different choices in an automated phone menu before they’re spoken, so you can tap nine to reach a live person and skip the recorded voice reading out the whole list. It even has real-time Scam Detection, alerting you when it thinks the person on the other end is scamming you.
Voice assistants handling phone calls is a little more accepted today than back in the Duplex days. Call screening features abound—whether on a Pixel, Samsung, or iPhone, onboard assistants routinely intercept unknown callers to ask why they’re calling.
But these kinds of features—much like hyped-up AI translation features—can often fall short. Calls are unpredictable, and the person on the other end may hang up, assuming it’s just another spam call. What happens if Gemini doesn’t understand a person’s accent all that well? Will it trap the clerk in an endless loop of asking them to repeat themselves? And if the shop doesn’t have the tool you need, does the bot know how to bow out politely—or just cut the line?
“That is exactly what we want to continue testing,” the Google spokesperson says. “With this experiment, we look forward to users testing a variety of cases, so that we can continue to improve the feature across accents and noisy environments.” And yes, Google says Gemini will “politely” hang up if the business can't accommodate your needs.
It still points to a future where robots may take over these kinds of business phone calls altogether. Businesses are also experimenting with artificial-intelligence tools to interface with customers, like local California pizza chain Pizza My Heart, which lets you text its Jimmy the Surfer chatbot to order pizza.
It doesn’t seem too far off that you’ll ask your phone to call a restaurant, and the restaurant’s AI will answer. The machines are talking to each other, except they’re just debating whether you want the stuffed crust.

Tension escalated at Lovely Professional University in Punjab following unrest triggered by rumours of rape. Protesting students clashed with law enforcement personnel on campus, resulting in stone pelting, arson, and damage to several vehicles, including media and police vehicles. Heavy projectiles were thrown at officers in riot gear, prompting police to deploy mild lathi charge to push back crowds. Protesters torched a Punjab Police vehicle as smoke billowed across the campus. The university administration denied the allegations of rape, stating that no such incident occurred, while an FIR has been registered and a Special Investigation Team constituted. Senior police officers, including Kapurthala Senior Superintendent of Police Gaurav Toora, arrived on the ground to take stock of the situation as additional forces were mobilised across university hostels to restore order.
In an exclusive conversation on India Today, filmmaker Meghna Gulzar and actor Prithviraj Sukumaran discussed their film Dhaira and its exploration of uncomfortable societal questions surrounding crimes against women, judicial delays, and extrajudicial encounter killings. Reflecting on public outrage and the growing demand for instant justice, Meghna Gulzar noted, "Hesitating to talk about it is not going to make it go away." Addressing the dilemma between the rule of law and vigilante justice, she clarified that her intent was not to advocate encounter culture, stating, "I don't believe that we need to become a banana republic and that our police should become trigger-happy." Prithviraj Sukumaran explained his character Raman as an argument reflecting societal frustration with an overburdened judicial system facing millions of pending cases. Gulzar highlighted how the narrative confronts moral gray zones, juvenile justice laws post-Nirbhaya, and the complex reality of justice delivery in India today.
A political controversy has emerged over allegations concerning the Chief Election Commissioner. A former Kerala Chief Secretary alleged that during a flight to Delhi in 2016, the official advised him to contest the 2019 Lok Sabha elections on a Bharatiya Janata Party ticket, an offer he stated he rejected. The opposition has questioned the neutrality of the Election Commission and demanded the resignation of the poll body chief following reports regarding internal rifts. Meanwhile, the ruling party dismissed the claims as fabricated, questioning why the allegations surfaced after an entire decade and raising doubts over the timing of the disclosure.
Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra has demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar following allegations by former Kerala Chief Secretary Jiji Thomson. Thomson claimed that in 2016, Gyanesh Kumar advised him during a flight to contest the 2019 Lok Sabha elections on a BJP ticket, win, and become a minister. Speaking on the revelations, Priyanka Gandhi termed the alleged action illegal, unconstitutional, and unethical, questioning how individuals actively propagating party leanings can oversee fair elections. The controversy comes amid wider opposition scrutiny and ongoing friction within the Election Commission, with Congress leaders warning that protests demanding the poll chief's resignation will escalate in the coming weeks.
Opposition parties are intensifying coordination to forge a united front against the Election Commission and central agencies. CPM General Secretary M.A. Baby met AAP National Convener Arvind Kejriwal in New Delhi to discuss a joint struggle, inviting him to participate in party programmes in Kerala. The discussions focused on allegations of authoritarian functioning within the poll body, targeting of opposition leaders, and central agency actions against political figures including Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, Arvind Kejriwal, and Manish Sisodia. The coordination comes ahead of a key INDIA bloc meeting scheduled for 30 September, where opposition leaders plan to outline a common strategy to challenge the central government and the election watchdog.

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by rebels from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara, and the formation of a new rebel coalition aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.
Fighting from 2020 to 2022 between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) killed about 600,000 people. Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.
On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.
TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse (AFP) there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.
TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.
The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital, Addis Ababa.
The federal army said it had killed 272 TPLF soldiers as they launched attacks in multiple parts of North Wollo Zone in Amhara. The figure has not been independently verified, and no casualties were given for the federal army or civilians.
Analysts say TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”
The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.
Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar accusations.
TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.
The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.
It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.
On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks.
An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

A video (here & here) of a young woman without arms wearing a tricolour leotard and performing gymnastics (floor exercise) is being shared on social media, claiming to show a real Indian gymnast. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of an armless Indian performing gymnastics in a tricolour leotard.
Fact: The video is AI-generated. Visual analysis reveals obvious inconsistencies, such as gibberish background text, distorted audience members, and the gymnast’s body momentarily disappearing. Furthermore, AI content detectors confirmed that the video is AI-generated. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we conducted a keyword search to see if any recent sporting events matched the viral visuals. However, we couldn’t find any news reports, event details, or any details of an Indian gymnast delivering such a performance.
We then analysed the footage carefully by slowing it down. This revealed several visual inconsistencies, such as gibberish text in the background, overlapping fingers and arms in the audience, and the gymnast’s legs and body momentarily disappearing mid-air during the performance. These visual errors strongly indicate that the video is AI-generated.
Next, we ran the video through AI-content detectors, which confirmed (here & here) that the video is indeed AI- generated. Similar AI-generated clips (here & here) are circulating online and are falsely passed off as real incidents.
To sum it up, an AI-generated video is being shared as a real incident of an armless Indian gymnast performing a routine.

India’s hopes of an individual medal in badminton at the ongoing Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 ended on Sunday as P.V. Sindhu and Unnati Hooda both suffered defeats in the quarterfinals.
World Championships bronze medallists Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, and the mixed doubles duo of Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto also bowed out of the competition at the same stage.
The 31-year-old Sindhu, a two-time Asian Games medallist, took the lead before losing 21-11, 18-21, 10-21 to China’s Chen Yu Fei in an hour and 15 minutes.
Sindhu’s loss came after Unnati Hooda played a gruelling 66-minute encounter against Akane Yamaguchi and almost pulled off another medal. The Japanese, a three-time World Champion, eventually kept her composure to clinch the contest 21-16, 14-21, 21-17.
Dhruv-Tanisha fought hard in their 14-21, 21-18, 18-21 loss to Chinese World No. 1 duo of Feng Yan Zhe and Huang Dongping.
Treesa and Gayatri were eliminated after an 18-21, 9-21 defeat against Malaysian World No. 5 pair of Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan.
Indian shuttlers failed to win a medal in individual events at the Asian Games for the first time since the 2014 edition in Incheon where only the women’s team had bagged a bronze. In the current edition, the only podium finish was achieved in the men’s team which settled for bronze after losing to China in the semifinals.

Venezuela releases dozens of prisoners following meeting between Trump and interim leader
Human rights groups in Venezuela said that significant numbers of political prisoners were released in the South American country on Saturday, though a total number of those released has still not been established
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Human rights groups in Venezuela said that significant numbers of political prisoners were released in the South American country on Saturday, though the total number of those freed has still not been determined.
The prisoner releases follow a meeting Tuesday between Interim President Delcy Rodríguez and President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. In her speech at the UN, Rodríguez said Venezuela, whose government has been widely accused of jailing dissidents, stealing elections and stifling freedom of speech, has “begun a process of democratic transformation.”
In a message posted on X, the Venezuelan human rights group Clippve said seven political prisoners were released from a prison on the outskirts of Caracas on Saturday morning, including Wilder Vasquez, a university student who had been sentenced to five years in prison for participating in a 2018 plot to kill former President Nicolás Maduro. Vasquez has long claimed he was innocent. His sentence had expired in 2023.
In another X message, the human rights group Justicia Encuentro y Perdon said that 29 people were released from Venezuelan prisons Saturday, including 12 inmates who were on its list of political prisoners.
“Seventeen of those freed were not in our database of political prisoners,” the organization said. “Our team continues to verify information to update our registry.”
Venezuela’s government did not make any statements on Saturday’s events.
Rodríguez's administration denies the country is jailing dissidents. However, it has said it is making an effort to release people who have been investigated or condemned for committing crimes that include attacking the nation’s institutions, as it seeks to promote national reconciliation.
Hundreds of people have been released from Venezuela’s prisons since Maduro was captured in January in a U.S. military raid and taken to New York, where he faces drug trafficking charges. But human rights groups argue that Venezuela continues to hold political prisoners. In a message posted on Friday, Justicia Encuentro y Perdon said that there are still 450 political prisoners in Venezuela, including 20 foreigners.
In a speech at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday, Rodríguez said that there “will be elections in Venezuela” but did not say when.
Democracy activists and human rights groups have been calling on Venezuela's government to hold new elections that would grant legitimacy to its institutions and express the will of the Venezuelan people. After Maduro was removed, Rodríguez, who was his vice president, stepped in as interim leader, and was given a six-month mandate by the nation’s supreme court. That mandate has now expired, raising questions about Rodríguez’s legitimacy.
At least 1,800 people were arrested in Venezuela in a crackdown that followed the nation’s 2024 presidential election, which Maduro was widely accused of stealing. Dozens of opposition activists went into hiding to avoid arrest and some also left the country, including opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who smuggled herself out of Venezuela last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Machado has been threatened with arrest by the Rodriguez administration if she returns to the country.

I was in a long-distance relationship when I moved from India to join my partner in Austria.
I first met him four years earlier while doing what I loved best — introducing travelers to India as an Airbnb experience host. We connected instantly. Two years later, in the middle of the pandemic, we became life partners.
After another gap for visa formalities, I joined him in Austria. Unlike most people who make this shift in their 20s, I was doing it in my late 40s. It was a difficult decision because I was at the peak of my career as a content creator at a New York-based agency and had built a life in a city I loved.
Many people said it was a mistake. But today, after relocating during a pandemic, making a cultural transition into another country, learning a new language, and reestablishing my career in the most unconventional way, we have built a life we love.
Our relationship is stronger
My move to Austria during the pandemic was slow. While cross-border moves usually involve bureaucratic hurdles, the pandemic made them even more complex.
But we prepared carefully and fulfilled all legal requirements. Facing uncertainty together made us more certain of our plans and drew us closer. It helped us build the resilience we needed for the path ahead.
Home is something you build together, not a place where you are born
One of the most difficult things I had to do was gather over 40 years' worth of belongings into a bag. Doing that showed me how to downsize my life to what really mattered.
When I arrived in Austria, my partner's things were still in boxes in our new house. I added my suitcase to them and we unpacked everything we owned. We built our home by making it a space that reflected both our identities.
It's never too late to start again
The difficult part about moving later in life is rebuilding your old systems from scratch. Not just the big things like settling into a new home or finding a job, but also the small things like figuring out how public transport works or navigating bureaucracy in a new country.
I rebuilt my old systems, from setting up a new bank account to getting an Austrian phone number, all with tremendous support from my partner. As an independent woman, I learned to be vulnerable and ask for support when I needed it.
Thinking in a new language is life-changing
I had already begun learning German before I moved. But for the first time, I was in a classroom where none of the other students knew English.
But we did learn to speak to each other. Our adult language classroom helped me meet incredible people from around the world who were also relocating. Learning a new language with them made me a better communicator.
Careers are connected to what you do, not where you live
The biggest problem with leaving a country later in life is letting go of the professional identity you have established. I stepped down from leading the content practice at a New York agency and left behind my identity as a bestselling author in India.
But the digital world helped me stay connected to both those identities. Instead of looking for employers, I looked for clients instead. I used my experience to become a content consultant to companies around the world, followed my passion as a travel writer, and published my first poetry anthology.
Having a personal network matters
The deep bond between my partner and me did not compensate for the loss of my friends and family back home. Unlike when you leave home earlier, I had built these friendships over the last four decades.
My first friends were my partner's friends. But one of the best decisions I made was to join a local book club. Not only did it help me to keep reading, but it also gave me a chance to meet people with similar interests.
You have to embrace your roots and wings
I also had to find my balance between the two countries I now call home. I was still keenly aware of my home country's history and cultural traditions.
But I also came to appreciate many things about being Austrian. As someone who had been an experienced host, I learned about Austrian history, culture, food, and traditions with the same enthusiasm. Embracing my new country helped me genuinely value and come to enjoy my new home.

How to use Android's Desktop mode to turn your phone into a tiny PC
You can plug recent Pixel phones into a monitor to get a desktop-style interface.
For years, the idea of smartphones connected to a monitor offering a desktop experience has fascinated manufacturers, developers and (to some extent) consumers. But hardware experiments like Asus' PadFone and the Motorola Atrix Lapdock didn't catch on with users as vendors expected.
Companies took to software experiences in their attempts to grant desktop-grade functionality. Microsoft's short-lived Continuum feature for Windows 10 Mobile was discontinued in 2017. Samsung's DeX lets its Galaxy phones deliver a PC-like workspace with a taskbar, optimized apps and wireless connectivity. And Motorola's phones continue to offer its Smart Connect experience.
Now, after months of being in beta, the Android 16 March Pixel Drop update brought Android Desktop Mode to the Pixel 8 and up. Let's get it set up.
How do I put my Android in desktop mode?
Connect your Pixel 8 or a newer Google phone to an external monitor with a high-speed USB-C cable, and a pop-up will prompt you to switch to Android Desktop Mode or use it as a mirror. Select the Desktop option. Attach a mouse and keyboard via Bluetooth or a USB hub, and you now have a mobile workstation with a desktop-style interface. Google hasn't announced the feature's availability on non-Pixel devices yet.
Apps open in windows that can be sized based on your needs, and a start menu opens the App Drawer. Pulling down from the top brings up your notifications. ZDNet noted that Desktop Mode ran smoothly with no hiccups while running multiple applications.
If you disconnect your phone from your setup and reconnect it, Desktop Mode preserves your active window layout to help you resume where you left things if you didn't already close them on your phone. You can't add apps to the desktop's home screen, so open them from the start menu. If gaming's on your mind, remember that most games built for phones won't support keyboard inputs. Content creator leepspvideo managed to run Steam games natively via Desktop Mode with the help of apps like GameNative.
What are the limitations of Android desktop mode?
Your mileage with Android's Desktop Mode will depend on your use case. While simple document editing and watching cat videos on YouTube will run smoothly, you may run into issues with meatier tasks like photo editing. While videos ran smoothly, HowToGeek found that the software currently caps the frame rate at 60 Hz. Users on Reddit noted its lack of 4K support, which is a big deal when connecting with large monitors.
Right now, your phone won't run Chrome extensions in Desktop Mode, even if they can run on Apple Silicon or Windows on ARM devices. That means editing tools like Grammarly and tab manager OneTab won't function as you'd expect.
Running a desktop UI with floating windows off a smartphone pushes its thermal envelope to its limits. Android Police's testing found that the phone turned hot to the touch in 30 minutes of light usage on Desktop Mode. Prolonged sessions of running Android like a desktop can weaken your battery's endurance at a higher pace than regular usage would. Despite these hiccups, Android Desktop Mode is a step in the right direction for mobile productivity, and it's worth testing out if you own a newer Pixel device.

The first in a new class of space telescopes is on track to reach the launch pad in the early 2030s, NASA announced this week.
The PRIMA mission will be the first of NASA’s Probe Explorers, a new line of observatories intended to do more science for less money. The agency’s space telescopes typically fall into lower-cost “Explorer-class” missions, with cost caps in the range of a few hundred million dollars, or flagship observatories like the recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which came with a price tag of some $4.3 billion.
With the Probe Explorers, NASA officials seek to find a better balance between the smaller Explorer missions and multibillion-dollar flagships. NASA has studied potential Probe Explorer mission concepts for several years after an independent panel of scientists recommended the new mission category. But it wasn’t clear until recently whether NASA’s science budget, which is under pressure from the Trump administration, would be sufficient to actually start developing one.
NASA announced Wednesday it will move forward with PRIMA, short for the Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics. PRIMA was the sole finalist for the first Probe Explorer mission after NASA disqualified a competing mission, an X-ray observatory known as AXIS, earlier this year. NASA said a concept study for AXIS indicated it would not meet the agency’s schedule and budget constraints.
The scientist leading the AXIS concept study blamed disruptions and mismanagement at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, the NASA location charged with leading the AXIS mission if it moved forward into development. PRIMA will be led by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, which has also found itself in an institutional crisis, with few missions in development and a series of layoffs.
Flagship missions can take decades to design, build, and test before they make it to the launch pad. The Roman Space Telescope was the exception. It took 10 years from NASA’s approval to proceed into development until Roman’s launch last month on the way to an observation post a million miles from Earth.
Leftovers from Webb
PRIMA, which has a cost cap of $1.2 billion excluding launch costs, will not be as big and complex as Roman, so it’s natural to assume a shorter development cycle. NASA wants to launch PRIMA seven years from now, in 2033. The telescope will observe the Universe in faint, far-infrared light in a range of wavelengths between 24 and 235 micrometers, requiring its primary optics to be cooled to 4.5 Kelvin, or minus 451° Fahrenheit.
This would usually require a brand-new build of a sophisticated cryocooler. PRIMA will instead use a spare leftover from the development of the James Webb Space Telescope, modified to use helium-3 instead of helium-4 as the cooling fluid. The focal planes of PRIMA’s kinetic inductance detectors will be chilled even lower to 100 milliKelvin, putting the mission’s optics in contention for the coldest ever sent into space.
Its far-infrared sensitivity will give PRIMA visibility into the origins of planets and their atmospheres, the coevolution of galaxies and black holes, and changes in the properties of dust and metals over cosmic time, according to the scientists heading the mission. PRIMA, with a 5.9-foot-diameter (1.8-meter) primary mirror, will set up shop in an orbit around the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point a million miles from Earth.
The mission will peer deeper into the infrared bands than any of NASA’s past or current infrared observatories, such as Spitzer and Webb, and will build on discoveries made by Europe’s Herschel space telescope, which gave astronomers new insights into the formation of cosmic filaments and the role of water in the formation of stars and planets.
PRIMA uses a modified spare cryocooler from the James Webb Space Telescope. The cryocooler for Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument is seen here.
