Srinagar, Sep 22: The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference Additional General Secretary and Rajya Sabha Member Choudhary Mohammad Ramzan Tuesday said that the discontinuation of the December 5 holiday commemorating the birth anniversary of Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and attempts to obstruct the elected government’s efforts to restore the holiday, raise serious questions about respect for the democratic mandate and public sentiment.
He said the manner in which BJP legislators reacted to the proposal in the Assembly to restore the holiday on Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s birth anniversary reflected their narrow-mindedness, communal outlook and hostility towards the National Conference.
Choudhary Ramzan, as per a party statement, said Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s stature and legacy do not depend on any official holiday. His historic struggle against subjugation, deprivation, poverty and economic backwardness in Jammu and Kashmir and his efforts to politically awaken and empower the people, remain deeply associated with the history of the region. The measures undertaken under his leadership concerning popular rights, land reforms and social justice constitute an important chapter of modern Jammu and Kashmir’s history.
He said the changes made to official holidays associated with July 13, Martyrs’ Day, and Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s birth anniversary are viewed by the National Conference in the context of its historical legacy and the memory of those who sacrificed their lives for the political rights of the people. He stressed that the martyrs of July 13, 1931, hold an important place in Jammu and Kashmir’s political history and that their sacrifices cannot simply be erased from public memory.
Choudhary Ramzan said the National Conference has, from the outset, expressed its concerns over the fundamental changes made to Jammu and Kashmir’s constitutional and administrative framework after August 5, 2019. He said the abrogation of Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status and its reorganisation into two Union Territories raised profound questions among the people regarding their political, constitutional and democratic rights.
He said the people of Jammu and Kashmir have elected their representative government through the democratic process and the elected government should be provided adequate constitutional and administrative space to implement its decisions and fulfil public expectations. If an elected government decides to restore a holiday associated with the birth anniversary of a historic personality, he said, the matter should not be subjected to unnecessary administrative hurdles.
He further said that decisions concerning the constitutional and democratic rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir, which have been altered or restricted over the past several years, should be addressed through democratic processes, constitutional institutions and in accordance with the aspirations of the people.

Telangana to remove eligible private properties from 22-A list
Telangana has removed private properties from the prohibited list for registration, benefiting 1.41 lakh homes and plots, amid political controversy.
The Telangana government on Thursday ordered the removal of all eligible private properties from the prohibited list under Section 22-A of the Registration Act, 1908, paving the way for their registration, people familiar with the matter said. The decision is expected to benefit around 1.41 lakh houses and plots across the state.
The orders issued by principal secretary (revenue) Lokesh Kumar, following a meeting led by deputy chief minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka, will allow registration of eligible houses, plots and flats that have valid layout, building or apartment approvals from competent government authorities.
According to a senior revenue department official, Section 22-A empowers the government to identify categories of properties whose registration should be prohibited. These include government waste lands, assigned lands, properties belonging to municipalities and government institutions, endowment and Wakf properties, surplus lands under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, forest lands, tribal lands covered by Regulation 1 of 1970, and properties under court orders or disputes.
The official said more than 3.72 lakh acres had been inadvertently included in the prohibited list while changes were being made to Dharani, the previous land registration portal, which has now been replaced by Bhu Bharati.
“Thousands of genuine private properties, including decades-old residential layouts, apartments and lands that had previously received clearances from government agencies, were brought under Section 22-A without adequate verification,” the official said.
The issue has triggered a political controversy over the past two months, with opposition parties accusing the government of harassing people by blocking property transactions. Thousands of complaints were received from owners who said the restrictions prevented them from selling or registering their properties.
The issue particularly affected areas in and around Hyderabad, including parts of Medchal-Malkajgiri, Rangareddy, Sangareddy and Hyderabad districts. When it came up in the state legislative assembly on September 16, chief minister A Revanth Reddy assured that the problems would be resolved shortly.
Revenue minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy said properties covered by the 22-A list can be considered for registration if they were developed with valid statutory permissions from competent authorities, including GHMC, HMDA, DTCP, municipal bodies and panchayats.
Owners will have to produce valid approvals and at least one link document relating to a registration carried out after the relevant approval was granted.
The government has also constituted district-level committees headed by collectors to scrutinise individual cases based on revenue records, statutory approvals, title documents and the legal status of the land.
“Eligible cases will be resolved at the earliest,” Reddy said.

Morwell community walks to remember those lost to violence, a year on from Kaiden Morgan-Johnston's death
In short:
About 300 people have walked Morwell's main street in solidarity, to condemn violence.
The walk marked a year since the alleged murder of Kaiden Morgan-Johnston by two boys and a man, 500 metres from his Morwell home.
What's next?
Mr Morgan-Johnston's mother says she will keep advocating to stamp out violence in the community.
Twelve months ago Sascha Johnston watched the AFL grand final with her 18-year-old son Kaiden.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are warned that this story includes names and images of Indigenous people who have died.
Hours later, he was allegedly murdered by three people, only 500 metres from his home in Victoria's east.
Instead of sharing a couch with him to watch the big game this year, she was preparing to march the streets of Morwell, to condemn violence in his honour.
She rallied a 300-strong crowd of people of all ages, and also managed to gather other Latrobe Valley families who have lost loved ones to violence.
They walked down the main street and gathered in the local park to talk about change and tell the young people of the Latrobe Valley that weapons and violence are never the answer.
Addressing the crowd, Ms Johnston said she was proud of her community.
"We've all just used our voices and our feet to say that we want a safe community," she said.
"We all deserve to be safe and we need to be teaching our kids and young people there's never ever the right time for a weapon.
"Young lives lost, young lives with so much future ahead of them that they would have contributed to society, and what's left is insurmountable pain.
"We deserve safe streets, [a] safe community for our children, for the young ones, for anyone."
A young life lost
Kaiden Morgan-Johnston was a proud Yorta Yorta, Wakka Wakka and Wurundjeri man living on Gunaikurnai country.
He worked at Bunnings, spent time with mates and was quickly becoming a young Aboriginal leader, dancing with local Indigenous dance group Boorun Boys.
"You know, he's not here to finish his story, but I'll be finishing it on his behalf," Ms Johnston said.
"I do this with Kaiden, I know he's with me, I do this with him,"
"That's my mission as his mum."
In the latest data from the Crime Statistics Agency, Latrobe Valley recorded the highest rate of criminal incidents in Victoria outside the City of Melbourne.
In the weeks before Kaiden died, the Victorian government introduced machete bins.
But Ms Johnston said she believed teaching young people not to carry them at all was the most important thing.
"There were probably machetes that went into those bins that were from someone's garden shed, but not the young people that are pulling them out and using them as weapons," Ms Johnston said.
"If someone feels they're at risk, they think their only way to keep safe is to carry a weapon, that's the problem.
"We just need everybody to put them down."
When Mr Morgan-Johnston was about 15 years old, he was robbed on a tram by a group of boys at knifepoint.
"You know, that was the path Kaiden wanted to go down after he got robbed," Ms Johnston said.
"And we worked through that, we said that's not the solution.
"He grew up and he realised that's not the way to solve anything, so he wasn't interested in carrying weapons or anything like that."
But above all, she wants society to be safer.
"In his short life, he was robbed for his shoes and his phone," Ms Johnston said.
"And then he's [allegedly] murdered at 18.
"What kind of world have we created that a young person can experience that level of violence?"
Families remember lost loved ones
Walking alongside Mr Morgan-Johnston's family were the families of slain GP Dr Ashley Gordon and Roy Poole, who was killed in Moe in 2011.
Dr Ashley Gordon grew up in the Latrobe Valley and went to school in Morwell. His family is well-known for running the local childcare centre.
Dr Gordon was murdered in 2024 by a teenager with a knife. He had chased a group of boys who had broken into his home.
His sister Natalie Gordon has since been vocal about preventing knife crime.
"I think it's amazing that so many people are getting behind it and so many young faces," Ms Gordon said.
"It's really, really nice to see so many young people understanding their actions have consequences and, you know, fighting against wrong."
Ms Gordon has campaigned for tougher penalties for youth crime and legislation like Jack's Law to be brought to Victoria.
The law allows police to check people for weapons in public places using metal detectors, without warrants.
Never-ending pain
In 2011, Bec Kennedy's brother Roy Poole was stabbed to death alongside his friend Evan Rudd, during an argument over a car park in a block of flats in Moe.
"Everyone's life moves on after such a tragedy, but for those that are directly impacted, it never, never stops," Ms Kennedy said.
"I don't think it matters how long ago that you lose a loved one."
She has never spoken publicly about her brother's death.
The man who was convicted of his manslaughter, and the murder of Mr Rudd, is serving a 31-year prison sentence.
At the time of the killings, he was on parole.
"We just want a safe community,"
"I think back when everything happened, I was a bit of a silent bystander.
"It was very, very hard for me to deal with.
"It was huge for me to be able to come today and walk beside everyone."
Victoria Police Detective Inspector Matt Gleeson said police supported the rally.
"It brings attention to the community and raising the awareness and for us, it supports the stopping of violence in our communities, which is a good thing," he said.
"There were no issues there yesterday, it was a good day for it, plenty of people turned out I'm told so the objective was achieved by the family."

Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces carried out 756 operations against Houthi military positions across several fronts over the past 72 hours and killed or wounded 2,316 Houthi members, the Yemeni armed forces said on Sunday. The military also claimed that four Iranian experts specialising in drone and missile operations were killed in Taiz governorate.
Brigadier general Majeed Abdullah Al-Nuzaili, spokesman for Yemen’s armed forces, said the operations targeted Houthi positions and movements in Kitaf and Al-Baqa, Alab, Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda, Lahij and Taiz. His statement was carried by Yemen’s Saba news agency and reported by Ajel News.
Al-Nuzaili said the operations involved aircraft, drones, snipers, field artillery and rocket launchers. He said the attacks “destroyed or disabled troop carriers, vehicles, military reinforcements, missile-launch platforms, weapons and equipment depots and other military hardware belonging to the Houthis”.
The spokesman said the deaths of the four Iranian specialists were “a new confirmation of the continued Iranian support and expertise” provided to the Houthi movement. 
He also said the presence of the experts demonstrated Iran’s continued provision of support and expertise to the group.
The figures and claims from the Yemeni government could not be independently verified. A separate report by Al Bawaba also cited the government’s claim of 756 operations and 2,316 Houthi casualties.
The latest claims came as fighting intensified around Taiz. On Sunday, a Saudi airstrike on a market in the province killed seven people and wounded 40, according to the Houthi-run health ministry and Houthi media. Al-Masirah TV said a Saudi fighter jet had targeted the area shortly before reporting the casualties.
Yemen’s government disputed the Houthi account of the market strike. Three government military sources told Reuters that Houthi fighters had recently established a military camp near the market, leaving the intended target and circumstances of the civilian casualties disputed.
The escalation follows a renewed Houthi offensive after years of relative calm. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi air forces had carried out 27 strikes across Taiz, Marib, Saada, Amran, Ibb and Hajjah.

US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
- Published
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

Heartburn is commonly described as acidity and treated with antacids. But gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is not simply acidity. It occurs when the stomach contents repeatedly move into the oesophagus because the normal anti-reflux barrier does not function effectively.
“GERD is not simply a problem of producing too much acid,” said Vishnu Abishek Raju, senior consultant, medical gastroenterology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. Heartburn, therefore, is a symptom, rather than a diagnosis. Some people living with reflux have visible inflammation of the oesophagus, while others have symptoms without any visible injury.
GERD is common in India. A 2021 analysis of nine Indian studies involving 20,614 people estimated its pooled prevalence at 15.6%.
How reflux occurs
The lower oesophageal sphincter acts as a valve between the oesophagus and stomach. It can undergo brief, inappropriate relaxations, allowing stomach contents to move upwards.
A hiatal hernia can weaken the anti-reflux barrier by allowing part of the stomach to move above the diaphragm. Obesity, particularly excess abdominal fat, increases pressure within the abdomen, while delayed gastric emptying can increase the volume and pressure inside the stomach.
The oesophagus also has protective mechanisms. Saliva helps clear refluxed material, while alkaline mucus helps limit acid-related injury.
“People may have acid reflux within a stipulated period. But if that goes beyond the protective mechanisms of the body, those defensive mechanisms fail and the food pipe can ger damaged, a condition called oesophagitis,” said Arul Prakash, clinical lead and senior consultant in medical gastroenterology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai.
Why symptoms can be misleading
The amount of reflux does not always correspond to the severity of symptoms.
“Some people have increased sensitivity of the oesophagus, so even normal amounts of reflux can produce significant burning or chest discomfort,” Dr. Abishek Raju said. This includes reflux hypersensitivity and functional heartburn. In reflux hypersensitivity, symptoms are linked to reflux events despite normal overall reflux exposure. In functional heartburn, symptoms occur without evidence that reflux is responsible.
“These are people who may feel a burning sensation with almost anything they eat because the nerves in the food pipe are very sensitive,” Dr. Arul Prakash said.
This is one reason why simply increasing acid-suppressing medicines does not necessarily resolve persistent symptoms.
Establishing the diagnosis
A response to a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) can support a diagnosis of GERD, but it does not prove that reflux is the cause.
When symptoms continue despite appropriately used treatment, doctors may need to investigate other causes, including oesophageal motility disorders and disorders of oesophageal sensitivity.
Endoscopy is particularly important when there are alarm symptoms such as difficulty or pain while swallowing, bleeding, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting or anaemia. It can detect oesophagitis, ulcers, strictures and Barrett’s oesophagus.
A normal endoscopy, however, does not exclude reflux. In such cases, 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring can measure reflux episodes, distinguish acid from non-acid reflux and assess whether symptoms occur in association with reflux.
Manometry assesses pressure and movement within the oesophagus and can identify motility disorders. It is also used in selected patients before anti-reflux procedures.
Chest discomfort should not automatically be attributed to GERD because cardiac pain can have a similar presentation. Even discomfort after a heavy meal cannot by itself establish reflux. In people with cardiovascular risk factors, cardiac causes may need to be assessed first.
Lifestyle measures
Weight loss can reduce reflux symptoms in people who are overweight or obese. Avoiding food for about three hours before lying down can help, particularly with night-time symptoms.
Food triggers vary. Rather than eliminating multiple foods routinely, patients should identify those that consistently worsen their symptoms. Coffee, spicy and high-fat foods, chocolate, mint and acidic foods can trigger symptoms in some people.
For night-time reflux, raising the head end of the bed and, for some people, sleeping on the left side may help.
Complications and treatment
Persistent GERD can cause erosive oesophagitis, ulcers and strictures. It can also lead to Barrett’s oesophagus, in which the lining of the lower oesophagus changes. Barrett’s is associated with an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
New difficulty in swallowing, painful swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools or persistent vomiting require medical evaluation.
For patients with objectively confirmed reflux who remain significantly symptomatic, endoscopic or surgical treatment may be considered in selected cases. Laparoscopic fundoplication is one surgical option, while endoscopic anti-reflux procedures are available for some patients.

Rio residents find their own way to tackle gangs as crime dominates Brazil's election
Crime is a key issue in Brazil's upcoming Oct. 4 election
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Crime is the top concern for Brazilians ahead of October’s presidential election, with candidates competing to offer the toughest — and most effective — approach to the deep-seated problem.
Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, is seeking to defeat President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with a promise to loosen organized crime’s grip on Brazil, particularly in Rio de Janeiro.
After Rio’s deadliest-ever police operation last year, in which more than 120 people were killed, polls indicated that the hard-line policies Sen. Bolsonaro touts are popular. Lula, meanwhile, has argued for a more prominent role of the federal government in the fight against organized crime as well as greater coordination between governmental institutions.
But while politicians trade barbs, residents in Rio de Janeiro have been designing their own responses, with ex-traffickers launching podcasts and grieving mothers stepping up to stop youth recruitment.
Many residents, community leaders and experts say that the current approach — which favors armed confrontations between police and the groups — is inefficient and often results in indiscriminate loss of life. They're taking on crime on their own to bridge that gap.
Here is a look at some local initiatives.
Once a week, a group of former drug-traffickers gather in a small recording studio on the outskirts of Rio to dissect their past lives of crime and those of their guests. They air the episodes of 01 Sobreviventes, or 01 Survivors, on YouTube and streaming platforms.
A painting of the four founders grinning hangs on the wall, while the podcast’s logo – a microphone breaking a chain – is projected on a screen over the desk.
“We want to propagate the idea that crime isn’t worth it," said host Fábio Santos, a 56-year-old ex-trafficker from the Manguinhos favela who spent 25 years in prison.
"We want them to follow our current lives so that they don’t go through what we went through,” he added after recording a recent interview with a former gang member who is now a pastor.
The podcast, launched in 2024 and followed by more than 225,000 people on Instagram, is both for those tempted by the allure of quick cash and for those who need convincing to course-correct. Crime leads to prison, a wheelchair or a coffin, they say repeatedly.
Santos says several people have said they have seen traffickers listening to the podcast and that he regularly hears about people who left the world of crime or didn't enter thanks to their work.
Alan Duarte, 38, grew up in Complexo do Alemao, one of the two sprawling complexes of favelas targeted in Rio’s lethal police operation last year. He lost a brother, uncle and cousins — 10 family members in all — to violence.
He credits the influence of a nonprofit offering martial arts classes in a nearby favela for keeping him from going down a perilous path. That insight inspired Duarte to create his own academy in his childhood neighborhood.
Since opening in 2014, Abraco Campeao, or Embrace Champions, has expanded into teaching boxing, jiu-jitsu, Muay Thai and capoeira, and providing educational talks. Duarte hopes to boost its current 600-student capacity to 1,000.
“I often say that martial arts, Abraco Campeao, offers the same things that draw youngsters to gangs: identity, respect, attention, authority and a sense of belonging,” Duarte said during a recent tour of the school.
Classes, uniforms and equipment are free. During one of the thrice-weekly classes, attendees have an hour-long discussion with an educator about themes ranging from environmental issues to relationships.
Mherrhy Esperança Rosário, a 23-year-old amateur boxer who has been part of the school for more than a decade, is studying software engineering at a nearby university. He said the school changed his life.
“Abraco Campeao offers a path that is different to what we often see around here," he said. “It shows that we can attain our dreams.”
When two armed men turned up to Vanderson Rocha Silva’s electricity course in a Rio favela asking if they could join, the 43-year-old didn’t turn them away. Today they are both working as electricians.
“If they want to leave crime but they don’t have an employment opportunity, any hopes for life, what are they supposed to do? A project changes everything,” Rocha Silva said.
Rocha Silva grew up in an abusive household in the famed City of God favela and was 8 when he entered the world of drug-trafficking.
After stints in prison and converting to Evangelical Christianity, he eventually left that life behind and now runs what he calls a therapeutic community, named “R3,” which stands for Rescuing, Resocializing and Resending. The organization offers psychological assistance as well as free electricity, refrigeration and English courses.
“I’m starting my life again,” said Danilo Gomes da Silva, 37, who was once addicted to cocaine and involved in a criminal organization. He now has a job in building maintenance and is slowly furnishing a small home; a fridge is on its way.
“Look at all (the pastor) is doing without help from the state. Imagine all the people he could resocialize,” he said.
Nadia dos Santos' son Cleyverson ran a social project that distributed food, medicine, clothes and other essentials to people in need in the Chapadao complex of favelas where he grew up. After police killed him in 2022 when he was 17, his mother shifted the focus of the project specifically to help youth under 26 get jobs and training.
“We have to get them out of the world of criminality where they are used to living," dos Santos said.
Due to funding challenges, the project is still in its early stages, hosting occasional events. Dos Santos plans on transforming a house she owns into its headquarters, with a room for computers and another for a community food center.
At a recent event she organized in her son's memory, other grieving mothers called for a change in the approach to security in Rio.
Maria Rubia Brito da Silva, a 61-year-old who was at the event, said her son and grandson became involved in drug-trafficking and were later killed.
“Even if our sons become involved in the wrong kind of life, the state doesn’t have a right to take their lives away,” she said.
Brito da Silva blamed the lack of educational, recreational and employment options for youth's gang involvement. She says her granddaughter hardly has class because of police operations.
“If there were opportunities for these children, I'm sure they would leave the streets and their self-esteem would soar,” she said.
“They would be able to lead a dignified life and bring lots of pride to us mothers who live with the fear of losing our sons.”

Malini (name changed) from Odisha’s Angul district did not have a conventional arranged marriage. Instead of matching horoscopes with her prospective husband, she and her family relied on the couple’s medical reports before agreeing to the marriage.
Malini, 42, has lived with sickle cell disease (SCD), a genetic disorder affecting red blood cells, since birth. Yet, she went on to have a successful marriage and is now the mother of a healthy 12-year-old son.
Asish, a manager with public-sector Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL), was not as fortunate. Despite having a stable and well-paying job, he could not convince his girlfriend’s family that there was no harm in marrying her. Even a renowned haematologist tried to mediate, but the couple’s nine-year relationship eventually failed to culminate in marriage.
Odisha is among the 17 states with a high prevalence of SCD. According to available data, around 10.61% of the population screened in the state has either sickle cell trait (SCT) or sickle cell disease.
Asish, a Homozygous Sickle Cell Anaemia patient, said he could endure the excruciating pain caused by the disease, but found it far more difficult to overcome the stigma associated with it.
“Social stigma affects people with sickle cell disease more than the disease itself,” members of the newly formed National Alliance for Sickle Cell and Thalassemia Control (NASCETC) said at its first meeting held on the sidelines of the 16th annual congress of the Odisha Haematology Association here on Saturday (September 26, 2026). The voluntary forum has been formed to create a stronger support system for people living with SCD and thalassemia.
The Union government launched the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Programme (NSCAEP) on July 1, 2023, across 17 high-prevalence states, including Odisha, with the goal of eliminating SCD as a public health problem by 2047.
“The programme is one of India’s largest initiatives to control a genetic disease and is being closely watched internationally because of its scale and comprehensive community-based approach. Besides medical interventions, we also need to address the taboos and social stigma surrounding the disease. People living with SCD themselves must take the lead in creating awareness about the condition,” said Professor R. K. Jena, a renowned haematologist.
Experts, including Ruby Khan, Deputy Director of the National Health Mission, Madhya Pradesh, and Manoranjan Mohapatra, Head of the Department of Haematology at AIIMS, Delhi, advised patients and their families that people living with sickle cell disease can lead a healthy married life if their partner does not have either sickle cell trait (SCT) or sickle cell disease.
“Kundli milao ya na milao, lekin sickle cell reports milana zaruri hai (Match horoscopes or not, but matching sickle cell medical reports is a must). Pregnant women should also undergo prenatal diagnosis, while screening of family members should be carried out as a preventive measure,” said Dr. Khan.
Prof Mohapatra said that, unlike thalassaemia, people with SCD can lead normal lives and that, not every patient requires a bone marrow transplant.
“Not every patient will require a bone marrow transplant. Patients must follow the advice prescribed by their doctors and overcome their fears,” he said.
Although medicines such as hydroxyurea, which helps reduce the frequency and severity of pain episodes, are available at government hospitals, and haematology departments have been opened at several government and private hospitals, patients and their families continue to face social stigma associated with the disease.
“In Kandhamal district, where we are studying the social stigma attached to blood disorders, we have found that some people collect medicines from places far from their homes to conceal their condition from neighbours. Marriages also take place without families disclosing the medical condition of their sons or daughters,” said Debarpita Mohanty, a scientist at the ICMR’s Regional Medical Research Centre, Bhubaneswar.

Chief Minister Rekha Gupta on Sunday rejected the Opposition’s allegations against the Election Commission, saying the revision of electoral rolls to remove deceased voters, duplicate entries and other invalid names was being dubbed “vote chori”.
Addressing a press conference at Jan Seva Sadan, Ms. Gupta said eligible voters remained on the rolls. “Everyone has the right to ask questions in a democracy, but such questions should be based on facts,” she said.
Her remarks came amid demands by Opposition parties and organisations for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar following an investigation by The Indian Express. The report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
The investigation also reported that the two Commissioners had objected to changes linked to Form 6, describing them as “illegal” and “unauthorised”. The revised process sought information on whether an applicant or their parents were on the electoral roll during the last SIR in the early 2000s.
Ms. Gupta said there had been no change in Form 6 and that, under the SIR, a separate declaration had been provided along with the form, according to the Election Commission.
Delhi Bharatiya Janata Party president and Union Minister Harsh Malhotra asked booth-level agents to coordinate with booth-level officers to ensure every eligible voter is enrolled. He said no name would be deleted without a hearing.
More protests planned
Meanwhile, the Delhi Congress plans to stage a protest outside Nirvachan Sadan on Monday over the issue. It will be the party’s second protest, after a demonstration on September 25.
The Cockroach Janta Party has also warned of a nationwide agitation, including “Jantar Mantar 2.0”, if Mr. Kumar does not step down.

The festive season has officially arrived, and Indian kitchens are once again coming alive with preparations of laddus, payasam, halwa, burfis, and other traditional sweets. With the rising awareness about the impact of sugar, however, some ingredients in popular sweets are being changed. Refined sugar is increasingly being replaced with jaggery, while some consumers are also experimenting with artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and of late, monk fruit sweetener.
The intention is understandable: enjoy festive food while reducing sugar use. The science behind these sweeteners however, is more nuanced. Not every alternative to sugar is nutritionally equivalent, and ‘natural’ does not automatically mean low-sugar. The important question is not simply what sweetener is being used, but how much sweetness and sugars a person consumes overall.
Jaggery counts as sugar
Jaggery has long been associated with traditional Indian cooking and is often perceived as a healthier alternative to refined sugar because it undergoes less refining and may retain small amounts of minerals. However, it remains a concentrated source of sugar.
This distinction becomes particularly important during festivals, when sweets are rarely eaten in isolation. A person may have a laddu, a serving of payasam/kheer, sweetened beverages and several savoury foods in the same day, or worse in a single meal.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that free sugars contribute less than 10% of total daily energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% providing additional health benefits. For a person consuming around 2,000 calories a day, 5% is roughly 20 to 25 grams, or 4 to 5 teaspoons of sugar.
Therefore, replacing sugar with jaggery does not make a sweet sugar-free. From a doctor’s perspective, portion size and the total amount of free sugar consumed during the day remain far more important than whether the sweetener is brown or white.
Artificial sweeteners
Across the country, many people are now using low-calorie or no-calorie sweeteners. These include artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, saccharin and aspartame, as well as naturally derived sweeteners such as steviol glycosides and monk fruit extract.
Monk fruit extract, the newest addition to sweeteners in the mass market, is particularly interesting because its sweetness comes from compounds called mogrosides. Monk fruit extracts can be approximately 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar, depending on their mogroside content. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted that the use of monk fruit extract is ‘generally recognised as safe’ under its intended conditions of use.
Artificial sweeteners work differently. They provide intense sweetness with little or no calories and are commonly used in products marketed as ‘sugar-free’, ‘light’ or ‘diet’. Approved high-intensity sweeteners are considered safe within their specified conditions of use, and several have established acceptable daily intake levels.
However, a ‘safe’ label does not necessarily mean beneficial. The World Health Organization currently advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners as a strategy for long-term weight control. Its recommendation is conditional and is based on evidence that replacing free sugars with non-sugar sweeteners does not provide a clear long-term benefit for reducing body fat.
This is an important distinction for consumers. A sweetener can be safe to consume and still not be a reason to increase the amount of sweet food in the diet.
A better approach
The biggest misconception is that changing the sweetener automatically changes the nutritional quality of the sweet.
A jaggery laddu is still sweet. A sugar-free dessert can be calorie-dense if it contains large amounts of ghee, nuts, cream or other ingredients. Similarly, replacing sugar with monk fruit does not make an otherwise highly processed dessert a health food.
The more useful approach is for us to look at our entire festive eating pattern. One traditional sweet enjoyed occasionally is very different from consuming several servings every day throughout the season. The goal is not to find a sweetener that allows unlimited sweetness; it should be to reduce excessive sweets while retaining the cultural and social pleasure associated with festivals.
So, if a festival sweet is made with sugar, moderation matters. If it is made with jaggery, moderation still matters. Monk fruit essence or other non-sugar sweeteners do not automatically bestow a license to eat more.
The aim should be not to move from sugar to jaggery or from jaggery to monk fruit. It should be to simply learn to enjoy our favourite sweets alittle less sweet, and a little less often. This also aligns with broader dietary recommendations from the WHO that advise building diets on minimally and unprocessed foods, and restricting free sugars.
There is no need to cut out every single sweet, but do practice portion control and choose wisely. Instead of five laddus, have one and enjoy it mindfully. Keep the overall diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and fibre, and let sweets remain a small part of the meal.
(Suparna Mukherjee is a dietician with Narayana Health City, Bengaluru. suparna.mukherjee@narayanahealth.org)

‘US won't let India become next China’: Russian envoy claims ‘Freudian slip’ revealed Washington's concerns
The envoy’s remarks come as India faces US pressure over its purchase of Russian crude oil, especially after the Graham Act was signed into law.
Russia's envoy to India Denis Alipov said on Sunday that a senior US official had publicly admitted that Washington would not let India become another China, a competitor, calling the remark a "Freudian slip".
Speaking at the NDTV Defence Summit, he said the US would “do everything possible to contain India” and pointed to the Graham Act as one such measure.
Russian envoy’s big claim
Alipov said the US official made the remark during this year's Raisina Dialogue in the national capital.
“I think this year at the Raisina Dialogue, one of the top US officials revealed and spoke publicly that the 'US will never allow India to become the next China' as a competitor. It was like a Freudian slip,” he said.
Notably, “Freudian slip” refers to an unintentional error in speech that is believed to reveal a person’s hidden thoughts or feelings.
He said the US would seek to contain India as the country grows stronger. “So as India becomes stronger and stronger, and eventually a superpower, which is inevitable, the US would be doing everything possible to contain India. And so, we regard this measure, the Graham Act, as such.”
The Indian government has not released an official statement on this remark yet.
US pressure over India’s Russian oil purchases
The envoy’s remarks come as India faces US pressure over its purchase of Russian crude oil.
Last week, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law, giving Congress-backed authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil - a group that, based on current import volumes, includes China and India. However, the law does not name any country as a target.
“India is buying Russian oil not for the sake of Russia. India is buying Russian oil for the sake of its own economy and its own people. Because it is there at a competitive offer," Alipov told NDTV.
He said such “tactics” would continue as India grows stronger. “In response to this, I think India has shown strategic autonomy and strength. The US has articulated its pressure on Russia with this act. It is, by itself, absurd. And the US, I would repeat, very well knows that. I think as India rises, this kind of pressure and these tactics will continue and will aggravate and increase,” he said.
What India said on Russia sanctions bill
Earlier this month, India said it would take all necessary measures to safeguard its trade and economic interests after the legislation was passed by the US House of Representatives.
The external affairs ministry said that India remained firmly committed to meeting the energy needs of its 1.4 billion people.
“The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” the ministry said in a statement, without specifying what steps could be taken. “Government will work closely with Indian trade and industry bodies to deal with the implications of these developments.”
The ministry added that India would continue to protect its energy security through “diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics”.

Just Like That: How social media is reshaping news, TV and the media landscape
The great transformation taking place in media is not merely technological. It is a redistribution of power.
There was a time when the morning newspaper told us what had happened yesterday, and the evening television bulletin told us what had happened today. That world has not quite disappeared, but it has lost its monopoly.
The great transformation taking place in media is not merely technological. It is a redistribution of power. The authority to decide what millions of people should see, hear and discuss is moving, slowly but unmistakably, from the newsroom to the smartphone.
The numbers are difficult to ignore. India had about 1.03 billion internet users by the end of 2025, representing 70 per cent internet penetration. It had about 500 million social media user identities. By March 2026, TRAI recorded more than 1.09 billion internet subscribers.
Television, however, is hardly dead. Indeed, the Indian television ecosystem remains enormous: the government estimated in 2025 that television reached roughly 900 million viewers across 230 million households. The more accurate conclusion, therefore, is not that social media has simply killed television. It is that television has ceased to be the unquestioned centre of the media universe.
In India, YouTube reported more than 650 million monthly logged-in viewers of Shorts alone in 2025, while more than 75 million adults were reached through connected television. The Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found that 77 per cent of respondents globally consumed online news video during the preceding week; in 45 of the 48 markets surveyed, online news video was watched by more people than broadcast television news.
India is particularly fertile territory for this revolution. The Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report says social/video networks have, for the first time globally, become the most widely used source of news, at 54%, while TV news usage has fallen substantially since 2020. The survey also indicated that 55 per cent of Indian respondents used YouTube for news, 37 per cent Instagram, 36 per cent Facebook and 16 per cent X. These figures come from an online, predominantly English-speaking sample and therefore should not be mistaken for a census of all Indians. But the direction is unmistakable.
Instagram had an estimated 414 million users in India in early 2025, according to Meta's advertising data. X's corresponding advertising reach was about 24.1 million. X may be much smaller than Instagram, but influence cannot be measured merely by numbers. A single post by a politician, journalist, celebrity, activist or public intellectual can become the subject of national conversation within minutes.
This is the extraordinary democratisation of contemporary communication. The citizen who once wrote a letter to the editor, unsure whether the editor would publish it, can now become their own publisher. The independent reporter can reach thousands without owning a printing press, a television studio or a satellite channel. The old gatekeepers have been joined by millions of new ones. And this has altered the nature of news itself.
Today, social media can sometimes show reality more immediately and graphically than conventional media. A citizen's mobile-phone recording of a road accident, police action, civic failure or public protest can reach millions before a television crew reaches the scene. CCTV cameras have multiplied the visual record of public life. Smartphones have converted millions of ordinary citizens into potential witnesses.
But there are pitfalls too. Evidence requires context, verification and interpretation. A 30-second video can reveal something important while concealing something equally important. A photograph can be authentic but misleading. An AI-generated video can be entirely fictitious while looking astonishingly real. And here lies the paradox of the new media revolution: the same technology that democratises truth can democratise falsehood.
The problem is compounded by algorithms. What we see is not necessarily what is most important; it is often what is most likely to keep us watching. Anger travels faster than nuance. Outrage is more transmissible than explanation. Abuse generates engagement. A lie repeated a million times acquires not truth, but familiarity.
Not that traditional media is completely pristine. Ownership structures, advertising dependence and corporate interests can influence editorial priorities. Yet, the newspaper still possesses something the influencer often does not: institutional memory. The change is that young readers now increasingly encounter a newspaper through a mobile screen rather than a printed sheet. Legacy organisations are consequently investing heavily in websites, apps, YouTube channels, podcasts, Instagram reels and other forms of digital distribution. Old media is becoming multi-platform media.
Perhaps this is the real significance of the revolution. The future newspaper may not look like a newspaper. The future television channel may not require a television set. The future journalist may appear simultaneously on a website, YouTube, Instagram, X and an AI-powered news interface.
The old media had too few voices. The new media has too many. The challenge of the future will be to ensure that abundance does not destroy judgement, that immediacy does not eliminate verification, and that democratisation does not become a licence for abuse.

It took Shannon Stokes two years and 11 days to successfully prosecute her former boyfriend for sexual assault and domestic violence offences. The lengthy trial left her feeling as though “there wasn’t going to be an end in sight”.
Prosecutors secured convictions on nine of the 11 charges, and he was later sentenced to five years in prison.
Stokes, 28, from New South Wales, said a “sense of doom” throughout the trial was compounded by a lack of appropriate legal assistance as she navigated the justice system, a world she said felt “so alien” to her.
She recalled receiving pamphlets in the lead-up to the trial that she said were “more or less about how to look presentable” in court.
“I also had a few pieces of paper handed to me on the day going into that courtroom, and that was what I had to kind of go off … it just makes you feel so isolated and like a number in the system rather than a person who has actually been victimised by violence.”
Experts say Stokes’ experience is common among sexual assault victim-survivors pursuing justice. Sarah Rosenberg, the executive director of the victim-led network With You We Can and an advocate for justice reform, has long called for greater support for victim-survivors navigating the legal system.
“They’re expected to navigate a very isolating, very complex system entirely alone,” she said. “They’d essentially have to become legal experts overnight just to figure out what is going on in a case that supposedly revolves around them.”
Rosenberg said an adversarial justice system often further traumatises victim-survivors.
“That process of having the victim-survivor be a witness opens them up to a lot of re-traumatising during the process … There is nothing that mimics the dynamics of abuse more than being relegated to just a witness in the accountability process.”
This week, the NSW government announced it would establish the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Legal Service, operating through Legal Aid NSW.
The $1.74m expansion will provide free legal support for a range of sexual assault matters, including advice about the criminal process, survivors’ rights during police investigations and prosecutions, and assistance with access to victims’ compensation.
The pilot program is part of the state government’s $6.2m strengthening sexual violence justice responses package announced last month, which is backed by federal funding.
Robyn Gilbert, a senior solicitor at Legal Aid NSW who will lead the service, said: “The point of the service is to bring some autonomy and choice back to survivors, to be better informed and have a clearer idea of their own rights and their role in the system.”She said the service would be “open to all callers” across the state.
“Really, the only eligibility criteria is to have experienced a sexual assault,” Gilbert said.
The NSW minister for the prevention of domestic violence and sexual assault, Jodie Harrison, said navigating the legal system could be overwhelming for many victim-survivors.
“Accessing the right support at the right time is an important part of ensuring they are treated with dignity and respect throughout the justice process,” she said.
Ged Kearney, the federal assistant minister for the prevention of family violence, said: “I have heard from many victim-survivors of sexual violence that their experience seeking legal advice after an assault can be traumatic during what’s already a very traumatic period.”
Stokes said she experienced those challenges during her own trial, when questions were dismissed or repeated, and she was required to submit evidence for victims’ compensation more than once.
The pilot program was a step towards addressing the trauma of navigating “a really hard legal system”, she said.
“Having such a big time pass between my assault and going to court definitely affected me more mentally … I say it light-heartedly, but I think it actually traumatised me more than my actual assault did.”

The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s survival and expansion over a century is among its biggest achievements, said BJP national general secretary B.L. Santosh in Puducherry on Sunday.
Speaking at an interactrive session on “The RSS at 100” organised as part of the Bharat Shakti Pondy Lit Fest 2026, he defended the organisation’s ideological framework and described political engagement as a means of broader social transformation.
He said the RSS, founded in 1925, had emerged when Indian society was fragmented and disconnected from its civilisational legacy. According to him, the organisation sought to bring society together around cultural values and create conditions for what it considers positive traditions to flourish.
The BJP leader also disputed the characterisation of the RSS as right-wing or centre-right, saying those labels were drawn from Western political categories. He described the organisation as centrist in an Indian ideological context and said this should not be seen as a compromise between the political left and right.
Addressing criticism about Brahmin dominance, he said the composition of local RSS units was shaped by the social networks of those who first joined, rather than by a policy to keep out particular castes. He maintained that organisational leadership could emerge from any community. The RSS shakha system was founded for men but women take part in public and nation-building activities as equal partners, he said.
On questions concerning Muslims, Christians and communists, Mr. Santosh said the RSS did not treat entire communities as threats. He said it identified issues such as religious conversion, “jihadi mindset”, and intolerance as social problems.
He described himself as having been sent to politics on “deputation.”
Responding to criticism over the induction of leaders from rival political parties, including concerns about “Trinamoolification” in West Bengal and “Congressification” elsewhere, the BJP leader called such moves a “necessary evil” in pursuit of larger political objectives.
He said a legislative majority was required to implement key reforms and address urgent problems, particularly where a party did not have sufficient organic growth. He said the BJP had the capacity to assimilate newcomers.
According to him, the Gen Z should not be assessed solely through social-media trends or protest spaces. The RSS camps continued to attract young participants, he said and described the popularisation of ideas such as Hindu Rashtra and Akhand Bharat as an ongoing exercise.
On Nepal, he said the RSS was involved in non-political cultural and social initiatives aimed at preserving Hindu ethos and building connections among Hindu, tribal and Buddhist communities. He said the organisation had limited direct influence in Bangladesh but supported Hindus through diplomatic channels, international agencies and local contacts within the limits of international law.
Earlier in the day, he participated in various events held as part of Seva Sankalp Abhiyan, organised by BJP to mark 25 years of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s public service. He had also called on Chief Minister and AINRC founder N. Rangasamy.

The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting with survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit to France.
Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday, Pope Leo XIV called on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.
“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.
Leo is due to privately meet seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.
Meeting French bishops earlier on Sunday, Leo said they had acted with determination against “the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context against minors”. He urged them “to continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance”, according to a transcript of his remarks released by the Vatican.
Arriving at Lourdes in a white popemobile on Saturday night, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing more than two dozen women over three decades.
Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.
Rupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.
Among the survivors who will meet the pope is a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, whose former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to be the biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.
In an interview published last year, the pope spoke of the “crisis” of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.
The first visit to France by the head of the Catholic church in 18 years follows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.
France’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation after a landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.
On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.
“You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération.
The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.
The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).

In October 2025, I packed up my 15-pound hairless Xoloitzcuintli, Troy, and the rest of my belongings and moved from the north of England back to my hometown in California. I was exhausted, relieved, excited, heartbroken, and so hopeful.
I'd been living outside the US for 14 years — a year in Taiwan teaching English, followed by 13 in York. I was there for over a third of my life. I had no idea I'd stay so long. Those years brought growth and hard choices: a master's degree, meeting and marrying a local, and a string of jobs unrelated to what I wanted, until I found work I cared about. I built a life through work, rugby, and volunteering, and could walk the medieval streets of York and run into someone I knew most days.
But underneath that friendliness, I was growing lonelier. Every new conversation brought the same questions: Where are you from? Why did you leave California? Will you move back? It took years to understand why. It was the feeling of always being othered, always just outside full belonging, no matter how hard I'd worked to build a life there.
What I thought I wanted versus what I actually needed
I hit some dark times and retreated inward for a few years. It was partly the pandemic, but mostly because life came at me all at once. My marriage hit a reckoning, and between May 2023 and May 2024, I lost four family members, including my eldest brother. Just as I gained the courage for a big change to move to Wales, I learned that an aunt was facing serious health issues. I flew home to care for her, pausing my move. I was suddenly living between two countries. It was also the longest I'd spent in my hometown since 2011, and I was forced to confront what actually made me happy, versus what I'd convinced myself I wanted.
I told myself California was temporary, I was just there for a few months to help out. But I started hiking the hills, watching the sun set over Monterey Bay, and spending time with friends, my mom, dad, sister, brother, nieces, and nephews. I began writing again after years of feeling stuck. I hadn't wanted to move back to the US and had resisted the idea for years. But when I got honest with myself, I realized that although I can make anywhere a home, I really just wanted to be "home home."
I made a few trips back and forth, packing what mattered and leaving the rest. I threw myself a goodbye party, left a secure job with nothing lined up, and spent my last two and a half months traveling the UK and continental Europe, closing out my to-do list, grieving, and hugging people goodbye without knowing when I'd see them again.
There is no place like "home home"
Back in the US, it's been hard. job hunting in, once again, one of the toughest markets my generation has faced, relearning systems other countries make simple, and reckoning daily with what it means to be American. But I'm still hiking and watching sunsets, learning to solo camp, reconnecting with distant family, and building new friendships through local creative and rugby communities. I'm taking road trips across the West with my dog, opening my eyes to places that had felt so far away for so long.
It's not the life I expected, and there's still so much I don't know. But when people ask why I moved back right now, I tell them the truth: I just knew I needed to be here, at least for now. And I know it was the right call, because despite everything, I'm somehow the happiest I've been in years.

Starting October 1, millions of additional Amazon Prime customers could receive automatic payments as part of an expanded federal settlement over billing and cancellation practices.
The upcoming distribution phase expands eligibility to consumers who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits during a single year, a group excluded from earlier distributions, according to the Federal Trade Commission.
The payments are part of a landmark $2.5 billion agreement resolving government allegations that Amazon enrolled consumers in Prime without explicit consent and created complex digital processes that hindered efforts to cancel memberships. Under the resolution, Amazon agreed to pay a $1 billion civil penalty and set aside $1.5 billion for direct consumer restitution.
Subscribers qualify for restitution if they are based in the U.S. and either enrolled through specific disputed checkout screens or attempted unsuccessfully to cancel their membership between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025.
Qualifying subscribers must also have used no more than 20 Prime benefits, such as Prime Video or Prime Music, in any 12-month period following enrollment.
A federal court recently approved modifications to the settlement terms that increased the maximum total payout per eligible customer from $51 to $200. Consumers who previously received the lower capped amount may receive supplemental payments of up to $149 to reach the revised cap, according to the FTC.
Eligible customers do not need to fill out forms, submit claims or respond to notices to receive compensation. Amazon will issue funds directly through PayPal, Venmo or mailed paper checks.
Recipients must cash or redeem checks or electronic payments within 60 days of issuance.
Amazon had already issued more than $845 million in refunds to affected customers as of September, FTC officials said in a news release. The full payment schedule under the modified agreement is set to conclude by April 2027.
Federal regulators are also urging consumers to remain alert for fraudulent activity related to the payouts. Neither the FTC nor Amazon will contact consumers demanding money, requesting personal details or requiring payment to release funds.
Officials warned that any third party promising expedited distribution or guaranteed access in exchange for a fee is attempting a scam.
