Bellamy 'hurting' as Denmark outclass Wales
- Published
Craig Bellamy says he is "hurting" after admitting Denmark were worthy winners against his Wales side in Copenhagen.
A Ben Davies own goal along with Gustav Isaksen's strike earned Brian Riemer's men a 2-0 victory over Wales at Parken Stadium.
It leaves Bellamy's team winless in six matches in 2026 and without a point from their away Nations League A double-header with Portugal and the Danes.
Despite the loss, Bellamy remains confident his side will improve by playing against Europe's elite on a consistent basis.
"I'm really hurting. When you see an athletic team run over you a little bit... but then, will we improve? I think we will," said the Wales head coach.
"This team will get better, these players will keep improving. There are young ones coming in well after I'm gone.
"For me now it's just focus, two more games to go. How can I help you improve for the next two games but also how can I improve?
"I'm probably more loving when I'm losing, I'm probably more of a pain in the backside when I'm winning."
Denmark dominated early on and Mikkel Damsgaard fired against the post shortly after Isaksen had a goal disallowed for offside.
Despite an improvement from Wales after the opening half an hour, they were ultimately undone from two set-pieces.
"I said to the players before the game, 'this is going to be tougher than Portugal'," Bellamy added.
"It was a different challenge but a very difficult one. The best team won overall.
"As disappointed as I am with that, the result I probably think was fair."
Defeat - which came just three days after a 1-0 loss to Portugal in Lisbon - has left Wales with plenty of work to do.
They will at least have home advantage at Cardiff City Stadium as they prepare for the remainder of the current international break, with matches against Norway on Thursday, 1 October, and then Denmark the following Sunday.
Captain Davies felt Wales were being taught some harsh lessons in what is their second stint in the top tier of the Nations League.
"It was a tough game. They are a good team and made it a hard game for us," the Spurs defender told BBC Match of the Day Wales.
"It was really frustrating to concede from two set-pieces. The Nations League games are against the best teams in Europe, it was always going to be tough.
"If you're not at 100% then you are going to get punished at this level. We have to regroup and go again on Thursday."
Despite the setback in the Danish capital, winger Sorba Thomas echoed Bellamy's sentiments.
"Thankfully we've got two games at home still to come. We'll have home advantage so we need to show a reaction," he told BBC Match of the Day Wales.
"We are just going to get better. We are a small nation but we've got big hearts and beliefs and for us it's about showing that more on the pitch."

Xi visit to Washington all pomp but little progress so far
- Published
At least so far, Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington has been all pomp and little obvious progress on pressing issues.
From the ceremonial welcoming at a military air base on Wednesday to the honour-guard arrival at the White House this morning, President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet – literally and figuratively – for his Chinese counterpart.
The public remarks from the two leaders have teemed with warm words and diplomatic niceties. In a statement before today's formal meetings, Xi announced a gift of Chinese pandas and unveiled a new student exchange programme.
"Let us keep advancing the cause of friendship between our two peoples and work together to build a better world," he said.
Trump, for his part, outlined some of the topics the leaders planned to discuss in their meetings, including "pressing issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence" - using his preferred term for artificial intelligence.
"The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come," he said.
The marching bands and military flyovers on Thursday may serve a larger purpose, however – at least for Trump.
"This is a little bit of intentional pageantry to talk up the positive vibes of the summit," Jennifer Welch, chief economic analyst for Bloomberg Economics, told the BBC. "This is very much how President Trump sees the summit and the role he plays in the US-China relationship, as ballast to provide stability."
Even so, there is still an edge to some of Xi's rhetoric, she notes.
In remarks at the White House, the Chinese leader again mentioned the "Thucydides trap" – a theory that shifts in global power tend to lead to conflict between rising and declining nations.
"China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust," Xi said.
The obstacles in the way of reaching any substantive agreement between the two nations are significant, however. When Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May, the men agreed to form boards of trade and investment to oversee economic interactions, and little more.
On Wednesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a year-long trade "truce" between the two nations that had kept tariffs lower would be extended another two months. Financial analysts expect a further extension could come before this week's summit ends, given that neither side wants a renewal of last year's trade war.
The outlook for progress is much dimmer on other topics, like the US war with Iran, the Ukraine war and regulating AI.
China's reneging on promises to buy more American agricultural products and to also sell more rare earth minerals to the US is helping cloud the outlook. China, meanwhile, is watching to see if Trump follows through on a proposed sale of American weapons to Taiwan, which has been on hold for months.
When it comes to AI, China and the US have two very different goals for any agreement on the race to develop the technology, Robyn Klingler-Vida, a professor of political economy at Kings College London, told the BBC.
"On the US side, it's about existential risk and slowing down AI potentially," she said. "Whereas in China, it's about acceleration, maybe winning the AI tech race and the application of AI to the real economy."
A number of leading American AI executives plan to attend tonight's formal state dinner at the White House, which many view as a means for the US side to tout its current technological advantage.
Muscle-flexing aside, more pageantry – and the promise of stability – may be the end result of Xi's China visit, even with additional face time between the two leaders to come before Xi departs on Friday afternoon.
"What China talks about is metaphysical and abstract. The United States wants to solve specific problems," Miles Yu, who served as principal China policy planner and strategist to Secretary of State Mike Pompeo during Trump's first term, told the BBC.
"These different approaches are not going to lead to any result."

Following his bilingual speech, in which he thanked his family and songwriting collaborators, Voisine performed an emotional, choir-backed duet of his ballad I'll Always Be There with French Canadian artist Isabelle Boulay.

"And light your phones up for Mr. Gord Downie."

Serbia’s populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned to pursue an attempt to become prime minister in an early parliamentary election that will test his firm rule in the Balkan country after nearly two years of protests.
Vučić’s second presidential term would otherwise end in May next year. He is banned by the constitution from seeking a third term and said he was resigning to lead his rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in the 25 October ballot.
The governing populists face a major challenge from a youth-backed movement that led protests triggered by a train station canopy collapse in November 2024 that killed 16 people in the northern city of Novi Sad.
University students demanded accountability for the tragedy. Their struggle for justice and against corruption has grown into a strong movement that will attempt to oust Vučić’s government after 14 years in power. Vučić has been either prime minister or president for the past 12 years.
“I am resigning the duty of the president of the republic,” Vučić said, reading the text of his resignation.
The ballot in October will be held against a backdrop of high political tensions as Vučić’s populists seek to remain in office despite widespread discontent. His decision to run for prime minister is seen as an attempt to retain a top position and boost his party’s chances against the student movement.
Vučić has toured the country in recent weeks with live coverage on pro-government media. He has opened new roads, offered assistance money and cheaper medicines and visited voters in their homes.
The prime minister in Serbia is formally more powerful than the president, but Vučić still played a dominant role during his two five-year terms, sometimes presiding over government sessions and routinely announcing all important decisions and plans.
Serbia’s independent Bureau for Social Research has filed a complaint alleging that Vučić has abused a public institution as president to promote his party, which he has dismissed. There has been no response from the anti-corruption authorities, which are under government control.
The new acting president will be Ana Brnabić, a close Vučić ally and former prime minister who is the outgoing speaker of parliament. Once a new parliament is elected, the new speaker will take over from Brnabić, appoint the prime minister and schedule a presidential vote.
Vučić and his party have been accused of rampant corruption, organised crime links and a clampdown on democratic freedoms, including critical media. The SNS has gradually taken control of all state institutions since coming to power in 2012, while denying abuse of office and repeatedly pledging to fight corruption.
The student-backed election list includes little-known experts, professors, teachers, athletes and other individuals from all walks of life. Groups of students have been touring the country on bicycles as part of their campaign urging the rule of law and an end to corruption.
Analysts say the student group and Vučić are polling closelyin a referendum-like atmosphere. Also running are Vučić’s allies, the Socialist party, a pro-EU opposition alliance and several smaller groups.
Authorities have pushed hard against protesters with police violence and detentions, as Vučić, without offering evidence, has accused his opponents and critical media of intending to destroy the state under unspecified foreign influence.
He told Serbia’s state RTS television on Sunday that foreign powers and unidentified people in the country planned to stir unrest on election night.
Serbia’s efforts to join the EU have stalled under Vučić because of democratic backsliding and a refusal to join sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.

No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains

It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case.
Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, the period in which they were accused of breaking Premier League financial rules?
Judging by social media, many fans of rival clubs are now hoping for such an outcome.
However BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and clubs - for past titles to be stripped from City
Does that put an end to it?
Not quite, as the decision will be made by an independent panel which is yet to hold a "sanction hearing". That means it cannot be ruled out, although a points deduction, huge fine or possibly even expulsion from the Premier League are thought to be more likely.
Here, BBC Sport analyses this difficult issue and decision the panel is now facing.
- Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City 
  - Published17 hours ago
"I think we still have a chance to win that league… and then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal."
It was almost two years ago that Jose Mourinho mischievously raised the possibility that his former club Manchester United could be handed the 2018 Premier League title held by Manchester City.
Under Mourinho, United finished second to City by 19 points in 2018, his final full campaign in charge at Old Trafford.
City have always denied wrongdoing. But now we know they have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges, was Mourinho right?
Premier League rules do not directly make reference to such a sanction, with a fine, points deduction or expulsion listed as possible punishments. However, they also allow for a disciplinary commission panel to impose a penalty "as it shall think fit". That theoretically could include retrospectively-applied points deductions, or the stripping of titles.
Many will argue that if upheld after any appeal, the nature and scale of the wrongdoing City have been found guilty of warrants such as sanction on the basis that titles were won unfairly, and any misrepresentation of revenue and costs gave them a crucial competitive advantage.
City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.
So with a cloud hanging over the trophy-laden era City have enjoyed since the takeover of the club by Abu Dhabi billionaire Sheikh Mansour in 2008, could asterisks now be applied to the titles City won during the period in which they have been found to have broken the rules?
Could they be left blank? Or, as implied by Mourinho, reallocated to those teams who finished runners-up to City?
Those clubs are:
Premier League
2011-12: Manchester United
2013-14: Liverpool
2017-18: Manchester United
FA Cup
2010-11: Stoke City
EFL Cup
2013-14: Sunderland
2015-16: Liverpool
2017-18: Arsenal
Community Shield
2012-13 Chelsea
Such a move would threaten to open the proverbial can of worms, raising questions over other accomplishments.
For instance, there is now scepticism towards the various trophies Chelsea won in the 2010s, after the club were found to have made a catalogue of secret payments to agents over transfers, between 2011 and 2018.
Some will ask that if retrospective action is applied to City, should the same not happen to Chelsea?
It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations.
And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations?
Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles.
Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023.
Does that era come into scope? Where does it end?
For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing.
And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan.
There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players.
There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place.
In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. Many will see it as unfair that players and fans unconnected to any rule breaches should suffer by losing titles.
And with some suggesting that relations between the United Arab Emirates and the UK could be put under serious pressure by this ruling, one can only imagine the diplomatic tensions if past titles were then taken away from the club.
On Friday, former City midfielder Rodri dismissed talk of the club being stripped of some of the titles they won.
"What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added.
"It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day.
"I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here."
Others, however, will insist the rewriting of history is the only way of restoring the competition's official record, and rewarding clubs that competed within the rules.
In terms of retrospective action, the compensation claims for lost earnings that several clubs are known to be considering launching against City are more likely than the stripping of titles.
A lawyer told me: "The question isn't whether the clubs can take legal action... it's: Where does the line of people who have a case actually end?
"The clubs who didn't win/qualify/stay up; the players who didn't get bonuses, contract extensions; the staff who missed out on bonuses; the agents who didn't get their uplift on their player deals...
"It's endless and potentially so destructive to the whole ecosystem."
Whatever happens, more division and disruption seems guaranteed.

Back and loving it - Pietersen on his history, Brook & helping win the Ashes
- Published
Kevin Pietersen is asked, after everything that came before, what he would have said if told he would work for the England and Wales Cricket board again one day.
In 2014, he was sacked by the ECB in one of most ugly and acrimonious periods in English cricketing history – a period that brought one of the most exciting but divisive international careers to an end.
"What do you think I'd have said," Pietersen says with a smile.
Bigger stars in English cricket are harder to find.
This is the man who had a brief but high-profile relationship with American celebrity Caprice, married a pop star, Jessica from Liberty X, and once tried to explain cricket to Taylor Swift on The Graham Norton Show.
Back in the dressing room as a mentor, he is speaking to the media at Headingley - the location of his famous "it's tough being me" press conference.
The hair is greyer, but he still carries all of that aura.
"I'm 46, man," he says, asked whether animosity remains.
"That stuff is so long gone. I am a completely different person.
"I live in South Africa. I love doing what I do. I am just here to help Brendon first and foremost, help the players try and become the best versions of themselves."
My preconceptions of England 'completely different' to reality
Pietersen was the most intriguing of appointments to England's dressing room staff because of his own history, but also what he has said before.
While commentating on England's white-ball tour of India last year, he suggested the Brendon McCullum outfit were not training enough.
"Clearly the perceptions I had before being asked to do the job were completely different to what I feel now," he says.
"It is nice to being part of an England team and set-up that is actually really, really driven."
Pietersen answers every question with poise. Almost all are given and lengthy, considered responses.
His only terse response comes when pushed on what exactly those preconceptions were - and how quickly they took to disappear.
"You know what the preconceptions were," he says. "I am not going near it."
I can help these players 'stay away from the ugly'
Despite that, he appears to be loving his return.
Pietersen is "not sitting here wanting to be the coach of England" but wants to help McCullum and the players, many of whom grew up idolising him.
One of those, Tom Banton, said last week he is still in awe of the four-time Ashes-winner, so much so he was struggling to build up the courage to speak to him.
"He wants a YouTube channel," Pietersen laughs. Pietersen, a 50-over great who played in a way ahead of his time, can also help him there.
His official title is "specialist mentor" and he will dip in and out to work with the white-ball teams through to the 50-over World Cup next autumn.
Before the first ODI in Durham, England posted a clip on social media of Pietersen leading a batting session.
Holding court, he had Joe Root and Rehan Ahmed alike involved in a batting drill on how to rotate the strike against spin.
"All I want to be is a great person to these guys," Pietersen says.
"I want to be the best guy in the room, so that they come to me, and they ask me for information, and if I've got stuff for them, I'll give it to them.
"I am lucky to have worn every T-shirt an England cricketer can wear – the good, the bad the ugly.
"I can potentially help them to stay away from the ugly."
'Frightening how good Brook could be'
Pietersen's eyes roll slightly when he is asked about Ben Stokes' recent comments comparing Harry Brook's talents to his.
Pietersen, like Brook, was a maverick – a batter capable of incredible highs. Those highs mean the lows come with a disproportionate level of criticism.
"Where I can help him is playing situations, because there was a lot of method in my madness," Pietersen says.
"Yes, occasionally, I got out to reckless shots and crazy shots in the '80s and '90s but there was a lot of structure to the way that I batted.
"I've still got notes on my phone on how I played in T20 cricket, one-day cricket, Test match cricket, and about hitting straight back at the stumps, and the techniques, and how I did it, and don't play certain shots.
"That all-round structure is something I could potentially help him with because he's so flipping good.
"It's actually frightening how good he is and how good he can be."
And Pietersen says he will not limit himself to working purely on white-ball cricket.
He has already spoken to new Test coach Stephen Fleming about how he can help the Test batters during his time with the white-ball squads.
Though he said he would not have time for a full-time role, he suggested he is open to working with the Test side before next summer's home Ashes series.
"I have got a pretty mad schedule," he says. "I wouldn't say no.
"I don't think that necessarily means I need to be in a dressing room.
"There is a lot of time in the lead up to an Ashes series and a tour of South Africa, when I will be with the Test batters.
"There are conversations I can have there."
Who knows how long this will last. England may as well make the most of this second chance.

National Conference leader and MLA Uri Dr Sajad Shafi Tuesday said the government must hand over the defunct Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre to local stakeholders for promotion of tourism.
Talking to Greater Kashmir outside the Legislative Assembly, Dr Sajad Shafi said the infrastructure at Salamabad has been lying unused since LoC trade was suspended several years ago.
“I requested the Chief Minister to hand over the tourism (facility) to us so that we can utilise it. Our local people can benefit from it,” he said.
The MLA said the trade centre was a source of livelihood for many local families before its closure.
“When the Salamabad Trade Facilitation Centre was there, many people got employment. Now they are unemployed. When the tourism facilitation centre will be back, unemployment among the youth will be reduced,” Dr Shafi said.
He said a road being built from Gulmarg by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) will touch Uri, opening new tourism circuits in the region.
“We are building a road from Gulmarg which will touch Uri. Tourists will come to Gulmarg. Beyond that, there are beautiful places — they will see our Pandu Temple, Chhatti Padshahi, Baba Rangi Imam, Baba Kazi Nag, Baba Fareed,” he added.
“People are tired of seeing Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Yusmarg, Sonmarg. They must come and explore Uri,” he added.
MLA Dr Sajad Shafi said Uri has two hydroelectric projects, one built by Sweden, which remained functional even during the 2005 earthquake as they are fully underground.
“From a security point of view, it is a border area. Operation Sindoor took place. There were many conflicts. Nothing happened to those powerhouses. That is also something to look at. I want Uri to be brought to the tourism map in a new way,” he said.
MLA Uri further said that the rare Markhor species is found only at the Limber Wildlife Centre in Lashipura. “I want to give a huge boost to tourism,” he said.

Bigg Boss 20 contestant Yung DSA has recently found himself at the centre of an online conversation surrounding his accent and manner of speaking. The discussion gained momentum after the latest Weekend Ka Vaar episode, during which host Salman Khan commented on the rapper’s behaviour and gameplay. Soon after, old interview clips of Yung speaking in both Hindi and English began circulating on social media, with some users comparing his communication style outside the show to the way he speaks inside the Bigg Boss house.
Bigg Boss 20: Yung DSA’s brother BREAKS silence on accent debate; says, “Being professional doesn’t mean being fake”
Former Bigg Boss contestant Gauahar Khan also weighed in on the discussion after a video of Yung went viral. She questioned whether the personality and tonality he displays inside the house are entirely natural or whether he could be adopting certain slang and mannerisms for the show.

In a statement shared on Instagram, Pranay said that Yung’s manner of communication changes depending on the setting and argued that this should not necessarily be interpreted as him being inauthentic.
“Being professional doesn’t mean being fake. YUNG is educated and smart enough to understand kidhar, kaise aur kis tone mein baat karni hai. He further addressed comparisons between Yung’s communication outside and inside the reality show, saying that the rapper does not need to imitate anyone.
“My brother doesn’t need to copy anybody, he is very much self-content, raw and REAL. So how is that ‘faking’ it? Both versions are real. He simply knows how to read the room. Surprisingly our rapper is educated. Support it rather than criticising an artist’s educational background and where he uses what when is his choice. That’s being convenient NOT FAKE. The discussion comes after Salman Khan addressed Yung during the latest Weekend Ka Vaar episode. Salman told Yung that he appeared to be a misfit within his current group and suggested that his association with the group could be affecting his individual game.

8 dead, 330 houses damaged as heavy rain batters UP's Hardoi
Heavy rainfall in Hardoi since September 25 has left eight people dead and hundreds of houses damaged or destroyed. Relief camps, drainage clearance and restoration work are continuing as the administration remains on alert.
Heavy rainfall in Uttar Pradesh's Hardoi district has claimed eight lives and damaged or destroyed around 330 houses since September 25, with rain-related incidents also killing nearly 30 animals, officials said.
Of the eight deaths, six were caused by walls or houses collapsing, while two people died of snake bites amid the heavy rain.
In the latest incident, 45-year-old Makrand, son of Shivlal, was killed after a mud wall collapsed on him in Ummarpurwa hamlet of Khajurahara village under the Sursa police station area. A cow and a bull were also killed in the collapse.
In Barbatapur village of Baghauli, 50-year-old Aarti Singh died after a mud wall collapsed on Saturday night. In Lakhamapur in the Pali area, 13-year-old Jeetu was killed when a brick wall collapsed.
Nisha, wife of Naseem, who was injured in a wall collapse in Garhi village in Shahabad on Friday, died while undergoing treatment.
In Fatehpur hamlet of Gaju in Kachhauna, 55-year-old Sunderlal was killed when a wall fell on him while he was taking out fodder. In Sikandarpur village of Beniganj, a tree fell and brought down a house wall, killing 11-year-old Monika after she was trapped under the debris.
Two other deaths were reported from snake bites. Nisha, daughter of Bhanu, died in Rasulpur in Sandila, while Ragini, daughter of Pankaj, died in Banamau in Sawayajpur.
Additional District Magistrate Dipali Bhargava said Hardoi has been severely affected by excessive rainfall since September 25 and that administration and police teams have been carrying out relief and rescue operations across the district.
"Waterlogging is being cleared continuously and our machines are working round the clock," Bhargava said. Roads affected by the rain have been restored, while repair work on damaged culverts is underway.
Power supply at electricity substations that were affected by waterlogging has also been restored, she said.
According to the ADM, five deaths have so far been officially reported due to excessive rainfall, apart from the two caused by snake bites. The administration has sent a request to the state government for financial assistance for the affected families and said immediate relief would be provided.
Relief camps are operating in the Shahabad, Sandila and Sawayajpur tehsils, where arrangements for food, drinking water and accommodation have been made for affected residents.
The administration said it remains on alert as rescue, drainage and restoration work continues in the rain-affected areas.

Israel revokes diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats in Ramallah
Foreign Minister Gideon Saar made the announcement in response to Dutch sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank
Israel said on Sunday it was revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats who represent the Netherlands at the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority, in response to Dutch sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Israel earlier this month ordered the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem, which is Britain’s representative with the Palestinian Authority, after London announced similar sanctions banning the import of goods from settlements.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said on social media that Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah must return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days, when their diplomatic privileges and immunities are due to expire.

Motorists have been demanding streetlights on the recently opened ₹90-crore Sathuvachari - VIT High Road, off the Chennai - Bengaluru National Highway (NH 48), near the Collectorate in Vellore.
Motorists said the new stretch, which was laid by the State Highways Department, provided the shortest route to reach key government offices like that of the Collectorate, Superintendent of Police (SP), EPFO, banks, and the zonal office of Vellore Corporation.
The stretch helped motorists avoid narrow stretches. ‘’Ambulances also use the new stretch to help victims reach in time, especially during night. Streetlights will help ensure safety of road users,” said G. Kumar, an ambulance driver.
Motorists said that of the entire 3.2 km of the VIT Road, only the new bridge across Palar River on the stretch had bright LED streetlights with tiled footpaths and a median. The new four-lane bridge is 475-metre-long and 15-metre-wide.
The remaining part of the carriageway remained dark in the night with no streetlights. “Crossing the new stretch during night is also risky due to speeding vehicles with flash headlights. The stretch does not have warning signages, reflectors, blinkers, and other road safety measures to restrict speed limit,” said E. Pavithra, a motorist.
Officials of the State Highways Department, which maintains the facility, said as per norms, installation of new streetlights and its maintenance, including electricity charges should be borne by respective civic bodies such as the Corporation and panchayats. “Despite the stretch being used by motorists, it is not completely ready in terms of road safety measures. Additional funds are required to execute such safety measures,” said a State Highway Department official.
The new bridge on the stretch is three metres higher than the flyovers in Katpadi, which was built in 2009, to prevent damage to its structure and inundation of its carriageway. The bridge was built at a height of 20 ft from the dry riverbed.

German town decision to halt Holocaust memorial plaques sparks outrage
Some of Merz’s conservatives joined the far-right in supporting the move.
GENEVA -- A decision by a city council in in eastern Germany to halt the laying of memorial plaques that honor Holocaust victims has sparked outrage, not least because some of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives joined the far-right Alternative for Germany in supporting the move.
The city council of Heidenau, southeast of Dresden, on Thursday voted to end the practice of laying the engraved brass plaques featuring the names of Holocaust victims into sidewalks — often in place of cobblestones and near the homes where they once lived.
Created by German artist Gunter Demnig, the Stolpersteine, or “stumbling blocks” in German, are the palm-sized memorial plaques that bear the names and fates of Jews and others persecuted by the Nazis. They have become a prominent form of Holocaust remembrance in Germany.
The first block was laid in the western city of Cologne in 1992, and today more than 126,000 can be found in over 30 countries across Europe, honoring some of the 6 million Jews and others killed in the Holocaust.
City councilors from the AfD and Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union came together behind the municipal action, whose promoters claimed that many relatives of Holocaust victims consider the stones to be an inappropriate form of remembrance because passersby walk on them.
But Israel’s ambassador to Germany, Ron Prosor, said he was “ashamed,” adding that some of the plaques in Berlin commemorated his own relatives. “And in Germany in the year 2026, a city council decides to no longer install new Stolpersteine,” he wrote on X.
Many Jews have traveled to Germany to attend the stone-laying ceremonies, often to remember victims who were gassed in Nazi concentration camps. The plaque-covered blocks amount to the closest thing to a grave or a burial.
Christian Meyer-Heidemann, the state commissioner for political education in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein, blasted the decision in Heidenau, telling the German news agency dpa that it amounted to "a deliberate attack on our culture of remembrance.”
The town of about 16,000 is not alone in rejecting the plaque commemorations. Munich does not permit Stolpersteine to be laid on city-owned land, and has come up with alternative memorials. Some Jewish leaders there have objected to them on the grounds that they allow victims’ names to be trampled on.
The anti-immigration AfD, which has a stronghold in eastern Germany, has been riding a wave of popularity. The party is fresh off electoral successes in two states, and polls suggest it’s now the most popular party in Germany.
Merz, the CDU leader, has rejected any cooperation with the AfD, which has been criticized for brushing aside memories of the Nazi era that have influenced Germany’s politics and mindset throughout the postwar era.
The AfD's successes have tested the longstanding policy of mainstream parties not to cooperate with it. The party has been classified by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as an extremist group in some regions.
“Following the AfD’s electoral successes, it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen,” Demnig was quoted as saying by dpa. He accused the CDU of “leaving their Christian roots behind.”

The Jammu and Kashmir government has approved the diversion of 51.501 hectares of forest land for 33 projects in Uri over the 2024-25 to 2026-27 financial years, with 20.9352 hectares allocated for the Srinagar-Baramulla-Uri Road, the Legislative Assembly was informed Tuesday.
The figures were disclosed by the Minister for Forest, Ecology and Environment Department, Javed Ahmad Rana in response to an unstarred question by Uri National Conference MLA Sajjad Shafi, who sought details of forest and agricultural land affected by government and private construction in the constituency.
The Ministry said the projects were cleared under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Abhiniyam and related rules.
These projects include work by the Jal Shakti Department, the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) and the Uri-II Stage-II hydroelectric project.
The government said the diversions were in the public interest and subject to “statutory environmental safeguards, conditions and compensatory measures” to minimise and mitigate their impact.
“Under the applicable provisions, user agencies must provide equivalent non-forest or State forest land for compensatory afforestation,” it said.
If such land is unavailable, the government said afforestation is carried out over twice the diverted area on degraded forest land.
Approved plans provide for 1,000 plants per hectare and 10 years of maintenance.
Depending on the project, agencies must also fund slope stabilisation, muck disposal, wildlife mitigation, Catchment Area Treatment and biodiversity management measures.
The Ministry said compensatory, mitigation and strip plantations have been undertaken near developmental and hydropower projects in Uri through CAPEX and CAMPA schemes, wherever feasible.
The response also lists the Uri-I Stage-II hydropower project and several water-supply schemes in Boniyar and Uri among the projects involving forest-land diversion.
Plantation and compensatory afforestation sites have been identified under approved plans, and the respective user agencies or companies are required to bear the costs, the Ministry said.

An event organized by the team of Ramayana yesterday, September 26, was attended not only by the film’s actors and makers but also by global YouTube sensation MrBeast. With more than 517 million subscribers, his main channel is the most subscribed channel on YouTube. However, what was meant to be a high-profile promotional event ended up leaving several members of the media frustrated, with a number of prominent journalists even walking out in anger.
SHOCKING: MrBeast’s Ramayana event leaves media FURIOUS; several journalists WALK OUT after 3½-hour delay
The confusion began even before the event. The invite was sent to members of the media on Friday, September 25, a day before the event. What raised eyebrows was that revised invites followed within a span of barely two hours, each mentioning a different timing. The first invite stated that the event would tentatively begin at 12:30 pm. Soon after, the media was informed that it would start at 12:00 pm. The call time was then changed to 1:00 pm, with the revised invite assuring journalists that the event would begin sharp at 1:30 pm. Accordingly, journalists, photographers, cameramen and paparazzi made their way to Film City, located far from the city’s central media hubs, and reached the venue around the prescribed time.
A journalist who attended the event told Bollywood Hungama, “The event didn’t begin at 1:30 pm, but we assumed that it would start by 2:00 pm or, at the most, 2:30 pm. The publicity team was unable to give us a proper answer regarding the reason for the delay or when the event would finally begin. It was only after 3:00 pm that we were informed that MrBeast’s flight from Bengaluru had been delayed and that was causing the hold-up.”
According to a report by India Today, when journalists questioned the lack of communication, members of the publicity team reportedly told the media that they were free to leave if they did not wish to wait. This reportedly angered several journalists, many of whom decided to stage a walkout.
The India Today report further stated that when Ranbir Kapoor was informed about journalists leaving, he remarked, “Aap logon ko jana hai toh chale jao.” However, the journalist who spoke to Bollywood Hungama stressed that Ranbir’s comment was not made arrogantly. He explained, “Ranbir didn’t mean it in an arrogant manner. When the journalists apprised him of the situation, he told them that if they felt like leaving, they could do so. Even Ranbir was irritated by the delay as he had arrived before the media. Sai Pallavi, too, had been present since morning and she also made her displeasure over the delay clear to the team.”
The journalist further claimed, “The PR team was kept in the dark by MrBeast’s team, which largely comprised foreigners. They were not giving proper and timely information about when he would land and reach the venue.”
A brief event after a very long wait
The event finally commenced at around 5:00 pm, that is, three-and-a-half hours after the promised 1:30 pm start. The media’s frustration might perhaps have subsided had the event turned out to be an elaborate or announcement-heavy affair. Instead, it concluded in barely 20 minutes, with no major new announcement being made. Moreover, except Ravie Dubey, no one from the team apologized for making the media wait endlessly.
Ranbir Kapoor, Namit Malhotra and Ravie Dubey were seen lifting the ‘Shiv Dhanush’, while MrBeast enthusiastically chanted “Jai Shri Ram”. The moments certainly made for striking photographs and social-media videos, but several journalists felt that making the media wait for hours for such a brief event was unreasonable.
The journalist remarked, “The event was held at Film City, which is around 5 kms away from the railway station and nearly 4 kms away from the nearest Metro station. If the makers knew that they had such a short event planned, they could easily have organized it in Juhu or Andheri. MrBeast could also have reached such a venue much faster from the airport.”
He continued, “By the end of it, everyone was exhausted. Many journalists had expected to be free by 2:00 or 2:30 pm, but the event wrapped up only around 5:20 pm. And imagine, many of them had left their homes at 11:00 am or 12 noon. For several people, it felt like their entire Saturday had gone to waste.”

England vs Sri Lanka: Tom Banton notches maiden ODI century as Harry Brook's side secure series victory after tourists collapse
England secured a 2-1 ODI series victory over Sri Lanka in the third ODI at the Oval after Tom Banton notched an imperious 126 off 105 balls; Jordan Cox and Harry Brook notched fifties on the way to England's 356; Pavan Rathnayake's run-out dismissal caused confusion
Sunday 27 September 2026 17:56, UK
Tom Banton posted an imperious 126 off just 105 balls to guide England to a dominant 223-run win in the third ODI against Sri Lanka to secure a 2-1 series victory at the Oval.
Banton top scored with his career-best but was aided by sizeable contributions by skipper Harry Brook (77 off 66) and the in-form Jordan Cox (76 off 52) as the batting side set the tourists a mammoth target of 356 after their 50 overs, with Dilhara Fernando (3-52) the pick of the bowlers - albeit with two of his wickets coming with the final two balls of the innings.
That target loomed even larger over Sri Lanka's innings when Sonny Baker nicked off Pathum Nissanka (1) for his maiden ODI wicket with just the eighth ball of their innings.
From there the wickets started to tumble for Sri Lanka who - despite the best efforts of captain Kusal Mendis (35 off 26) - went from 36-1 to 82-6 in just 10 overs, including the confusing run-out dismissal of Pavan Rathnayake (18), which was still given as out despite Jordan Cox taking the bails off before Archer's direct-hit throw dismantled the stumps.
The impressive bowling of Liam Dawson (3-17) and Gus Atkinson (2-26) then ensured Sri Lanka's tail went out with a 50-run whimper, handing England the series victory and marking a successful end of the home summer for Brendon McCullum's side after 12 wins in 14 white-ball games.
Banton brilliance headlines complete England performance
Despite England's eventual victory, it took just eight balls for Sri Lanka to take their first wicket as Ben Duckett (0) was clean bowled by Dilshan Madushanka (1-49), before Joe Root was dismissed by Janith Liyanage in an uncharacteristically stiff cameo that saw him notch just 18 off 37 balls.
It was then the partnership of Brook and player-of-the-match Banton that made the difference for England, putting on 150 runs in a lucrative partnership that was eventually ended when the former was caught on the boundary by Dunith Wellalage.
Banton's majestic innings - featuring 21 boundaries and including five sixes - came to a conclusion when his effort to hit a sixth maximum was caught by Malinga at long-on.
But England were not done there - alongside Will Jacks (25 off 21), Cox spearheaded a late flurry of runs, notching his half-century off 42 balls before Fernando took his and Dawson's wickets with the final two balls of the 49th over, leaving England in the ascendancy after posting a formidable score of 355-7.
Sri Lanka were immediately left reeling after Baker's early wicket and found it difficult to recover, with no batter scoring above 20 bar their captain Mendis, with their woes being immediately compounded by the controversial run out of Pavan Rathnayake.
Cox appeared to have made a mishap after taking the bails off the stumps before he was in control of the ball, but - after a near five-minute period of discussion involving both umpires and players - Archer's direct-hit throw uprooting the stump was ruled legitimate.
His dismissal was followed by that of Charith Asalanka and Wellalage within the next eight balls, leaving Sri Lanka on the brink of defeat at 82-6 with no recognised batters left, before the excellent work of Dawson - taking three of the last four Sri Lanka wickets - ensured England's dominant victory was confirmed with 21.5 overs to spare.
Brook: That was a near-perfect performance
England captain Harry Brook, speaking to Sky Sports:
"I thought that was a near-perfect performance there - I thought everyone chipped in and it was an exceptional win.
"There was some tough periods, but I thought the patience we showed, it was exceptional.
"We want to be able to adapt to conditions every game. Every surface has been slightly different. That is the side we want to be - we want to win when they are not in our favour and when they are, we want to nail sides.
"We are building towards a squad where someone can come into roles and fill it exceptionally well. We are building to a strong squad and I have full trust in anyone who comes in."
Mendis: We made too many mistakes
Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis:
"We struggled with the batting and then we made some mistakes in the field, including me.
"I think we played good cricket in the second ODI and when go to Pakistan after this, we need to be better.
"We made too many mistakes."

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Iran says it will wait for official US response after Trump rejects Strait of Hormuz proposal
- Published
Iran has said it will wait for an official response from US negotiators after President Donald Trump rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within seven days.
In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but accused the president of previously making contradictory statements.
Earlier, Trump told reporters at the White House that Tehran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that they wanted to make a deal to open the strait immediately because "they're losing so badly".
On Friday at the UN, Araghchi told reporters that an agreement could be reached if "necessary conditions are met" between the two countries.
Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran that was signed in June.
Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.
The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it.
Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".
"We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them," Araghchi said.
Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.
Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.
Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by the US ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker.
Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage".
"President Trump's right to reject it," he said.
Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic pressure from the US was taking a toll on Tehran.
Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.
The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran as "Operation Economic Outcast", and is using sanctions to pressure Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.
But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.
These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

On Thursday, the Senate health committee met with Heidi Overton, nominee for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. When asked about her views on mifepristone, a key abortion medication, Overton danced around the issue.
As the CEO of Reproductive Futures, a legal organization advocating for reproductive rights, I am deeply concerned. Overton’s anti-abortion views are crystal clear. As FDA commissioner, she would have a chance to implement them and do serious harm.
When her nomination was first announced, anti-abortion groups cheered it as an opportunity to remove access to mifepristone. The head of Americans United for Life said he had spoken with Overton five or six times and predicted that she would “expose this drug.”
With this latest appointment, mifepristone has a new boss but an old problem. Few medications have been sued, petitioned against, and unnecessarily hauled before Congress as often as this one has. For the past two decades the U.S. has probed, cross-examined, and disparaged mifepristone, despite the medication’s well-documented safety. Even under this unprecedented scrutiny, mifepristone’s impressive safety and efficacy record stands strong in the U.S. and globally.
As a human rights lawyer, I spent more than a decade working with women in Ireland to challenge the country’s complete ban on abortion. Back then, those who needed an abortion made “the Irish Journey,” traveling by ferry or flight to England, sometimes using borrowed money, often in isolation and always with unnecessary hardship. That work inspired me to launch Reproductive Futures, an organization that brings legal firepower to the fight for patients to have the option to access abortion through telemedicine and avoid “the American journey.”
The vast majority of all abortion now relies on mifepristone and patients should not have to travel to a clinic to receive the same safe, effective medications they could receive at home.
So you can see why mifepristone makes abortion opponents lose their minds.
Paired with a second drug, misoprostol, mifepristone is standard care around the world. An estimated 7.5 million Americans have used it. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends it for early pregnancy loss too. Yet the FDA has never added miscarriage management to mifepristone’s label. Patients experiencing miscarriage get tangled in the same medically unnecessary red tape — and today’s hearing indicated that birth control is next.
The red tape wrapped around mifepristone is thick. FDA regulations require clinicians to be specially certified to prescribe mifepristone. Because pharmacies must join a unique registration system in order to dispense mifepristone, very few do even in abortion-friendly states. Patients must sign a special agreement form that creates another layer of exposure and bureaucracy for them.
All this unneeded rigamarole for a safe drug, with a comparatively very low rate of reported deaths across its decades of use in the U.S., none of which the FDA can attribute to the drug with certainty. Meanwhile acetaminophen, sold next to the gum at the local gas station, is far less safe and directly linked to an estimated 458 deaths a year. Birth control pills went over the counter in 2023. Emergency contraception has safely sat on drugstore shelves for years. Mifepristone still needs a permission slip.
None of that caution is driven by the data. Abortion opponents see red when they see mifepristone because it makes abortion simple and safe, affordable and accessible. Opponents are willing to undermine the FDA’s reputation and the drug approval process itself just to take mifepristone away from women. They repeatedly have challenged mifepristone in courts. In 2024, the Supreme Court unanimously threw out a nationwide challenge to the FDA’s approval and regulation of mifepristone in FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, because the doctors who sued lacked standing.
Louisiana then filed its own suit to stop remote prescribing of mifepristone and end telemedicine nationwide. This spring, a 5th Circuit order briefly reinstated in-person dispensing nationwide, but thankfully the Supreme Court stepped in to pause that order and preserve access while the case continues.
But just weeks ago, Louisiana was back at the 5th Circuit seeking the same restrictions again, and the FDA’s own review of mifepristone has been conveniently scheduled to finish after the midterms. Overton acknowledged that the FDA’s internal research safety study of mifepristone would “immediately be on [her] desk,” and said she is eager to get to work to respond to Louisiana’s anti-mifepristone litigation — presumably to support it.
In response to that case, a biotech CEO recently warned in these pages that letting courts and politicians second-guess the FDA’s scientific judgment endangers the whole drug pipeline. Overton inherits an agency that has fired more than 3,000 staff in the past year, whose last commissioner resigned after clashing with the White House. During Thursday’s Senate hearing, she continuously sidestepped questions about renouncing or correcting the White House’s misinformation about vaccines schedules, food safety, and tobacco use, frustrating both Republican and Democratic Senators alike.
Her inability to prioritize science over the White House’s political agenda was so obvious that Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) outright asked Overton to name one thing she thought the president had ever been wrong about, but she received no answer. Overton will now be the fox guarding the hen house.
Public trust in the FDA approval process took decades to earn. It will not survive a commissioner who treats settled scientific evidence as negotiable to appease the Trump administration.
For more than 30 years, abortion opponents have harassed patients outside clinics, threatened providers, and attacked facilities with arson and bombings. Clinics were targets because they were visible. Telemedicine took that target away. With mifepristone, a patient can consult a clinician by video, receive pills by mail, and end a first trimester pregnancy at home. No hassle or expense of a journey across state lines and past protesters needed. About 30% of U.S. abortion patients now choose to receive care via telehealth, many prescribed by clinicians working from states where telemedicine shield laws offer them protections from anti-abortion elected officials.
That is what truly alarms abortion opponents: safe, affordable abortion on a patient’s own terms. During Overton’s hearing, anti-abortion Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) noted his distress that telemedicine has allowed greater access to abortion despite the overturn of Roe v. Wade, and reiterated his desire to halt it in its tracks.
But make no mistake: The horse has left the stable. Messing with mifepristone will not make abortion disappear. Care will continue, including through clinicians who prescribe misoprostol alone, an effective regimen with more side effects or new medications being developed. And some patients will access pills through other channels, without the guidance of a licensed medical professional.
While they can’t eliminate access to abortion medications, what we all stand to lose is abortion care from doctors in the US offering the best possible care, a government that respects scientific rigor and a country that embraces reproductive rights as human rights. Let’s stand strong for our rights, and circle up to protect mife, and science.
Julie F. Kay, a human rights attorney, is the founder and CEO of Reproductive Futures and co-author of “Controlling Women: What We Must Do Now to Save Reproductive Freedom.”

Temba Bavuma and David Miller both struck centuries as South Africa defeated Australia by 32 runs in a high-scoring second one-day international in Johannesburg on Sunday to claim the three-match series with a game to spare.
Australia sent its host in to bat and South Africa amassed 365 for nine in its 50 overs, before bowling the visitor out for 333 in 49.5 overs as it continued its dominance over its rival with a 19th ODI win in their last 25 meetings.
Australia was again undone by spin in the middle of the innings after a fast start to their reply and were not helped by the continued absence of seamer Pat Cummins and a side strain suffered by Nathan Ellis in the match that meant he bowled only four overs.
South Africa made a cautious start to its innings and was rocked by the loss of Aiden Markram off the first ball, with Cooper Connolly taking a superb one-handed catch above his head off the bowling of Josh Hazlewood.
Bavuma scored his 103 from 116 balls for his sixth ODI century in a measured innings where he scored all around the wicket.
Miller was more explosive, with nine sixes in his 142 from 93 balls, clearing the ropes with ease as he struck his career-best score and eighth ODI ton.
There was little else of substance as the pair put on 156 for the fourth wicket and Jack Edwards, playing in his second ODI, was the pick of the bowlers with 5-67 in 10 overs.
In a carbon-copy of Thursday’s 67-run win for South Africa in Durban, Australia made a lightning start to its reply as Mitchell Marsh (84 from 53 balls) and Travis Head (84 from 76 balls) put on 130 in 17 overs for the first wicket.
But the middle order struggled to score freely and South Africa’s three spinners tightened the screw.
Keshav Maharaj (2-54), Bjorn Fortuin (2-70) and Markram (1-55) were all effective in their 10 overs on a very good batting wicket.
Xavier Bartlett kept Australia in the game with a fine 50 runs from 28 deliveries but it was not enough.

The Tamil Nadu Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) has proposed to outsource the bi-monthly assessment of meter readings of domestic consumers in the State as a short-term measure for six months, until the smart meters have been fixed.
The TNPDCL has been reeling from a severe manpower shortage in all categories, including linemen, wiremen, supervisors, and assessors. At present, the TNPDCL faces a 60% vacancy crunch in assessor positions, with only 3,063 assessors available against a sanctioned strength of 7,565, serving roughly 3.50 crore low-tension connections.
Particularly the shortage of assessors in Chennai, where there are nearly 40 lakh domestic consumers, has resulted in hundred of complaints regarding the low-tension (LT) consumers receiving inflated electricity bills due to delayed assessment of meters and table reading of meters (without visiting the houses).
Under this proposal, the TNPDCL has also given the authority to Executive Engineers (who would be controlling 20 section offices) to call for tenders to appoint private contractors for the exercise. .
A senior official said the interim measure has been proposed to ensure prompt assessment of all LT (non-commercial) connections and also to avoid complaints from consumers regarding delayed meter readings.
As per the tender document, the private contractor has been stipulated to assess 250 meters per day in Greater Chennai Corporation limits, 220 in other corporations, 200 in municipal towns, 180 in town panchayats, 110 in rural areas, and 80 in hill regions. The private assessors would have to carry out the assessment by using a mobile app through an optical probe, a Bluetooth transmitter, or a manual key by engaging outside staff.
While the proposal was welcomed by a section of the operation and maintenance engineers, who are facing hardships in carrying out their regular duty because of the assessors shortage, several electricity trade unions are concerned that the interim outsourcing would lead to privatisation of more works.
An electricity official at a section office in South Chennai said that several retired assessors have been engaged to carry out meter assessment by fixing an amount of ₹5 per meter, but still, not many retired staff were willing to take up the job.
A. Sekkizhar, secretary of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Board Employees’ Federation, requested the TNPDCL Chairman and Managing Director V. Arun Roy to cancel the appointment of private contractors for meter assessment, and said the federation has planned to hold a protest on Monday. He said the assessment of meters was a specialised job that demands a certain level of educational qualification. Moreover, once it is privatised it could lead to more job privatisation, he alleged.
Consumer activists are likewise concerned about the efficiency of assessment that would be carried out by private contractors, who they said, may not bear the responsibility in their job of assessing 250 meters a day.
Social activist S. Kumararaja said the best way for the TNPDCL is to speed up the installation of smart meters, at least in the city, and also allow self-assessment as a temporary measure.

NEW DELHI: 
Virat Kohli
 added another major milestone to his remarkable ODI career on Sunday. The India star became only the second batter after 
Sachin Tendulkar
 to score 15,000 runs in One-day Internationals.
Kohli reached the landmark during India's chase in the first ODI against the West Indies in Thiruvananthapuram. He completed 15,000 runs with a four off Alzarri Joseph.
Standing ovation for Kohli
As Kohli pulled the short ball past mid-wicket for four, the crowd rose to its feet and applauded the Indian batter.
Kohli acknowledged the cheers by raising both arms. The moment marked another milestone in a career filled with records.
The 15,000-run mark puts Kohli in an elite club led by Tendulkar, who finished his ODI career with 18,426 runs.
Kohli reached 15,002 runs from 315 matches and 303 innings. He has scored 54 centuries and 80 fifties in ODIs, with a highest score of 183. His ODI batting average stands at 58.83, while his strike rate is more than 94.
Tendulkar remains the leading run-scorer in ODI cricket with 18,426 runs from 463 matches. He scored 49 centuries and 96 fifties during his ODI career.
Kohli has been the second-highest run-scorer in ODI cricket since going past former Sri Lanka captain Kumar Sangakkara in October 2025. Sangakkara scored 14,243 runs in the format and remains third on the all-time list.
Former Australia captain Ricky Ponting is fourth with 13,704 runs in 375 ODIs, while former Sri Lanka opener Sanath Jayasuriya is fifth with 13,430 runs in 448 matches.

Tenth woman's body found in South Africa suburb as police probe killings
- Published
Police in South Africa say that they have found a woman's body in a Johannesburg suburb, the tenth in recent months.
The body was found on Saturday morning and identified by the friend with whom she had been at a bar the previous evening.
The local police commissioner said his force could not rule out the possibility that there was a serial killer on the loose, noting similarities across the 10 deaths in Ekurhuleni, as well as another in Soweto.
The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
The latest body was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg.
Police issued a statement a short while later saying crime scene investigators were at the scene gathering evidence. Officials have yet to publicly identify the victim.
The woman's friend told national broadcaster SABC that she recognised her friend's clothes from the previous night when shown a picture of the body.
"I don't know what I'm going to say to her children," she said while wiping away tears. "It's painful."
Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said that, at this early stage in the investigation, it was too soon to say whether the woman's death was linked to the others.
He told reporters that the other bodies shared a "similar victimology" that indicated a shared "modus operandi" of killing, which would allow police to determine whether this latest death was linked to the others.
"For now, it's not something which we can overrule to say there's a serial killer, but we cannot conclusively indicate as such," Lt Gen Mthombeni said.
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates - with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
But it is the nature of the recent killings around Johannesburg that has left many women there reeling from the growing death toll.
The 10 other bodies have been found in similar circumstances to one another since July. Most of them were found in Kempton Park, one neighbourhood over from Tembisa.
Many of the bodies were those of young women and almost all had suffered extreme violence prior to their deaths.
The deaths have placed pressure on the national government less than a year after ministers declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.
Three men appeared in court earlier this week accused of being involved in one of the nine murders, with police working to track down others who may have been involved.

McNulty first US world road race winner in 33 years
- Published
Brandon McNulty became the first American winner of the men's road race world title in 33 years with a stunning victory in Montreal.
The 28-year-old put his hands on his head in disbelief as he crossed the line 13 seconds clear of the chasing pack, completing the gruelling 273.4km course in six hours and 17 minutes.
Australian Michael Matthews was second, with former winner Mathieu van der Poel, of the Netherlands, in third.
The last American winner of the race was Lance Armstrong in 1993.
"Until the last 800m I didn't believe, I was so tired," said McNulty.
"I'm at a loss for words. I knew something could happen but it would take a miracle and I guess today a miracle happened".
He launched an attack going into the final 30km and was 50 seconds clear going into the last lap.
McNulty visibly began to tire on the final climb and his lead was cut to just 10 seconds, but the chasing pack were unable to reel him in.
Britain's Tom Pidcock finished seventh, with Ireland's Ben Healy 10th and Remco Evenepoel of Belgium in 12th place.
'One of the best races of a long season'
Even without injured riding legend Tadej Pogacar, Montreal 2026 was still full of favourites who were expected to dictate the shape of this monumentally long race.
Van der poel, Evenepoel, Wout van Aert, Paul Seixas and Pidcock were all there, all animating and pushing to breakaway from one another under gradually yellowing Canadian maples.
But timing, not power or race craft, proved crucial.
Such was the distance all attacked far too early, and it was McNulty - a time triallist and domestique to Pogacar by trade - who took off and emptied himself.
The unassuming and, at times, seemingly timid American is a very popular winner of what was unquestionably one of the best races of a long season.

The Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) is planning to set up an Amma Canteen at the Omandurar Government Multi Super Speciality Hospital, with an estimated additional annual expenditure of ₹20.53 lakh, after accounting for projected food sales.
Recently The Hindu had reported on the need for low cost food at the hospital.
An online petition was also launched by some members of civil society appealing to the Chief Minister to establish an Amma Canteen at the hospital.
The civic body has now said the facility would provide quality, low-cost food to patients and their attendants.
The GCC has sought retrospective government approval to establish the Amma Canteen and permission to undertake the building, electrical, equipment, raw material and other works required to commence operations.
With an estimated 150 beneficiaries a day, annual sales are projected at ₹16.43 lakh. The balance expenditure of ₹20.53 lakh will have to be met from Corporation funds, according to the civic body.
According to the GCC, a site near Tower-7, close to the outpatient department entrance, has been identified. The existing children’s ward was subsequently inspected and found suitable. It has a kitchen, dishwashing and food distribution facilities, dining space, raw material storage, handwashing facilities and toilets. Only minor infrastructure improvements are required, the GCC said.
The facility is expected to involve a first-year expenditure of ₹36.96 lakh, including ₹5.52 lakh for building maintenance, ₹6.50 lakh for machinery and utensils, ₹16.80 lakh for raw materials, ₹7.12 lakh towards wages for six Women Self-Help Group members and ₹1.02 lakh in petty expenses .The six workers will be paid ₹325 a day each.
Food will be sold at subsidised rates: idli at ₹1; pongal, sambar rice, lemon rice and curry leaf rice at ₹5 each; and curd rice and two chapatis with dal at ₹3 each.
